approach: Introduce one canonical scheme/provider table (name, aliases, credential env vars, cloudpathlib prefix) and derive all four call sites from it, so adding a scheme cannot leave a gate behind. Decide explicitly whether abfs:// is supported: if yes it must classify as cloud and stage like abfss:// (PR #1303 routes abfss via CloudStagingPath); if no, it must be rejected loudly rather than silently becoming a relative directory.
description: Same defect class as classify-snowflake-stage-paths-as-non-local (PR #1299), still live. is_cloud_path's scheme list is [s3, gs, gcs, az, abfss, azure, dbfs] -- 'abfs' is absent, so abfs://container@account.dfs.core.windows.net/data returns False and create_path_handler yields a RELATIVE PosixPath. Generated data therefore lands in a local 'abfs:' tree under the current working directory, exactly the mechanism behind the 319MB @~/ spill. Verified on develop: is_cloud_path=False, handler=PosixPath, relative=True. Meanwhile azure_synapse.py:93 gates on path_info['provider'] in ('az','abfs','abfss'), but get_cloud_path_info sets provider=parsed.scheme, which yields 'azure' for the documented azure:// form -- so Synapse REJECTS a valid, advertised output location, while accepting 'abfs' which the classifier can never produce. Third instance: validate_cloud_credentials' env_checks map (cloud_storage.py:710) has keys s3/gs/gcs/abfss/azure but NOT 'az', so the canonical az:// form skips the Azure credential env check entirely while its alias azure:// gets checked. Root cause is shared: scheme and provider strings are duplicated across classification (is_cloud_path), reporting (get_cloud_path_info), credential validation (env_checks) and platform gating (azure_synapse), with no single source of truth.
preserves: Snowflake stage paths keep routing through CloudStagingPath as PR #1299/#1303 established
s3://, gs://, gcs://, az://, azure://, abfss:// and dbfs:/ keep their current classification and handler types
title: abfs:// classifies as local and spills to cwd; provider strings diverge across classify/validate/platform gates

approach:
Follow a profiling-first workflow. For each heavy file, identify dominant costs
(subprocess startup, data generation, full benchmark execution, real sleeps),
then apply the smallest refactor that preserves the same assertion semantics.

tests/integration/_cli_e2e_utils.py to centralize CLI invocations and avoid
duplicated subprocess runs. Keep one or a few true subprocess smoke tests per
behavior class, then validate remaining parameter matrices via shared fixtures
or in-process CLI runners where equivalent.

For integration suites, convert repeated setup into module/session-scoped
fixtures and keep exactly one full-fidelity path in stress. Preserve contract
checks by ensuring smoke tests still execute the same public APIs.
description:
Reduce wall-clock time of slow and resource-heavy test lanes by at least 4x
while preserving behavioral fidelity and overall coverage guarantees.

Profiling shows heavy concentration in E2E subprocess-heavy suites and a
small set of expensive full-benchmark integration paths. The implementation
should separate default-fast confidence checks from full-fidelity stress paths
without dropping assertions or removing benchmark correctness validation.

Primary hotspots from recent profiling:
- tests/e2e/test_local_platforms.py (slow subset ~6m18s; sqlite full run dominates)
- tests/e2e/test_dataframe_platforms.py (slow subset ~2m38s; pyspark+dask dominate)
- tests/e2e/test_cli_options.py (~1m07s; 31 CLI subprocess invocations)

- tests/integration/test_tpcds_query_generation.py (~1m07s; class fixture setup ~57s)

description:
Adapter instances currently behave as serial, run-scoped objects that hold
connection state, plan-capture flags, dry-run state, execution metadata, and
phase result caches. That is acceptable if documented and tested. It becomes
fragile if service-mode reuse or concurrent execution is a near-term product
goal.

This item decides the adapter lifecycle contract, adds a sequential reuse
regression test for the current model, and only introduces AdapterRunContext
if the project chooses reusable/concurrent adapters.

work.notes:
Decision recorded in docs/reference/public-contracts.md and
docs/development/adapter-refactor-map.md: PlatformAdapter instances are
serial execution objects. One instance may run multiple benchmarks
sequentially. Concurrent run_benchmark calls on one adapter are not
supported.

The base adapter owns the active per-run connection and closes it in
finally. Cached phase results, database reuse decisions, sorted-ingestion
counters, plan-capture counters, and dry-run captured SQL are run-scoped and
reset at run start. Run-config plan-capture overrides are per-run and
restored at run end; direct adapter attributes such as dry_run_mode and
table_mode remain adapter-scoped caller controls.

description:
chatgpt-codex-connector review finding on merged PR #1261 (P1, benchbox/platforms/base/adapter.py:790). Deferred from the PR-review sweep in PR #1292 because it is an adapter-lifecycle change affecting exported evidence and needs live verification on a schema-tuned platform; tracked in GitHub issue #1293.

For platforms whose tuning is rendered into CREATE TABLE during schema creation, the ledger is initialized in the adapter but _setup_fresh_database_phases still calls create_schema with the RAW connection, before any DDL-recording wrapper is in play. ClickHouse injects tuned PARTITION BY / ORDER BY clauses in create_schema and executes them directly, so a run whose physical tuning is ONLY schema DDL can export noop / no applied_ledger_hash even though the database was genuinely tuned.
Thread: https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/pull/1261#discussion_r3630131939

Related: clickhouse-applied-ledger-fidelity-20260724 covers the ClickHouse-side recording; this item covers the base-adapter lifecycle seam. Sequence them to avoid double-recording the same DDL.
preserves: No statement is recorded twice when a platform already records its own schema DDL
Platforms with no schema-phase tuning export exactly the ledger they do today
title: Schema-phase tuning DDL bypasses the ledger recorder (ClickHouse exports noop despite physical tuning)

description:
Implement a unified Firebolt platform adapter supporting both Firebolt Core (free, self-hosted)
and Firebolt Cloud (managed service). Firebolt is a PostgreSQL-compatible cloud data warehouse
with a vectorized query engine optimized for analytical workloads.

**Key Discovery: Firebolt Core**
Firebolt provides a genuinely free, self-hosted version called "Firebolt Core" that runs locally
via Docker with the same distributed, vectorized query engine as the cloud version. This enables
cost-free development, testing, and benchmarking without cloud dependencies.

**Unified Adapter Strategy**
A single adapter can support both deployment modes with minimal conditional logic:
- Local (Core): `connect(database='firebolt', url='http://localhost:3473')`
- Cloud: `connect(auth=ClientCredentials(...), engine_name=..., account_name=...)`

This approach mirrors DataFusion's lesson of handling local vs cloud seamlessly.
title: Add Firebolt Platform Adapter (Core + Cloud)

description:
Analysis of the full test suite (~16,800 test functions) identified ~20 tests
across 5 categories where property-based testing would genuinely add value by
replacing or augmenting manual parametrize lists with generated inputs.

These are pure-function tests asserting PROPERTIES (invariants that hold for
any valid input), not specific behaviors (exact output for exact input). The
remaining ~98% of the suite tests exact SQL strings, mock call sequences,
golden-file snapshots, or integration paths - none of which benefit from
Hypothesis.

Estimated impact: ~400 lines of manual test code replaced or augmented,
with significantly better edge-case coverage on those specific paths.

This is a quality enhancement, not a gap. The suite already has 1,352+
error-path tests and 161 parametrized test sets covering similar ground
manually.

CI test time increase < 15 seconds total across all new property tests

work.notes:
Create `docs/operations/release-guide.md`. Structure:

  # Cutting a BenchBox release

  ## Overview
  One short diagram: private -> curated public tree -> squash -> tag ->
  wheel -> archive. Plain text or simple ASCII, not a graphics file.

  ## Before you start
  - On private main, clean, fetched.
  - ../BenchBox-public clone exists, on main, clean, fetched.
  - PyPI token configured.
  - The two-remote rule (CLAUDE.md): push to `private`, never `public`
    without intent.

  ## The one command
  ```bash
  uv run python scripts/automate_release.py --version 0.2.2 -y --push
  ```
  What each phase does, with one-liner descriptions and source pointers
  (e.g., "Phase 4 builds the curated public tree - see
  benchbox/release/workflow.py::prepare_public_release").

  ## What automation handles vs what you handle
  Two-column table.
  Automation: version bump, changelog, CI, content checks, size guard,
  public divergence preflight, squash, tag, build, archive.
  You: write user-facing changelog blurb, decide patch vs minor,
  communicate the release.

  ## Recovering from common failures
  - CI check fails -> fix on private, re-run.
  - Size check fails -> identify file, add to HOLD_BACK_PATHS or shrink.
  - Content validation fails (em-dash etc.) -> fix in source, re-run.
  - **Public divergence preflight fails** -> run `benchbox-sync pull
    --revspec <last-tag>..HEAD`, commit on private, re-run. Use
    `--allow-public-divergence` ONLY if you intentionally want to
    overwrite those commits.

  ## When to use benchbox-sync (and when not to)
  Table:
  | Subcommand | Use when |
  | status | Sanity check before release. |
  | pull | An external PR landed on public; bring it back to private. |
  | push | Almost never - prefer cutting a patch release. |

  ## Glossary
  - Squash anchor - previous v* tag, where the next release squashes from.
  - Normalized timestamp - most-recent-whole-hour UTC.
  - Source fingerprint - hash of the curated tree.
  - Curated tree - the subset decided by `is_public_path` (single-source
    predicate in benchbox/release/workflow.py).

  ## Reference
  - Source: `scripts/automate_release.py`, `benchbox/release/workflow.py`,
    `benchbox/release/sync.py`.
  - Related: AGENTS.md (dependency bounds), CONTRIBUTING.md.

Style: myst-parser markdown (.md). Triple-backtick fences with language
hints. H2 sentence case. Frontmatter copyright header consistent with
other docs/operations/*.md files - check
`docs/operations/results-phase-2-runbook.md` and copy the header style.
Length target: ~1500 words. If it grows past 2500, split.

description:
The strategy doc differentiates BenchBox vs. ClickBench on three axes,
the first being **multi-benchmark coverage**: TPC-H + TPC-DS + SSB +
more. The current corpus has only TPC-H and SSB. A third benchmark
family is needed before that differentiation claim is credible to a
visitor who actually clicks around the explorer.

This item picks one of TPC-DS or ClickBench, generates a 3-platform
cohort at SF 0.01 (and SF 0.1 if budget allows), and lands it via the
same submit→PR→merge flow used for SF 0.1 expansion. The choice between
TPC-DS and ClickBench is itself a decision (TPC-DS is more standard,
ClickBench is a direct head-to-head with the comparison site we
differentiate against) - w1 makes that call explicitly.
preserves: Cohort isolation per strategy doc - never compare across benchmark families.
Existing TPC-H and SSB cohorts untouched.
Maintainer-run trust label on all generated bundles.
title: Add a third benchmark cohort (TPC-DS or ClickBench) to the public corpus

description:
Implement TPC-H Skew benchmark based on the research published at
https://www.tpc.org/tpctc/tpctc2011/slides_and_papers/introducing_skew_into_the_tpc_h_benchmark.pdf
and reference implementation at https://github.com/YSU-Data-Lab/TPC-H-Skew

For comparative analysis (uniform vs skewed), the existing TPCHBenchmark must be used
for uniform data generation and execution. Do NOT duplicate TPC-H functionality within
TPC-H Skew - instead, orchestrate both benchmarks when comparison is needed.

approach:
Sequence is deliberate and dependency-aware:
- w1-w3 (Critical) ship first, individually. Each is a contract bug
  that breaks production and needs no shared infrastructure.
- w4-w5 (shared-helper foundation) ship next. They are the leverage
  that makes w8/w11 mechanical instead of bespoke per-adapter.
- w6 (P11 visibility cluster) and w7 (N1 throughput inflation) are
  independent of the foundation work — can ship in parallel with w4/w5.
- w8/w9/w10 (modularity-drift extractions) ship after w4/w5.
- w11/w22/w23/w12 (per-adapter regex fixes) ship after w5 in bounded
  adapter-family slices.
- w13/w14 are independent one-liners.
- w15 (ABC test) ships after w3 and gates future regressions.
- w16/w17/w24/w25/w18/w19/w26/w20 are cleanup; ship last.

Reference the canonical fixes already in the repo:
- benchbox/platforms/_spark_helpers.py for balanced-paren walker,
  SparkLikeAdapterMixin, "Import discipline" docstring block
- benchbox/platforms/{spark,lakesail,velox}.py for the lambda-capture
  pattern (w10-style), the on_pre_loop hook wiring, the
  --platform-option error message rewrite (P3 canonical fix)
- docker/velox/docker-compose.yml for the canonical tmpfs pattern
  that w20 should mirror

Grep before each work unit:
  git diff 73f3a582e -- <file>     # confirm file hasn't drifted from audit baseline
  grep -n '<exact snippet>' <file> # confirm line numbers
Audit lines were captured at 73f3a582e; subsequent commits may shift them.

description:
A 13-pattern defect audit across 30 platform adapters (excluding the
already-fixed spark/lakesail/velox triple), shared helpers in
benchbox/platforms/base/, cloud_shared.py, presto_trino_utils.py,
questdb_rewriter.py, datafusion_*.py rewriters, benchbox/sql_compat/,
and all docker/*/ surfaced 33 actionable findings: 3 Critical, 22 Required,
and 8 Nit/Consider. Those findings span the original 13-pattern catalogue
plus 4 newly-named patterns (P14 stale-flag-coexistence,
P15 reference-before-assignment, N1 COUNT(*) throughput inflation,
N2 ABC contract divergence).

The audit ran on commit 73f3a582e (post velox/lakesail/spark fixes for
W8/W9/W10). The canonical fixes for patterns 1-13 already exist in
benchbox/platforms/_spark_helpers.py (`_strip_balanced_paren_constraints`,
the "import discipline" docstring block, the SparkLikeAdapterMixin)
and benchbox/platforms/{spark,lakesail,velox}.py — implementers should
port those patterns rather than reinvent.

Work units are sequenced by blast radius and dependency order: Critical
contract bugs first, then shared-helper drift (highest leverage), then
destructive-op visibility, then the silent-throughput bug, then
modularity-drift extractions, then the long tail of P1/P2 regex bugs
in individual adapters.

Audit report and pattern catalogue are in conversation context (not
committed). This TODO is intended to be self-contained enough to start
implementation, but every work unit must still confirm the cited snippet
against the current file before editing because line numbers were captured
at commit 73f3a582e.
preserves: All currently-passing fast tests continue to pass: `uv run -- python -m pytest -m fast -q`
Existing CLI invocations using legacy `--<adapter>-<flag>` flags continue to work where w17 keeps a shim (deprecation must not be a hard break)
PlatformAdapter ABC method signatures stay stable; w15's conformance test enforces them going forward
PostgreSQLAdapter.create_schema(self, benchmark, connection) -> float signature stays canonical for the entire PG family
Spark/lakesail/velox triple continues to pass tests/unit/platforms/test_{spark,lakesail,velox}_*.py — they are the canonical reference for patterns 1-13
_strip_balanced_paren_constraints behavior in _spark_helpers.py is unchanged when lifted to base/ — re-export must keep import paths stable
title: Address cross-adapter 13-pattern audit findings (3 Critical, 22 Required, 8 Nit/Consider)

description:
Every PR-gating job in .github/workflows/pr.yml runs on `ubuntu-latest`,
but the project is developed on Apple-silicon macOS. So every PR is a
macOS -> Linux leap of faith: a pure-Python check can pass locally on
macOS and then fail in CI on locale, path-case, float formatting, dict/
hash ordering, line endings, or `uv` lock/arch resolution differences.
The correctness-gate and the *-cross-surface-equivalence-report jobs are
the sharp edge here -- they compare result digests against pinned Linux
reference results, exactly the class of value that can format/round
differently across OS.

Apple's `container` (v1.0.0, GA) runs Linux containers as lightweight VMs
on Apple silicon and ships a `container machine` mode: a persistent Linux
environment with the Mac home directory mounted in, so you "edit on the
Mac, build inside Linux". This lets us reproduce the *pure-Python* Linux
PR gate locally before submitting -- the one capability native macOS
cannot provide.

Scope of THIS TODO is the runtime/agent substrate only: stand up Apple
`container` + a `benchbox-agent` machine, run the pure-Python gate inside
it, decide whether in-Linux digests actually diverge from macOS-local,
and (if warranted) add an opt-in `make ci-linux` wrapper. It explicitly
does NOT cover Docker Compose / `make test-docker-*` (no Compose support
in `container`); that is tracked separately in
migrate-test-docker-stacks-to-mocker.

Spike evidence (2026-06-30, host macOS 26.5 / arm64): `brew install
container` -> container CLI 1.0.0; `container system start` +
`container system kernel set --recommended` (kata-static 3.28.0) brought
the runtime up; a single Linux container published ports to the Mac
`localhost` and served real traffic (questdb REST `localhost:19000/exec`
-> result; postgres `localhost:5432` psycopg round-trip -> PostgreSQL
18.4, RW returned 42). `container machine` mode is documented and GA but
was NOT itself exercised in the spike -- w0/w1 must confirm it.

FINDINGS (2026-07-03, container 1.0.0 / macOS 26.5 / arm64):
- w0 PASS: container 1.0.0, apiserver running, arm64/macOS 26.5, mocker 0.5.4.
- w1/w2 PASS: `container machine` boots ONLY with an init in the rootfs
  (ubuntu:24.04 needs systemd-sysv for /sbin/init); home-mount exposes the
  worktree rw at its Mac path via virtiofs. Image: docker/benchbox-agent.
- w3: correctness-gate + ssb equivalence ran inside the machine on a targeted
  lock-pinned env (core + duckdb 1.3.2 + polars); full `uv sync --group dev` +
  `make ci-local` exceeded this host's ~6.6 GiB free disk (the VM sparse disk
  only grows). Digest is DuckDB-build-tied, so the subset does not weaken w4.
- w4 = DIVERGES (central finding): identical DuckDB 1.3.2/arm64, TPC-H SF=1 --
  Linux correctness-gate PASS (18/18 match pinned ref); macOS FAIL on Q2/Q10/
  Q15 (same cardinality, different value digests, deterministic over 2 runs).
  ssb cross-surface equivalence PASS on both (self-referential -> OS-insensitive).
  The pinned references are effectively Linux-specific, so `container` parity is
  the only way to validate the correctness-gate pre-PR from a Mac -> shipped the
  opt-in `make ci-linux` wrapper (w5) + AGENTS.md (w6).
preserves: No PR-gating CI job gains a dependency on Apple container; .github/workflows/ stays ubuntu-latest.
make ci-local and the correctness-gate / *-cross-surface-equivalence-report targets keep working unchanged when run natively on macOS (ci-linux is purely additive).
test-docker-* targets are untouched by this TODO.

approach: Decide the intended contract first: either the guard recognizes an ephemeral/CI clone directly (no sibling worktree pool present, or an explicit signal such as CI), or BENCHBOX_AGENT_PRIMARY_CLONE becomes the documented supported path for these sessions and the refusal message names it alongside worktree-claim. Either way the refusal must keep firing unchanged in a real primary clone, and the message should stop implying BENCHBOX_ALLOW_MAIN_CLONE_WRITE is the only way out. Extend tests/unit/test_agent_write_preflight.py, which already covers the reject/allow/worktree cases.
description: scripts/agent_write_preflight.sh refuses whenever the working tree is not a linked worktree: it derives primary_clone from dirname(git rev-parse --git-common-dir) and rejects when that equals the toplevel. In a remote/ephemeral session (Claude Code on the web, CI, any container) the repo is a plain fresh clone, so the guard fires even though there is no primary clone to protect - the machinery it protects, and the pool it tells you to use, live on the maintainer's Mac. Its remedy 'make worktree-claim BRANCH=...' cannot work there: the pool targets sibling BenchBox.pool-NN directories that do not exist in a container. The only escape the message offers is BENCHBOX_ALLOW_MAIN_CLONE_WRITE=1, documented for 'emergency main-clone hotfix work' needing explicit user authorization. That is semantically wrong for a container session and actively harmful as habit: it trains agents to reach for the broad override routinely, which erodes the guard in the one place it does matter. Note a targeted escape already exists and is untested for this case - BENCHBOX_AGENT_PRIMARY_CLONE (agent_write_preflight.sh:15) repoints the comparison without granting main-clone write - so the fix may be detection plus documentation rather than a new knob. Encountered while opening PR #1374 from a container, where the guard blocked 'make pr-open'.
preserves: A real primary clone still refuses without an override, and the existing BENCHBOX_ALLOW_MAIN_CLONE_WRITE escape keeps working
make pr-open and make skill-sync keep running the preflight before write work

work.notes:
textcharts added `subject: str | None = None` to all chart constructors.
When set, the title is composed as f"{subject} {default_title}".

Example: `subject="Query Latency"` on Histogram → "Query Latency Histogram"

Current BenchBox pattern:
  `ASCIIQueryHistogram(data=data, title="Query Latency Histogram", ...)`
Could become:
  `ASCIIQueryHistogram(data=data, subject="Query Latency", ...)`

Evaluate for each of the ~14 constructor calls in ascii_runtime.py whether
subject= would be cleaner. The benefit is avoiding title string duplication
with the chart type name. The risk is titles that don't compose well with
the generic default (e.g., subject="Performance" + "Bar Chart" = "Performance
Bar Chart" - fine, but subject="Phase Breakdown by Platform" + "Stacked
Breakdown" = nonsense).

Decision criteria:
- Use subject= when the domain qualifier composes naturally with the generic
  chart type name (e.g., "Query Latency" + "Histogram" → good)
- Keep explicit title= when the desired title doesn't match the pattern
  (e.g., "Cost vs Performance" doesn't compose with "Scatter Plot")
- Keep explicit title= for dynamic titles (f-strings with platform names)

Done criteria: Adopt subject= if 5+ of the ~14 call sites compose cleanly.
If fewer than 5 compose well, skip - the consistency benefit is too small
to justify a mixed approach (some subject=, some title=). Document the
evaluation result either way in a commit message or code comment.

Scope: ascii_runtime.py constructor calls only. Do NOT touch MCP dispatch
or exporters.py - those pass title= from external input and must remain
explicit.
work.summary: Evaluate adopting subject= parameter for cleaner title composition

approach: Change the ANCHOR, not the directory name. In resolve_benchmark_runs_dir(), when the resolved root is still the bare DEFAULT_BENCHMARK_RUNS_ROOT sentinel, walk up from Path.cwd() for a '.git' entry (a directory in a clone, a FILE in a linked worktree — both must be accepted via .exists()) and return <worktree_root>.parent / 'benchmark_runs'. When cwd is not inside a work tree (installed package, arbitrary cwd) keep returning Path.cwd() / 'benchmark_runs' so published behaviour for non-repo users is byte-identical. Precedence --output > BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR > default must be untouched: resolve_benchmark_runs_root() and the explicit/env branches keep their current semantics, and only the default branch changes. Guard against the degenerate case where the work tree root is the filesystem root (parent == self) by falling back to cwd. Then rewrite the 11 assertion sites that assert the literal cwd path so they assert against the resolved default root instead of a hardcoded shape, and add a positive regression test that the resolved default is never contained in a Git work tree.

description: benchbox/core/runtime_paths.py::DEFAULT_BENCHMARK_RUNS_ROOT is the RELATIVE Path('benchmark_runs'), and benchbox/utils/path_utils.py::resolve_benchmark_runs_dir anchors that fallback to Path.cwd(). benchbox/cli/config.py::DirectoryManager.__init__ then eagerly mkdirs results/, datagen/ and databases/ under it. Consequence: any `uv run benchbox run` launched from a checkout with no BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR set writes generated data, loaded databases and result JSONs INTO that checkout. Verified on 2026-07-24 @ 14b0271c1: the main clone held 1.9 GB of in-tree artifacts (datagen 1.0 G, databases 936 M, results 704 K) from a 2026-07-24 08:18-08:40 multi-platform session, while the intended shared root /Users/joe/Developer/benchmark_runs received nothing from that day. Direct probe from a scratch cwd returned `resolve_benchmark_runs_dir() = <cwd>/benchmark_runs`. The maintainer convention is `../benchmark_runs` — a SIBLING of the checkout — which works uniformly because every pool worktree (BenchBox.pool-NN, BenchBox.findings-pN) is itself a sibling of the main clone. Both existing guards miss the no-env case: tests/unit/core/test_benchmark_output_root_guard.py only forbids HARDCODED Path.cwd()/'benchmark_runs' in benchmark sources (it enforces routing through the very helper that is cwd-relative), and tests/uat/artifact_hygiene.py::configured_external_root is a no-op when BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR is unset. .env.example:81 actively recommends the in-repo path (`BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR=./benchmark_runs`). Scope note for the test rewrite: grepping the literal pattern yields 13 hits, but 2 of them live in tests/unit/core/test_benchmark_output_root_guard.py - a comment at :41 and a deliberate fixture string at :166 that the guard asserts its own regex still matches. Those 2 must NOT be rewritten; doing so defeats the guard. The real work is 11 assertion sites across 9 files, enumerated in w3.
preserves: A cwd that is NOT inside a Git work tree still resolves to Path.cwd()/'benchmark_runs', so installed-package users see no change
All pool worktrees and the main clone continue to resolve to the SAME shared root, preserving datagen reuse across checkouts
BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR continues to be expanduser()'d and to accept both relative and absolute values
DirectoryManager still creates results/, datagen/ and databases/ under whatever root is resolved
Resolution precedence stays explicit --output > BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR > default; neither the explicit nor the env branch changes behaviour
The directory name stays 'benchmark_runs' so the existing /Users/joe/Developer/benchmark_runs corpus and every BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR-based UAT flow keep working

description:
From the 2026-07-31 adversarial review (leak demonstrated by executing the real scrub code).

Leak 1: IntrospectionReceipt.to_payload() emits a top-level 'error' (benchbox/core/tuning/introspection.py:211-212), and every degraded entry gets reason=f'introspection degraded: {state_error}' (introspection.py:531) where state_error embeds the raw driver exception from the platform introspectors (clickhouse/introspection.py:78, duckdb_introspection.py:61, snowflake_introspection.py:99) - connection strings, hostnames, usernames, cert paths. _sanitize_applied_receipt (benchbox/core/results/exporter.py:478-503) pops statement/diff/evidence/table/name/columns but never receipt['error'], and deliberately retains 'reason' (docstring wrongly classifies reason as structural). After ResultExporter(anonymize=True) the 'anonymized' companion still contains the full raw driver string in applied_receipt.receipt.error and entries[].reason - next to statement_redacted:true.

Leak 2: ABSENT verdicts set reason=f'no {intent.kind} on {intent.table} found in catalog' (introspection.py:553); intent.table is captured by [^\s(]+ regexes so it carries fully-qualified catalog.schema.table - the exact identifier class the exporter pops from the sibling 'table' field.

Propagation: the explorer pipeline ingests the receipt verbatim (_project/scripts/explorer_pipeline/transformer.py:303-332), RunReceipt.tsx:371 renders reason, and publish/submit copy companions byte-for-byte (benchbox/validation/bundle.py COMPANION_SUFFIXES, cli/commands/submit.py:665-667), so export-time scrubbing is the only gate. Contradicts the design note's own claim at docs/development/tuning-introspection-receipts.md:136-137 ('Anonymized exports scrub the receipt's free-text / identifier fields exactly like the ledger statements').

Adjacent smell (fix here too): dropped[].intent/reason are retained wholesale on an unenforced 'code-authored strings' convention (exporter.py:424-426); today's call sites are safe (duckdb.py:1360-1376) but nothing stops a future adapter passing exception text into record_dropped.
preserves: Non-anonymized exports keep full statement/error/reason text - the honest local record must not lose diagnostics.
Receipt structure stays backward-compatible for the explorer's verbatim ingestion (additive markers only, no renamed fields).
The upgrade gate's fail-closed behavior on degraded introspection is unchanged; only the TEXT carried in the receipt changes.
Verdicts, summary counts, and the corroborated flag are untouched by scrubbing - anonymization must never change trust semantics.

description:
Survey approximate analytics support and performance across all major cloud SQL
platforms by running the read_primitives (one-shot approx aggregates) and
write_primitives SQL sketch category (persist + merge + requery) benchmarks at three
scale factors (SF=0.1, SF=1, SF=10).

The goal is a complete support matrix — which platform supports which sketch family,
at what latency, and how latency scales with data volume — plus identification of
any gaps or regressions not yet captured in the cross-engine docs.

Target platforms (SQL mode):
- Databricks SQL (enabled, credentials available)
- ClickHouse Cloud (enabled)
- Firebolt Cloud (enabled)
- Starburst/Trino Cloud (enabled)
- MotherDuck (enabled)

import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

root = Path(os.environ["BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR"]) / "results"
platforms = {"databricks", "clickhouse-cloud", "firebolt", "starburst", "motherduck", "snowflake", "bigquery", "redshift"}

    "clickhouse-cloud": "clickhouse-cloud",
    "databricks-sql": "databricks",
    "google-bigquery": "bigquery",
}
found: set[tuple[str, str]] = set()
for path in root.glob("*.json"):
    data = json.loads(path.read_text())
    benchmark = data.get("benchmark", {})
    benchmark_id = str(benchmark.get("id", ""))
    if benchmark_id not in benchmarks or float(benchmark.get("scale_factor", -1)) != 1.0:
        continue
    platform_name = str(data.get("platform", {}).get("name", "")).lower().replace(" ", "-")

            assert queries, f"{path}: missing query statuses"
            assert all("status" in query for query in queries), f"{path}: query without status"
            found.add((expected, benchmark_id))
missing = sorted((platform, benchmark) for platform in platforms for benchmark in benchmarks if (platform, benchmark) not in found)
assert not missing, f"missing result bundles: {missing}"

approach:
Reuse the grid-based rendering pattern from benchbox/core/visualization/ascii/line_chart.py
(grid creation, Bresenham-like line drawing, axis rendering) but with CDF-specific logic:

1. Create CDFSeriesData (name, values list[float]) dataclass.
2. Create ASCIICDFChart(ASCIIChartBase) with render().
3. For each series: sort values, compute cumulative proportions (i/n for each value).
4. Plot on a grid where X = execution time, Y = cumulative proportion (0-100%).
5. Reuse the marker system from ASCIILineChart (*, +, o, x, ^, v, #, @) for multi-series.
6. Add percentile annotations: vertical dashed lines at P50, P95, P99 positions.
7. Add from_query_results() factory.

Keep Y-axis fixed at 0-100% (no auto-scaling). X-axis scales to data range.
description:
Add a new ASCII chart type that renders a cumulative distribution function (CDF) plot
showing the proportion of queries completing within a given time threshold. The X-axis
is execution time, the Y-axis is the cumulative proportion (0% to 100%), and each
platform is a separate line/curve.

CDF plots are the standard academic and industry method for visualizing latency
distributions, used extensively in TailBench, YCSB, and database vendor whitepapers.
They answer: "what percentage of my queries finish within T milliseconds?" which maps
directly to SLA compliance analysis.

Example output:
```
Cumulative Distribution of Query Latency
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
100%│                         ****+++++++++++
    │                    ****++++
 75%│                ****+++
    │            ***++++
 50%│         **+++
    │       *+++
 25%│     *++
    │    *+
  0%└────────────────────────────────────────
    0      50    100    150    200    300 ms
  * DuckDB    + Polars
```

Steeper curves indicate more consistent performance. Curves that rise quickly and
plateau show tight latency distributions; long tails that slowly reach 100% reveal
problematic outlier queries.

This is distinct from the Box Plot (quartile summary statistics that collapse
distribution shape), the Histogram (per-query latency, not cumulative), and the
Line Chart (time-series trends over runs, not distribution functions). CDF reveals
bimodal distributions, heavy tails, and performance cliffs that quartile summaries hide.
preserves: ASCIILineChart behavior unchanged (CDF is a distribution chart, line chart is time-series)

approach:
Follow the pattern in benchbox/core/visualization/ascii/diverging_bar.py for the
centered-zero layout with bars extending left and right from a reference line:

1. Create SpeedupData dataclass (name, ratio, is_baseline).
2. Create ASCIINormalizedSpeedup(ASCIIChartBase) with a render() method.
3. Draw a vertical baseline reference line at 1.0x in the center.
4. Ratios > 1.0 extend right (faster, green), ratios < 1.0 extend left (slower, red).
5. Add from_normalized_results() factory that computes ratios given results + baseline name.
6. Use logarithmic scaling for the bar width to handle large ratio ranges (e.g., 0.1x to 50x).

The baseline platform selection should accept either a platform name or "slowest"/"fastest"
as convenience aliases.
description:
Add a new ASCII chart type that shows platform performance as a ratio relative to a
user-selected baseline platform (e.g., "DuckDB is 3.2x faster than SQLite"). The
baseline is rendered at 1.0x with a vertical reference line. Platforms faster than
baseline extend right, slower ones extend left.

This is the standard way TPC and SPEC results are formally reported. When comparing
platforms that span orders of magnitude (50ms to 50,000ms), absolute bar charts make
fast platforms invisible slivers. Normalized ratios make relative performance
immediately clear regardless of absolute magnitude.

Example output:
```
Normalized Performance (baseline: SQLite = 1.0x)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         Slower          │         Faster
SQLite                   │█  1.0x
Pandas             ██████│   0.4x
DuckDB                   │████████████████████  8.2x
Polars                   │██████████████████  7.5x
ClickHouse               │██████████████████████████  12.1x
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

This is distinct from the existing bar chart (absolute values) and the diverging bar
chart (percentage change between two runs of the same platform). The normalized speedup
chart shows cross-platform comparison ratios with a centered baseline reference.

description:
Add a new ASCII chart type that visualizes percentile latency bands (P50, P90, P95, P99)
for each platform. Each platform gets a single row showing nested/layered bar segments
where each percentile extends further right, creating a "ladder" appearance.

This chart answers: "what fraction of queries finish within X ms?" which is the gold
standard for tail-latency analysis in database benchmarks. The difference between P50
and P99 reveals consistency - a platform with a tight spread is more predictable than
one with a wide gap.

Example output:
```
Percentile Latency by Platform (ms)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
              P50         P90     P95   P99
DuckDB   ░░░░░░░░░▒▒▒▒▒▓▓██                12 | 45 | 78 | 120
Polars   ░░░░░░░░░░▒▒▒▒▒▒▓▓▓▓██████        15 | 52 | 95 | 310
Pandas   ░░░░░░░░░░░░░▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▓▓▓████      25 | 85 | 140 | 280
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
░ P50   ▒ P90   ▓ P95   █ P99
```

This is distinct from the existing Box Plot which shows IQR-based quartiles with
outlier whiskers. The Percentile Ladder emphasizes specific tail-latency thresholds
(P90/P95/P99) that are standard SLA metrics, rendered as layered horizontal bars
rather than box-and-whisker diagrams.

description:
The ASCII charting module (benchbox/core/visualization/ascii/, ~2,976 lines across 11 files) is
functionally complete with 11 chart types, but real-world usage reveals several UX issues that make
charts harder to read and interpret. These are cosmetic/readability issues, not functional bugs -
all chart types render correctly and return valid strings.

Issues identified from head_to_head and comparison template output with DataFusion SQL vs DataFrame:

1. **Asymmetric series naming**: When comparing SQL vs DataFrame, one series is labeled
   "DataFusion" and the other "DataFusion (dataframe)". Both should carry their mode suffix
   for symmetry - e.g., "DataFusion (sql)" vs "DataFusion (df)". Prefer abbreviated mode
   labels: "df" not "dataframe", "sql" stays "sql".

2. **Aggressive label truncation**: Platform names are truncated to as few as 8 characters
   (comparison_bar.py:81), causing "DataFusion" → "DataFu..". Labels should accommodate full
   names by shrinking the data area or wrapping to a second line.

3. **No chart metadata**: Scale factor, platform version, and tuning configuration are available
   in NormalizedResult but never displayed. Charts should include a subtitle line showing key
   run parameters (e.g., "SF=1 | DataFusion 44.0.0 | tuned").

4. **Inconsistent color application**: Bar chart labels are not colored (bar_chart.py:141) while
   histogram bars and box plot lines are colored. Colors should be applied uniformly across all
   chart types that display series data.

5. **Missing axis labels**: Charts lack axis title annotations (e.g., "Query ID →" on x-axis,
   "↑ Execution Time (ms)" on y-axis). Only tick values and query IDs are shown.

6. **Heatmap readability**: Column headers are severely truncated. The green→yellow→red color
   scale (heatmap.py:32-38) is hard to distinguish in many terminals. User requests red→blue
   diverging palette for better contrast.

7. **Histogram outlier bars**: All bars use the same █ block character regardless of whether
   they represent outlier values. Outlier columns should use a visually distinct character
   (e.g., ▓ or hatched pattern) so extreme values are immediately recognizable.

8. **Summary box dot-leader gap**: In comparison summary boxes, the percentage change is
   right-justified against the border while metric text is left-aligned, leaving a wide blank
   gap (80+ chars of whitespace). Replace with dot-leader pattern (·····) so the eye can trace
   from the value to its percentage.

description:
Add a new ASCII chart type that shows a ranked leaderboard table with each platform's
rank position per query, plus aggregate win/loss/tie counts and an overall geometric
mean rank. Each cell shows a compact rank indicator (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) with color
coding. The footer summarizes total wins, losses, and the overall ranking.

This is how ClickBench presents its results. When comparing 4+ platforms across 22+
queries, it is hard to determine an overall winner from raw timing data. A rank table
immediately shows: "DuckDB wins 18 of 22 queries, Polars wins 3, SQLite wins 1."

Example output:
```
Query Rankings (1st = fastest)
──────────────────────────────────────────────
Query    DuckDB  Polars  SQLite  Pandas
Q1        1st     2nd     3rd     4th
Q2        2nd     1st     3rd     4th
Q3        1st     1st     3rd     4th
Q4        1st     2nd     4th     3rd
...
Q22       1st     3rd     2nd     4th
──────────────────────────────────────────────
1st wins    15      5       2       0
GeoRank    1.2    1.8     2.8     3.9
──────────────────────────────────────────────
```

This is distinct from the Heatmap (shows absolute times color-coded by magnitude,
not relative rankings), the Comparison Bar (handles only two platforms), and the
Bar Chart (one aggregate metric, not per-query ranking). Rank tables answer
"which platform wins the most queries?" rather than "how fast is each platform?"

description:
`tests/contracts/visualization/test_ascii_golden_output.py::test_golden_output`
(parametrized over all 15 ASCII chart builders) is meant to catch
unintended rendering changes by diffing against a stored golden file per
chart, with regeneration gated behind an explicit `--update-golden` CLI
flag (registered in `tests/contracts/visualization/conftest.py:9`).

The gate works correctly for the "intentional change, want to update"
path (lines 342-345: `if update_golden: ... write ... pytest.skip(...)`).
It does NOT work for the "golden file is simply missing" path
(lines 347-350):

    if not golden_path.exists():
        golden_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        golden_path.write_text(normalized, encoding="utf-8")
        pytest.fail(f"Golden file did not exist - created {golden_path}. Re-run to verify parity.")

This block writes the golden file unconditionally (without
`--update-golden`) and then fails once with a message telling the human
to re-run. On the very next run, the freshly-written file exists and the
test passes by construction - there was never an actual parity check.

Concretely, this means: if a golden fixture file under
`tests/fixtures/golden/ascii/` is accidentally deleted, renamed, or
gitignored, or if a rebase/merge drops it, CI fails ONCE (as a
`pytest.fail`, indistinguishable at a glance from a real mismatch), then
quietly self-heals and goes green on the next CI run or re-run - with
whatever the current (possibly buggy) rendering happened to produce
baked in as the new "golden" answer. Nobody has to run `--update-golden`
or review a diff for this to happen. This defeats the purpose of a golden
test, which is specifically to catch renders changing without human
review.

description:
The current Athena adapter uploads text files (pipe-delimited .tbl) to S3 and creates
external tables pointing directly to them. This works but is suboptimal for query
performance - text file queries scan 100x more data than columnar formats.

AWS documentation shows text table scans use 20GB vs Parquet using only 135MB for
the same data, with corresponding cost and performance improvements.

The recommended approach is:
1. Upload text files to S3 staging location
2. Create external staging table pointing to text files
3. Use CTAS to convert to Parquet:
   CREATE TABLE {table} WITH (format='PARQUET', external_location='s3://.../')
   AS SELECT * FROM {table}_staging
4. Query the optimized Parquet table
5. Optionally clean up staging data

This should be the default behavior for Athena, with an option to use text-only
for debugging or when Parquet conversion is not desired.
title: Athena: Convert text tables to Parquet using CTAS for query performance

description:
Release-readiness reports under `_project/audits/` describe a tree. If
the tree the report describes is not the tree that ships, the verdict
is structurally unreliable — even when every individual check passes.
PR #269 demonstrated this: a release-readiness report and capture
generated against the PR branch were squash-merged onto a develop tip
that included PR #268's literal-styled `Result summary` panel and
`Compare guardrails` section, and the report still claimed READY.
PR #271 (commit `274a4a11e`) closed the immediate token regression
manually, but the framework gap remains.

This TODO adds a durable, audit-agnostic gate so the same class of
regression is caught at PR time across every structured audit, not
only retheme work:

1. Every `_project/audits/*.md` audit landing after the cutoff date
   must include a `develop_sha:` frontmatter field naming the develop
   SHA the report describes.
2. The capture flow that authors release-final reports
   (`results-explorer/e2e/captures/release-final.spec.ts` and any
   sibling `*-final.spec.ts` drivers) records the develop SHA at
   run-start so the human author copies it into the audit
   frontmatter.
3. A small validator (`_project/scripts/audit_sha_check.py`) and a
   `make audit-sha-check FILE=…` target verify the field is present,
   resolves to a SHA reachable from `origin/develop`, and is not too
   far behind the merge target's tip.
4. A path-aware CI hook on `_project/audits/**` and
   `results-explorer/e2e/captures/**` runs the validator on every PR
   and refuses to merge a release-readiness audit whose recorded SHA
   is missing or stale relative to the merge target.

Complements (does not replace)
`results-explorer-token-scan-ci-gate.yaml`: that gate prevents the
literal-color regression class from shipping; this gate makes every
release-readiness audit's tree-claim auditable so future cross-PR
races on any surface (security, performance, docs migration) are
caught at the audit-author step rather than after merge.

description:
Systematic, evidence-based review of every dependency declared in the
project with the goal of pruning anything that is not absolutely required.

Motivation:
  - `pyproject.toml` declares ~15 core deps and ~50 optional-extra groups
    covering SQL platforms, cloud storage, DataFrame engines, benchmarks,
    docs, and MCP. Extras have accreted organically as platforms were
    added and it is no longer self-evident which imports are live, which
    are dead, and which are redundant with something already pulled in
    transitively.
  - Supply chain surface: every declared dep is an install target, a
    vulnerability surface, and a version-resolution constraint. Dropping
    unused deps shrinks install size, speeds CI, and reduces the matrix
    the release gate has to keep green.
  - Complements (does NOT replace) `review-dependency-upper-bounds-quarterly.yaml`.
    That item watches caps on *kept* deps for breakage; this item asks the
    prior question: does the dep belong in the manifest at all?

Scope:
  - All `[project] dependencies`, `[project.optional-dependencies]`,
    `[dependency-groups]` in `pyproject.toml`.
  - Any `uv.sources` overrides, git pins, or platform markers.
  - Any runtime imports in `benchbox/`, `scripts/`, `tests/`, `docs/`
    that name a third-party package not declared in the manifest
    (the inverse check - declared-but-unused AND used-but-undeclared).

Non-goals:
  - Not a version-bump exercise. Upper-bounds review is separate.
  - Not a rewrite of extras topology. Consolidation proposals are fine,
    but execution of breaking extras renames is out of scope and would
    be split into a follow-up.
  - Does NOT touch `_binaries/` bundled C++ binaries or dsdgen/dsqgen
    toolchain - those are artifacts, not Python deps.

Deliverable:
  - A committed markdown inventory at
    `docs/development/dependency-inventory.md` listing every declared
    dep, its extras group(s), every source file that imports it, and
    a one-line justification for keeping it. Deps with no live imports
    or with justification "covered by <other dep>" are flagged as
    elimination candidates.
  - A short follow-up TODO (or set of TODOs) proposing concrete
    removals, gated on maintainer sign-off. No deps are deleted under
    this item - only inventoried and flagged.
preserves: Existing `review-dependency-upper-bounds-quarterly.yaml` scope stays intact - this audit explicitly complements, does not subsume

`pyproject.toml` is NOT modified by this audit - only inventoried
`scripts/check_dependency_bounds.py` behavior and CLI unchanged
`uv.lock` is NOT regenerated as part of this work

description:
`.github/workflows/auto-merge-on-open.yml` (lines 31-48: the checkout, base-branch
fetch, and "Check soundness-critical paths" step) checks out the PR at its own
HEAD and then runs `_project/scripts/auto_merge_soundness_paths.py` *from that
same checkout*. For a same-repo (non-fork) PR — the normal case for this
single-maintainer-owned repo where contributors push branches directly — the
script executing the predicate is whatever version the PR itself introduces. A
PR that edits `auto_merge_soundness_paths.py` (e.g. narrows `SOUNDNESS_PREFIXES`,
or the workflow file itself) evaluates its own diff against its own modified
rules, so it can neutralize its review gate in the same commit that would
otherwise have triggered it.

Note honestly: with the repo-layer ruleset review requirement from
auto-merge-review-gate-admin-enforcement enforced (once its deferred admin
action lands), this workflow's withholding behavior is defense-in-depth, not
the primary control — the ruleset's `pull_request` rule would block a
zero-approval squash-merge regardless of what this workflow decides. This item
is still worth doing because (a) the ruleset enforcement is not yet live, and
(b) even once it is, a same-commit self-neutralization that quietly avoids
ever showing "review required" is a bad signal for reviewers relying on the
auto-merge state as a triage cue.

description:
Follow-up to auto-merge-review-gate-soundness-paths (PR #912, already DONE). The
adversarial holistic-review found the gate is only half-real in production. The
code side is correct and sound: pr-open (Makefile:1161) and the
auto-merge-on-open.yml workflow share one predicate
(_project/scripts/auto_merge_soundness_paths.py, invoked with --no-renames) and
correctly WITHHOLD auto-merge enablement for PRs touching comparator/plan-parser
soundness paths. But nothing ENFORCES a review: the develop ruleset
`develop-squash-only` has required_approving_review_count: 0 and
require_code_owner_review: false (verified via `gh api repos/.../rules/branches/develop`;
legacy branch protection returns 404 "Branch not protected"). So a soundness-path
PR can still be squash-merged with zero approvals — manually or by re-enabling
auto-merge. The DONE item's success_metric ("PRs touching the comparator or plan
parsers cannot squash-auto-merge without a review") is NOT met at the repo level.

Two parts: (1) a CI meta-check that makes the gap LOUD and self-healing so it
cannot silently regress once set; (2) the actual ruleset change, which requires
a repo admin and is tracked here as the gating human action.
preserves: Non-soundness-path PRs keep squash auto-merge on CI-pass; this item only hardens the soundness exception.
The code-side withholding behavior (pr-open + auto-merge-on-open.yml shared predicate, --no-renames) is unchanged.

description:
Nine numbered "PR review follow-up sweep" PRs landed this month fixing REAL
defects on already-merged PRs - including comparator-soundness holes in a
correctness gate (e.g. #862: the tie-aware comparator used a constant/literal
column as the boundary-tie key, letting an arbitrary row-swap pass; #872/#878:
unconditional multiset acceptance in the final ORDER BY group; #894: a Spark
parser accepting an EXPLAIN-failure sentinel as a one-node plan). These landed up
to ~3 weeks after merge because squash-auto-merge-on-CI-green makes human review a
post-merge activity, not a merge precondition.

Escaped defects cluster in a small set of files: the result comparator and the
query-plan parsers. Require one approving review for PRs touching those paths
before auto-merge, while leaving the cheap-merge default intact for everything
else.
preserves: No change to CI checks themselves; this adds a human-review precondition for a narrow path set.
The cheap squash-auto-merge default is unchanged for all non-soundness paths.
The local pr-open path and the GitHub auto-merge-on-open backstop use the same soundness-path predicate.

work.notes:
.github/workflows/auto-merge-on-open.yml currently runs `gh pr merge --auto
--squash` UNCONDITIONALLY for every non-draft PR opened against develop. That is
the GitHub-side backstop for PRs opened via the UI, `gh pr create`, or any path
that skips `make pr-open`. While it stays unconditional it RE-ENABLES auto-merge
on soundness-path PRs even when w2 opened them without it, defeating the
review-before-auto-merge goal.

Gate this workflow on the SAME soundness-path predicate w2 uses: detect whether
the PR diff intersects the soundness paths (e.g. a paths/paths-ignore filter or
a diff --name-only check in the job) and SKIP the `gh pr merge --auto --squash`
step for those PRs. Keep the cheap auto-merge default for every non-soundness
diff. The predicate MUST be the single shared source the regression test pins,
so the local pr-open guard and this backstop never diverge.
work.summary: Gate the auto-merge-on-open backstop workflow on the same soundness-path predicate

(1) A 2026-07-23 API snapshot showed auto_merge: null on open PRs whose auto-merge-on-open `enable` job had succeeded. description:
The auto-revert-on-failure job in .github/workflows/develop-post-merge.yml
fires on ANY gate-job failure and reverts `github.sha` unconditionally. On
2026-07-10 two real breakages (#1093 test-side, #1100 code-side) produced
15 consecutive red runs and ~14 auto-revert PRs, of which only 2 (#1099,
#1112) blamed the guilty commit. TODO-only and docs-only merges (#1118,
#1123) got revert PRs. When the pile of revert PRs was bulk-closed at
19:22, the one correct revert (#1112) was discarded with the noise.

Fix: attribute by failure signature, not by newest SHA.

- Each gate job (lint, fast-test, explorer-tokens, medium-test) exposes a
  machine-readable failure signature (for pytest lanes: the set of failed
  test node IDs; for lint/token lanes: the failing job name + step is
  enough) uploaded as a per-run artifact.
- auto-revert-on-failure downloads the signature artifact of the PREVIOUS
  completed develop-post-merge run and diffs:
    * previous run green, or new failure IDs appeared -> this merge
      introduced them: open the revert PR (current behavior), listing the
      new failure IDs in the body.
    * previous run red with an identical-or-superset signature and no new
      IDs -> do NOT open a revert PR; upsert a single open
      "develop red" incident issue (label incident:develop-red) appending
      the run link, so persistent red is one issue, not N PRs.
- A plain green->red transition guard is NOT sufficient: #1100 added a
  second failure to an already-red develop and a transition guard would
  have skipped the one revert PR that was actually correct. Signature
  diffing handles both cases.

Also in scope (same file):
- When all gate jobs succeed, auto-close any open auto-revert/* PRs and
  open incident:develop-red issues with a comment naming the green run
  (extension alongside close-orphaned-prs).
- Fix the stale metrics-job comment (lines ~448-451) claiming
  MEDIUM_TEST_RESULT is inert under continue-on-error; medium-test was
  promoted to blocking on 2026-07-06.
preserves: A genuinely new failure on an already-red develop STILL opens a revert PR (the #1100 case)
Existing conflict fallback: git revert conflict still opens the incident:develop-red-revert-conflict issue with SHA-in-body dedup
Idempotency: re-runs for the same SHA must not open duplicate revert PRs or issues
Metrics artifact stays a superset of the current JSON schema (existing keys unchanged)
close-orphaned-prs semantics untouched

description:
`results-data/corpus-inventory.json` is currently maintained by hand. It
enumerates every bundle in the seed corpus with metadata (benchmark,
platform, scale, trust label, hash). Once Phase 2 community PRs start
landing, hand-maintenance will drift: contributors will forget to update
the inventory, maintainers will forget to nudge them, and the explorer
static-build pipeline will silently see a stale view of the corpus.

This item replaces the hand-maintained file with a generated one. The
generator scans `results-data/bundles/` recursively, extracts metadata
from each bundle's schema-v2 header (and sidecar manifest where present),
and writes a deterministic, sorted `corpus-inventory.json`. A pre-commit
hook and a CI step prevent drift.
preserves: Existing fields/shape consumed by any downstream tool referencing `corpus-inventory.json`. Audit consumers in w5 before changing the shape.
Existing pipeline at `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` - it builds its own manifest; the inventory is a separate, lighter index.
The schema-v2 bundle format and the trust-label sidecar contract - generator reads, never mutates.
title: Automate corpus-inventory.json generation from results-data/bundles/

description:
Add support for Apache DataFusion Ballista, a distributed SQL query engine built on
Apache DataFusion and Apache Arrow. Ballista extends DataFusion's single-node execution
to a distributed cluster architecture with a scheduler and multiple executor nodes.

Ballista is notable for:
- Distributed SQL execution across a cluster (scheduler + executors)
- Built on DataFusion - same SQL dialect, same query planning, same Arrow-native execution
- Python bindings built from source (BallistaBuilder and BallistaSessionContext APIs)
- Supports Parquet, CSV, and other Arrow-compatible formats on shared storage
- Kubernetes-native deployment with Helm charts
- Standalone mode for single-machine testing
- Columnar execution via Apache Arrow with query vectorization
- Claims 2.9x speedup over Spark on TPC-H at 100GB scale factor

Since Ballista uses DataFusion internally, the existing DataFusion adapter provides
a strong foundation. The key differences are: (1) connection via BallistaBuilder to a
remote scheduler instead of a local SessionContext, (2) data must reside on shared
storage accessible to all executors (S3, GCS, HDFS, or shared filesystem), and
(3) distributed execution semantics (partitioning, shuffles, task scheduling).

IMPORTANT: The `ballista` name on PyPI is occupied by an UNRELATED package (a PyTorch
helper). The Apache Ballista Python bindings are NOT published to PyPI as prebuilt
wheels. Users must build from source using maturin from the main Ballista repo
(apache/datafusion-ballista/python/). This significantly affects installation UX
and CI integration.

Reference: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-ballista
Python bindings: https://github.com/apache/datafusion-ballista/tree/main/python

description:
Implement a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that enables AI agents like Claude Code
to run benchmarks, analyze results, and interact with BenchBox programmatically.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI systems to
external tools and data sources. By implementing an MCP server, BenchBox becomes
accessible to any MCP-compatible AI agent, enabling natural language benchmark
orchestration.

The MCP server will expose BenchBox functionality through three primitives:
- **Tools**: Executable actions (run benchmarks, export results)
- **Resources**: Read-only data (benchmark metadata, historical results, system info)
- **Prompts**: Reusable templates (analysis patterns, comparison queries)

This enables use cases like:
- "Run TPC-H at scale factor 1 on DuckDB and show me the results"
- "Compare my last 3 benchmark runs and identify regressions"
- "Which platforms support the TPC-DS benchmark?"
- "Analyze query 5 performance across all my runs"
title: BenchBox MCP Server for AI Agent Integration

description:
The public BenchBox site currently ships multiple independent header
implementations. The landing page uses `landing/index.html` and
`landing/style.css`; docs/blog inject a Furo-adjacent header from
`docs/_templates/page.html` and `docs/_static/custom.css`; Results Explorer
renders a separate Preact header in `results-explorer/src/components/Layout.tsx`.
Those headers differ in link set, CTA presence, max width, fixed/sticky/static
positioning, spacing, mobile behavior, active state, and theme assumptions.

This is a product-shell defect: the user should experience one BenchBox
global header everywhere, including `/`, `/docs/`, `/blog/`, and `/results/`.
Results Explorer may keep a secondary Results-specific navigation row below

description:

named `get_benchmark_class` intentionally return different surfaces:

    -> benchbox.core.tpch.benchmark.TPCHBenchmark

The same split was confirmed for `vector_search` and `datavault`. Both
returns are callable benchmark classes, so importing the wrong function can
silently select the public wrapper surface where a core implementation was
expected, or vice versa. Existing tests already alias these functions to keep
them straight, which is evidence that the ambiguity is real.

Independent verification also confirmed the constructor fallback concern in
`benchbox/core/benchmark_loader.py`: a class whose constructor accepts

returning successfully in the mocked harness after constructor calls

"constructor accepted `parallel` but had an internal TypeError" are currently
indistinguishable.

cheapest credible per-benchmark oracle (w2), reusing existing harnesses

description:
The TPC-Havoc equivalence work established that a benchmark can have a real
correctness oracle without a hand-maintained answer key (variant-vs-canonical
and SQL-vs-DataFrame, compared live on a bounded DuckDB cell). Applying that
lens across the suite exposes how little of it is actually guarded:

- Stored expected results exist for ONLY tpch and tpcds
  (benchbox/core/expected_results/tpch_results.py, tpcds_results.py).
- Live equivalence gates exist for ONLY tpchavoc (SQL variant + DataFrame),
  plus cross-engine sampling for tpchavoc (PRs #803/#806).
- Every other benchmark - ssb, clickbench, amplab, coffeeshop, datavault,
  flightdata, joinorder, joinorder_synthetic, nyctaxi, tsbs_devops, tpcds_obt,
  tpch_skew, and the primitive suites (read/write/transaction/metadata/ai),
  tpcdi - executes "green" with NO automated check that any result is correct.

Two complementary mechanisms cover most of this gap. The cross-surface
SQL<->DataFrame gate (owned by benchmark-cross-surface-equivalence-gate)
handles dual-surface benchmarks. THIS item owns (a) the coverage map itself -
a single authoritative matrix of which oracle, if any, guards each shipped
benchmark - and (b) the benchmarks that cross-surface cannot reach: single-
surface benchmarks (one of SQL or DataFrame only) and benchmarks whose two
surfaces are not result-comparable. Those need a different oracle: a
differential check against a second engine on the same SQL, a small curated
expected-results subset, or a documented structural invariant - chosen per
benchmark from evidence.

The end state is a policy: every shipped benchmark declares its correctness
oracle, and a benchmark with "none" is visible (and ideally flagged), so the
suite cannot quietly grow more unverified surfaces.
preserves: Existing oracles (tpch/tpcds expected results, tpchavoc gates) are unchanged and remain authoritative for their benchmarks.
No new hard CI gate lands noisy/flaky; advisory-first, promote to blocking only once stable.
benchbox run default behavior is unchanged for every benchmark; coverage work is additive.

approach:
Generalize the proven TPC-Havoc DataFrame gate rather than inventing a new
comparator: extract a shared harness (w0), inventory applicability (w1), stand
up a production-faithful DataFrame-loading substrate (w5) and fix the loader
bugs it surfaces (w6), re-base ssb onto it (w7), then land report-mode across
the ungated dual-surface benchmarks (w2), burn down (w3), and flip bounded CI
gates with fast-lane companions (w4). SQL is the live reference for its own
DataFrame surface; no hand-maintained answer keys; the DataFrame surface runs
on its real production data path so divergences are real, not dtype artifacts.

description:
TPC-Havoc now ships two result-equivalence gates that proved a discipline:
execute a candidate query and a trusted reference over the SAME bounded
small-SF DuckDB dataset and compare results live (order-insensitive, float-
tolerant), with no hand-maintained expected answers. The SQL gate
(benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py) compares each SQL variant to canonical
TPC-H; the DataFrame gate (benchbox/core/tpchavoc/dataframe_equivalence.py)
compares each DataFrame variant to canonical TPC-H SQL. Together they found and
fixed ~42 silent correctness defects.

That discipline is currently TPC-Havoc-only, by construction. But ~14
benchmarks ship a DataFrame query surface (amplab, clickbench, coffeeshop,
datavault, flightdata, joinorder, nyctaxi, read_primitives, ssb, tpcds,
tpcds_obt, tpch, tpch_skew, tsbs_devops) in ADDITION to their SQL surface, and
nothing checks that the two surfaces agree. Worse, stored expected results
exist for ONLY tpch and tpcds (benchbox/core/expected_results/tpch_results.py,
tpcds_results.py) - so for every other dual-surface benchmark there is NO
correctness oracle of any kind: SQL and DataFrame implementations both execute
"green" while their results are unverified and may silently disagree.

Cross-surface equivalence is the cheap, maintenance-free oracle for exactly
this gap: SQL and DataFrame are independent implementations of the same logical
query, so a divergence proves at least one is wrong - without needing a
hand-curated answer key. This work generalizes the TPC-Havoc DataFrame-gate
harness into a shared, benchmark-agnostic helper, then rolls out a bounded
SQL<->DataFrame equivalence gate to the dual-surface benchmarks, SQL as the
reference for its own DataFrame surface.

Note: for tpch/tpcds the expected-results registry already validates each
surface against a stored answer key (transitive equivalence), so they are
lower priority here; the highest value is the dual-surface benchmarks with NO
oracle today (ssb first - canonical and small - then clickbench, joinorder,
coffeeshop, etc.).
preserves: ResultValidator tolerance/checksum semantics are unchanged; reuse, do not fork, the comparator and the DuckDB SQL-reference data builder.
The TPC-Havoc SQL and DataFrame gates stay green with empty KNOWN_DIVERGENCES and unchanged behavior.

The production DataFrame loader/adapters are reused, not forked; any change there (w6) is a genuine loader bug fix that keeps the real DataFrame run path working (re-verify the DataFrame benchmark run), never gate-only special-casing.
benchbox run default (execution-only) behavior is unchanged for every benchmark; the gates are additive.

BURN-DOWN PROGRESS (full detail:
_project/analysis/clickbench-cross-surface-divergences.md):
  - DETERMINISM FIX (prerequisite): the ClickBench generator was UNSEEDED, so
    every run produced different data and top-N/tie-sensitive cells flipped
    divergence run-to-run (the gate was flaky). Added random.seed(42) in
    _generate_data_local (mirrors SSBDataGenerator); the gate is now
    deterministic (verified: two runs report the identical divergence set).
  - ALL 10 engine/error-category cells FIXED: added UnifiedStrExpr.replace
    (Q29) and UnifiedLazyFrame.slice (Q39-42) to the shared abstraction;
    compared EventDate to native date literals not strings (Q37-43); pandas
    `<> ''` filters now exclude NULL via .notna() to match SQL/Polars
    (Q25/27). 1129 dataframe/clickbench unit tests still pass.
  - REMAINING: 27 stable value-divergence cells across 14 queries. TRIAGE
    (verified by direct SQL-vs-DataFrame set/count comparison): these are
    mostly NOT logic bugs. The DataFrame computes CORRECT aggregates; the
    divergences are the gate's order-sensitive row-by-row comparison of
    tie-ambiguous top-N (`ORDER BY col ... LIMIT N` with ties spanning the
    cutoff). E.g. Q32/Q33 top-10 are all count=1 (thousands of count-1
    groups, LIMIT keeps an arbitrary 10); Q16 count distribution is IDENTICAL
    on both surfaces (only tied rows reorder). So the fix is GATE-LEVEL
    (deterministic total-order tie-breaker on both surfaces, OR a tie-aware
    validator, OR classify tie-ambiguous queries), NOT per-query ClickBench
    fixes. Exception: Q17/Q24 empty-string-vs-None is the deferred loader
    null/dtype materialization issue (see joinorder_synthetic). Detail:
    _project/analysis/clickbench-cross-surface-divergences.md.
So ClickBench has ~no genuine DataFrame logic bugs; promote STAGED_GATES->GATES

instead of applying schema types: "expected String type" on 1a/1b/5a/8a/9a/10a;

loading the DataFrame surface (types now available from column_sql_type). Detail:
_project/analysis/joinorder-synthetic-cross-surface-divergences.md.

work.notes:
DONE. Made ResultValidator.validate_results_exact opt-in tie_aware (additive,
default False so the TPC-Havoc gates are byte-unchanged). Chose option (b) (a
tie-aware comparator) over (a) (the ClickBench SQL queries are also the perf
queries, so adding tie-breaker ORDER BY columns would pollute the benchmark)
and over weakening to set-equality.

MECHANISM: the relaxation engages ONLY after the strict sorted-positional
comparison fails, and accepts a divergence iff it is exactly an ambiguous
top-N boundary tie - deterministically, independent of run-to-run tie
reordering:
  - the differing rows are the multiset difference each way (the swapped tie
    members); the rest are byte-identical (the deterministic remainder);
  - there must be an order-key column c that is monotonic across the
    reference result (the ORDER BY key is; a grouped non-key column is not),
    whose value on EVERY swapped row equals the reference's boundary value
    original[-1][c] (stable even when tied rows reorder), the boundary value
    occurs >=2 times (a genuine tie, not a unique last row), and is an
    extreme (min/max) of the column.
So a real value-misplacement bug outside the tie (wrong order-key value,
wrong non-key value on a determined row, wrong row count, unique-last-row
change) puts a non-boundary value into the swap and still FAILS. The
cross-surface gate passes tie_aware=True; TPC-Havoc keeps the default.

An EARLIER attempt inferred the key by splitting on all monotonic columns
jointly; DuckDB's non-deterministic tie order made a non-key column
(SearchPhrase) coincidentally monotonic in ~1/3 of runs, so the gate was
flaky. The multiset-difference + boundary-value formulation is order-stable
(the count column always qualifies); verified 5 consecutive clean runs.

Q18 (`... GROUP BY ... LIMIT 10` with NO ORDER BY over ~97k groups) is the
one genuinely order-less query - any 10 rows are valid and the two surfaces
pick different subsets (both verified subsets of the full grouped result).
It is the last-resort option (c): classified in clickbench's
known_divergences with justification, NOT masked (the tie-aware comparator
handles every ORDER BY ... LIMIT case; only this order-less LIMIT needs a
baseline entry).

ROOT CAUSE (verified by direct SQL-vs-DataFrame set/count comparison): the 27
remaining ClickBench divergences are NOT logic bugs. The DataFrame computes
CORRECT aggregates; the gate's comparator (ResultValidator.validate_results_exact
in benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py) sorts both sides then compares
row-by-row, so for `ORDER BY <col> ... LIMIT N` queries whose ties span the
LIMIT cutoff it reports a false divergence: SQL and the DataFrame each keep a
different (equally valid) subset of the tied rows. E.g. Q32/Q33 top-10 are all
count=1 (thousands of count-1 groups; LIMIT 10 keeps an arbitrary 10); Q16's
count distribution 4,4,4,4,4,4,3,3,3,3 is IDENTICAL on both surfaces, only the
tied rows reorder/swap at the boundary.

FIX (gate/validator-level, NOT 27 per-query ClickBench changes - pick one):
  (a) append a deterministic total-order tie-breaker (remaining columns / a
      stable key) to the ORDER BY on BOTH surfaces before comparison, or
  (b) make the comparator tie-aware: compare the MULTISET of rows sharing the
      boundary order-key value instead of position-by-position, or
  (c) classify genuinely tie-ambiguous queries as accepted/justified
      divergences (last resort - prefer a real total order).
Reuse, do not fork, ResultValidator; keep it able to catch genuine
value-misplacement bugs (do not weaken to set-equality across all columns).

work.summary: Make the cross-surface comparator tie-aware for top-N queries (clears ClickBench's 27 tie-ambiguous cells)

work.notes:
DONE. Made the production DataFrame loader apply the schema's declared column
TYPES (and DuckDB-matching empty-field semantics) instead of per-file
inference. Three loader-layer fixes, all additive, no per-query changes:

  1. SQL-type -> Arrow-type map was incomplete. The CSV->Parquet conversion
     (the Polars/expression path, which reads read_parquet) only typed the
     handful of names in SchemaMapper.PYARROW_TYPE_MAP (VARCHAR/CHAR/INTEGER/
     DATE/...), so declared TEXT/STRING/BIGINT/NUMERIC/... columns fell
     through to PyArrow inference - an all-NULL TEXT column (joinorder
     movie_companies.note) inferred as Null, a numeric-looking TEXT column
     (movie_info_idx.info ratings) as float64. Added
     SchemaMapper.sql_type_to_pyarrow() covering every SQL type family
     (TEXT/STRING/CHAR -> string, INT family -> int64, DECIMAL/FLOAT family
     -> float64, DATE -> date32, TIMESTAMP/DATETIME -> timestamp[us]) and
     routed _extract_arrow_types through it. Cleared the 6 Polars
     "expected String type" cells (1a/1b/5a/8a/9a/10a) and the float64-vs-str
     cells (4a/12a).
  2. Pandas reads CSV, not Parquet (its recommended_data_format is CSV), so
     the Parquet fix did not reach it. read_csv now (a) reads declared text
     columns as object (so numeric-looking text is not inferred float64) and
     (b) parses a declared DATE/TIMESTAMP column as temporal even when its
     NAME does not match the date-suffix heuristic (ClickBench
     ClientEventTime TIMESTAMP was read as a raw string vs DuckDB's datetime).
     Date detection is now TYPE-aware (extends the w6 numeric-exclusion).
  3. Empty-string vs NULL (ClickBench Q17/Q24): the DataFrame surface emitted
     None where the SQL surface emits "". Root cause was the per-benchmark
     CSV null_marker, NOT dtype: DuckDB resolves nullstr via
     resolve_csv_dialect (ClickBench null_marker=None -> empty kept "";
     JoinOrder null_marker="" -> empty -> NULL), while the DataFrame path
     always nulled empties (coincidentally matching JoinOrder, diverging from
     ClickBench). Threaded the SAME resolved null_marker into both surfaces:
     the Parquet conversion sets strings_can_be_null = (null_marker is not
     None); pandas restores "" on declared string columns when null_marker is
     None; pandas load_table now resolves null_marker via resolve_csv_dialect
     (not the file-extension heuristic) so JoinOrder still nulls empties.
     Bumped the DataFrame Parquet cache v3->v4 (conversion rules changed).

The orchestrator (_get_benchmark_instance) only forwards a fixed set of kwargs (scale_factor, compress_data, compression_type, compression_level, verbose, quiet, parallel). description:
PR #759 made benchmark datagen roots honor BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR at construction
and added GeneratorOutputDirMixin so a post-construction output_dir
reassignment propagates to nested generators. Several generator-backed
benchmarks (h2odb, ssb, tpch, nyctaxi, etc.) opted into the mixin; a few did
not because their generators are lazy or intentionally point elsewhere.

Two benchmarks build a generator (or derive directories) in __init__ but have
no synchronizing output_dir setter, so an explicit CLI --output root that
differs from the construction default does NOT reach them:

- tpcds: builds its data_generator in __init__ and has no output_dir setter, so
  a post-construction reassignment (runner _resolve_output_dir_handler) leaves
  the generator pointed at the construction-time path.
- tpcdi: derives source_dir/staging_dir/warehouse_dir and builds its
  data_generator in __init__ from self.config.output_dir; a later output_dir
  reassignment updates neither the ETL subdirs nor the generator.

This is a pre-existing residual gap, NOT a regression. The reported failure

description:

ignored BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR and wrote datagen output under a worktree-local

enforced for every current and future benchmark, and add a cheap static guard
that fails when a benchmark constructor hardcodes a cwd-local benchmark_runs
default instead of the shared resolver.

description:
PR #759 fixed the output-root propagation bug with two cooperating mechanisms:
an env-aware default in BaseBenchmark, and an opt-in GeneratorOutputDirMixin
whose setter re-syncs nested generators when output_dir is reassigned after
construction. This works, but it leaves the original architectural smell that
the TODO's w2 explicitly preferred to fix: the orchestrator still constructs
the benchmark BEFORE the final output root is resolved, then mutates
benchmark.output_dir afterward (orchestrator data-sharing redirect, runner
_resolve_output_dir_handler).

Consequences of keeping post-construction mutation as the contract:

- Footgun: any new generator-backed benchmark that builds its generator in
  __init__ and forgets the mixin silently reintroduces the bug. The mixin is
  opt-in, so correctness depends on author memory.
- Duplication: GeneratorOutputDirMixin now overlaps with the bespoke output_dir
  setters in read_primitives/benchmark.py and transactional/benchmark_base.py.
- Residual gaps: benchmarks with lazy/derived layouts (tpcds, tpcdi) need the
  separate explicit-override fix tracked in
  benchmark-output-root-explicit-override-propagation.

Investigate resolving the benchmark-specific datagen directory once at the call
boundary and injecting it into the constructor, so generators capture the
correct root immediately and post-construction mutation (and the mixin) can be
retired or reduced to a thin compatibility shim. If adopted, this would subsume
the explicit-override item and let the duplicated setters collapse onto one
mechanism.
preserves: BENCHBOX_OUTPUT_DIR remains the shared-root mechanism; cwd-local default preserved when neither is set.
CLI --output remains the highest-precedence output root.
Data-sharing benchmarks (read/write/transaction primitives) keep reusing the source benchmark's datagen dir.
External callers that still assign benchmark.output_dir after construction continue to work (compatibility shim).
