Finding 1 (P1, Axis 3): the command uses
`git log --since="$START_DATE" --until="$END_DATE"`, which makes
the upper bound midnight at the *start* of `END_DATE`. Test changes
merged later on the closing day are excluded — exactly the axis
meant to catch missed coverage downgrades silently misses them.

Finding 2 (P2, Axis 2): the template says `make blind-spots-list`
is a more *precise* way to get findings in the review window, but
that target maps to `sweep_blind_spots.py list`, which only filters
by status/kind and does not support date-window filtering. In
practice it can pull unrelated historical open findings and omit
in-window non-open findings, so weekly sweep scope becomes
inconsistent.

Current evidence on `origin/develop`:
  - `_project/audits/codex-weekly-sweep-template.md:55-62` — Axis 2
    presents `make blind-spots-list` as the more-precise option.
  - `_project/audits/codex-weekly-sweep-template.md:88-92` — Axis 3
    uses bare `--since`/`--until` with no inclusive end-of-day.

Recommended fix:
  - Axis 3: align with Axis 1's inclusive end pattern (e.g.
    `--until="$END_DATE 23:59:59"` or
    `--until="$(date -d "$END_DATE + 1 day" +%Y-%m-%d)"` — match
    whichever idiom Axis 1 already uses).
  - Axis 2: replace the "more precise" guidance with an actual
    date-bounded query. Option A: keep the `ls` glob with explicit
    start/end dates. Option B: extend `sweep_blind_spots.py list`
    with `--since`/`--until` and use that. Option A is lower-risk
    and ship-now; Option B can be filed as a follow-up if the
    team wants a CLI affordance.

Must preserve:
  - Axis 1 (the existing reference for the inclusive bound) keeps
    its current command exactly.
  - The cross-link to the cold-load-rowcount blind-spot example at
    line 74-77 stays intact.

Verification:

work.notes:
Source review comment:
  - PR #141, P1, `benchbox/core/results/schema.py`
  - https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/pull/141#discussion_r3177580644

Finding: re-exporting previously saved results silently drops
`cost.total_usd`. `reconstruct_benchmark_results()` calls
`_extract_cost_summary()` which only rebuilds `total_cost` and
`cost_model` and does not restore `normalized_cost`, so this
guard rejects emitting totals for any legacy bundle. Comparison
and reporting flows that depend on `cost.total_usd` break for
anything written before normalized_cost existed.

Current evidence on `origin/develop`:
  - `benchbox/core/results/schema.py:578-589` — `_add_cost_section`
    emits `cost.total_usd` only when
    `_normalized_cost_allows_direct_total(normalized_cost)` is true.
  - `benchbox/core/results/schema.py:592-598` — that helper returns
    `False` whenever `normalized_cost` is not a dict.
  - `benchbox/core/results/loader.py:394-401` —
    `_extract_cost_summary` returns only
    `{"total_cost": ..., "cost_model": ...}`. No `normalized_cost`
    key is restored, so re-exports always hit the False branch.

Recommended fix: restore `normalized_cost` during reconstruction so
round-tripped bundles preserve the contract. Update
`_extract_cost_summary` to also pull
`cost_section.get("normalized_cost")` (preserve the dict shape) and
put it in `cost_summary["normalized_cost"]`. As a defensive backstop,
treat "no normalized block at all" (legacy) as "allow direct total"
in `_normalized_cost_allows_direct_total` so a missing-vs-rejected
block has different semantics.

Must preserve:
  - Bundles that have `normalized_cost` with `cost_status` outside
    `{"normalized", "not_applicable_local"}` continue to suppress
    `cost.total_usd` (this is the original P1 fix from PR #141).
  - `cost.model` field continues to round-trip from `cost_model`.
  - Empty `cost_summary` (no cost data at all) emits no `cost`
    section — current behavior must hold.

Verification:
  - description: "Pytest: legacy bundle (no `normalized_cost`) →
      re-export → `cost.total_usd` survives. Modern bundle with
      `cost_status='unavailable'` → re-export → no `cost.total_usd`."
  - command: "uv run -- python -m pytest tests/unit/core/results/ -v -k 'cost or round_trip or legacy'"
  - expected_output: "Both the legacy round-trip and the modern
      suppression cases pass; legacy bundle keeps its total_usd."
work.summary: Round-trip `cost.total_usd` for legacy bundles that have no normalized_cost block

Finding: the new skip logic unconditionally excludes Q10 for any
benchmark detected as TPC-H, regardless of whether the run is
using the constrained local envelope. Users who provide a remote
`scheduler_address` or provision enough resources still lose Q10
coverage, producing incomplete TPC-H results and preventing valid
full-suite runs.

Current evidence on `origin/develop`:
  - `benchbox/platforms/dataframe/dask_df.py:447-455` —
    `_collect_skip_query_ids` only checks `_is_tpch_benchmark`
    before adding `_RESOURCE_ENVELOPE_SKIP_QUERY_IDS`.
  - `benchbox/platforms/dataframe/dask_df.py:178,239,298` —
    `self.scheduler_address` and `self.use_distributed` flags are
    available; an external scheduler is treated as
    "not local cluster".

Recommended fix: gate the Q10 skip on a local-envelope predicate.
Initial proposal: skip when `not self.scheduler_address and not
self.use_distributed`. When the user provides an external
scheduler, run Q10 normally. Update the diagnostic message to
explain *why* it skipped and how to opt out (provide a remote
scheduler).

Must preserve:
  - The OOM exit-137 protection still applies for actual local-
    cluster TPC-H runs (the original incident).
  - `_build_skipped_results` continues to attach
    `dask_resource_envelope_guarded=True` and the diagnostic
    string for the queries it actually skipped.
  - No change to skip lists for non-TPC-H benchmarks.

Open question (resolve before edit):
  - Is the OOM gate `not scheduler_address` (covers user-supplied
    remote schedulers) or also `cluster_mode != "local"` (covers
    managed-Dask/Coiled distributed clusters)? Verify against
    how the original OOM was reproduced; default to the broader
    predicate if both are needed.

Verification:

work.notes:
Source review comment:
  - PR #145, P1, `benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py`
  - https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/pull/145#discussion_r3177722807

Finding: when `file_paths` contain multiple shard names that do
not share a leading substring (UUID- or hash-named parts),
`os.path.commonprefix(...)` returns `""`, so `location` becomes
`"<parent>/*"`. DataFusion will then register every file in the
directory, pulling in other tables' data and silently corrupting
row counts.

Current evidence on `origin/develop`:
  - `benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py:909-921` — multi-file branch
    builds `location = str(parent_dir / f"{common_prefix}*")` with
    no check that `common_prefix != ""`.

Recommended fix: when `common_prefix == ""`, fall back to one of
(a) registering each file by exact path and unioning, (b) using
DataFusion's `LISTING_TABLE` with an explicit file list, or
(c) the existing single-file fallback applied per shard. Pick the
least-disruptive option that preserves row counts (likely (a) — a
union view over explicit paths).

Must preserve:
  - Single-file branch (`len(file_paths) == 1`) keeps its current
    behavior unchanged.
  - Multi-directory fallback (line 916-921) keeps its current
    "first file with warning" behavior.
  - Schema-clause inference (lines 899-906) is independent of
    this fix; do not touch.

Verification:
  - description: "Pytest: multi-file with uuid-style names (no
      common prefix) → registered location does not glob the
      parent directory. Multi-file with shared prefix → glob still
      works."
  - command: "uv run -- python -m pytest tests/unit/platforms/test_datafusion.py -v -k 'glob or common_prefix or external_table'"
  - expected_output: "New no-common-prefix test passes; existing
      shared-prefix glob test continues to pass."
work.summary: Guard empty common prefix in DataFusion CSV multi-file glob

description:
Address two UX issues with the `benchbox compare` command:

1. **Superfluous --run flag**: The `--run` flag is awkward and inconsistent with
   `benchbox run` which doesn't require a `--run` flag. Mode should be inferred
   from the arguments provided.

2. **No interactive guidance**: Unlike `benchbox run`, `compare` has no interactive
   wizard when called without arguments. Users must already know the exact syntax.

Current state:
- benchbox compare --run -p duckdb -p sqlite  # Awkward --run flag
- benchbox compare result1.json result2.json   # File comparison
- benchbox compare                              # Error - no guidance

Target state:
- benchbox compare -p duckdb -p sqlite          # Run mode (inferred from -p)
- benchbox compare result1.json result2.json    # File mode (inferred from args)
- benchbox compare                              # Interactive wizard
title: Compare Command UX Improvements

description:
The `benchbox compare` command's interactive file comparison mode needs significant
UX improvements. Currently it shows a flat list of JSON files with just paths,
requiring users to manually identify which results they want to compare.

Users should be able to either:
A) Specify files directly by path (keep existing behavior)
B) Interactively filter by benchmark/platform/scale, then select from the 10
   most recent matching results

This makes the compare workflow much more intuitive for users with many result
files accumulated over time.
title: Improve interactive file selection in compare command

approach:
Use an evidence-first workflow:
1) Build a complete classification matrix for every flagged function.
2) Apply ignore entries only for truly irreducible complexity with explicit rationale.
3) Refactor accidental complexity in subsystem batches with focused tests.
4) Re-run complexity and regression tests after each batch.

approach:
Three patterns to apply:
1. Enumeration loop: FIELDS = [("src_attr", "dst_attr"), ...]; for s, d in FIELDS: setattr(dst, d, getattr(src, s))
2. Conditional accumulation: CONDITIONS = [(predicate_fn, value), ...]; result = [v for fn, v in CONDITIONS if fn()]
3. Optional dict builder: KEYS = [("src", "dst"), ...]; return {d: src[s] for s, d in KEYS if s in src}

Keep field definitions close to the function (module-level constant or near the function).

description:
There are three overlapping concurrent-stream executors plus a dead stub. This
fragmentation is a maintenance and correctness hazard: fixes to one path (the
production one) do not reach the others, and it is not obvious which is live.

- LIVE: benchbox/core/throughput/runner.py:StreamRunner — the real executor
  used by the CLI/adapter throughput path.
- EFFECTIVELY DEAD: benchbox/utils/execution_manager.py:ConcurrentQueryExecutor
  (+ PowerRunExecutor) — config-driven, reachable only through the stubbed
  run_concurrent_streams paths below.
- UNUSED EXTERNALLY: benchbox/core/tpc_patterns.py:StreamExecutor — a full
  concurrent framework instantiated only inside its own module; external
  consumers import only generate_official_benchmark_audit_trail from it.
- NON-EXECUTING STUB: benchbox/core/tpch/streams.py:TPCHStreamRunner.run_stream
  (~lines 431-454) counts `-- Query` comment lines and marks every query
  successful WITHOUT executing SQL. Any path through
  run_concurrent_streams (tpch/streams.py, and the parallel
  tpcds/benchmark/runner.py:988-1011 path) measures nothing real. A test or
  caller that reaches this reports fake success.

Fix: make StreamRunner the single throughput executor; delete or clearly
quarantine the dead/unused executors; and either remove the non-executing
stub or make it raise NotImplementedError so it cannot silently report fake
success.

approach:
Work in phases, each independently testable and committable:

Phase 1 (w1-w2): Extract shared infrastructure for the primitives fork. These are the
highest-value targets with byte-for-byte identical code. Create new shared modules,
update imports, verify with existing tests.

Phase 2 (w3-w5): Consolidate benchmark base class methods and query infrastructure.
These are lower-risk refactors touching well-tested code paths.

Phase 3 (w6-w8): Minor utility extraction, ignore-list configuration, and threshold
adjustment. This is the cleanup phase.

For each consolidation:
1. Read both/all copies side-by-side to confirm true equivalence
2. Create the shared module with the canonical implementation
3. Update all call sites to use the shared version
4. Run targeted tests for affected modules
5. Run make duplicate-check-verbose to confirm line count drop
6. Commit

description:
21 platform adapters each have a _build_<platform>_config function that performs
the same 4-step operation: (1) instantiate CredentialManager, (2) merge
options/saved_creds/explicit_options/overrides, (3) extract fields into a dict,
(4) return DatabaseConfig(**config_dict).

benchbox/platforms/base/config_utils.py already contains build_platform_config()
implementing this exact pattern, but only 3 of 21 platforms use it
(velox.py:761, lakesail.py:811, azure_synapse.py:1300).

The credential merge order bug (commit d41c56980) required patching 18 separate
files because each had its own inline copy. If the builders used the shared helper,
the same fix would have been one edit.

Platforms are divided into four groups based on consolidation difficulty:

  Group A (5 platforms) - clean drop-in, no complications:
    databend, clickhouse_cloud, spark, snowflake, databricks

  Group B (4 platforms) - minor audit needed before consolidating:
    trino, presto, starburst (conditional schema key), firebolt (deployment_mode sourcing)

  Group C (3 platforms) - need base_options parameter added to helper:
    pg_duckdb, pg_mooncake, timescaledb (pre-seed merged_options with {"schema": "public"})

  Group D (6 platforms) - investigation gate required before any code:
    singlestore, doris, starrocks (os.environ fallbacks + int() coercions)
    athena (dual-source region: region or aws_region)
    bigquery (multi-step staging_root derivation from default_output_location)
    redshift (admin_database="dev" hardcoded default, conditional database handling)

Groups C and D must complete investigation work units before any consolidation
is attempted. The investigation may conclude that some Group D platforms should
stay inline - that outcome is acceptable if properly documented.
title: Consolidate platform config builders to use shared build_platform_config helper

work.notes:
Three specific questions to answer before w4 can proceed:

Q1: trino/presto/starburst conditional schema
  Current code: `if "schema" in overrides and overrides["schema"]: config_dict["schema"] = ...`
  build_platform_config would emit schema=None when not set.
  Action: grep each adapter's __init__ and from_config() for schema access patterns.
    - config.get("schema") → safe (None is handled)
    - config["schema"] → NOT safe (KeyError if key absent, or TypeError if None used as schema)
  Read: benchbox/platforms/trino.py TrinoPlatform.from_config()
        benchbox/platforms/presto.py PrestoPlatform.from_config()
        benchbox/platforms/starburst.py StarburstPlatform.from_config()
  If all three use config.get("schema"), include "schema" in platform_fields (emitting None is safe).
  If any uses config["schema"], exclude "schema" from platform_fields and note it in w4.

Q2: databricks missing benchmark/scale_factor/tuning_config
  build_platform_config always adds these three fields (from overrides).
  Current _build_databricks_config omits them - they'd be added as None.
  Action: Check DatabaseConfig Pydantic model for Optional annotations on these fields.
  Read: benchbox/core/schemas.py DatabaseConfig definition.
  If Optional, adding them as None is safe → databricks can go in Group A (w3).
  If required/non-Optional, databricks needs special handling in w4.

Q3: firebolt deployment_mode sourcing
  Current: "deployment_mode": overrides.get("deployment_mode") or options.get("deployment_mode")
  With helper: merged_options.get("deployment_mode") - since overrides is merged last, this
  should be equivalent. Verify by tracing: if deployment_mode is in overrides, it appears in
  merged_options (overrides.update last). If it's only in options, it also appears in merged_options.
  Confirm there's no case where options.get() would find it but merged_options.get() wouldn't.

Record findings as annotations in w4 notes before marking w1 done.

work.notes:
These builders use os.environ.get() and int() coercions for field defaults:
  singlestore: SINGLESTORE_HOST, SINGLESTORE_PORT, SINGLESTORE_USER, SINGLESTORE_PASSWORD
  doris:       DORIS_HOST, DORIS_PORT (int), DORIS_HTTP_PORT (int), DORIS_BE_HTTP_PORT (int),
               DORIS_USER/DORIS_USERNAME, DORIS_PASSWORD, DORIS_DATABASE
  starrocks:   STARROCKS_HOST, STARROCKS_PORT (int), STARROCKS_USER, STARROCKS_PASSWORD,
               STARROCKS_DATABASE, STARROCKS_HTTP_PORT (int)

Investigation questions:
1. Are these platforms' PlatformOptionSpec defaults currently hardcoded strings
   (e.g., default="localhost") or do they already read from env vars?
   Read: benchbox/platforms/__init__.py option spec registrations for singlestore, doris, starrocks
2. Could PlatformOptionSpec.default be changed to a callable or env-var-aware value?
   Or could the default= argument read os.environ at registration time?
   Read: benchbox/cli/platform_hooks.py PlatformOptionSpec definition
3. Are there existing unit tests that mock the env vars and assert specific values?
   These tests constrain how safe the migration is.
4. The int() coercions in doris/starrocks (e.g., int(merged_options.get("port") or "9030")):
   are these needed because the registry/options dict stores port as a string?
   If so, this is a type-coercion concern separate from the env-var question.

Decision framework:
- If env-var fallbacks CAN move to registry defaults cleanly: add to w9 as consolidation candidates
- If env-var fallbacks require PlatformOptionSpec changes that affect other platforms: too risky, leave inline
- If int() coercions are needed because of string→int type conversion: note in w9 as a blocker
  (build_platform_config would return string where adapter expects int - a silent type bug)

w7 FINDINGS:
  - PlatformOptionSpec.default is a static value. PlatformHookRegistry.get_default_options() returns that raw value
    unchanged; there is no callable/env-aware default hook today.
  - Reading os.environ at registration time would only snapshot the environment once, but the existing tests patch env vars
    around builder/direct-construction calls after import. That means moving env fallbacks into today's registry mechanism
    would break current behavior and tests.
  - Existing tests explicitly lock in env-var resolution:
    singlestore -> tests/unit/platforms/test_singlestore_adapter.py
    doris       -> tests/unit/platforms/test_doris_adapter.py
    starrocks   -> tests/unit/platforms/test_starrocks_adapter.py
  - int() coercions are load-bearing:
    singlestore coerces port
    doris coerces port/http_port/be_http_port
    starrocks coerces port/http_port

Verdicts:
  - singlestore: Can consolidate: NO. Reason: builder-level env fallback and port coercion are runtime behaviors, not static defaults.
  - doris: Can consolidate: NO. Reason: env fallback plus multi-port int coercion are load-bearing and covered by tests.
  - starrocks: Can consolidate: NO. Reason: env fallback plus int coercion for FE/HTTP ports are load-bearing and covered by tests.
work.summary: Investigate Group D env-var platforms (singlestore, doris, starrocks) - can env-var fallbacks move to registered defaults?

approach:
The smart field-count detection from FormatConverter._needs_trailing_dummy_column() is the
canonical approach: read the first non-empty line, split by delimiter, compare field count
to expected column count. This correctly handles both TPC-H files (which have trailing |)
and TPC-DS files like time_dim.dat (which do not). Move this logic to file_format.py as
the single source of truth, then update all 13 call sites to use it. For SQL adapters,
only standardize the column name -- the unconditional add-then-drop pattern is safe there.
description:
TPC benchmark data files (.tbl/.dat) use | as a field terminator (not separator),
creating an extra empty field when split. This is currently handled in 13+ locations
across 9 files using 3 different detection approaches and 3 different dummy column
names (_trailing_, _trailing_delimiter, _trailing_ignore). The inconsistency caused
regressions (e.g., time_dim.dat conversion failure where the naive "ends with |"
check incorrectly added a dummy column).

Approach: Extract the smart field-count detection logic into benchbox/utils/file_format.py
as a shared utility. Update all 13 locations to use the shared constant and, where
appropriate, the shared detection function. Remove has_trailing_delimiter from
FileFormatInfo (it's always False -- dead code).
preserves: All existing TPC-H and TPC-DS data loading must continue to work identically
Compressed file support in trailing delimiter detection (via CompressionManager)
DuckDB SQL EXCLUDE pattern and PyArrow include_columns filtering remain unconditional (they handle both with/without trailing delimiter)
Schema-less fallback for has_trailing_delimiter when column_names is None
title: Consolidate trailing delimiter handling into shared utility

description:
The CLI currently has two separate tuning command structures that should be unified:

Current (inconsistent):
- `benchbox create-sample-tuning --platform duckdb` (top-level, 20 chars)
- `benchbox df-tuning create-sample --platform polars` (nested group)
- `benchbox df-tuning validate config.yaml`
- `benchbox df-tuning show-defaults --platform polars`

Proposed (unified):
- `benchbox tuning init --platform duckdb` (SQL platforms)
- `benchbox tuning init --platform polars --mode dataframe` (DataFrame platforms)
- `benchbox tuning validate config.yaml --platform polars`
- `benchbox tuning defaults --platform polars`

This consolidation improves discoverability, reduces cognitive load, and provides
a consistent interface for all tuning-related operations.
title: Consolidate tuning commands under unified `tuning` group

description:
An adversarial falsification review of the value-digest oracle (PR #867,
reviewed on develop @ e4a04484 — confirmed an ancestor of origin/develop, all
18 stored digests reproduced by running `make test-correctness-gate` on the
pinned DuckDB 1.3.2) confirmed the headline win is REAL: a wrong-but-same-
cardinality TPC-H answer at SF=1 now turns the gate RED, the check is CI-wired
as a hard blocker (.github/workflows/pr.yml correctness-gate job; the aggregator
requires CORRECTNESS_RESULT == success for any code PR), and #867's CI ran it
green for ~11.5 min (not skipped). The strict arming
(`digest_evaluated == digest_reference_count`) was reproduced locally to require
all 18 digests to evaluate and match, so a missing digest disarms RED not green.

The same review reproduced four residual fidelity gaps that the AI-implemented,
AI-reviewed, AI-merged chain did not surface. None is a correctness regression;
each narrows what "value-level" actually proves and should be either fixed or
honestly documented:

- PRECISION FLOOR IS ABSOLUTE, NOT RELATIVE (MEDIUM). The digest normalizes real
  numbers with `f"{value:.4f}"` (benchbox/core/results/result_digest.py
  _format_real, _DIGEST_FLOAT_PRECISION=4). Reproduced: an error <5e-5 ABSOLUTE
  in any single cell is invisible regardless of column magnitude
  (delta=4.9e-5 -> identical digest; 5.0e-5 -> differs). On large-magnitude
  columns (TPC-H revenue ~1e10) 5e-5 absolute is ~1e-15 relative — effectively
  perfect. But on small-magnitude averaged ratio columns it is coarse: Q1's
  `avg_disc` is ~0.049985 (a float), so a sub-5e-5-absolute (~0.1% relative)
  aggregate/rounding bug on that column survives the gate
  (compute_result_digest([(0.05,)]) == compute_result_digest([(0.05004,)])).

- DIGEST CONFLATES VALUE WITH TYPE REPRESENTATION (LOW). _normalize_cell renders
  int exactly ("1478493") but float/Decimal at fixed precision
  ("37734107.0000"). The SAME numeric value with a different Python type hashes
  DIFFERENTLY. Stable today on pinned DuckDB 1.3.2, but it means the digest is a
  value+type-rendering digest, and it is the blocker for any cross-engine reuse.

- EMISSION IS ENGINE-WIDE BUT THE ORACLE IS DUCKDB-ONLY (LOW). compute_result_digest
  is called both in benchbox/platforms/duckdb.py:999 AND in the shared DBAPI
  helper benchbox/platforms/base/sql_execution.py:80 (sqlite/postgres/datafusion/
  ...). It is harmless today — `_stored_value_digest` only returns a reference for
  tpch SF=1, so a non-DuckDB digest is computed-but-never-compared — but combined
  with the type-sensitivity above it is a latent trap for the cross-engine
  independence work below, and it sits outside the original TODO's scope_limit
  (benchbox/platforms/) by the implementer's own admission.

- THE VALUE REFERENCE IS A SELF-SNAPSHOT, NOT AN INDEPENDENT ORACLE, AND HAS NO
  AUTOMATED REGENERATION (MEDIUM). The 18 reference digests in
  benchbox/core/expected_results/reference_digests/tpch_value_digests_sf1.json
  were produced by running benchbox-on-DuckDB-1.3.2 and HAND-COPYING the emitted
  digests (provenance note says exactly this; no script/make target writes the
  file — grep confirms only loader.py reads it). So the oracle detects CHANGE
  from the frozen baseline (a genuine regression tripwire) but NOT correctness vs
  an authority outside benchbox: a conceptual value bug present at freeze time is
  enshrined, never caught. This is the same hand-curated-answer-key fragility the
  effort claimed to avoid, one level down. There is also no one-button
  regeneration, so a legitimate DuckDB bump means a manual re-copy.

- THE NONE-SAFE SORT PATH IS UNTESTED BY THE GATE (LOW). calculate_checksum sorts
  rows by the None-safe `_row_sort_key`. Reproduced: 0 of the 18 SF=1 gate result
  sets contain a NULL or mixed-type column, so for the gate's inputs the None-safe
  surrogate is order-identical to a plain sort and its NULL/mixed-type branch
  never fires in the gate. (Note: the None-safe sort PREDATES #867 — it existed at
  parent ce999bd7 — so #867 only promoted the helper to module level; this is a
  coverage gap, not a #867 regression.)

This item fixes or honestly documents each gap. It is the fidelity complement to
the value axis shipped in bounded-correctness-gate-value-oracle (#867, DONE); it
does NOT re-do the digest emission, the strict arming, or the row-count work.
preserves: The #867 value axis is unchanged: digest emission behind BENCHBOX_EMIT_RESULT_DIGEST, the strict arming (digest_evaluated == digest_reference_count), and the additive row-count check keep working exactly as today.
The TPC-Havoc gates that share calculate_checksum stay green — reuse the one digest definition, never fork it.
`benchbox run` default behavior, payload shape, and cost stay unchanged when the digest flag is unset (digest emission stays gate-only).
`make test-correctness-gate` stays green on a correct tree and on the required PR path after any normalization change (regenerate the reference in the same change).

_project/DONE/main/planning/bounded-correctness-gate-value-oracle.yaml — the effort this hardens; w3 already proved sensitivity to gross mutations, w1 chose absolute rounding as a non-gating open question. This item revisits that choice with the reproduced floor quantified.

description:
PR #756 fixed three TPC-Havoc SQL variants where a correlated subquery's
UNQUALIFIED correlation column silently bound to the INNER alias instead of
the outer table, degenerating the intended correlation into an uncorrelated
scan. That sweep covered the SQL variant_sets only, by hand. Two reachable
surfaces were never checked, and the manual sweep is not a durable guard.

Scope of this audit:

1. TPC-Havoc DataFrame variants (benchbox/core/tpchavoc/dataframe_queries/).
   The DataFrame implementations of the correlated queries (Q2 min-cost,
   Q11 threshold, Q17 per-part avg, Q20, Q21, Q22) must encode the SAME outer
   correlation as the canonical query. DataFrame code does not "self-bind" the
   same way, but the equivalent mistake - joining/filtering on the inner frame
   instead of the outer row - is possible and equally silent.

   Review evidence (PR #770): the DataFrame variants are INDEPENDENT designs,
   not mirrors of the SQL variants - e.g. DataFrame q9_v10 is an algebraic
   reformulation while SQL q9_v10 had nation-bucketing/clamping defects. None
   of the 24 SQL-side divergences PR #770 fixed has a mirrored DataFrame
   analog, but the same variant ID means a DIFFERENT transformation per
   surface, so the SQL equivalence gate proves nothing about this surface.

   NOTE: broad DataFrame result-equivalence vs canonical TPC-H is now owned by
   its own work item, tpchavoc-dataframe-variant-equivalence-gate. THIS audit's
   DataFrame scope is the narrower, targeted self-binding / inner-frame-
   correlation check on the correlated queries (Q2, Q11, Q17, Q20, Q21, Q22);
   run it alongside, or fold it into, that gate rather than duplicating the
   harness.

2. Other SQL benchmarks with correlated subqueries: TPC-DS, SSB, join-order,
   read-primitives (subquery category), and write-primitives
   (update_with_subquery). Grep evidence already shows correlated patterns and
   a "self-join pattern" comment in tpcds/dataframe_queries. Apply the same
   qualify-the-outer-correlation audit.

3. A DURABLE detector so this class cannot silently reappear: a static check
   (sqlglot-backed) that flags a correlated subquery whose correlation
   predicate has an unqualified column also present in an inner aliased
   relation. A binder-level check is hard to make exact, so a conservative
   lint that surfaces candidates for human confirmation is acceptable.

Provenance question worth answering during the audit: how were these variants
authored? If LLM-generated or mechanically transformed, self-binding is likely
a SYSTEMATIC generation artifact, implying more instances and a generator that
needs a correctness contract rather than per-instance patches.
preserves: Each variant keeps its declared structural identity; only the correlation binding is corrected.
Existing DataFrame and SQL benchmark results that are already correct are unchanged.

approach:
Follow existing test patterns in tests/unit/{cli,core,tpcdi,platforms} and
prefer fast unit tests with mocks over integration tests. Implement coverage
lift in waves ordered by fastest impact (near-50% quick wins first, then
medium-effort modules, then large modules requiring 5-10 tests each, then
CLI, then TPC-DI). Recompute and checkpoint coverage after each wave using
coverage.json plus the per-file checker to keep progress measurable.

Naming convention: new files are named test_{module}_coverage.py when an
existing test file covers the same source module. All tests marked
@pytest.mark.fast and @pytest.mark.unit, pure mocks only.

Within each phase, batches are independent and can be parallelized via
Task agents. Each batch creates all its test files, then runs verification
before proceeding to the next phase.

   boosts measured coverage to ~76.3%. Gap after omit: 3,928 lines.

     commands, DF benchmark_suite, runner, base.py, utils)

Anti-coverage-theater principles:
- Every test must call a function and assert on specific output values
- Use real engines (DuckDB, Polars, DataFusion) not mocks where possible
- Test behavior not implementation - if the function changes how it works but
  produces the same result, the test should still pass
- No import-only tests, no `assert result is not None`, no `assert True`
- Cloud platform tests assert on generated SQL strings, not mock.called
- Mark genuinely untestable code for exclusion rather than writing useless tests

description:
PR #1332 fixed Windows CRLF trailing-delimiter misdetection by routing benchbox/core/data_organization/sorting.py::_source_has_trailing_delimiter through the shared helper benchbox/utils/file_format.py::has_trailing_delimiter. The fix is correct, but it is correct for an IMPLICIT reason: has_trailing_delimiter reads via _check_first_nonempty_line, which opens 'rt' (and mode='rt' for the compressed branch), so Python universal-newlines translates 
 to 
 before either checker runs. Both checkers then rstrip('
') only. Nothing pins that. If any read path is ever switched to binary for throughput - plausible for multi-GB TBL files - CRLF stops being normalized, the field count or the ends-with check shifts, and the original Windows bug returns silently. Second, narrower point: the merged CRLF tests only feed trailing-delimiter input. _write_tbl_crlf() has no clean variant, so of the four cells in (LF|CRLF) x (clean|trailing-delimiter), only clean-CRLF is unexercised end-to-end. Note the LF clean case IS covered by test_reads_normalized_tbl_with_no_trailing_delimiter, so a checker hardcoded to True would already be caught - this is coverage symmetry and invariant pinning, not a live defect. Also note has_trailing_delimiter's column_names=None fallback (ends-with check) is reachable but unused by all 10 platform callers, which all pass column names; it deserves the same CRLF assertion.

macOS/Linux fast lane stays green and the fast-lane test cap is not exceeded

Honest note on what this case does and does not catch: under a simulated binary-read regression it PASSES, because a failed probe returns False and clean input needs no synthetic column. Points at the test that enforces it. The enforcement is behavioural, not a source grep: simulating the regression by switching the uncompressed read to 'rb' fails 6 of the 10 framing tests and 2 of the 3 writer CRLF tests. description:
Follow-up spun out of PR #878 (review-sweep pass 3) and the order-aware
comparator landed in #872. It records a known, accepted limitation in the
shared cross-surface SQL<->DataFrame validator so it is tracked rather than
forgotten.

`ResultValidator.validate_results_exact(order_aware=True, tie_aware=True)`
(benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py, `_validate_order_aware`) partitions the
returned rows into consecutive same-order-key groups and, for the FINAL group
under a trailing `LIMIT`, tolerates a membership difference as an
equally-valid tie pick across the LIMIT cutoff. #878 tightened that acceptance
to require a genuine tie of `len(orig_rows) >= 2` rows sharing the final key,
so a deterministic single-row final-group difference is CAUGHT instead of
masked.

Codex review on #878 (discussion r3462372977) correctly observed the residual
edge: when a `LIMIT` cuts mid-tie, a legitimate boundary tie can leave exactly
ONE of the tied rows visible (keys `10, 5a, 5b` with `LIMIT 2` -> `[10, 5]`).
Two surfaces picking different `5` rows is valid SQL, but the `>= 2` guard now
flags it as a mismatch.

The root cause is fundamental: from the TRUNCATED result alone, a one-visible-
row boundary tie and a genuine unique-final-key value change (e.g.
`(2,"good")` vs `(2,"bad")`) are structurally identical - same final order
key, differing non-key column, a single row in the group. The comparator
cannot distinguish them without signal from outside the LIMIT.

Accepted tradeoff (decided on #878): land the `>= 2` guard as-is. Its failure
mode is a LOUD false positive (a gate fails when it should not), which is
recoverable and safer than the prior behavior (#872 accepted ALL final-group
differences, silently MASKING real single-row value bugs). All five enforced
cross-surface gates currently pass (0 unclassified divergent), so the false
positive is latent and data-dependent, not an active breakage.

title: Cross-surface comparator: make the final-tie-group guard boundary-aware (one-visible-row LIMIT ties)

work.notes:
The comparator needs signal it does not have today to tell a truncated
boundary tie from a genuine deterministic last row. Candidate approaches,
to be evaluated for cost vs. value:
  - Have the cross-surface gate run each trailing-LIMIT query at `LIMIT N+1`
    (or unbounded) to learn whether the final order key is genuinely tied
    beyond the cutoff, and pass that fact into validate_results_exact so a
    single-visible-row final group can be accepted ONLY when the key is
    actually tied past the LIMIT.
  - Or thread the resolved `ORDER BY` / `LIMIT` structure plus a
    tie-multiplicity hint from the SQL surface into the comparator.
Keep the change ADDITIVE: the TPC-Havoc strict path (no order_aware/
tie_aware) must stay byte-identical, and the default must remain catching
single-row value bugs. Add a regression test for the keys `10,5,5`
`LIMIT 2` boundary-tie case (currently a false positive) alongside the
existing `(2,"good")` vs `(2,"bad")` true-positive case.

RESOLVED: took the first approach (LIMIT N+1 probe). The cross-surface gate
now re-runs each trailing-LIMIT order-aware query one row wider
(`cross_surface._bump_trailing_limit` / `_final_key_tied_beyond_limit`) and
threads `final_key_tied_beyond_limit` into
`ResultValidator.validate_results_exact`. `_validate_order_aware` accepts a
single-visible-row final tie group ONLY when that probe confirms the final
order key recurs past the cutoff; otherwise the lone row is treated as a
deterministic last row and a value change there is still CAUGHT. The same
change also lands #878's `len(orig_rows) >= 2` tightening of the order-aware
final-group accept (#878 was still open against develop), so a >= 2-row
visible tie remains an accepted boundary swap. ADDITIVE: callers that pass
neither `order_aware` nor `tie_aware` (the TPC-Havoc strict path) are
untouched - verified 220/220 variant and 440/440 DataFrame equivalence, and
all five enforced cross-surface gates green (0 unclassified divergent). The
probe runs once per query (memoized across backends). Regression tests:
tests/integration/test_validator_order_aware.py (one-visible-row tie accepted
with the probe, caught without; the `(2,"good")` vs `(2,"bad")` unique-key
bug still raises) and tests/unit/core/equivalence/test_cross_surface.py
(`_bump_trailing_limit`, `_final_key_tied_beyond_limit`, and the end-to-end
gate accept/catch cases).

description:
Follow-up spun out of PR #886 (the boundary-tie probe, w1 of
cross-surface-comparator-boundary-tie-soundness) and its self-review. It records
a known, accepted residual limitation in the order-aware tie-aware validator so
it is tracked rather than forgotten.

`ResultValidator._validate_order_aware` accepts a differing FINAL tie group under
a trailing `LIMIT` when:

    if i == last_index and tie_aware and (len(orig_rows) >= 2 or final_key_tied_beyond_limit):
        continue

The `len(orig_rows) >= 2` branch (landed by #878, preserved by #886) accepts a
membership difference in any final group that has >= 2 visible rows sharing the
order key - WITHOUT evidence that the `LIMIT` actually truncated that tie. That
is unsound for a COMPLETE, non-truncated final tie group: e.g.
`... ORDER BY a DESC LIMIT 10` over a table with exactly 10 rows whose last two
rows tie at `a`. There is no truncation, so both surfaces should return the SAME
two tied rows; a membership difference like `[(5,'a'),(5,'b')]` vs
`[(5,'a'),(5,'c')]` is a genuine value bug, yet the `>= 2` branch accepts it as a
"boundary swap" and the gate goes silently green.

#886's boundary-tie probe (`final_key_tied_beyond_limit`) is the exact signal
needed to distinguish a truncated tie from a complete one, but #886 scoped it to
the single-visible-row case only (its stated charter). For the >= 2 case the
probe is deliberately NOT consulted, and `cross_surface._final_key_tied_beyond_limit`
even short-circuits (returns False, skipping the extra query) whenever the
reference's final group already spans >= 2 rows - so today the >= 2 branch has no
truncation evidence at all.

Accepted tradeoff (decided on #886): the failure mode is a MASKED bug (a false
negative) confined to a narrow shape - a complete, non-truncated, multi-row final
tie group whose members differ between surfaces. All six enforced cross-surface
gates currently pass with 0 unclassified divergent, so this is latent and
data-dependent, not an active breakage. It is documented in-code at the guard
site. Closing it is a deliberate, separately-scoped change (below), not a
drive-by, because it alters the #872/#878 established semantics and forces a
test + cost change.

Priority raised Low -> Medium (2026-06-28, holistic-review remediation): for a
benchmark tool, false confidence in a correctness gate is the worst outcome, so a
documented masked-value-bug path in the comparator warrants Medium and should be
closed before the next published cross-platform comparison claim. (The fix is
already scoped in w1; this is the only change to this item.)
preserves: All enforced cross-surface gates remain green with 0 unclassified divergences after the tighter final-tie check.
TPC-Havoc strict validation behavior is byte-identical when order_aware/tie_aware is disabled.
The fix remains targeted to boundary-tie soundness; it does not rewrite queries or compare untruncated result sets.
Truncated ORDER BY/LIMIT boundary swaps remain accepted only when the probe proves the final key extends past the LIMIT.

description:
Cross-surface gates carry classified known_divergences (e.g. ClickBench Q18's
order-less LIMIT, _H2ODB_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES). These entries are reported but do
NOT fail the gate when they no longer reproduce. That asymmetry lets a stale
exception linger: once a known divergence is silently resolved (by a loader fix,
a query change, or a comparator improvement), the baseline entry stays, and a
FUTURE regression on that same cell would be masked as "known" instead of caught.

Add baseline hygiene: a known-divergence entry whose cell now matches must either
fail the gate or force a baseline update (an --update-baseline discipline), so the
exception list cannot drift ahead of reality. This mirrors the empty-baseline,
fail-on-divergence discipline the TPC-Havoc gates already enforce, extended to the
"resolved exception" direction.

description:
An adversarial review of the cross-surface SQL<->DataFrame equivalence campaign
(PRs #826-#848 on develop) reproduced every finding by running the gates and
found the oracle is real but narrow, oversold, and partly vacuous. This TODO
addresses ALL of those findings. The committed evidence the review draws on
lives in _project/analysis/clickbench-cross-surface-divergences.md,
_project/analysis/joinorder-synthetic-cross-surface-divergences.md, and
_project/analysis/oracle-coverage-map.md; reproduce any cell with
`make <benchmark>-cross-surface-equivalence-report`.

The headline problem: PR #848 concluded "ClickBench has ~no genuine DataFrame
logic bugs" and triaged 27 divergences as "tie-ambiguous top-N." That is false.
Re-running the gate shows at least three REAL, deterministic DataFrame bugs that
#848 rationalized away as ties:
  - Q6_pandas: wrong COUNT(DISTINCT SearchPhrase) (18 SQL vs 17 pandas), a
    scalar with NO ORDER BY and NO LIMIT - a tie is impossible. Root cause: the
    DataFrame loader maps empty-string -> None and pandas .nunique() drops the
    null. SearchPhrase has 74,724 empty strings / 0 nulls.
  - Q17_pandas / Q18_pandas: wrong GROUP BY - pandas default groupby(dropna=True)
    silently drops ~74k null-key rows, so the query runs over ~25% of the data.
    The count multiset differs, which a boundary tie cannot cause.
  - Q24 / Q17 col-1 "" vs None: the SAME root cause #848 deferred as a cosmetic
    "dtype" issue. It is not cosmetic - it changes COUNT(DISTINCT) and GROUP BY
    membership.

Compounding issues the review proved by reproduction:
  - NON-DETERMINISM: the ClickBench gate returned 27 -> 25 -> 26 divergent cells
    across three identical runs, with per-query values changing run to run. The
    generated DATA is byte-identical across runs (verified by md5), so the wobble
    is ENGINE tie-ordering (DuckDB/Polars thread parallelism under
    LIMIT-without-total-ORDER), NOT data. random.seed(42) cannot fix it, and a
    known_divergences baseline is therefore un-pinnable.
  - ORDER-BY BLINDNESS: ResultValidator.validate_results_exact sorts FULL ROWS
    before comparing (tpchavoc/validation.py:54-79), so ORDER BY is never checked
    except via which rows survive LIMIT. A reversed ORDER BY passes silently;
    equally-valid tie picks are flagged as false divergences; a column mixing
    None and non-None crashes Python sorted() and is mislabeled "error:".
  - VACUOUS CELLS: at SF=0.1, 6 of 13 SSB queries (Q2.1-2.3, Q3.3, Q3.4, Q4.3)
    return ZERO rows on both surfaces, so 12 of 26 SSB cells pass empty-vs-empty
    while the report counts them as "compared". The build guards empty TABLES
    (cross_surface.py:261) but not empty RESULTS.
  - FALSE INDEPENDENCE: SSB and ~40/43 ClickBench DataFrame queries are GENERATED
    from a compact DSL spec, and BOTH "independent backends" are emitted from the
    SAME spec row - so a spec-level logic error appears identically on both, and
    the docs' "two independent implementations" claim (cross_surface.py:3-6,
    dataframe_surface.py:48-50) is false for them. CoffeeShop (hand-written) is
    the genuine exception.
  - LOADER BYPASS: the gate materializes contexts straight from typed DuckDB
    Arrow (dataframe_surface.py:74-125), never through DataFrameDataLoader, so a
    green gate proves NOTHING about the production CSV->parquet loader's dtype
    fidelity (leading-zero VARCHAR->int, empty->null). #847 "deferred dtype" is
    docs-only and the bug is still live; the #846 DDL parser is a naive
    whitespace tokenizer that breaks on DECIMAL(p, s), quoted names, and
    multi-word types.
  - GOVERNANCE: STAGED gates are not run in CI and have no promotion forcing
    function; "guarded" in the coverage map means "registered in the GATES dict",
    not "verified green"; the "12 gateable" applicability headline counts 6
    benchmarks whose SQL<->DF id mapping was never verified (the team's own TODO
    says "do NOT guess").
preserves: All TPC-Havoc SQL and DataFrame equivalence gates stay green with empty baselines and byte-identical output - the comparator change (w2) is additive, never a fork.
SSB and CoffeeShop enforced gates stay green throughout (CoffeeShop is the reference 'good' gate).
The bounded one-cell-per-benchmark cost model is preserved; no full platform matrix in routine PRs.

title: Remediate the cross-surface equivalence oracle: fix the bugs it found-and-dismissed, make it deterministic, order-aware, non-vacuous, and honest

work.notes:
The DataFrame surface conflates SQL '' with None, which changes results, not
just presentation. Two layers must be decided and fixed:

ROOT FIX (preferred) - loader fidelity: a CSV empty field in a declared
string/VARCHAR/TEXT column must materialize as '' (matching DuckDB/SQL), not
Arrow null. Today convert_csv_to_parquet passes strings_can_be_null=True
(data_loader.py:329) and pandas read_csv uses default na_values, so empties
become null on the production path; the gate path (DuckDB->Arrow) keeps ''.
Decide the canonical contract (recommend: declared-string empties stay '',
matching the SQL reference and the upstream ClickBench data) and enforce it on
BOTH load paths. This is the true fix and also resolves Q24/Q17-col1.

SYMPTOM FIX (only if the loader contract cannot be '' for a real reason):
make the generated factories null-correct - groupby(..., dropna=False) in
_make_group_pandas (clickbench queries.py:291; mirror in ssb) and a
null-aware distinct count instead of bare pandas .nunique() (queries.py:206/
285). But note this only patches generated factories; hand-written impls and
future benchmarks would still be exposed - which is why the loader fix is
preferred.

Whichever path: verify against the REAL DataFrame run (dataframe_runner /
benchmark_mixin), not the gate only - the gate bypasses the loader (see w6),
so a gate-only fix would be invisible to production.
work.summary: Fix the empty-string/null conflation in the DataFrame load path (C1: Q6, Q17, Q18, Q24 are REAL bugs)

work.notes:
The campaign measured only that the gates PASS (specificity); it never measured
whether they CATCH a seeded bug (sensitivity). Add a mutation-test harness that,
per gated benchmark, injects a known DataFrame error and asserts the gate goes
RED:
  - flip a filter comparator (< -> <=),
  - drop a GROUP BY key,
  - reverse a sort direction (this is the BS2 regression guard),
  - drop a join.
For each mutation that the gate does NOT catch, document why (e.g. an empty-
result query from BS3, or an order-only change the comparator ignores) and feed
it back into w2/w4. This closes the central unanswered question: is the oracle
strong enough to find logic bugs, or did it find "no bugs" because it is too
weak/vacuous?
work.summary: Mutation-test the oracle to measure SENSITIVITY, not just specificity (C2 - the central question)

work.notes:
validate_results_exact (validation.py:54-79) sorts full rows then compares
positionally, so it is simultaneously BLIND to real ORDER BY bugs (a reversed
order passes - DEMO1) and NOISY on legitimate ties (two equally-valid tie
picks fail - DEMO2), and it crashes on a column mixing None with non-None
because Python sorted() cannot order None vs int (DEMO3), which
find_surface_divergences (dataframe_surface.py:234) then mislabels as
"error:" instead of a clean result.

Add an ORDER-AWARE comparison mode for queries that declare an ORDER BY:
  - compare the ordered prefix up to the first tie group exactly (this
    restores ORDER BY signal), then
  - treat the rows sharing the boundary order-key as a MULTISET (this removes
    the tie noise that #848 mistook for the whole story).
For queries with no ORDER BY, keep multiset/set comparison.
Fix the sort key to place None deterministically (e.g. sort on a (is_none,
value) surrogate) so a NULL-bearing column never raises, and so a genuine
None-vs-value difference is reported as a MISMATCH, not an "error:".

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: this comparator is shared with the TPC-Havoc SQL and
DataFrame gates, which rely on its current semantics and run with empty
baselines. The order/tie-awareness must be additive (opt-in per query/gate)
and MUST keep all TPC-Havoc gates byte-identical-green. Do NOT fork the
validator for cross-surface only; extend it.
work.summary: Make the comparator order-aware and tie-aware; fix the None/NaN sort crash (BS2)

work.notes:
The wobble is engine tie-ordering, not data. Pin it at the gate:
  - run the gate's DuckDB connection and the Polars/pandas execution
    single-threaded (PRAGMA threads=1; pl.Config / POLARS_MAX_THREADS=1), AND
  - have both surfaces apply a deterministic TOTAL-ORDER tie-breaker before any
    LIMIT (append all remaining columns / a stable key to ORDER BY on the SQL
    reference and the DataFrame impls), so LIMIT truncation is reproducible.
Document explicitly (in cross_surface.py and the review's "determinism" claim)
that random.seed(42) makes the DATA reproducible but does NOT make the GATE
deterministic; the tie-breaker + single-thread is what does.
work.summary: Eliminate engine nondeterminism at the gate boundary (H1)

work.notes:
6/13 SSB queries return 0 rows at SF=0.1, so 12/26 cells pass empty-vs-empty.
Two parts:
  1. Gate hygiene: track per-query reference row count in
     find_cross_surface_divergences; in _report, count a both-empty cell as
     NON-discriminating. The gate should FAIL (or require an explicit
     classified "legitimately-empty" entry) if any gated query's reference is
     empty, and the "compared N of M cells" line must exclude vacuous cells
     from the discriminating count.
  2. Data discrimination: for SSB, choose query parameters (or a per-benchmark
     SF) so Q2.1-2.3/Q3.3/Q3.4/Q4.3 return rows at the bounded cell. Prefer
     parameterization over raising SF globally (keep PRs cheap).
Apply the same empty-result audit to coffeeshop (currently 0/11 empty - good),
clickbench, and joinorder_synthetic before promotion.
work.summary: Fail (not silently pass) on vacuous empty-vs-empty cells; make every gated query discriminating (BS3)

work.notes:
The gate's loader bypass (dataframe_surface.py:74-125 materializes from typed
DuckDB Arrow) means it cannot see production CSV->parquet dtype corruption.
  - Add a gate cell/mode that loads each gated benchmark through the REAL
    DataFrameDataLoader (CSV->parquet->read_parquet) and compares both dtypes
    and values to the SQL reference, so loader corruption is observable.
  - Carry the w1 empty-string->'' contract to the remaining raw-CSV adapters.

  - Harden schema_utils.column_name/column_sql_type (schema_utils.py:29-51):

  - Extend PYARROW_TYPE_MAP and the polars/pandas maps (data_loader.py:191-199)
    to cover TEXT, BIGINT, REAL, DOUBLE PRECISION, NUMERIC, BOOLEAN so declared
    string/numeric types are applied at conversion instead of inferred.
  - Apply declared STRING dtypes on the production load path (not just date-
    name suppression) so a leading-zero VARCHAR is not inferred as int.
Re-verify the real DataFrame benchmark run still works (this is a loader fix,

work.summary: Add a production-loader-path gate cell + harden the DDL parser and type maps (M4, L1, L2)

description: Found 2026-07-31 during the credential-egress review. ResultExporter anonymizes only the main JSON payload (exporter.py:320) and the .plans/.applied companions (:271-292). Three export surfaces never consult self.anonymize: _export_csv_detailed (exporter.py:515) writes a raw error_message column (:524) - driver error text that can carry DSNs/paths/secret assignments; _export_html_detailed (:579) renders the same data; and the .tuning.json companion (:279-284) is written with no anonymization branch at all. anti_patterns.dont: skip research units to save time

anti_patterns.why: incorrect assumptions for cloud warehouses could produce silently incorrect benchmark data

anti_patterns.dont: use CTAS for Databricks/Delta Lake
anti_patterns.instead: the correct mechanism is OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY
anti_patterns.why: CTAS creates an unmanaged table losing Delta transactional metadata

approach:
Research units (w1, w3, w5, w7, w9) can all run in parallel - they are read-only.
Implementation follows research findings. Where the answer is "unsupported / return None",
the implementation is 5-10 lines (override + docstring); prioritize getting the documentation
right over speed.

For cloud platforms that are unsupported, rely on the existing base-class skip logging from
ctas-sort-dataloader-connectivity. If gaps are discovered, capture them as a follow-up TODO
instead of modifying base adapter code in this item.

Do not attempt live platform tests - unit tests with mocked connections are sufficient
for verifying SQL generation. The verification commands use only unit tests.
description:
With the centralized apply_ctas_sort() in PlatformAdapter (ctas-sort-dataloader-connectivity),
cloud data warehouse platforms gain sorted-data loading by overriding only
_build_ctas_sort_sql(table_name, sort_columns). This item implements those overrides.

Each cloud platform has a distinct approach to physical data ordering:

Snowflake
  Snowflake already applies SORT configuration via clustering keys in apply_unified_tuning().
  A post-load CTAS (CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t AS SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY col) will
  re-materialize data sorted but without Automatic Clustering - this may be counterproductive.
  Research whether post-load CTAS sort is beneficial in addition to or instead of clustering.
  If clustering already covers the use case, _build_ctas_sort_sql should return None and the
  sort should remain in apply_unified_tuning() / apply_table_tunings().

Databricks / Delta Lake
  Delta Lake does not guarantee physical sort order on disk via CTAS ORDER BY.
  Physical ordering is achieved post-load via OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (Z-ordering) or
  OPTIMIZE ... with liquid clustering. The _build_ctas_sort_sql hook is not the right
  mechanism; instead, an apply_post_load_optimize() pattern may be needed, or the existing
  Z_ORDERING TuningType support can be extended. Return None from _build_ctas_sort_sql
  and document the correct path.

BigQuery
  BigQuery CTAS supports ORDER BY (CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM ... ORDER BY).
  However, BigQuery is distributed and row order is not preserved after DML, so a post-load
  CTAS sort does not produce persistent physical ordering. Clustering keys (via partition/
  cluster config) are the correct mechanism. Return None and document.

Redshift
  Amazon Redshift supports SORT KEYS defined at table creation. A post-load CTAS
  (CREATE TABLE t_sorted AS SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY col) followed by DROP+RENAME is
  valid but loses distribution style and sort key metadata. The correct approach is to
  define the SORT KEY in CREATE TABLE DDL. Investigate whether a VACUUM SORT ONLY t
  command (which re-sorts in-place) is a better post-load mechanism than CTAS.

ClickHouse / ClickHouse Cloud
  ClickHouse table ORDER BY is defined immutably at CREATE TABLE time (ENGINE = MergeTree
  ORDER BY col). Post-load CTAS sort is not applicable. Return None from
  _build_ctas_sort_sql and document. The correct path is to include ORDER BY in CREATE
  TABLE DDL generation - this may require a separate tuning TODO for ClickHouse DDL.

Athena
  Athena (Presto/Trino-based) queries S3 directly. CTAS (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT ...
  ORDER BY) writes new Parquet files to S3. This IS meaningful for query performance if
  the output is partitioned or sorted - but Athena's distributed nature means ORDER BY in
  CTAS only produces local file ordering, not global ordering across the dataset. Research
  whether this provides zone-map-equivalent benefits for Athena queries.

Azure Synapse
  Azure Synapse Analytics supports CTAS (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT ... ORDER BY).
  Physical ordering depends on the distribution style (hash, round-robin, replicated).
  Investigate whether CTAS ORDER BY produces useful clustering for Synapse's columnar storage.

description:
The initial CTAS sort implementation (ctas-sorted-data-loading) placed apply_ctas_sort()
directly on DuckDBAdapter and used a duck-typed hasattr() check in DataLoader. This works
for DuckDB today, but extending to additional platforms would require copy-pasting the common
lookup/validation/logging logic into each adapter.

This item centralizes apply_ctas_sort() in PlatformAdapter (base class) so that all common
behavior - case-insensitive table lookup, sort column extraction, validate_sql_identifier call,
dry-run capture_sql, success logging, and debug logging on skipped paths - lives in exactly
one place. Each platform adapter overrides only the SQL generation hook
_build_ctas_sort_sql(table_name, sort_columns) -> str | None, returning None if the platform
does not support CTAS-based sorting.

Secondary items in scope:
- Wire tuning_config into the DataLoader calls for ClickHouse, StarRocks, SQLite, and
  MotherDuck (currently they construct DataLoader without tuning_config, so CTAS sort
  never fires even when tuning is enabled).
- Rename the misleadingly named if_not_exists parameter in DuckDBDDLGenerator.generate_ctas_ddl()
  to or_replace (the parameter generates CREATE OR REPLACE, not IF NOT EXISTS).
- Remove or simplify the hasattr(adapter, "apply_ctas_sort") guard in DataLoader now that
  the method is guaranteed by the base class; keep the tuning_config None check as the opt-in.
- Add debug-level logging on all early-return paths in the base apply_ctas_sort() so
  operators can understand why sorting was skipped.

description:
With the centralized apply_ctas_sort() in PlatformAdapter (ctas-sort-dataloader-connectivity),
each local SQL platform needs only to override _build_ctas_sort_sql(table_name, sort_columns)
to gain CTAS-based sorted loading. This item implements those overrides.

Platforms in scope (MotherDuck is handled in ctas-sort-dataloader-connectivity as it shares
DuckDB's SQL syntax):

DataFusion
  DataFusion's SQL dialect supports CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT ... ORDER BY ...
  (same pattern as DuckDB). Verify the exact syntax against DataFusion's SQL reference and
  implement the hook.

PostgreSQL
  PostgreSQL does not support CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT. The closest equivalent is:
    CREATE TABLE {t}_sorted AS SELECT * FROM {t} ORDER BY col;
    DROP TABLE {t};
    ALTER TABLE {t}_sorted RENAME TO {t};
  This is safe within a single connection but requires the table to exist first (post-load).
  Wrap in a transaction to keep it atomic.

StarRocks
  StarRocks supports CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT (CTAS) with ORDER BY via its sort keys.
  However, StarRocks sorts are defined at table-creation time (via ORDER BY in CREATE TABLE),
  not on a post-load CTAS. Investigate whether a post-load CTAS reorders physical data or
  just creates an unsorted replica. If CTAS does not physically sort: return None and document
  as unsupported; the correct path for StarRocks is to define ORDER BY in CREATE TABLE DDL.

SQLite
  SQLite has no efficient physical sort; INSERT ORDER determines storage order. A CTAS pattern
  (CREATE TABLE t2 AS SELECT * FROM t1 ORDER BY col; DROP TABLE t1; ALTER TABLE t2 RENAME TO t1)
  is syntactically valid but requires recreating indexes and constraints. Given SQLite's use
  as a development/testing platform (not production), assess whether the overhead is justified.
  If not: _build_ctas_sort_sql returns None with a logged debug message.

description:
BenchBox's tuning infrastructure generates sort clauses via DuckDBDDLGenerator
(e.g., `ORDER BY L_SHIPDATE, L_ORDERKEY`), but the data loader uses INSERT INTO
statements that don't preserve sorting.

DuckDB doesn't support inline ORDER BY in CREATE TABLE. Sorted tables must be
created via CTAS patterns:
  CREATE TABLE sorted_table AS SELECT * FROM source ORDER BY col;

The current DataLoader uses INSERT INTO with VALUES, which doesn't apply sorting.
This gap was discovered during sorted data performance experiments showing 5-28x
speedups for selective queries when data is properly sorted (zone map pruning).

The fix requires modifying the data loading path to:
1. Detect when tuning config specifies sorting for a table
2. Use CTAS pattern instead of INSERT INTO for those tables
3. Support both fresh load (CTAS) and append scenarios

description:
Dask runs fail on all 22 TPC-H queries due to API incompatibilities between
Dask and Pandas. The root cause is that pandas_impl query functions call
.groupby(as_index=False) directly, which Dask doesn't support.

Errors by category:
- as_index=False not supported: Q1-Q5, Q10-Q13, Q15-Q18, Q20, Q22 (16 queries)
- .dt.year on DatetimeIndex: Q7, Q8, Q9 (3 queries)
- nunique aggregate: Q16, Q21 (2 queries)
- Lazy scalar conversion: Q6, Q14, Q19 (3 queries)

Solution: Created UnifiedPandasFrame wrapper (following Expression family pattern)
that intercepts DataFrame operations and routes to adapter for platform-specific
handling. Also made minor query adaptations to handle lazy scalar computations.
title: Fix Dask DataFrame Platform Compatibility

description:
dask-df pre-emptively SKIPPED TPC-H Q10 in the default local envelope via a
resource guard (benchbox/platforms/dataframe/dask_df.py:
_RESOURCE_ENVELOPE_SKIP_QUERY_IDS = {"Q10"}, _guarded_resource_query_diagnostic,
_collect_skip_query_ids override). The guard's premise was that Q10's
Pandas-family Dask graph terminates the parent process with exit 137 (OOM) on
local runs.

Investigation on 2026-05-29/30 (during uat-dask-stability-under-sweep) showed
the guard was OBSOLETE:

  raises NotImplementedError ("The legacy implementation is no longer
  supported"). The optimizer auto-applies projection + filter pushdown, so the
  naive Q10 graph that OOMed on legacy Dask no longer materializes.

  envelope at SF1 in 2.6s (parquet) and 13.9s (CSV, the real benchbox IO),
  producing 37,967 groups — no OOM, no exit 137.
- A projection-pushdown rework (select needed columns, push the
  l_returnflag='R' filter before the lineitem join, group by the narrow
  integer keys c_custkey/c_nationkey then rejoin detail columns) is byte-
  identical to the current result (same all_hash, same top-20) and also fits.

approach:
First make the critical section explicit: only one process should decide and
populate a shared archive path at a time. Then switch the downloader to a
process-unique temporary path plus atomic replace, so the final path is
either absent or checksum-verified. Keep the implementation generic in

description:
Housekeeping for the JoinOrder canonical cutover audited
`benchbox/core/data_fetch/` and found that archive downloads are not guarded
against concurrent callers writing the same destination file.

`fetch_data()` resolves the archive path under the benchmark output
directory and calls `download(manifest.url, archive_path, ...)` when table
files are missing. `download()` writes directly to `dest_path`, resumes from
existing bytes with a Range request, and verifies the final checksum. There is
no per-archive lock, no unique `.part` path per process, and no atomic
`os.replace()` from a completed temp file. Two processes that start with a
missing archive can therefore append/truncate the same file concurrently and
either corrupt the archive or waste a large download before checksum failure.

This affects every benchmark that uses `benchbox/core/data_fetch/`, not just
JoinOrder, so the housekeeping TODO deliberately records it as a separate
follow-up instead of fixing it inline.

Pre-populated verified table files still skip network access

approach:
Follow the ClickHouse 3-mode pattern precisely:
  - deployment_mode.py for normalization/resolution (clickhouse/deployment_mode.py)
  - Thin first-class adapters that force their mode (clickhouse_local.py)
  - Mode-specific setup methods inside the base adapter (clickhouse/setup.py)
  - No eager process startup - start the standalone binary only inside
    create_connection(), not in __init__
Unlike ClickHouse local mode (chDB, in-process), standalone requires external
process lifecycle via process_manager.py. Treat this as the most complex part:
write it defensively with timeouts, port conflict detection, and clean failure
modes. Do not attempt to make process management "clever" - sequential start
with polling is correct and sufficient.
description:
Databend currently supports two implicit modes - remote self-hosted (Docker +
MinIO) and Databend Cloud - but they aren't modelled as distinct deployment
modes. This TODO adds a ClickHouse-style 3-mode architecture:

  standalone  Native macOS binary, local disk storage, no Docker or object
              store required. Manages databend-meta and databend-query
              processes in-process during the benchmark run.
  server      Current Docker-based mode (MinIO + databend-query). Unchanged.
  cloud       Databend Cloud managed service (HTTPS, existing credential
              flow). Promoted to a first-class named platform.

--- COMPLEXITY NOTICE ---
This is significantly harder than the ClickHouse equivalent. ClickHouse local
mode uses chDB, an embedded in-process Python library with zero binary
management. Databend standalone requires managing TWO separate external OS
processes with ordered startup and teardown:

  1. databend-meta  (Raft consensus / metadata service, gRPC port 9191)
  2. databend-query (compute / SQL layer, HTTP port 8000)

The meta service must be healthy before the query service starts. Shutdown
must be reversed. Both binaries must be downloaded and cached per architecture
(arm64 vs x86_64). Two TOML config files must be generated per run. This is
closer in complexity to an embedded-PostgreSQL lifecycle manager than to
DuckDB or chDB. The work should not begin until the validation gate (w2)
confirms the standalone mode is reliable enough to be worth this investment.

--- KEY RESEARCH FINDINGS (2026-04-20) ---
From prior conversation analysis:
  - Databend releases macOS arm64 + x86_64 binaries on GitHub releases
  - supports storage_type = "disk" (no MinIO) for development/testing
  - DSN format unchanged: databend+http://user:pass@localhost:8000/db
  - adapter.py create_connection(), create_schema(), load_data() all survive
    unchanged - they already use the DSN, no mode-specific logic needed
  - deployment_mode.py, process_manager.py, config_generator.py are all new
    files (none exist today); pattern follows clickhouse/deployment_mode.py
  - Raft data dir, ports 9191 (meta gRPC), 8000 (query HTTP), 3307 (MySQL)
    all need to be configurable and default to localhost with no port
    conflicts against other platforms

Docker docker-compose.yml for databend is not modified or removed
Existing 'databend' platform behavior (server/Docker mode) is completely unchanged - default deployment_mode must remain 'server'

description:
Implement Databend (https://github.com/databendlabs/databend) as a supported platform
in BenchBox. Databend is a cloud-native, Rust-based data warehouse with Snowflake-
compatible SQL, compute/storage separation, and object storage backend.

**Key Technical Approach:**
- Use Snowflake SQLGlot dialect as translation proxy (Databend claims ~100% compatibility)
- Leverage `databend-driver` (v0.28.2+) for DB-API 2.0 connectivity
- Implement lightweight QueryTransformer for edge cases if needed
- Deploy Databend + MinIO via Docker Compose for CI testing

**Rationale for Low Priority:**
Based on comprehensive analysis (Jan 2025), integration was deferred because:
1. SQLGlot does NOT support Databend as a native dialect
2. Significant platform overlap with ClickHouse, Snowflake, and Firebolt
3. Lower enterprise adoption compared to alternatives
4. Medium-high integration complexity due to custom translation layer

**Conditions for Prioritization:**
- SQLGlot adds native Databend dialect support
- User demand accumulates (3+ explicit requests)
- Databend Cloud enterprise adoption grows
- TPC-certified benchmark results published

description: Found 2026-07-31 by sentinel sweep. description:
Follow-up to generalize-tpc-tuning-base. The generalized TPC profile work
correctly moved Databricks TPC-H/TPC-DS tuning columns into a reusable
logical profile, but review exposed a Databricks-specific blind spot that can
corrupt tuned-run comparisons: the current checked-in Databricks TPC examples
still render the logical profile through the legacy Z-ORDER path, while
modern Databricks guidance treats Liquid Clustering as the preferred table
layout for new Delta tables.

The goal is not to make Databricks special again. The goal is to separate
three concerns cleanly so the TPC tuning base stays reusable across platforms:
logical workload candidates, platform physical rendering strategy, and
execution/result metadata. Databricks must support at least Z-ORDER and
Liquid Clustering as distinct renderings of the same logical TPC profile, and
result comparisons must expose which rendering was actually requested and
applied.

Current external evidence checked on 2026-05-26:
- Databricks liquid clustering docs describe Liquid Clustering as a data
  layout optimization that replaces table partitioning and ZORDER, supports
  CREATE/ALTER TABLE CLUSTER BY, and supports CLUSTER BY AUTO for automatic
  key selection.
  Source: https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/delta/clustering
- Databricks optimize-layout docs recommend Liquid Clustering instead of
  partitions, ZORDER, or other layout approaches; OPTIMIZE groups data by
  Liquid Clustering keys for clustered tables.
  Source: https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/optimize
- Databricks data-skipping docs state that ZORDER cannot be used with Liquid
  Clustering and recommend Liquid Clustering for new tables.
  Source: https://docs.databricks.com/gcp/en/delta/data-skipping

Current BenchBox facts to revalidate before implementation:
- `TuningType.LIQUID_CLUSTERING` and Databricks liquid configuration fields
  already exist in `benchbox/core/tuning/interface.py`.
- `DatabricksAdapter` can resolve `databricks_clustering_strategy` and emit
  `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...)`, but the TPC profile capability mapping
  currently reports Databricks logical locality as `z_order`.
- The checked-in Databricks TPC YAMLs set `z_ordering_enabled: true` and keep
  per-table `partitioning` fields, which is not a valid Liquid Clustering
  rendering without a deliberate conversion rule.
- Unified tuning application currently runs before data loading for fresh
  native tables, while Databricks post-load layout operations and metadata
  need to distinguish create-time `CLUSTER BY`, post-load `OPTIMIZE`, and
  Z-ORDER statements.
preserves: DuckDB tuned templates and mappings remain free of Databricks vocabulary such as Z-ORDER or Liquid Clustering.
Existing Databricks Z-ORDER tuned templates remain available for legacy strategy comparisons unless a migration is explicitly approved.
Liquid Clustering, Z-ORDER, and basic-constraints fallback are distinguishable in result metadata and comparison semantics.
New routine tests carry explicit `unit` and `fast` pytest markers.
No live Databricks/cloud tests run without explicit user approval.
No result metadata claims a tuning mechanism was applied unless BenchBox attempted and recorded that operation.
The logical TPC profile remains platform-neutral; Databricks is one renderer, not the source of truth.

work.summary: Revalidate Databricks Liquid Clustering guidance and current BenchBox execution semantics

work.notes:
Extend the profile/capability model so Databricks mapping is strategy
aware instead of hardcoded to Z-ORDER.

Required concepts:
  - logical profile: reusable TPC candidate source, currently `tpc-v1`;
  - physical rendering: platform-specific representation of the logical
    profile;
  - Databricks rendering ids:
      databricks_z_order
      databricks_liquid_manual
      databricks_liquid_auto
  - physical mechanisms:
      z_order
      liquid_clustering
      liquid_clustering_auto
      partitioning
      optimize
      optimize_full
  - unsupported/waived decisions with explicit reasons.

The mapping must answer:
  - for Z-ORDER rendering, which logical roles map to partitioning,
    clustering, distribution hints, and ZORDER operations;
  - for manual Liquid rendering, which logical roles become clustering
    keys, which legacy partition/ZORDER columns are folded into those
    keys, and which candidates exceed Databricks key limits;
  - for automatic Liquid rendering, how BenchBox reports logical intent
    when Databricks chooses keys asynchronously from workload history;
  - how distribution candidates should be represented when Databricks has
    no user-managed physical distribution key.

Resolve the default-selection decision before w2 starts. Unless the
implementation records an explicit migration decision with tests, docs,
and release-note guidance, preserve the current `--tuning tuned`
Databricks behavior as the legacy Z-ORDER rendering and expose Liquid
through an explicit rendering/template/strategy path.

Do not claim that Databricks Liquid, Databricks Z-ORDER, DuckDB sorting,
BigQuery clustering, Redshift sort/dist keys, and Snowflake clustering are
performance-equivalent. Report logical coverage and physical mechanism
differences separately.
work.summary: Define Databricks physical rendering variants for the logical TPC profile

work.notes:
Choose one of these implementation shapes and document the tradeoff:
  - generated Liquid variants from the logical profile; or
  - checked-in Databricks Liquid YAML variants, e.g.
    `examples/tunings/databricks/tpch_liquid_tuned.yaml` and
    `examples/tunings/databricks/tpcds_liquid_tuned.yaml`.

Minimum requirements for Liquid variants:
  - `z_ordering_enabled: false`;
  - `liquid_clustering_enabled: true` or
    `databricks_clustering_strategy: liquid_clustering`;
  - no per-table legacy `partitioning` fields in Liquid-rendered Delta
    templates; logical partition candidates must be converted into Liquid
    clustering-key candidates or moved into a separate unsupported/waived
    decision list with rationale;
  - logical ZORDER candidates are explicitly converted into Liquid
    clustering-key candidates or moved into a separate unsupported/waived
    decision list with rationale;
  - key-count limits are enforced or explicitly handled;
  - template metadata records both `logical_tuning_profile_id` and
    `physical_rendering_id`.

Preserve existing Z-ORDER YAML behavior for users who intentionally want
legacy comparisons. Do not silently reinterpret existing
`tpch_tuned.yaml` or `tpcds_tuned.yaml` as Liquid Clustering unless a
migration decision is made explicit in docs, tests, and release notes.
work.summary: Add explicit Databricks Liquid TPC template/rendering artifacts without breaking Z-ORDER templates

work.notes:
Add validation that hard-fails invalid or misleading Databricks
effective configurations. Do not allow waivers for runtime config
conflicts that Databricks treats as mutually exclusive. At minimum,
reject:
  - `liquid_clustering_enabled: true` with `z_ordering_enabled: true`;
  - Liquid rendering with non-empty `z_ordering_columns`;
  - Liquid rendering with per-table partitioning on Delta tables where
    legacy partitioning would conflict with Liquid Clustering;
  - `databricks_clustering_strategy: none` with Liquid fields;
  - generic `distribution` fields being reported as a real Databricks
    physical distribution mechanism.

Waivers are only acceptable for logical profile candidates that cannot be
represented in a selected rendering, not for contradictory effective
Databricks configuration fields.

Add this validation in the lowest shared layer that can see the full
unified tuning configuration, then add adapter-level guardrails where
runtime table format or Databricks-specific constraints are only known by
the adapter. Error messages must name the conflicting fields and the
migration path.

description:
Implement DataFrame versions of AI Primitives benchmark operations. The current
benchmark has **16 SQL queries** across 4 categories testing AI/ML functions:

**Categories (16 queries total):**
- Generative (4): text completion, customer profile summary, Q&A, SQL generation
- NLP (5): sentiment analysis (single/batch), classification (priority/segment), entity extraction
- Transform (4): summarization (short/long), translation, grammar correction
- Embedding (3): single embedding, batch embeddings, large-dimension embeddings

**DataFrame Implementation Approach:**
The SQL benchmark uses platform-specific AI functions (Snowflake Cortex, BigQuery ML,
Databricks AI). DataFrame implementations would use:

- **PySpark MLlib**: Native ML functions, model inference pipelines
- **Sentence Transformers**: For embeddings via Hugging Face integration
- **Polars + NumPy**: Vector operations, embedding similarity
- **Pandas + scikit-learn**: Classification, NLP pipelines

Not all 16 SQL queries translate directly - generative queries require LLM APIs
while embedding/vector operations map well to DataFrame native operations.
title: Implement DataFrame Version of AI Primitives Benchmark
