description:
The empty-string-vs-null contract is centralized at the Parquet conversion layer
(data_loader.py, strings_can_be_null = null_marker is not None), and
prefer_parquet=True is the default - so the DEFAULT path is consistent. But on the
prefer_parquet=False CSV-direct path the contract is NOT uniform:
  - pandas_df.py:378 and polars_df.py:283 restore '' for empty fields when
    null_marker is None (dask/modin/cudf do likewise).
  - pyspark_df.py:461 returns directly after CSV load (Spark emits null for empty
    fields by default).
  - datafusion_df.py:511 documents null_marker as "Unused".
So for a null-marker-less benchmark (e.g. ClickBench), a prefer_parquet=False run
on PySpark or DataFusion emits NULL where the SQL reference (and the other
adapters) emit "" - the exact Q6/Q17/Q18 divergence class the polars adapter's own
comment warns about. It is non-default, hence latent, but it is a real
cross-surface fidelity gap and will silently mis-compare if that path is exercised.

Prefer a SINGLE shared post-coercion (so future adapters inherit it) over
per-adapter patches.
preserves: JoinOrder and other null_marker='' benchmarks still map empty -> NULL; the fix is null_marker-driven, not a blanket empty->'' for all.
The production DataFrame run path is reused, not forked; the change is additive.
prefer_parquet=True (default) load behavior is byte-unchanged for every adapter.

approach: Thread has_header from the benchmark's csv_has_header attribute (resolved next to the existing csv_delimiter) through _convert_table_files into convert_csv_to_parquet, and set ReadOptions(skip_rows=1) when a header is declared AND explicit column names are supplied. Gate the pass-through on format_type == 'csv' so .tbl stays headerless regardless of the attribute. Bump DATAFRAME_CACHE_VERSION so stale caches built from the broken path are not reused.
description: FormatConverter.convert_csv_to_parquet passes the schema's column names to pyarrow.csv.ReadOptions(column_names=...). That REPLACES the header names but does NOT skip the header LINE, so a headered CSV is parsed with its own header as the first data row. With declared numeric/date column types the conversion then FAILS ('CSV conversion error to int64: invalid value day_of_week'), and _convert_table_files logs 'Failed to convert <table>, using source file' and falls back to the RAW CSV -- an untyped read where date columns stay strings. Every downstream date filter then matches nothing, so the DataFrame surface silently returns zero rows instead of erroring. Headerless TPC .tbl is unaffected (it has no header), which is why this survived: every gated benchmark so far is .tbl or headerless. Found by wiring a FlightData cross-surface gate, whose CSVs carry headers -- all 20 queries x 2 backends diverged. The benchmark already declares csv_has_header=True; the converter simply never received it.
preserves: Declared column types still apply; the fix must not reintroduce PyArrow type inference
Headerless sources (TPC .tbl, headerless CSV) keep every row -- no off-by-one from skipping a line that is not a header
title: DataFrame loader parses a headered CSV's header row as data, then silently falls back to an untyped read

verifications.description: a headered CSV converts with declared types and does not count its header as a row

verifications.description: the full DataFrame loader suite is unregressed

work.evidence: Threaded has_header from the benchmark's csv_has_header attribute (resolved beside the existing csv_delimiter) through _convert_table_files into convert_csv_to_parquet, setting ReadOptions(skip_rows=1) only when a header is declared AND explicit column names are supplied. Pass-through gated on format_type == 'csv' so .tbl stays headerless regardless of the attribute. DATAFRAME_CACHE_VERSION v4 -> v5 so caches built from the broken path are not reused.
work.summary: Thread has_header into the converter and skip the header line; bump the cache version

work.evidence: 3 tests in TestHeaderedCsvConversion. Mutation-proved: reverting ONLY the skip_rows line fails test_headered_csv_converts_with_typed_columns and test_header_row_is_not_ingested_as_data (conversion returns FAILED with 'CSV conversion error to int64: invalid value id'), while test_headerless_source_is_unchanged still passes -- confirming the guard is header-specific and does not touch .tbl. Empirically end to end: before the fix the FlightData cross-surface probe logged 'Conversion failed ... invalid value day_of_week' and 'Failed to convert flights, using source file'; after the fix both disappear.

description:
Implement maintenance operations (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE equivalents) for DataFrame
platforms, enabling full TPC-H and TPC-DS compliance in DataFrame mode.

Currently, `get_maintenance_operations_sql()` only supports SQL mode. When users
run `--platform polars-df --benchmark tpch --phases maintenance`, no error is raised
and the maintenance phase silently does nothing useful.

DataFrame platforms like Spark (Delta Lake, Iceberg), Polars, and others support
write operations that can implement TPC maintenance semantics:
- Delta Lake: MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE operations
- Iceberg: Row-level deletes, upserts
- Polars: write_parquet() with append/overwrite modes
- Parquet files: Partition-based updates

This work involves:
1. Adding validation to error when maintenance+dataframe is attempted (short-term fix)
2. Designing a unified maintenance abstraction that works for both SQL and DataFrame
3. Implementing platform-specific maintenance operations
title: Implement DataFrame Maintenance Operations for TPC-H/TPC-DS

description:
Implement DataFrame versions of Metadata Primitives benchmark operations. This
benchmark tests metadata introspection operations: schema discovery, column
introspection, table statistics, and query introspection.

DataFrame platforms have metadata capabilities through various APIs:

**PySpark:**
- spark.catalog.listDatabases(), listTables(), listColumns()
- spark.sql("SHOW TABLES"), spark.sql("DESCRIBE TABLE")
- Delta Lake: DESCRIBE HISTORY, DESCRIBE DETAIL
- Iceberg: metadata tables (snapshots, manifests, files)

**Polars:**
- df.schema, df.dtypes, df.describe()
- Limited catalog capabilities (file-based, no central catalog)

**Pandas:**
- df.dtypes, df.info(), df.describe()
- No catalog capabilities

The benchmark should focus on operations that are meaningful across platforms,
with platform-specific extensions for lakehouse metadata.
title: Implement DataFrame Version of Metadata Primitives Benchmark

approach:
MINIMUM-CHANGE STRATEGY - inject parameters through centralized parameter functions,
not through DataFrameContext Protocol changes.

Key insight: TPC-DS already has a single choke point - every query calls
get_parameters(query_id) from parameters.py. Adding an optional `overrides` parameter
to this function is the minimum fix for all 99 TPC-DS queries: zero query function
modifications needed.

TPC-H is harder: queries inline values directly (TPCH_PARAMS dict is dead code).
The minimum fix requires: (1) consolidate inline values into a TPCH_DEFAULT_PARAMS dict,
(2) create get_tpch_parameters(query_id, overrides=None), (3) refactor 44 query functions
(22 expression + 22 pandas) to call it. This is unavoidable scope.

Parameter extraction from binaries:
1. Run qgen/dsqgen for each query with a given seed/SF/stream
2. Parse substitution values from generated SQL using regex anchored to SQL keywords
3. Return dict structure matching the existing parameter formats
4. Cache results per seed/SF/stream combination

Override injection mechanism: Use a module-level _parameter_overrides dict in each
parameters module. The dataframe_runner sets it before query execution and clears it
after. The get_*_parameters() functions check overrides first, then fall back to static
defaults. This avoids touching DataFrameContext, DataFrameQuery, or any platform adapter.

Phase 6 approach: Fix the 3 identified gaps with minimal scope:
- Q7/Q8: Add start_date/end_date to TPCH_DEFAULT_PARAMS, update 4 functions to read from params
- Q96: This is the sole TPC-DS query that bypasses get_parameters() - add the call to both impls
- Tests: Add integration-level tests that verify query functions actually consume overrides
description:
DataFrame query implementations for TPC-H (22 queries) and TPC-DS (99 queries) use
hardcoded static parameter values instead of deriving parameters from the same
seed-based generation that SQL queries use via the qgen/dsqgen binaries. This means:

1. SQL queries produce different parameter values for each stream/seed combination
   (as the TPC spec requires), while DataFrame queries always use the same fixed values
   regardless of stream_id or seed.
2. SQL and DataFrame modes cannot be meaningfully compared because they execute
   different workloads when using any non-default seed.
3. Multi-stream throughput tests in DataFrame mode repeat identical parameters across
   streams instead of varying them per the TPC specification.

The ordering permutation logic is already correct - both SQL and DataFrame modes use
TPCHStreams.PERMUTATION_MATRIX and TPCDSPermutationGenerator respectively. The gap
is purely in parameter substitution.

IMPORTANT: The two benchmarks have different parameter access patterns:
- TPC-DS: All 99 queries call get_parameters(query_id) from parameters.py - a single
  centralized choke point. Minimum fix: modify get_parameters() to accept overrides.
- TPC-H: All 22 queries INLINE parameter values directly (e.g., cutoff_date = date(1998, 9, 2)).
  The TPCH_PARAMS dict at module top is dead documentation - never referenced by any
  query function. Minimum fix: create a get_tpch_parameters(query_id) function, then
  refactor each query to call it instead of using inline literals.

POST-IMPLEMENTATION REVIEW (2026-02-06):
Phases 1-5 are complete and the core mechanism works. An adversarial code review
identified 3 defects that require a follow-up Phase 6:
- BUG: TPC-H Q7/Q8 have hardcoded date parameters that bypass the override system
- BUG: TPC-DS Q96 bypasses get_parameters() and uses hardcoded literals directly
- GAP: Missing integration-level tests that verify query functions consume overrides
- STYLE: Misplaced import in parameter_extractor.py
preserves: All 22 TPC-H query functions produce identical results when no overrides are set (static defaults match current inline values exactly)
All 99 TPC-DS query functions continue to call get_parameters(N) with no signature change - overrides parameter is optional with default None
DataFrameContext Protocol and all 5 implementations unchanged: DataFrameContext (Protocol), DataFrameContextImpl (ABC), PolarsDataFrameContext, ExpressionFamilyContext, PandasFamilyContext
Existing DataFrame benchmark results at default seed remain reproducible
Q7/Q8 dates are spec-fixed at 1995-01-01 to 1996-12-31 regardless of seed - Phase 6 parameterizes them for architectural consistency but the default values MUST remain these exact dates
TPCDSPermutationGenerator ordering logic is unchanged - permutations are already correct
TPCHStreams.PERMUTATION_MATRIX ordering logic is unchanged - permutations are already correct

description:
Implement DataFrame (Polars, Pandas, PySpark, DataFusion) versions of all 136 Read
Primitives queries. This benchmark tests fundamental database read operations and is
the ideal candidate for DataFrame expansion - it uses the TPC-H schema (already
supported by DataFrame loaders) and covers operations that map well to DataFrame APIs.

The Read Primitives catalog includes queries across 29 categories:
- Aggregation (13 queries): COUNT, SUM, AVG, COUNT DISTINCT, GROUP BY
- Filter (10 queries): WHERE clauses, predicate pushdown
- Optimizer (13 queries): Subquery decorrelation, join reordering, constant folding
- Array (9 queries): ARRAY operations, UNNEST, array aggregations
- String (11 queries): LIKE, CONCAT, SUBSTRING, string functions
- Order By (8 queries): Sorting, TOP-N, ORDER BY ALL
- Window (6 queries): ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, aggregate windows
- Qualify (6 queries): QUALIFY clause for window filtering
- Shuffle (5 queries): Data redistribution patterns
- Group By (5 queries): GROUP BY ALL, GROUP BY ROLLUP/CUBE
- And 19 more categories with 1-4 queries each

Implementation follows the established TPC-H DataFrame pattern using:
- Expression family (Polars, PySpark, DataFusion): ctx.col(), ctx.lit(), lazy expressions
- Pandas family (Pandas, Modin, Dask, cuDF): df['column'], boolean indexing, eager ops
title: Implement DataFrame Version of Read Primitives Benchmark

description:

Current state: 102 queries implemented, 34 remaining

marked 49 queries as "skipped" or "expression-family-only" when they should have

description:
Implement DataFrame versions of Transaction Primitives benchmark operations. This
benchmark tests database transaction semantics: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, savepoints,
isolation levels, and multi-statement transactions.

DataFrame platforms with table formats have ACID transaction support:

**Delta Lake (Full ACID):**
- Atomic writes with automatic commit
- Optimistic concurrency control
- Time travel (query historical versions)
- VACUUM for garbage collection
- Isolation: serializable snapshot isolation

**Iceberg (Full ACID):**
- Atomic table operations
- Snapshot isolation
- Time travel via snapshots
- Schema evolution with transactions
- Partition evolution

**PySpark (Spark SQL):**
- Transaction support via Delta Lake or Iceberg
- Streaming transactions (structured streaming)
- Batch transaction patterns

Platforms without transaction support (Polars, Pandas) should be skipped
for transaction-specific operations.
title: Implement DataFrame Version of Transaction Primitives Benchmark

DataFrame tuning focuses on runtime execution parameters, memory management, and

Current State:
- DataFrame adapters have ZERO tuning framework integration
- SQL adapters use UnifiedTuningConfiguration with 13 TuningType options
- DataFrame adapters only accept constructor parameters for basic settings
- No way to load/save DataFrame tuning configs from YAML
- No validation or platform compatibility checking

This TODO implements a parallel tuning system designed for DataFrame semantics.
title: DataFrame Tuning Configuration Support

description:
Implement DataFrame versions of Write Primitives benchmark operations. This benchmark
tests fundamental write operations: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, BULK_LOAD, MERGE, DDL,
and TRANSACTION operations.

DataFrame platforms have extensive write capabilities that map to these operations:

**PySpark + Delta Lake:**
- INSERT → df.write.mode("append").saveAsTable()
- UPDATE → DeltaTable.update()
- DELETE → DeltaTable.delete()
- MERGE → DeltaTable.merge()
- DDL → spark.sql() for schema operations

**PySpark + Iceberg:**
- INSERT → df.writeTo().append()
- UPDATE → Row-level updates via MERGE
- DELETE → Row-level deletes
- MERGE → df.writeTo().overwritePartitions()

**Polars:**
- INSERT → write_parquet() with append
- BULK_LOAD → scan_parquet() + write_parquet()
- File-level operations (no row-level UPDATE/DELETE)

**All DataFrame Platforms:**
- BULK_LOAD → read + write with compression, partitioning, sorting
- Physical layout tuning (row groups, dictionary encoding)
title: Implement DataFrame Version of Write Primitives Benchmark

family (like Polars), offering lazy evaluation, Arrow-native execution, and
competitive single-node performance.

Current State:
- BenchBox has no DataFusion integration (neither SQL nor DataFrame)
- Expression family base class exists (ExpressionFamilyAdapter)
- Polars adapter serves as reference implementation for Expression family

- Fastest single-node Parquet engine (ClickBench 2024)
- Apache Arrow native - zero-copy data interchange

- Rust core with Python bindings - memory safe, performant

approach:
Follow the ClickHouse query transformer pattern exactly:
- Reference: benchbox/platforms/clickhouse/query_transformer.py (class structure, transform() entry point, transformations_applied tracking)
- Reference: benchbox/platforms/clickhouse/workload.py:293-295 (integration into execute_query())
- Reference: benchbox/core/tpch/dataframe_queries.py (DataFrame implementations of Q11, Q16, Q18, Q20 show the correct algorithmic approach to translate into SQL rewrites)

Each rewrite method extracts parameterized values (nation names, thresholds,
dates) from the qgen SQL via targeted regex, then reconstructs the query with
DataFusion-compatible structure. Literal values are preserved; only structure changes.
description:
DataFusion's SQL engine misexecutes 4 TPC-H queries (Q11, Q16, Q18, Q20) that
use SQL patterns it handles differently from PostgreSQL: HAVING with scalar
subqueries, NOT IN subqueries, IN with HAVING, and nested correlated subqueries.

These failures were exposed when the seed parity fix changed validation from
"loose" (±50% tolerance) to "exact" (0% tolerance). The DataFrame implementations
of the same queries produce correct results because they use explicit joins,
anti-joins, and semi-joins instead of these problematic SQL patterns.

The fix follows the established ClickHouse pattern: create a DataFusionQueryTransformer
that rewrites the 4 problematic queries before execution, transforming them into
semantically equivalent SQL that DataFusion handles correctly.

Row count discrepancies at SF=1 with qgen -d defaults:
  Q11: Expected 1,048 → Got 1,289 (HAVING + scalar subquery threshold)
  Q16: Expected 18,314 → Got 18,200 (NOT IN subquery, NULL semantics)
  Q18: Expected 57 → Got 9 (IN subquery with HAVING clause)
  Q20: Expected 186 → Got 173 (nested IN with correlated subquery)
preserves: All 18 non-affected TPC-H queries (Q1-Q10, Q12-Q15, Q17, Q19, Q21-Q22) pass through transformer unchanged
ClickHouseQueryTransformer remains independent and unchanged
DataFusion DataFrame mode (datafusion-df) execution path is not affected
DataFusionAdapter.execute_query() continues to work for non-TPC-H queries (no transformer applied when query_id is not Q11/Q16/Q18/Q20)

description:
DataFusionAdapter.load_data cannot ingest raw TPC-H .tbl (or TPC-DS .dat) data
files that carry a field-TERMINATING trailing delimiter - the format dbgen/dsdgen
emit by default, where a row of N values ends with a trailing `|` and so splits
into N+1 fields. BOTH of the adapter's load paths fail on it:

  - Parquet path (the default, data_format="parquet"): _build_pyarrow_columns
    returns the N schema column names; _write_csv_file_to_parquet then calls
    pyarrow.csv.read_csv with column_names=<N names>, and the trailing pipe makes
    PyArrow see N+1 fields, raising `ArrowInvalid: CSV parse error: Expected N
    columns, got N+1` (observed on customer.tbl: "Expected 8 columns, got 9").
  - CSV external-table path (data_format="csv"): _load_table_csv builds a
    CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE with an N-column schema and relies on DataFusion's CSV
    reader, which "doesn't have a direct 'ignore trailing delimiter' option"
    (the adapter's own comment, ~benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py:923), so the
    extra field shifts/!breaks parsing.

This was hit directly while building the third-engine TPC-Havoc equivalence
sample (PR #806). Because the adapter was out of that change's scope, the sample
had to HAND-ROLL a PyArrow load in
benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py:build_datafusion_with_tpch (reading the
.tbl with the shared trailing-delimiter helpers, dropping the dummy column, and
registering Arrow batches) and reach into the private
DataFusionAdapter._map_schema_type_to_pyarrow - a workaround the PR review
flagged (reuse / private-access / load-fidelity-drift). Fixing the adapter lets
that workaround be removed and lets ANY real DataFusion .tbl/.dat ingest work.

The correct fix already exists and is used by the OTHER adapters: the shared
helpers benchbox/utils/file_format.has_trailing_delimiter +
get_column_names_with_trailing + the TRAILING_DUMMY_COLUMN sentinel. The
COPY/CTAS loaders in benchbox/platforms/base/data_loading.py (~lines 1083 and
1168) detect the trailing delimiter per file and append a dummy column for the
extra field; the DataFusion adapter is the one that skips this step. Critically,
has_trailing_delimiter is field-count-aware (it returns False for TPC-DS
time_dim where dsdgen emits exactly N values with a terminating delimiter), so
the fix must NOT blindly append a dummy column to every file.
preserves: No on-disk rewriting of source data files; handle the trailing delimiter at read time only.
Non-trailing files (e.g. TPC-DS time_dim, where field count already equals the schema) are not regressed - rely on has_trailing_delimiter's field-count awareness, never a blind append.
Query results and row counts are unchanged: the trailing dummy column never leaks into a result schema, COUNT(*), or row total.
The DataFusion TPC-Havoc equivalence sample stays green (206/206, DATAFUSION_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES empty).

benchbox/platforms/base/data_loading.py (~1083, ~1168) - the reference pattern: other adapters detect trailing delimiter per file and add the dummy column.

benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py:_build_pyarrow_columns (~1257), _convert_and_register_parquet (~1331), _write_csv_file_to_parquet (~1276) - the parquet path that reads CSV with the bare schema column count and errors on the trailing field.
benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py:_load_table_csv (~845) and its comment (~923) - the CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE path with no ignore-trailing-delimiter handling.
benchbox/utils/file_format.py:has_trailing_delimiter (404), get_column_names_with_trailing (468), TRAILING_DUMMY_COLUMN (401) - the field-count-aware detection + dummy-column helpers to reuse.

SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS in benchmark.py is the single source of truth after
this work. Any future algorithm addition touches that constant and nothing else.
description:
The DataVault benchmark's hash key columns are defined as VARCHAR(32), sized for
MD5's 32-char hex output. MD5 has known collision vulnerabilities that make it
unsuitable for Data Vault 2.0 in any production-representative benchmark - the
whole point of DV2.0 hash keys is collision-free surrogate identity.

A root-cause analysis revealed a five-layer inconsistency across the codebase:

  1. BenchmarkOptionSpec (benchmark.py:485) declares choices=("md5", "sha256") -
     the CLI accepts sha256 and the docs advertise it.
  2. SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS = ("md5",) (benchmark.py:56) immediately rejects
     sha256 at construction time with ValueError.
  3. HashAlgorithm = Literal["md5"] (hash_functions.py:16) narrows the type to
     match the runtime - the unreachable sha1/sha256 branches were cleaned up in
     fc6509c35 along with the [:32] truncation; sha256 must now be added back cleanly.
  4. (Resolved by fc6509c35) The sha256 branch truncated to [:32], destroying
     half the entropy. That branch is gone; the function now raises ValueError for
     non-md5 inputs. Remaining work is to add sha256 properly post-schema migration.
  5. DataVaultETLTransformer hard-codes `if hash_algorithm != "md5"` (transformer.py:136)
     independently of SUPPORTED_HASH_ALGORITHMS.

The fix has two sequential phases: (a) immediately stop the CLI from advertising
sha256 while the schema cannot support it, and (b) migrate the schema to VARCHAR(64)
and wire sha256 through all remaining layers cleanly.

After this work, `benchbox run --platform duckdb --benchmark datavault
--benchmark-option hash_algorithm=sha256` must execute successfully end-to-end.
preserves: Existing VARCHAR(32) test fixtures remain valid - stored MD5 hashes are still 32 chars and fit in VARCHAR(64) without truncation
MD5 remains the default - hash_algorithm defaults to 'md5' in all constructors and CLI options
SHA-1 stays unsupported - 40-char output doesn't align with either VARCHAR(32) or VARCHAR(64), and SHA-1 is cryptographically weaker than SHA-256
generate_hash_key_sql() remains MD5-only - DuckDB's md5() SQL function is the only hash SQL available without custom extensions; that restriction stands

Extract a `_generate_table(self, conn, table_name, num_records, insert_sql)`
helper that handles: progress logging, timing via mono_time/elapsed_seconds,
conn.execute(insert_sql), stats dict updates (records_generated, tables_generated,
generation_times, sql_operations), completion logging.

The helper should accept an optional `num_records` parameter. When provided,

description:

scaffolding in benchbox/core/tpcdi/generator/sql.py:

- generate_security_dimension (line 315)
- generate_customer_dimension (line 359)
- generate_account_dimension (line 427)
- generate_trade_facts (line 467)

All 6 share the same pattern: progress log → mono_time() → conn.execute(sql)
→ elapsed_seconds → stats update (4 keys) → completion log → return count.

rather than pre-computing it. generate_account_dimension derives its count
from a formula (num_customers * 1.5) rather than base_X * scale_factor.

description:
The `make duplicate-check-verbose` report (2026-03-12, post wave-2) shows 344
duplicate groups / 8,051 duplicated lines (threshold 9,476). Wave-3 triage of
the top-30 groups identifies 13 groups that are intentional boilerplate, wave-2
extraction residuals, protocol conformance, TPC spec-mandated query patterns,
or AST structural false positives. These should be suppressed via ignore_rules
to reduce noise and focus the checker on genuine consolidation targets.

Groups to mark as ignored (by current report rank):

G1  (68 lines): generate_company_dimension / generate_customer_dimension /
    generate_security_dimension in tpcdi/generator/sql.py. Wave-2 residual:
    these are thin wrappers calling _build_dimension_sql with domain-specific
    column expressions. The 34-line structural match is the wrapper pattern,
    not duplicated logic.

G2  (55 lines): aggregation_distinct_groupby_expression_impl /
    aggregation_distinct_groupby_pandas_impl /
    aggregation_groupby_large_expression_impl in
    read_primitives/dataframe_queries.py. H2O.db benchmark spec-driven query
    variants. Wave-2 extracted aggregation_groupby_impl for some pandas variants;
    the remaining 6 copies (expression + large) are spec-mandated groupby patterns
    varying only by column names and cardinality.

G3  (55 lines): classify_error / date_add / date_sub across 6 files.
    AST false positive - these are different functions with different return
    types and semantics (error classification vs datetime arithmetic) that
    happen to share the facade/delegation AST shape.

G5  (48 lines): get_operations_by_category / get_queries_by_category across
    5 primitives modules (ai_primitives, metadata_primitives, read_primitives,
    transaction_primitives, write_primitives). Query catalog lookup methods
    with type variance (dict[str, str] vs dict[str, Operation]). The 12-line
    pattern is intentional per-type catalog API. Not worth a shared base class
    for the type generics overhead.

G6  (48 lines): get_all_create_table_sql in amplab, read_primitives, ssb.
    Wave-2 residual: all three now delegate to schema_utils.collect_create_table_sql.
    The structural match is the wrapper (passing table_order + per-table fn).

G7  (48 lines): supports_acl_introspection / supports_column_grants /
    supports_role_hierarchy in metadata_primitives/ddl.py. Intentional
    capability-matrix methods. Each defines a different platform set.
    Consolidating would require a capability-type string parameter that
    obscures the intent.

G8  (48 lines): generate_data / get_all_aliases / get_benchmark_info across
    platform_registry.py, datavault.py, nyctaxi.py, tpch_skew.py, tsbs_devops.py.
    Facade API conformance methods - same pattern as __init__ facades already
    ignored in wave-2.

G9  (48 lines): get_queries_by_category in tpcdi/query_analytics.py,
    tpcdi/query_etl.py, tpcdi/query_validation.py. Same catalog lookup pattern
    as G5. Extend existing wave-2 rule for TPC-DI query modules.

G19 (44 lines): get_dataframe_metadata_manager / get_dataframe_transaction_manager /
    get_dataframe_write_manager across 3 primitives dataframe_operations modules.
    Wave-2 residual: these now delegate to _get_dataframe_manager in
    dataframe_manager_factory.py. Structural match is the wrapper pattern.

G20 (44 lines): validate_customer_tier / validate_gender / validate_trade_type
    in tpcdi/etl/validation.py. Domain-specific validators that intentionally
    follow the same isin(valid_set) pattern with different column names and
    valid value sets.

G21 (44 lines): __init__ across 5 unrelated classes (tpcdi/tools/data_cleaners.py,
    base/data_loading.py x2, unified_frame.py x2). Constructor boilerplate:
    docstring + attribute assignment. Different classes, different attributes.

G22 (44 lines): calculate_official_metrics / execute_operation / get across
    5 files. AST false positive - three different function names with different
    purposes that share the delegation/accessor AST shape.

G27 (43 lines): q26_expression_impl / q7_expression_impl in
    tpcds/dataframe_queries/queries.py. TPC-DS spec pair: Q7 and Q26 both
    compute aggregated metrics from item-joined fact tables with promotional
    filtering. Same structural pattern, different dimension tables and measures.

anti_patterns.instead: use standalone utility functions or thin mixins
anti_patterns.why: platform adapters are frequently added/modified by contributors unfamiliar with the class hierarchy; utility functions are easier to discover and compose than deep class chains

anti_patterns.why: other platforms (BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB) use radically different tuning mechanisms (clustering, micro-partitions, pragmas) and a universal abstraction would be leaky

anti_patterns.instead: keep explicit parameters matching the current signatures

description:
Wave-3 duplicate-check triage (2026-03-12, post wave-2) identifies 7
consolidation-worthy groups in the SQL platform adapter layer. These are
parallel implementations across platform adapters that can share a base
implementation via utilities, mixins, or extraction to existing shared modules.

Targets (report rank -> dup lines):

G11 (48 dup lines): apply_table_tunings in firebolt.py:1227, lakesail.py:604,
    presto.py:1051. 3 copies with 97% identical logic: check has_any_tuning() ->
    get partitioning columns -> sort by order -> log. Only ImportError handling
    and log messages differ across platforms.

G12 (47 dup lines): _build_lakesail_config and _build_synapse_config in
    azure_synapse.py:1341 and lakesail.py:686. Identical Azure-compatible
    config builder pattern. Both construct connection configs from the same
    parameter set with platform-specific defaults.

G16 (46 dup lines): create_schema in presto.py:635 and trino.py:647.
    Byte-for-byte identical schema creation logic. Textbook extension of
    the existing presto_trino_utils.py from wave-2 (which already holds
    the shared _validate_catalog_exists utility).

G18+G28 (88 dup lines combined): _execute_statement in
    fabric_spark_adapter.py:419 and synapse_spark_adapter.py:402, plus
    _wait_for_statement in fabric_spark_adapter.py:465 and
    synapse_spark_adapter.py:448. Two pairs of identical methods in the
    Azure Spark adapter family. Both adapters use the same Livy-based
    statement execution and polling pattern.

G23 (44 dup lines): get_query_plan across 5 platforms: athena.py:1193,
    azure_synapse.py:1200, firebolt.py:1124, presto.py:958, trino.py:956.
    Verbatim identical: cursor -> EXPLAIN query -> fetchall -> join rows.
    No platform-specific differences whatsoever.

G24 (44 dup lines): _parse_gcs_url and _parse_s3_url in
    clickhouse_cloud.py:880/:904 and firebolt.py:999. Cloud storage URL
    parsing utilities duplicated across platforms. These extract bucket
    and path from gs:// and s3:// URLs using the same regex/split logic.

G26 (44 dup lines): _extract_table_name across 6 platforms:
    firebolt.py:1063, lakesail.py:504, presto.py:913, redshift.py:1692,
    spark.py:539, trino.py:913. Identical SQL table name extraction from
    CREATE TABLE with shared regex pattern (IF NOT EXISTS variant) and
    try/except/pass structure. 4 additional platforms (azure_synapse:1102,
    athena:1176, fabric_warehouse:1223, questdb:437) have platform-specific
    regex variants (bracket-quoting, EXTERNAL TABLE, schema-qualified names,
    quote-handling) and are excluded from this consolidation.

approach:
Treat the canonical schema-v2 bundle as input, not as the full hosted public
contract. Add hosted result identity, visibility, and trust semantics above

description:
A hosted results platform is not just an upload endpoint. BenchBox needs a
durable contract for what a hosted result is, how it relates to the canonical
schema-v2 bundle, who can see it, how trustworthy it is, and which runs are
valid to compare or rank together.

This item defines the canonical hosted object model and the governance rules
around visibility, trust promotion, compatibility cohorts, privacy, and
public claims. Without this layer, the API, UI, and ranking surfaces will
drift into misleading or contradictory behavior.

**Phase assignment:** Phase 2-3 preparation. NOT required for Phase 1 (all
results are maintainer-curated, so trust labels and governance are trivial).
The cohort compatibility rules (w3) are partially relevant to Phase 1 compare
views but can be handled with simple same-benchmark/same-scale validation
without a full governance model.
preserves: BenchBox does not imply TPC certification or equivalent official standing for ordinary hosted submissions
Canonical BenchBox result bundles remain downloadable and distinguishable from any derived hosted metadata
title: Define hosted results contract, trust labels, and governance model

description:
The strategy doc explicitly defers Phase 3 (hosted submission API) until
Phase 2 PR volume justifies the operational cost. It cites indicators
("submission volume exceeds ~50/month sustained", "maintainer review
becomes a sustained bottleneck", etc.) but no one is currently measuring
those indicators, and there is no decision moment where someone is asked
to look.

Without measurement and a forcing function, the Phase 3 promotion
decision will be made by whoever feels frustrated first - which is
exactly the kind of ad-hoc engineering decision the strategy doc is
trying to prevent. This item operationalizes the trigger: pick the
metrics, build the cheapest possible dashboard, and put a review on
someone's calendar.

description:
BenchBox currently blurs together three different concerns:
1) local/cloud artifact publication,
2) hosted result submission,
3) public result browsing and analysis on benchbox.dev.

That ambiguity makes the existing publishing TODO too large and too vague to
execute safely. This item defines the product boundary between those concerns,
chooses the initial site topology, and sequences the launch so BenchBox does
not jump directly from local result files to an open public submission portal.

The target output is a high-confidence strategy that distinguishes
`benchbox publish`, `benchbox submit`, and `benchbox.dev/results/`, plus a
delivery sequence the rest of the TODO cluster can depend on.

**Phase assignment:** This is a prerequisite planning item. Must complete before
any Phase 1 implementation begins. The refined strategy memo at
`_project/analysis/benchbox-results-platform-strategy.md` contains the current
recommended phasing: Phase 1 (static explorer MVP with repo-local
`results-data/`), Phase 2 (PR-based community contributions against that
corpus), Phase 3 (hosted API, only if demand warrants).
preserves: The existing static GitHub Pages deployment for landing/docs/blog remains a valid baseline during planning
The schema-v2 result bundle remains the single canonical artifact for all downstream publishing and submission flows

description:
`psycopg2-binary` is a legacy PostgreSQL driver with known packaging
fragility (ships pre-compiled C extensions in a binary wheel, no async
support, soft-deprecated in many CI environments). `psycopg3` (package:
`psycopg[binary]`) is the successor — async-compatible, PEP 249 v3 compliant,
and actively maintained.

Surfaced as a deferred item in the DONE file for `tighten-dependencies-phase-plan`
(completed 2026-04-15): "Migration off psycopg2-binary to psycopg3 — driver
modernization — out of scope for an *elimination* audit. File separately when
product is ready."

This is not an elimination audit item — it is a deliberate driver swap that
may require updating connection-string parameters, cursor usage, and any
code that imports psycopg2 directly. Scope must be confirmed before
committing to the swap.
preserves: All Redshift and PostgreSQL benchmark runs produce identical results before and after the swap
Connection factory interface remains unchanged for any callers outside benchbox/platforms/

description:

Capture a dated baseline snapshot under _project/analysis/.

No new required CI check is introduced by this item

promoted to `merged-to-todo` -> this TODO on 2026-05-11, so the
blind-spot log records that they are integrated into a planned item
rather than sitting in the `actionable` re-triage queue:

  - 2026-04-30-114723-queue-dwell-contract — treat dwell-time

approach:
Build the targets in dependency order: pool-init (w1) is foundational,
then claim (w2) and release (w3) are the core lifecycle, then status
(w4) and reset (w5) are operational tooling, then docs (w6) and
deprecation (w7-w8) update the rest of the surface.

Use a portable lock wrapper for atomic claim. `flock(1)` is not present
on the macOS workstation, so the Makefile cannot assume it. Prefer
`lockf` on macOS, `flock` on Linux when available, or a small Python
helper that calls `fcntl.flock`. Lock file stays at
`<main-clone>/.git/pool.lock`. Single shared lock across all pool
worktrees — claim is fast (seconds) so contention is fine.

For state detection in worktree-pool-status:
  - free: `git symbolic-ref -q --short HEAD` is empty AND
          `git rev-parse HEAD` == `git rev-parse origin/develop` AND
          `git status --porcelain` is empty
  - claimed: not on develop, working tree may or may not be clean
  - stale: claimed AND `gh pr view --json state` returns MERGED
  - dirty: claimed AND `git status --porcelain` non-empty

Refer to existing `make worktree-add` and `make worktree-prune`
targets for patterns; reuse their git-worktree command structure.

description:
Replace the create-and-destroy worktree model with a retained pool of
worktrees. Default pool size is 10 (`POOL_SIZE ?= 10`), but the targets
must keep the size configurable so the workstation can be tuned without
editing Makefile logic. New agent sessions claim an available worktree,
update it from current `develop`, work there until merge, then release
it back to the pool.

This formalizes how concurrent agents share the workstation. The default
size of 10 bounds routine parallelism (which is also why Step 1 keeps
the test lock global — even with the pool bounded, 10 concurrent xdist
runs would saturate the machine).

Single PR via `make pr-open`.

## Post-merge runbook (not part of the PR diff)

After this PR merges to develop, perform on Joe's workstation:

  make worktree-pool-init

Then verify:
  - 10 worktrees present at `BenchBox.pool-01..10`
  - Each is detached at `origin/develop` and clean
  - Each has `.venv/` populated
  - `make worktree-pool-status` shows all 10 free
  - Each free worktree is detached and clean, NOT on the local
    `develop` branch; claim refreshes free slots to current
    `origin/develop`

Tracked as a follow-up checklist item in the PR description, not as a
work unit, because the work unit DAG is for code changes that can be
marked done by `todo-cli done <slug> <work-id>` against a commit.
preserves: Atomic claim semantics — two concurrent `make worktree-claim` calls must always pick different pool-NN worktrees, never collide
Existing make worktree-add target keeps working — only adds deprecation notice; do not break legacy non-pool worktree workflows mid-session
Pool worktrees retain their .venv/ across release/claim cycles — uv sync only runs at claim time after a fetch, and only if pyproject.toml/uv.lock changed
make worktree-pool-init is idempotent — re-running must not destroy or reset existing pool worktrees

Selects the first **Free** pool worktree (detached HEAD, working
tree clean, no local feature branch checked out). Claim fetches
and resets the selected worktree to current `origin/develop`
before creating the branch. Pool worktrees must not check out the
local `develop` branch because the main clone keeps `develop`
checked out and Git does not allow the same branch in multiple
worktrees.
Steps:
  1. Acquire a portable file lock on `<main-clone>/.git/pool.lock`
     (timeout 30s). Use `lockf` on macOS, `flock` on Linux if
     available, or a tiny Python helper using `fcntl.flock` so the
     target works on Joe's macOS workstation and CI.
  2. Iterate pool-01..POOL_SIZE; first match is "Free"
  3. In that worktree: `git fetch origin`, `git reset --hard
     origin/develop`, `git checkout -b $BRANCH`, `uv sync --group dev`
  4. Release flock
  5. Print: `WORKTREE_PATH=<absolute-path>`
Refuses (exit 1) if pool is fully claimed; suggests
`make worktree-pool-status` to investigate.

  3. `git checkout --detach origin/develop`
  4. `git fetch origin`
  5. `git reset --hard origin/develop`
  6. `git branch -D <feature-branch>` (the one just released)
  7. `git remote prune origin`
Worktree returns to **Free** state.

minimal, so the implementation should not touch GitHub protection/ruleset
settings. The highest-risk design point is check-name stability: GitHub

approach:
Minimum implementation surface: `.github/path-filters.yml`
(ruleset), the PR-tier workflow (`test.yml` or `pr.yml`) that adds
`ci-paths`, `content-guard`, `code-lint`, `code-test`, and
`ci-required-result`, plus a small local helper for `make pr-preflight`
and the pre-push hook.

Final implementation uses `scripts/path_filter_decision.py`, a stdlib-only
helper, instead of a third-party path-filter action. That keeps CI and local
`make pr-preflight` on the same code path, avoids a mutable action tag, and
lets content-only PRs classify paths before dependency installation.

Required-check aggregation has one hard GitHub Actions constraint:
`needs:` only works inside one workflow. If the required `lint` gate
stays in `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, `ci-required-result` cannot
observe it. Move/duplicate the required develop PR lint/type work into
the umbrella workflow before making `ci-required-result` the only
required check.

For the umbrella aggregation step, the explicit pass/fail script
(rather than relying on `needs:` propagation alone) is intentional:
it makes the "content-only can pass without Python tests" semantic visible in the workflow
log, and it correctly handles the case where `needs.lint.result` is
the literal string `"skipped"` (which evaluates truthy in some
comparison contexts).

Sequence the rollout: workflow changes first (w6 merged to develop),
THEN branch-protection/ruleset change (w7). Reverse order leaves develop
unmergeable for whatever interval because the required umbrella check name
will not exist on the base branch yet.

description:
Companion to Step 3. After Step 3 removes broad non-required lanes
from routine develop PR CI while preserving the existing lint +
Ubuntu 3.12 fast-test required contexts, this step closes the remaining waste:
PRs that touch zero code (TODOs, blind-spots, decisions, blog drafts,
agent-doc edits) still run the surviving 2-3 jobs unnecessarily.

Evidence: PR #66 and PR #67 — both pure `_project/TODO/**` changes —
triggered ~16 jobs each (full matrix + integration + parity + PySpark)
pre-Step-3, and would still trigger ~3 jobs post-Step-3. Both rounds
of waste are unnecessary; nothing in those PRs could possibly affect
the test suite.

Approach: introduce a single always-reporting required check
(`ci-required-result`) that classifies the PR's diff, runs a cheap
content guard for content-only PRs, and dispatches the Step-3 code
PR-tier (`lint`/type + Ubuntu 3.12 fast tests) only when code paths
changed. For TODO/blog/agent-doc-only PRs, the required check should
report green in <60 seconds without running Python fast tests.

Branch protection contract: `ci-required-result` becomes the required
status check on develop. Any jobs whose failures should block merge
must be in the same workflow dependency graph as the result job, because
GitHub Actions `needs:` cannot aggregate jobs from separate workflows.
The current `lint.yml` workflow therefore moves its develop PR gate
under the umbrella. Leave `lint.yml` for main/push/manual use, or for
non-required reporting only.

Single PR via `make pr-open`. Independently shippable AFTER Step 3
lands so the PR-tier workflow shape is stable. The starting required-checks
list is already established by the live `develop` ruleset; Step 3a is the
later step that changes it to the umbrella result check.
preserves: Branch-protection contract — required check always reports a status; the umbrella is the new required check, not a removal of all required checks
Code-touching PRs continue to run full PR-tier CI as today (post-Step-3 narrowed) — the skip applies only when every changed path is in the safe content-only allowlist
Content validation — content-only PRs skip Python fast tests but still run cheap TODO/markdown/docs hygiene relevant to the changed paths
Existing PR-tier code checks from Step 3 — Step 3a gates them, it does not remove lint/type or Ubuntu 3.12 fast tests for code/infra/unknown-path PRs
Fail-closed path behavior — unknown paths, .gitignore, .gitattributes, workflow/config/tooling changes run full PR-tier unless explicitly and safely reclassified
Single source of truth for the path ruleset — `path-filters.yml` is referenced by both CI and local pr-preflight; do not duplicate the rules
Step 4's develop-post-merge.yml safety net is unchanged — post-merge auto-revert still runs on every landed SHA, doc-only or not

work.notes:
Decide what is explicitly safe to treat as content-only. The rule is
fail-closed: a PR can skip code CI only when EVERY changed path is in
the safe content-only allowlist. Any path outside that allowlist is a
code/infra path and runs the full post-Step-3 PR-tier.

Safe content-only paths (skip Python fast tests; run content guard):
  - `_project/TODO/**`, `_project/DONE/**`
  - `_project/blind-spots/**`
  - `_project/decisions/**`
  - `_project/handoffs/**`
  - `_project/notes/**`, `_project/research/**`, `_project/planning/**`
  - `_blog/**`
  - `docs/**` ONLY if the content guard includes docs validation for
    develop PRs; `docs.yml` currently runs PR checks for `main`, not
    `develop`, so do not rely on it as-is.
  - `*.md` at repo root (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, etc.)
  - `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`

Examples that MUST run full PR-tier (non-exhaustive; unknown paths
also run full PR-tier):
  - `benchbox/**`, `tests/**`, `scripts/**`, `examples/**`
  - `landing/**`, `results-data/**`, `results-explorer/**`, `docker/**`
  - `_binaries/**`, `_sources/**`
  - `_project/scripts/**`, `_project/config/**`, `_project/compat/**`
  - `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `Makefile`
  - `.github/workflows/**`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`
  - `.claude/commands/**` (slash-command behavior affects agents)
  - `.gitignore`, `.gitattributes` (repo behavior and tracked-file
    conflict guardrails; `.gitignore` also has gitignore-lint)

Edge case: a single PR that touches BOTH categories runs full
PR-tier (failsafe). The filter is "all paths safe → skip code CI";
anything else runs code CI.

Document the ruleset in `.github/path-filters.yml` (a reusable
filter file referenced by the umbrella and local helper) so it has
a single source of truth.

Implementation record (2026-04-30):
  - Added `.github/path-filters.yml` with a `safe-content` allowlist
    covering TODO/DONE records, blind spots, decisions, handoffs, notes,
    research/planning records, blog drafts, docs, root markdown, and
    agent docs.
  - Added `content-guard` patterns matching the safe content surface so
    content-only PRs still run targeted validation before the umbrella
    can report green.
  - Added explicit `code-ci` examples for code, tests, tooling, workflow,
    Makefile, config, lockfile, git behavior, and agent-command paths.
  - Kept unknown paths implicit and fail-closed so a new top-level path
    runs full PR-tier CI instead of silently skipping code checks.
  - W1 review issue fixed: removed a broad `**` code-ci pattern because
    it would make path-filter tooling report code CI for every content
    change and defeat the skip.

work.notes:
Edit the workflow that runs on `pull_request` to develop (Step 3
may have split test.yml; if so, edit the new pr-tier workflow;
otherwise edit test.yml). Add:

  - `ci-paths`: always runs, checks out the PR, uses
    `dorny/paths-filter@<pinned-sha>` (not `@v3`) or the shared helper
    to emit:
      - `safe-content-only: true|false`
      - `needs-code-ci: true|false`
      - `changed-paths` / optional debug summary
      - optional metric line/artifact: content-only?, skipped code
        CI?, estimated runner minutes saved (for Step 5)
  - `content-guard`: runs when a PR contains safe content paths. This
    is intentionally cheap and targeted: TODO YAML validation,
    markdown/YAML hygiene, docs validation for `docs/**` develop PRs,
    and gitignore-lint if `.gitignore` is ever routed through this
    workflow. It must catch the kind of markdown/YAML errors that
    mattered on PR #66/#67.
  - `code-lint`: the post-Step-3 lint/type gate, gated on
    `needs-code-ci == 'true'`.
  - `code-test`: Ubuntu 3.12 fast tests, gated on
    `needs-code-ci == 'true'`.
  - `ci-required-result`: always runs, aggregates all of the above,
    and is the required check name.

Do not try to aggregate the existing `.github/workflows/lint.yml`
`lint` job from `ci-required-result`: `needs:` cannot cross workflow
boundaries. Move/duplicate the required develop PR lint/type gate
into the umbrella workflow before making `ci-required-result` the
sole required check. Leave `lint.yml` for main/push/manual surfaces
or non-required reporting only.

Required behavior:
  1. `ci-paths` and `ci-required-result` always run (no `if:`
     condition on those jobs).
  2. Content-only PRs run `content-guard`, skip `code-lint` and
     `code-test`, and pass only if `content-guard` succeeds.
  3. Code/infra/unknown-path PRs run `content-guard` as applicable
     plus `code-lint` and `code-test`.
  4. If `needs-code-ci == true`, `ci-required-result` fails unless
     both `code-lint` and `code-test` succeeded.
  5. If `needs-code-ci == false`, `ci-required-result` fails unless
     `content-guard` succeeded or no content guard was needed.

Concrete shape (sketch):

  jobs:
    ci-paths:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      outputs:
        needs-code-ci: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.needs-code-ci }}
        safe-content-only: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.safe-content-only }}
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        - uses: dorny/paths-filter@<pinned-sha>
          id: filter
          with:
            filters: .github/path-filters.yml
        - id: classify
          run: scripts/path_filter_decision.sh

    content-guard:
      needs: ci-paths
      if: needs.ci-paths.outputs.safe-content-only == 'true' ||
          needs.ci-paths.outputs.needs-code-ci == 'true'
      ...

    code-lint:
      needs: ci-paths
      if: needs.ci-paths.outputs.needs-code-ci == 'true'
      ...

    code-test:
      needs: ci-paths
      if: needs.ci-paths.outputs.needs-code-ci == 'true'
      ...

    ci-required-result:
      needs: [ci-paths, content-guard, code-lint, code-test]
      if: always()
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - run: |
            set -euo pipefail
            if [ "${{ needs.ci-paths.outputs.needs-code-ci }}" = "false" ]; then
              if ! { test "${{ needs.content-guard.result }}" = "success" ||
                     test "${{ needs.content-guard.result }}" = "skipped"; }; then
                echo "content-guard=${{ needs.content-guard.result }}"
                exit 1
              fi
              echo "Content-only PR — skipped Python code CI."
              exit 0
            fi
            if [ "${{ needs.code-lint.result }}" = "success" ] && \
               [ "${{ needs.code-test.result }}" = "success" ]; then
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "code-lint=${{ needs.code-lint.result }} code-test=${{ needs.code-test.result }}"
            exit 1

The required check on develop branch protection becomes
`ci-required-result`, NOT bare `lint` or `test` directly, only after
the workflow has landed on develop.

  - Added always-reporting `ci-paths` and `ci-required-result` jobs.
    `ci-paths` writes a JSON decision artifact and exposes

  - Added `content-guard` for content paths. It validates changed YAML

  - Added gated `code-lint` and `code-test` jobs. Their displayed check

  - Added `scripts/path_filter_decision.py`, a stdlib-only classifier

    local/CI callers without duplicating rules.
  - W2 review issue fixed: added explicit `git fetch` steps for the base

approach:
Build the workflow changes incrementally:
  1. cancel-in-progress (w1) is a small, low-risk YAML edit
  2. Auto-revert (w2) is the substantive change — use peter-evans/
     create-pull-request@v6 (mature, well-tested) rather than rolling
     a custom revert script
  3. Metrics (w3) is independent of auto-revert; both can run in
     parallel jobs in the same workflow
  4. Make target (w5) is the human-facing surface for w3
  5. Docs (w4) once the behavior is confirmed
  6. Smoke test in fork (w6) BEFORE merging — auto-revert that
     opens spurious PRs would be very noisy to roll back

For revert conflicts: the fallback to "open an issue" is intentional.
An auto-revert that conflicts probably means later commits depend on
the broken one, so a human needs to decide whether to revert the
whole stack or fix forward.

For metrics: keep it simple. JSON files in workflow artifacts, no
database, no service. Step 5 reads the last 30 days and aggregates.
If we end up wanting longer retention, push to a `metrics` orphan
branch instead — but that's a Step 5 decision, not Step 4.

work.notes:
New job `auto-revert-on-failure` triggered by
`workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure'` (or as a continuation
job in the same workflow with `if: failure()`). Steps:
  1. Identify the failing SHA (`github.sha` of the post-merge run)
  2. Identify the PR that introduced the SHA via
     `gh pr list --state merged --search "<sha>"`
  3. Create branch `auto-revert/<short-sha>` from develop
  4. `git revert --no-edit <sha>` (single SHA, no merge commits)
  5. If revert succeeds: push branch, open PR with title
     `Revert <pr-title> (#<pr-num>) — develop went red post-merge`,
     body includes failing run URL + originating PR link, label
     `incident:develop-red`, request review from PR author
  6. If revert fails (conflict): open issue with same metadata,
     label `incident:develop-red-revert-conflict`, no PR
Use `peter-evans/create-pull-request@v6` action or a small
gh-cli script.

work.notes:
Add a `metrics` job that runs with `if: always()` for every push to
develop, so both green and red post-merge runs emit a machine-readable
record. Computes and writes JSON artifact:
  {
    "merged_at": "<ISO-8601>",
    "pr_number": N,
    "pr_open_to_merged_seconds": N,
    "post_merge_red": false,
    "develop_red_detected_at": null,
    "auto_revert_pr_opened_at": null,
    "time_to_revert_pr_seconds": null,
    "next_green_develop_run_at": null,
    "time_to_recover_red_seconds": null,
    "conflict_on_merge": <bool from PR labels/comments>,
    "orphaned_failed_pr": false,
    "ci_runner_minutes": N
  }
On failure, the auto-revert job should update or emit the same shape
with `post_merge_red: true`, `develop_red_detected_at`, and
`auto_revert_pr_opened_at`. `next_green_develop_run_at` and
`time_to_recover_red_seconds` may be null at artifact creation time;
`make dev-loop-metrics` must fill them by scanning later successful
develop-post-merge runs. Artifact retention: 90 days (covers the
Step 5 measurement window). One file per merge. Step 5 aggregates
these records plus the explicit PR audit sources named there.

    auto-revert PR timestamp when one was opened, recovery placeholders,

approach:
This is a deliberately low-effort TODO. The work is "wait, then look
at numbers and write down the answer." The goal is a forcing
function: without this gate, Step 6 might get built reflexively
("we said we would") rather than because it's needed.

Be honest about what the metrics show. If the numbers are clearly
below threshold (e.g., P95 PR-to-merged is 8 minutes), DO NOT BUILD
is the correct call. If they're clearly above, BUILD. If they're
ambiguous, REASSESS — don't force a binary decision on noisy data.

For "sustained" interpretation: use 70% of days above threshold as
the rule. One bad week shouldn't trigger a queue; sustained pain
should. Adjust if 70% turns out wrong empirically.

description:
RESOLVED by merged PR #1054 "fix(cli): key DataFrame platform options by base
name so run can reach them" (branch fix/dataframe-platform-option-keying,
merged 2026-07-08) plus review follow-up PR #1062 "fix: forward DataFrame
platform options to adapter construction (#1054 review)". This TODO fell out
of the PR #1042 (fix/datafusion-df-mode-erasure) audit; the in-flight session
task_ce5bd997 that was implementing it landed as #1054. No re-implementation
was needed. See the "resolution" block below for the empirical confirmation.

---

All DataFrame-platform `--platform-option` specs are registered under
suffixed keys (`datafusion-df`, `polars-df`, `pandas-df`, `modin-df`,
`cudf-df`, `dask-df`) in the `_OPTION_SPEC_ROWS` table in
benchbox/platforms/__init__.py (~lines 768-786). But `benchbox run` parses
platform options with the POST-alias platform key:
benchbox/cli/commands/run.py `_parse_plat_bench_options` (:584) calls
`PlatformHookRegistry.parse_options(s.platform_key, ...)` where
`s.platform_key` has already been normalized by PLATFORM_ALIASES in
benchbox/cli/platform.py (datafusion-df -> datafusion, polars-df -> polars,
etc.). The specs are registered under the suffixed key, so the base-name
lookup finds nothing.

Result: `benchbox run --platform datafusion-df --platform-option
target_partitions=4` fails with
"Unknown platform option 'target_partitions' for platform 'datafusion'".
Verified empirically on develop 2026-07-07. Every DataFrame platform option
(streaming, rechunk, n_rows, dtype_backend, engine, device_id,
target_partitions, repartition_joins, parquet_pushdown, batch_size,
memory_limit, temp_dir, n_workers, ...) is unreachable from the run CLI.

Same key mismatch affects the sibling lookups in run.py:
`PlatformHookRegistry.get_default_options(s.platform_key)` (:645) and
`list_option_specs(platform_key)` (:658). Note an asymmetry to preserve or
reconcile: `_describe_platform_options` (:453-455) lowercases the raw name
WITHOUT alias normalization, so `--describe-platform-options datafusion-df`
DOES list the options — while `run --platform datafusion-df` then rejects
them. Describe and parse must agree after the fix.

Distinct from qpc-16 (that TODO is about plan_max_depth /
plan_capture_timeout_seconds in benchbox/core/results/platform_options.py, a
different allowlist). This one is the cli.platform_hooks PlatformHookRegistry
used by `run`.

IN FLIGHT: a background session (spawned task task_ce5bd997) is actively
implementing this fix as of 2026-07-07. If that lands a PR, complete this
TODO against it rather than starting fresh work.

Context: PR #1042 (fix/datafusion-df-mode-erasure) added
`_apply_dataframe_suffix_mode` in run.py so `-df` names resolve DataFrame
mode while the platform key stays the base name by design. DO NOT undo that;
the option-spec fix must keep the base-name platform key and instead make
the specs reachable under it.
preserves: PR #1042 behavior: `-df` names resolve DataFrame mode and the platform key stays the base name.
Registered default values for DataFrame options unchanged when the option is not set.
SQL-platform --platform-option behavior (e.g. databricks, postgresql) unchanged.

description:
Add dual-family DataFrame query implementations (expression + pandas) for all 20
FlightData OLAP queries, enabling execution on Polars, PySpark, DataFusion, Pandas,
Modin, cuDF, and Dask platforms.

FlightData is a 3-table benchmark (flights fact table + airlines/airports dimensions)
with 20 queries across 5 categories: on-time performance (5), delay analysis (4),
route analytics (4), temporal patterns (4), and carrier comparisons (3). The queries
use standard OLAP patterns - GROUP BY with aggregations, LEFT JOINs to dimension
tables, CASE expressions, HAVING clauses, date filtering, and ROUND/AVG/SUM/COUNT.

This is one of the simpler benchmarks to port because the schema is small (3 tables),
joins are straightforward (single-key LEFT JOINs to dimension tables), and query
patterns are standard aggregation/filter operations that map cleanly to both
expression-family and pandas-family APIs.

Motivation: FlightData uses real-world aviation data and is popular for OLAP
demos. DataFrame support enables benchmarking DataFrame platforms on realistic
analytics workloads beyond TPC-H/TPC-DS.

anti_patterns.dont: attempt to replicate SQL optimizer stress-testing in DataFrame mode
anti_patterns.instead: focus on correct multi-join execution and performance measurement
anti_patterns.why: DataFrame APIs define explicit join order, there is no optimizer to stress

anti_patterns.dont: use nested loops or iterative joins

approach:
Follow the read_primitives/dataframe_queries.py single-file pattern with QueryRegistry.
Use get_dataframe_queries() fallback method on the benchmark class.

Start with 4-5 table queries (w1) to establish the multi-join translation pattern,
then scale to 7-9 table queries. The central translation challenge is converting
implicit cross-joins (comma-separated FROM with WHERE conditions) into explicit
.join() chains. Use the title table as the hub for most queries since most
junction tables reference title.id.

For the expression family, the join pattern is:
  title.join(movie_companies, left_on="id", right_on="movie_id")
       .join(company_type, left_on="company_type_id", right_on="id")
       .filter(col("kind") == lit("production companies"))
       .select(col("title").min().alias("movie_title"))

Use QueryCategory.JOIN for all queries, plus AGGREGATE and FILTER as appropriate.

description:
Add dual-family DataFrame query implementations (expression + pandas) for all 13
JoinOrder benchmark queries, enabling execution on Polars, PySpark, DataFusion,
Pandas, Modin, cuDF, and Dask platforms.

JoinOrder is based on "How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really?" (VLDB 2015) and uses
a 21-table IMDB-like schema to stress-test query optimizer join ordering. The 13
queries (1a through 12a, plus 1b) feature complex multi-table joins (5-9 tables),
LIKE predicates, IN clauses, cross-table filtering, and MIN aggregations.

This is the most challenging benchmark to port to DataFrames because:
1. Multi-table joins (5-9 tables per query) require careful chaining of .join() calls
2. Implicit cross-joins in FROM clauses (comma-separated tables with WHERE join
   conditions) must be translated to explicit .join() sequences
3. LIKE patterns with wildcards need string method equivalents
4. Join order matters for performance, and DataFrame APIs may not preserve the
   optimizer stress-testing intent - document this caveat

The purpose of DataFrame JoinOrder is NOT to test optimizer join ordering (DataFrames
define explicit join order), but to measure multi-join execution performance across
platforms with identical join sequences.
preserves: JoinOrderBenchmark SQL execution path unchanged - embedded queries and file-loaded queries work identically
JoinOrderGenerator synthetic data generation produces files loadable by both SQL and DataFrame paths
get_queries_by_complexity() classification still works for SQL mode
title: Add DataFrame execution support to JoinOrder benchmark

operations (stateful, sequential). For schema introspection operations that are

pattern instead - this enables the standard DataFrame runner to execute them.

description:
Add DataFrame variant implementations for TPC-Havoc, enabling execution of
structurally diverse TPC-H query variants on Polars, PySpark, DataFusion, Pandas,
Modin, cuDF, and Dask platforms.

TPC-Havoc generates 10 structural SQL variants per TPC-H query (22 queries x 10
variants = 220 total). Each variant is semantically equivalent but uses different
SQL constructs (CTEs, scalar subqueries, window functions, UNION, etc.) to stress
different optimizer components.

For DataFrame execution, the concept translates differently: instead of varying SQL
syntax, DataFrame variants vary the API call sequence - different join orders,
different aggregation strategies (pre-filter vs post-filter), lazy vs eager
evaluation patterns, and different window function formulations. The goal shifts
from "stress the SQL optimizer" to "measure how different DataFrame API patterns
affect execution performance on the same logical query."

TPC-H already has DataFrame queries (tpch/dataframe_queries.py) with 22 queries
in both expression and pandas families. TPC-Havoc DataFrame extends these with
alternative implementations that use structurally different DataFrame API patterns.

This is architecturally unique - no other benchmark has the variant concept in
DataFrame mode. Requires designing a new variant registration pattern for
DataFrameQuery objects.
preserves: ResultValidator variant equivalence checking still works for SQL mode
TPCHBenchmark base class DataFrame queries (tpch/dataframe_queries.py) are NOT modified - TPC-Havoc imports them as baselines
TPCHavocBenchmark SQL variant generation unchanged - all 220 SQL variants still work via VariantGenerator/StaticSQLVariant

title: Add DataFrame execution support to TPC-Havoc benchmark

work.notes:
Design how DataFrame variants integrate with the existing DataFrameQuery/QueryRegistry
system. Key decisions:

1. Query ID scheme: Use "Q1v1", "Q1v2", ... "Q1v10" or "Q1-scalar-subquery",
   "Q1-cte-rewrite"? The former is consistent with SQL variant IDs; the latter
   is more descriptive for DataFrame where structural names matter.

2. Registry structure: One flat QueryRegistry with all 220 entries, or a nested
   structure (VariantRegistry wrapping QueryRegistry)? Flat is simpler and works
   with the existing dataframe_runner dispatch.

3. Variant categories for DataFrame (map from SQL variant types):
   - join-reorder: Different .join() sequences for same result
   - pre-filter: Filter before join vs after join
   - window-alternative: Window function vs groupby+join for same logic
   - cte-inline: Intermediate DataFrame vs chained expression
   - aggregation-strategy: Multiple small groupbys vs single large groupby
   - broadcast-hint: Explicit broadcast for small tables vs default
   - lazy-eager: .collect() placement variations (expression family only)

4. How variants relate to base TPC-H queries: Import from tpch/dataframe_queries.py
   as the "v0" baseline, then define v1-v10 as alternatives.

Write a short design doc in benchbox/core/tpchavoc/DATAFRAME_VARIANTS.md
documenting the chosen approach before implementation.

description:
Complete and integrate the existing DataFrame operations module for the Transaction
Primitives benchmark, enabling execution on PySpark + Delta Lake/Iceberg platforms.

Transaction Primitives tests ACID transaction semantics: commit, rollback, savepoints,
isolation levels, and multi-statement transactions using 23 SQL operations on TPC-H
staging tables (txn_orders, txn_lineitem, txn_customer).

A substantial dataframe_operations.py already exists (1290 lines) with:
- TransactionOperationType enum (10 operation types: ATOMIC_INSERT, ROLLBACK_TO_VERSION,
  TIME_TRAVEL_QUERY, CONCURRENT_WRITE, etc.)
- DataFrameTransactionCapabilities dataclass (per-platform capability tracking)
- Integration with DataFrameMaintenanceCapabilities and TransactionIsolation
- Platform-specific support declarations (PySpark+Delta, PySpark+Iceberg)

Key constraint: DataFrame transaction semantics are fundamentally different from SQL.
SQL uses BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; Delta Lake uses atomic writes with RESTORE for
rollback; Iceberg uses snapshot-based isolation. Polars/Pandas have NO transaction
support. This benchmark is PySpark-only in DataFrame mode.

The work is primarily integration - wiring the existing operations module into the
benchmark class, runner, and registry - plus filling in any incomplete operation
implementations and adding tests.

approach:
New file: docs/usage/driver-version-management.md

Structure:
  1. How BenchBox selects a driver version (no pin = use installed, pin = validate/install)
  2. Why uv run may not respect manually-installed versions (uv.lock sync behavior)
  3. Three reliable patterns:
     a. driver_version + driver_auto_install=true (BenchBox manages the install)
     b. uv run --with "duckdb==X" (inline uv override, no lock mutation)
     c. uv add "duckdb==X" --allow-prereleases (update the lock file)
  4. Verifying the actual version used: result JSON platform.client_version and
     execution.driver_version_actual fields

description:
BenchBox's driver version selection logic is non-obvious to users who approach it from
the Python packaging angle (e.g., "I installed version X, why didn't it use X?"). The
behavior is correct but the interaction with uv.lock and uv run is undocumented.

Current documentation gaps:
  1. No explanation of how BenchBox selects a driver version when none is specified
     (it uses whatever is installed, as reported by importlib.metadata)
  2. No explanation that `uv run` syncs the environment to uv.lock before launching,
     which can silently revert manually-installed versions
  3. No dedicated "How to test a specific driver version" guide - examples exist in
     --help-topic examples but not in docs/
  4. The docs/reference/cli/configuration.md driver_version/driver_auto_install entries
     describe the flags but not the underlying selection algorithm or the uv.lock
     interaction

Target: a clear, concise explanation in docs/concepts/ (or docs/usage/) that answers:
  - How does BenchBox decide which driver version to use?
  - Why might my manually-installed version not be respected?
  - How do I reliably benchmark a specific version (including dev/pre-release)?
  - How do I verify which version actually ran?

This should reference the result JSON's driver_version_actual field as the source of truth.

description:
PR #681 fixed the v0.3.0 clean-install failure (`import benchbox` raised
ImportError without pandas) by adding `pandas>=2.0.0` to
`[project.dependencies]` (`pyproject.toml:50-52`). That treated the symptom,
not the cause.

Root cause: `import benchbox` eagerly pulls an engine-specific module that
imports pandas at module top level. The reachable chain is
`benchbox/__init__.py:28` -> `platforms/__init__.py:286` ->
`adapter_factory.py:17` -> `clickhouse/__init__.py:5` -> `adapter.py:13` ->
`setup.py:9` -> `client.py:11 import pandas as pd`. `platforms/__init__.py`
already lazy-loads `ClickHouseAdapter` via `__getattr__`, but
`adapter_factory.py:17` reaches through the package `__init__`, defeating that
lazy design. `client.py` uses pandas at exactly one runtime site
(`client.py:144`, an empty-result `pd.DataFrame()`), so it is trivially
lazy-able.

Consequences of the patch: every install — including a DuckDB-only SQL run —
now pays ~49 MB (pandas + pytz, tzdata, python-dateutil, six) for a library it
may never touch. pandas is simultaneously a hard core dep AND an optional
extra (`pandas`, `dataframe-pandas`, `tpcdi`, `modin`, `dask`, `all`), an
incoherent manifest. This contradicts the project's own documented thin-core
philosophy: `docs/development/dependency-inventory.md:159` classifies pandas
as "DF/BM" (DataFrame/Benchmark-specific, not core), and finding F1
(`:209-227`) recommends removing engine-specific libs from core for exactly
this reason.

v0.3.1 is UNRELEASED, so the correct fix lands NOW: make the import surface
minimal and drop pandas back to extras before the cut, rather than shipping
the heavy patch and deferring. Everyone who needs pandas still gets it via the
extras and transitively via `chdb` (which requires pandas).

This TODO is a gate on `release-recovery-v0-3-1` w3 (`make release-cut
VERSION=0.3.1`): the cut should carry the minimal-surface fix, not the patch.
preserves: DataFrame mode, TPC-DI, and ClickHouse-local (chdb) runs must keep working — they receive pandas via their extras.
Do not re-tag, force-push, or alter the immutable v0.3.0 tag/PyPI artifact.
Do not weaken the release-required context or the core-only smoke gate to land this.
`import benchbox` MUST succeed on a clean core install at every step; w1 satisfies this before pandas leaves core in w6.
title: Drop pandas from core dependencies for v0.3.1 by fixing the eager import surface

exporters.py, visualization.py) that have both Plotly and ASCII paths. After removal, unify the

description:
Remove Plotly and the entire HTML chart rendering pipeline from BenchBox. The ASCII charting
system (2,255 lines, 6 chart types, zero dependencies) is the actively-used visualization
path for CLI, MCP, and CI. The Plotly/HTML path (~1,750 lines source + ~1,260 lines tests)
generates static .html files that nobody opens - there is no browser integration, no HTTP
server, no CI usage, and no documented user workflow that depends on HTML output.

Removing Plotly eliminates:
- Two parallel rendering pipelines with incompatible data models
- ~2,300 lines of source + test code (37% reduction in visualization module)
- 46 MB optional dependency weight (plotly 43 MB + narwhals 3.3 MB)
- The dual data model problem (BarDatum vs BarData, etc.) that forces every new chart type
  to be implemented twice
- Three test files that use pytest.importorskip("plotly") and may skip silently

This clears the path for the ASCII charting enhancement (enhance-ascii-charting.yaml) by
establishing a single canonical data model and removing the need for conversion layers.

Decision rationale: Evaluated in depth - HTML charts are the default format but disconnected
from real usage. MCP returns file paths for HTML (useless to LLMs) vs inline content for ASCII
(immediately useful). CLI generates files users must manually locate and open. No blog workflow
references chart generation. The feature is vestigial.
preserves: ASCIIChartBase interface and render() -> str contract must not change
All 6 ASCII chart types (bar, histogram, heatmap, box, line, scatter) must remain fully functional
CLI benchbox visualize command must continue to work (ASCII output)
Chart templates (default, flagship, head_to_head, trends, cost_optimization) must work with ASCII
MCP generate_chart tool must continue to work (ASCII format)
MCP suggest_charts tool must continue to work (format-agnostic logic)
NormalizedResult and NormalizedQuery dataclasses must be preserved (shared data loading)
ResultPlotter.from_sources() must continue loading and normalizing result JSON files
tests/unit/visualization/ascii/test_ascii_charts.py (934 lines) must pass unchanged

description:
`benchbox submit` writes a 16-line CONTRIBUTING.md into every submission
bundle (hardcoded as `_CONTRIBUTING_TEXT` at
`benchbox/cli/commands/submit.py:29-46`), and the CLI's "Next step"
message tells contributors to follow it. That file does NOT include
three steps the canonical `docs/contributing-results.md` requires:

  1. Regenerate `corpus-inventory.json` before commit.
  2. Target the `published-results` branch (not `main`).
  3. Optionally validate the bundle locally with
     `scripts/validate_submission.py`.

A contributor who reads only the in-bundle file will open a PR against
`main` with a stale inventory. CI catches it, but that's wasted
maintainer cycles and a worse first-time UX. Surfaced by the
agent-proxy dry-run on 2026-04-28
(see `_project/handoffs/external-dry-run-retrospective-2026-04-28.md`).

Fix options (pick one):
  A. Generate the in-bundle file from `docs/contributing-results.md`
     at package-build time so the two cannot drift.
  B. Replace the in-bundle file with a one-page checklist that points
     to the canonical doc URL and lists the three required commands
     inline.

work.notes:
A vs B is a real architectural call:
  - A: harder-to-drift but introduces a build-time read of
    `docs/contributing-results.md` from `submit.py`. Requires
    packaging the doc into the wheel or reading it relative to
    the repo root.
  - B: simpler; ships a checklist that names the four required
    steps and points contributors to docs.benchbox.dev for the
    full doc. Requires updating the checklist whenever the
    canonical doc changes -- but the checklist is small and
    stable.
Default recommendation: option B unless wheel-packaging the doc
is already cheap. Document the choice + rationale in a one-line
comment above `_CONTRIBUTING_TEXT` so future maintainers don't
re-litigate it.

description:
The `scripts/validate_submission.py` on the `published-results` branch
(pinned at v0.2.1, commit `0182c9556`) uses a per-DIRECTORY hash
algorithm (`hashlib.sha256()` over `path.encode() + file.read_bytes()`
for every file in `bundle_dir` excluding the manifest). The same
script on `develop` (post-PR #33) uses a per-FILE hash (just
`sha256(bundle_file)` plus a `companion_hashes` map). The writer in
`develop`'s `submit.py` also uses per-file. Result: a bundle produced
by current `develop`'s `benchbox submit` will fail CI on
`published-results` with `Bundle hash mismatch: manifest says XXXX,
computed YYYY`.

This was confirmed empirically during the 2026-04-29 Codex
agent-proxy dry-run:
  - Codex's manifest: `bundle_hash: 799c80a2...` (per-file SHA-256)
  - Validator on published-results computed: `8a89ab6f...` (per-dir)
  - `shasum -a 256` on the actual bundle file: `799c80a2...` (matches
    the manifest exactly)

Forensic and full reproduction at
`_project/handoffs/external-dry-run-retrospective-2026-04-29.md`
(Appendix B).

This is a release-blocker for the community submission flow: until
the validator on `published-results` matches the writer's contract,
no contributor can successfully submit a result regardless of how
closely they follow the docs. The bug is invisible to maintainers
who only run the validator inside `develop`, because both sides
agree there.
preserves: Backwards-compat with already-merged community submissions in results-data/bundles/ (zero exist today, so this is theoretical)
develop's per-file hash contract (per-file is the right design -- bundles are individually addressable in results-data/bundles/)
