description:
Code review (2026-02-27) found that the current get_query_plan() uses EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)
without ANALYZE, capturing ESTIMATED plans only - timing and cardinality fields are absent
in stored plans. Switching to EXPLAIN ANALYZE (FORMAT JSON) by default will capture actual
per-operator execution statistics while keeping the existing JSON schema intact.

Decision: EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the new default for capture_plans=True.
PRAGMA enable_profiling was rejected (different JSON schema, version-dependent inline
reading, not thread-safe in file mode) - see context_sections for full rationale.

Schema compatibility: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (FORMAT JSON) produces the same field names as
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON): name / timing / cardinality / extra_info / children.
The DuckDBQueryPlanParser already handles timing+cardinality when present - proven by
the DUCKDB_1_0_JSON_WITH_TIMING fixture (tests/fixtures/duckdb_plans_by_version.py:177).
The core get_query_plan() change is one word: EXPLAIN → EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Trade-off acknowledged: EXPLAIN ANALYZE re-executes each query (2× cost per captured
query). This is acceptable for plan capture runs where rich operator data is the goal.
An opt-out config key (analyze_plans: false) must be available for users who want
structural-only plan capture without the execution overhead.

Note: plan fingerprinting is unaffected - it already excludes timing/cardinality by
design (structural comparison only).

Reference: /Users/joe/.claude/plans/temporal-kindling-tarjan.md
preserves: Opt-out path MUST remain available: analyze_plans: false in config (or equivalent) restores EXPLAIN without ANALYZE for users who need minimal overhead
Parser behavior for plans without timing fields MUST continue working unchanged (backwards compatibility with stored plans from before this change)
Plan fingerprinting MUST NOT include timing/cardinality (QueryPlanDAG.compute_plan_fingerprint excludes these by design - structural comparison only)
title: Switch DuckDB plan capture to use EXPLAIN ANALYZE by default for actual per-operator timing

description:
SCD2 adversarial audit findings N6 and N7.

N6 - benchbox/sql_compat/rules/execution_filter/duckdb_write_primitives.py:
40-42 tests "MERGE INTO" in write_sql.upper(). Verified (scratchpad repro3.py)
false positives and false negatives, both real against DuckDB 1.3.2:
  - false positive: token only in a comment ('-- ... MERGE INTO ...') -> gate
    skips an op DuckDB would run fine.
  - false positive: token only in a string literal ('MERGE INTO staging')
    -> same.
  - false negatives: 'MERGE  INTO' (two spaces), 'MERGE\nINTO', and MERGE
    reached via a CTE -> gate does NOT skip, and DuckDB 1.3.2 raises
    ParserException on all three (confirmed).
No live instance today (all 21 catalog ops with the token use the exact
single-space form), so this is a regression trap for the next MERGE op added:
it would run and hard-error instead of skipping cleanly. The gate also reads
operation.write_sql (benchmark.py:422) and runs BEFORE platform_overrides
resolution (benchmark.py:428-432), so it does not see the effective SQL.

    the operation_id lookup at :43-45 are dead code.
  - the REGISTRY.register loop at :49-66 registers 1 duckdb execution-filter

    decorative today - but a future consumer (coverage matrix, compat report)

    the same write-only-registry shape.
  - tests/integration/test_write_primitives_duckdb.py:515 repeats the
    "112 - 20 failing MERGE INTO" arithmetic.

description:
DuckDB + TPC-DS loading fails after TPC-DS datagen was changed to remove trailing
delimiters from generated .dat files. The pipe-delimited loader in
DuckDBNativeHandler.load_table() unconditionally appends a _trailing_delimiter_
dummy column and uses SELECT * EXCLUDE (_trailing_delimiter_), which causes a
Binder Error when the file has no trailing delimiter.

Observed in a 72-run DuckDB version matrix (1.0.0-1.5.0rc1) across tpch/tpcds/
clickbench/ssb - TPC-H succeeds but TPC-DS consistently fails with:
  - "Binder Error: Column '_trailing_delimiter_' in EXCLUDE list not found in FROM clause"
  - "Data validation failed - benchmark execution halted"
  - "Empty tables detected: ..."

Additionally, `benchbox run` exits with code 0 even when the benchmark status is
FAILED, masking failures in automation pipelines. No result JSON is written for
failed runs.

Utility functions `has_trailing_delimiter()` and `get_column_names_with_trailing()`
already exist in benchbox/utils/file_format.py but are not used by the loader.
preserves: DuckDBNativeHandler.load_table() continues to handle CSV and Parquet inputs via their existing code paths (only pipe-delimited path is affected)
DuckDBNativeHandler.load_table() continues to load TPC-H .tbl files (which still have trailing delimiters) correctly
Successful benchmark runs still exit with code 0 and produce result JSON
title: Fix DuckDB TPC-DS loader regression: trailing delimiter detection and CLI exit code

description:
Extend the DuckLake platform adapter (see ducklake-platform-adapter) beyond the
default DuckDB-file catalog + local storage to the full v1 scope:

  - Catalog metadata backends: SQLite and PostgreSQL (in addition to DuckDB).
  - Data storage: S3 / cloud object storage for DATA_PATH (in addition to local).

DuckLake's catalog backend is chosen by the ATTACH connection string, each
needing a DuckDB extension:
  duckdb  : ATTACH 'ducklake:meta.ducklake'          (default; done in base item)
  sqlite  : INSTALL sqlite;   ATTACH 'ducklake:sqlite:meta.sqlite'   (DATA_PATH ...)
  postgres: INSTALL postgres; ATTACH 'ducklake:postgres:dbname=... host=...' (DATA_PATH ...)
(MySQL is explicitly excluded — DuckLake docs flag it as not recommended.)

Cloud storage is orthogonal to the catalog: DATA_PATH can be 's3://bucket/prefix/'
with httpfs + a DuckDB secret:
  INSTALL httpfs;
  CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, PROVIDER credential_chain);  -- or KEY_ID/SECRET/REGION
  ATTACH 'ducklake:...' AS lake (DATA_PATH 's3://bucket/bench/');

Selection is surfaced via --platform-option catalog=duckdb|sqlite|postgres and
--platform-option data_path=<local|s3://...>.

Sources: https://ducklake.select/docs/stable/duckdb/usage/choosing_a_catalog_database ,
https://duckdb.org/docs/lts/core_extensions/ducklake
preserves: Existing PostgreSQL-family platforms (postgresql, pg_duckdb, timescaledb) and their option plumbing are unaffected
No new hard dependency: sqlite/postgres/httpfs are DuckDB runtime extensions, not Python packages; the global pyproject `duckdb` pin is untouched
The default DuckDB-file catalog + local storage path from ducklake-platform-adapter keeps working unchanged when no catalog/data_path option is given

description:
Add DuckLake as a runnable BenchBox platform so it can be benchmarked on
TPC-H/TPC-DS/etc. alongside the other 45 SQL engines.

DuckLake (GA v1.0, April 2026 — https://ducklake.select) is an open lakehouse
format: table DATA is Parquet on local disk or object storage, and all catalog
METADATA (schemas, snapshots, stats, file lists) lives in a standard SQL
database (DuckDB / SQLite / PostgreSQL) instead of Iceberg manifests or Delta
JSON logs. It ships as a DuckDB extension and uses DuckDB's engine + SQL
dialect unchanged:
  INSTALL ducklake;
  ATTACH 'ducklake:<catalog>' AS lake (DATA_PATH '<parquet_dir_or_s3>');
  USE lake;  -- then normal CREATE TABLE / COPY / SELECT

Current state: DuckLake already exists in BenchBox as a table *format*
(converter benchbox/utils/format_converters/ducklake_converter.py,
DUCKLAKE_CAPABILITY in benchbox/platforms/base/format_capabilities.py:180,
DataFrame maintenance ops in
benchbox/platforms/dataframe/ducklake_maintenance.py) but NOT as a *platform*.
There is no DuckLakeAdapter and no `ducklake` entry in PlatformRegistry. This
TODO adds the adapter and wires it in.

This item = the MVP: DuckLakeAdapter subclassing DuckDBAdapter, with a
DuckDB-file catalog + local Parquet storage, full registry wiring, docs, and
live TPC-H/TPC-DS validation. SQLite/PostgreSQL catalogs and S3 storage are a
follow-on (see ducklake-catalog-storage-backends).

Evidence (pinned): the worktree venv resolves duckdb==1.3.2; the `ducklake`
extension requires DuckDB >= 1.3 (spec 0.1/0.2; 1.4 for 0.3). The global
`duckdb` pin in pyproject.toml is intentionally `>=1.0.0,<2.0.0` (kept at 1.0
floor for duckdb-wasm on-disk-format compatibility — see the comment at
pyproject.toml:90-94). Do NOT raise that floor; enforce the >=1.3 requirement
at runtime in the adapter instead.
preserves: DuckDBAdapter behavior is unchanged — DuckLakeAdapter only overrides create_connection (+ catalog targeting if w3 requires it); all existing tests/integration/*duckdb* keep passing
PlatformRegistry metadata/support-status validation continues to pass for all platforms
The existing DuckLake table-FORMAT path (ducklake_converter.py, DUCKLAKE_CAPABILITY) is untouched
The global pyproject.toml `duckdb` pin stays >=1.0.0,<2.0.0 (duckdb-wasm on-disk-format compat)

description:
CONFIRMED credential leak found in a post-merge review of the shipped DuckLake
adapter (#1082, #1096; both in _project/DONE/).

When catalog=postgres and the ATTACH fails (server unreachable OR wrong
password -- the *normal* first-run case), DuckDB raises an IOException whose
message echoes the full libpq connection string, INCLUDING the plaintext
password, twice. benchbox/platforms/ducklake.py create_connection() catches
this and re-raises it verbatim via `... Underlying error: {e}` (around
ducklake.py:684-695), so the password propagates to:
  - stderr / console / --verbose output
  - the runner's serialized error list (benchbox/core/runner/runner.py:209,253
    stringify exceptions into errors=[...]), which for this tool can be
    exported to result JSON and potentially published.

Reproduced live (bogus PG target, connection refused):
  ATTACH 'ducklake:postgres:dbname=cat host=127.0.0.1 user=bob password=SuperSecretPw123 port=5432' AS lake (DATA_PATH ...)
  -> IOException: "... password=SuperSecretPw123 port=5432 ... Unable to connect
     to Postgres at dbname=cat host=127.0.0.1 user=bob password=SuperSecretPw123 ..."
  -> `SuperSecretPw123` present in str(e): True

Asymmetry that makes this clearly a miss (not a design choice): the S3 secret
path in the SAME function already redacts (ducklake.py:669-678 catches the
CREATE SECRET failure and suppresses key/secret material). The postgres ATTACH
path was not given the same treatment.
preserves: Non-postgres (duckdb/sqlite) ATTACH failures keep their informative metadata_path/data_path context
The S3 CREATE SECRET redaction at ducklake.py:669-678 stays intact
get_platform_info() continues to omit pg_user/pg_password

description:
A targeted architectural review found 5 confirmed non-data-loading instances
of wrong-layer compensation.

Confirmed findings:
1. SQL lifecycle omits canonical benchmark identity even though the caller
   already has it, so the base adapter infers benchmark type from benchmark
   object internals for routing, dialect selection, and row-count validation.
2. Live result creation and export paths re-derive benchmark_id from
   benchmark names instead of receiving a caller-supplied canonical id.
3. Dry-run query extraction and resource estimation ignore
   BenchmarkConfig.name and re-infer benchmark identity from benchmark
   object attributes.
4. Doris resolves host/user/password/database in the config builder, then
   re-resolves env/defaults again in from_config() and __init__().
5. SingleStore has the same duplicated connection/database ownership split.

The fix is not to centralize more inference. The fix is to make the caller
pass the context it already owns, then delete downstream compensation in the
live execution path. Historical artifact compatibility fallbacks and
legitimate owner-layer discovery are explicitly out of scope.

DataFrame execution already receives benchmark_config explicitly and must not regress while SQL is brought to the same contract quality
Explicit CLI database/schema overrides still win over generated names for Doris and SingleStore
Historical artifact compatibility fallbacks in benchbox/core/results/schema.py and result-loading code remain intact
The original data-loading-only wrong-layer-compensation fixes remain untouched

description:
Integrate the full tuning configuration directly into benchmark result output files.

Currently, benchmark results reference the tuning file path but do not capture the
actual tuning configuration content. This is problematic because:
- The tuning file could be modified by subsequent runs
- Results become non-reproducible without the exact tuning config used
- Comparing results across different tuning configs becomes unreliable

Unlike query text (which is deterministically generated from benchmark definitions),
tuning configurations are user-defined and can vary between runs. The actual tuning
content must be captured at execution time to ensure result reproducibility.

Solution: Embed the complete tuning configuration (clauses, indexes, constraints,
etc.) directly in the result output, either inline or as a companion file.
title: Embed Full Tuning Config in Result Output

description:
Successful datagen-only runs (--phases generate) produce results JSON with
near-zero metrics: run.total_duration_ms is always 0, phases.data_generation
has only {"status": "COMPLETED"} with no duration_ms, and no per-table stats
are surfaced anywhere.

Three distinct bugs prevent existing timing and manifest data from reaching
the JSON output:

1. duration_seconds kwarg silently dropped: runner.py captures datagen_duration
   and passes it to create_enhanced_benchmark_result(), but that method does
   not declare duration_seconds as an explicit parameter - it lands in **kwargs
   and is never extracted. ResultBuilder._calculate_duration() then returns 0.0
   (no query times, no loading time). Fix: add set_total_duration() to builder
   and wire the param through.

2. duration_ms missing from phases dict: runner.py passes
   phases={"data_generation": {"status": "COMPLETED"}} without duration_ms.
   Fix: include "duration_ms": int(datagen_duration * 1000) in the dict.

3. Manifest-level per-table stats never surfaced: the manifest
   (_datagen_manifest.json) written by every generator contains per-file
   row_count and size_bytes. After _ensure_data_generated() completes these
   sit on disk but are never read back. Fix: add _read_datagen_stats_from_manifest()
   helper that aggregates tables_generated, total_rows, total_size_bytes and
   merges them into the phases dict.
preserves: All existing callers of create_enhanced_benchmark_result() continue to work - duration_seconds was previously silently accepted via **kwargs; making it explicit must not break any call site
ResultBuilder._calculate_duration() fallback logic (start/end times, then query time sum) remains intact for non-datagen paths
Standard benchmark runs (load+power) report correct total_duration_ms and phase timings - no regression
_ensure_data_generated() return type (bool) and calling convention in runner.py unchanged
title: Emit meaningful datagen metrics in results JSON

Full test suite passes with no regression

approach:
Do not introduce a custom forked build of duckdb-wasm unless every
other avenue fails. Prefer a library upgrade, then a supported config
entry point, then an upstream fix. The goal is to keep the explorer's
HTTP attach logic conventional so future maintainers do not carry a

blocked_reason: imported from YAML status: Blocked
description:
The explorer attaches `results.duckdb` at
`results-explorer/src/db.ts` via
`registerFileURL("results.duckdb", url, DuckDBDataProtocol.HTTP, true)`
followed by `ATTACH 'results.duckdb' AS bench (READ_ONLY)`. The RG-2
gate for the canonical browser read model requires that a cold
single-row lookup transfers ≤10% of the on-disk DB, i.e. DuckDB-WASM
should use HTTP `Range:` requests rather than a single whole-file GET.

In practice, with duckdb-wasm 1.32.0, the runtime's HTTP file-info
defaults (`reliableHeadRequests=false`, `allowFullHttpReads=true`)
short-circuit the Range probe even when `directIO=true` is passed to
`registerFileURL`, and the runtime falls back to a single whole-file
GET on ATTACH. There is no stable per-URL API to override those
defaults from the main thread:

- `db.open({filesystem: {reliableHeadRequests: true, allowFullHTTPReads: false}})`
  resets the WebFileSystem and breaks the already-registered URL.
- `SET reliable_head_requests = true` affects only the httpfs extension
  HTTP client, not the runtime's built-in HTTP file reader.
- The per-file `_globalFileInfo` object that carries these flags lives
  inside the DuckDB-WASM worker and is not reachable from the page.

The e2e harness already serves the snapshot with `Accept-Ranges: bytes`
and honours `Range: bytes=...` with `206 Partial Content` (see
`results-explorer/scripts/serve-browser-tests.mjs` and
`results-explorer/e2e/capability/range-read-budget.spec.ts`), so the
moment the browser runtime starts issuing range reads, the RG-2
byte-budget assertion can be re-introduced without any server change.

Deliverables:
1. Confirm the library-level behaviour against the current
   duckdb-wasm version at the time of work start (it may have
   gained a supported override by then).
2. Pick a path from: (a) upgrade duckdb-wasm to a version that
   supports per-URL range-read flags, (b) patch the runtime via a
   supported entry point such as a config object accepted by
   `registerFileURL`, or (c) file an upstream issue/PR and pin to a
   build that includes the fix.
3. Re-enable the byte-budget assertion in
   `results-explorer/e2e/capability/range-read-budget.spec.ts` using
   the server-side `/__test/transfers` accounting already in place.
preserves: The server-side transfer log at `/__test/transfers` remains available for the re-enabled assertion.
The test server's `Accept-Ranges`/`Range` handling in `results-explorer/scripts/serve-browser-tests.mjs` is not regressed.
`results-explorer/src/db.ts` continues to ATTACH the snapshot READ_ONLY and must not fall back to a JSON-only path.
title: Enable DuckDB-WASM HTTP range-reads for URLs registered via registerFileURL

work.notes:
Audited duckdb-wasm 1.32.0 (latest stable as of 2026-04-27;
1.33.x exists only as dev pre-release builds). Findings:

- `DuckDBConfig.filesystem` in
  `dist/types/src/bindings/config.d.ts` exposes three booleans:
  `reliableHeadRequests`, `allowFullHTTPReads`, and
  `forceFullHTTPReads`. There is no per-URL override on
  `registerFileURL`.
- `db.open({filesystem: {...}})` is the public entry point.
- Order matters: `open` AFTER `registerFileURL` resets the
  WebFileSystem and breaks the registration; `open` BEFORE
  registration is the supported sequence.
- `allowFullHTTPReads: false` makes the runtime error on
  first ATTACH ("IO Error: Cannot open database 'results.duckdb'
  in read-only mode: database does not exist"). This matches
  upstream issue duckdb/duckdb-wasm#1984's analysis: when the
  flag is false the runtime "always errors". So we cannot use it
  to force range-only reads.
- With `reliableHeadRequests: true` + `forceFullHTTPReads: false`
  + the default `allowFullHTTPReads: true`, the page loads but
  the runtime still issues a single whole-file GET against the
  registered URL (verified by the test harness transfer log:
  total 6,565,888 bytes = full DB size, no 206 responses).
- Issue #1984 documents the underlying buggy code path: even
  when the runtime first attempts a range read, an extra "full
  GET anyway" code block runs after. This block has not been
  removed in 1.32.0.

Conclusion: there is no flag combination on duckdb-wasm 1.32.0
that yields range-only reads against an HTTP-registered URL.
The fix must come from upstream (or from a 1.33.x stable
release once one ships). The byte-budget assertion has been
added to range-read-budget.spec.ts under `test.skip` so it
auto-enables when the runtime starts issuing 206s.

Update 2026-04-27: also verified against `@duckdb/duckdb-wasm@
1.33.1-dev53.0` (the latest dev pre-release). Same behavior —
whole-file GET on ATTACH, zero 206 responses, byte-budget
exceeded by 10x. Upstream has not addressed this in any 1.33.x
build to date. Reverted to 1.32.0.
work.summary: Re-audit duckdb-wasm runtime flags and the HTTP file-reader code path for the current version

work.notes:
Update 2026-05-01: still blocked on upstream. Current npm metadata
shows no stable `@duckdb/duckdb-wasm` release beyond `1.32.0`; the
package dist-tags point at dev builds (`latest=1.33.1-dev45.0`,
`next=1.33.1-dev53.0`). Upstream issue duckdb/duckdb-wasm#1984 is
still open, with no maintainer resolution or release note indicating
a supported range-only path for HTTP-registered URLs.

`/code review W2`: no required code changes are available under the
TODO guardrails. Upgrading to a dev pre-release or carrying a private
patched runtime would violate the `approach` constraint unless the
maintainer explicitly accepts that tradeoff.

Of the three candidate paths:

1. **Library upgrade** — no stable 1.33.x release is available
   (only dev builds 1.33.1-dev1 through 1.33.1-dev53 as of
   2026-05-01). Pinning to a dev pre-release violates the
   `approach` constraint ("Do not introduce a custom forked build
   of duckdb-wasm unless every other avenue fails").
2. **Supported runtime API** — w1 verified that no flag
   combination on the public `DuckDBConfig.filesystem` API yields
   range-only reads. The buggy "Perform a full GET anyways" code
   path in runtime_browser.ts is not toggleable from the page.
3. **Upstream issue/PR** — this is the path forward. File or
   comment on duckdb/duckdb-wasm#1984 with a minimal repro
   showing that even `reliableHeadRequests: true` +
   `forceFullHTTPReads: false` produces a whole-file GET on
   ATTACH against an `HTTP, directIO=true` registration. Pin to
   the first 1.33.x stable that includes the fix.

This work unit unblocks once a 1.33.x stable release with the
fix is published OR a private patched build is acceptable.
work.summary: Pick an unblock path and prototype it

work.notes:
Partially landed: the byte-budget assertion is now coded in

description:
Query result rows currently rely on fallback inference for `run_type` in several
paths (especially SQL `standard` execution), while other paths set run_type
explicitly (`warmup`/`measurement`, and DataFrame metadata/summary rows).

This creates ambiguity and repeated fallback logic in normalization/schema code,
and can cause inconsistent downstream analytics semantics when producer paths
omit run_type.

This TODO defines canonical run_type semantics and ensures all producer paths
explicitly stamp run_type before result building/export. It also aligns
enhanced execution-phase objects and adds contract tests so missing run_type
cannot regress silently.

approach:
Work units are sequenced: extend the existing pytest_collection_modifyitems hook
in warning mode first (w1), placing conflict detection BEFORE the deselection

while violations are fixed (w2-w13 can run in any order or in parallel - one

description:
43 tests across 12 files currently carry mutually exclusive marker combinations
that undermine the fast/medium/slow speed-lane semantics and cause selection
ambiguity for both humans and automation.

Discovered violations (as of 2026-04-01):
  fast + slow        : 13 tests in 5 files
  medium + slow      : 26 tests in 6 files
  fast + resource_heavy: 4 tests in 1 file

Conflict rules to enforce:
  Speed-lane mutual exclusion: a test may carry at most one of {fast, medium, slow}
  Exclusion-set incompatibility: fast is incompatible with {slow, stress, resource_heavy, live_integration}

The fix has two parts:
1. Conflict detection merged into the existing pytest_collection_modifyitems hook in
   tests/conftest.py, running BEFORE the deselection slice so all collected items
   (including those about to be deselected by -m filters) are inspected. Starts in
   warning mode, promoted to error mode once all violations are remediated.
2. Remediation of all 43 existing violations - each test gets a single correct
   speed marker based on what it actually does.

This makes the pytest_collection_modifyitems exclusion hook (added in
d84c897a8) a belt-and-suspenders safety net rather than the primary guard.
preserves: BENCHBOX_SKIP_MARKER_CHECK=1 suppresses validation errors after w14 promotion (escape hatch preserved); during w1-w13 migration, BENCHBOX_ENFORCE_MARKER_CHECK=1 opts into early error mode
No test logic changes - only marker annotations modified

make test-slow, make test-stress, make test-all still collect their expected sets - hook must not block explicit marker opt-in
title: Enforce no conflicting test markers: detection hook + remediation of 43 existing violations

1. Paired comparison bar chart - side-by-side bars (e.g., SQL vs DataFrame) with inline percentage
   change annotations, regression/improvement color coding, and scale notes

Library evaluation conclusion: Keep custom implementation. Evaluated 10+ terminal charting libraries
(plotext, plotext-plus, termgraph, plotille, uniplot, rich, textual, asciichartpy, drawille,
bashplotlib). None can replace the existing module without significant adaptation. Key reasons:
- BenchBox needs render() -> str pattern; most libraries print to stdout
- Benchmark-specific features (Pareto frontiers, best/worst markers, grouped multi-platform bars,
  auto-chunking) don't exist in any library
- Sub-character bar precision (1/8 Unicode blocks) exceeds all library implementations
- 4-tier terminal color degradation (truecolor -> 256 -> 16 -> none) with NO_COLOR support is
  more robust than any library
- Zero dependency advantage is significant
Closest competitor was plotext-plus (7/10 fit) but still needs wrappers for string output,
benchmark annotations, and regression highlighting. Full evaluation documented in this item.

description:
The shared result comparator silently widens equivalence in two engine-justified
but globally-applied ways, each of which can mask a real cross-surface value
divergence:
  - validation.py:718 (_numeric_values_equal) treats float('nan') and None as
    both "missing" and reports two missing values as EQUAL. Combined with
    _normalize_value mapping NaN->None, a DataFrame surface that produces a
    spurious NaN (e.g. 0/0 from a division bug) compares EQUAL to a SQL NULL.
  - validation.py:693 strips leading/trailing whitespace unconditionally
    (val1.strip() == val2.strip()), so "foo " vs "foo" is declared equal - masking
    a real transcription difference.
Both are justified for specific engine decode paths (e.g. ClickHouse Arrow/pandas
NULL decode, CHAR padding) but are applied engine-agnostically with no flag to
disable, so they widen equivalence for every gate.

Make both behaviors explicit comparator flags (e.g. treat_nan_as_null,
strip_strings) that default to STRICT, enabled only where an engine genuinely
needs them and documented at that call site.
preserves: Engine decode paths that genuinely need NaN-as-null or CHAR-padding tolerance still pass, via the explicit opt-in flag at that site.
Float relative-tolerance (1e-10) comparison semantics are unchanged.

{'ref': 'benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py:718', 'note': '_numeric_values_equal NaN/None handling - add a treat_nan_as_null flag, default False (strict).'}

title: Make equivalence-comparator value-widening (NaN==NULL, whitespace strip) opt-in instead of unconditional

description:
SOUNDNESS-CRITICAL COMPARATOR SURFACE: this TODO's work touches
benchbox/core/equivalence/cross_surface.py (covered by .github/CODEOWNERS as
`benchbox/core/equivalence/** @joeharris76`) and
benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py (adjacent to, and sharing the same
waiver-baseline discipline as, benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py, which
IS covered as `benchbox/core/**/validation.py @joeharris76`; note that
tpchavoc/equivalence.py itself is not literally matched by an existing
CODEOWNERS glob - verified against the current 3-line .github/CODEOWNERS -
but should be treated as soundness-critical and reviewed by the code owner
regardless). Its PR will require code-owner review before merge.

Verified by reading both modules on this branch: no known-divergence waiver
entry, in either file, carries any date or expiry field.
  - cross_surface.py's `known_divergences: dict[str, str | ClassifiedDivergence]`
    (CrossSurfaceGate field, line 371) holds bare strings (e.g.
    `_READ_PRIMITIVES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`, cross_surface.py:859-885) and
    `ClassifiedDivergence` instances (cross_surface.py:338-357, e.g.
    `_H2ODB_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES` at 813-816, `_CLICKBENCH_TIE_AMBIGUOUS` at
    619-624+) - neither the `str` nor the `ClassifiedDivergence` dataclass
    (fields: `reason`, `accepts`, `requires_live_divergence`) has a date field.
  - equivalence.py's four engine-keyed baselines (`KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`,
    `POSTGRES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`, `DATAFUSION_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`,
    `CLICKHOUSE_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`, all `dict[str, str]`) are plain
    key->reason-string maps with no date field either.

The only existing staleness signal in either module is "stale-baseline
failure": a waiver whose divergence has stopped reproducing is caught (in
cross_surface.py's `_report`, the `resolved` check at line ~1188-1192; in
equivalence.py's shared `_report`, a `resolved` PRINT only - see the sibling
TODO tpchavoc-duckdb-gate-vacuity-guard w3 for that gap). But a waiver whose
divergence is STILL LIVE (e.g. an "irreducible engine-semantic difference" or
an "approximate by construction" classification) never gets re-examined - it
can sit correct-when-written but stale-in-spirit indefinitely: the engine
version that produced the documented behavior may have changed, the
benchmark's data/queries may have evolved, or the original rationale may no
longer hold, and nothing forces a human to re-look.

This TODO adds a lightweight, OPTIONAL `review_by:` date to waiver entries
(both the bare-string form, by upgrading it to a small structured wrapper or
a side-table, and the `ClassifiedDivergence` form, as a new optional field),
and a warning-or-failure when a `review_by` date has passed, so long-lived
waivers are periodically forced back into review even when their divergence
never disappears on its own.
preserves: The existing stale-baseline (resolved-divergence) failure behavior in both modules' _report functions is unchanged by this addition - review_by is a new, independent check, not a replacement.

cross_surface.py's GATES stay green and equivalence.py's tpchavoc-equivalence-report* targets stay green after this lands (no waiver in either module should already have an accidentally-past-due review_by introduced by this change).
review_by is OPTIONAL - every existing waiver entry with no review_by continues to behave exactly as today (no forced migration, no new failure for entries that omit it).

work.notes:
DECISION, matching the open_questions defaults exactly (directed as the
policy for this batch and independently confirmed sound):
  (a) cross_surface.py: option (i) - added `review_by: date | None = None`
      as a third field on `ClassifiedDivergence`. Bare-`str` entries
      CANNOT carry a review_by (documented explicitly in both the
      dataclass docstring and the module's new "waiver review policy"
      section) - no bare-string waiver was converted to
      ClassifiedDivergence to add one. Verified this does not complicate
      the sibling read-primitives-waivers-classified-divergence TODO:
      `_READ_PRIMITIVES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES` (read_primitives gate) still
      has its existing bare-string entries untouched; nothing in this
      change forces or blocks that sibling's future conversion.
  (b) equivalence.py (tpchavoc): option (ii) - a side-table
      `dict[str, date]` per baseline, keyed identically to the baseline
      it annotates (e.g. `CLICKHOUSE_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES_REVIEW_BY`), passed
      into the shared `_report` as a new optional `review_by` parameter.
      No existing `dict[str, str]` baseline's value type changed.
  (c) WARN, not fail - matches the default exactly. A past-due
      `review_by` prints a "WAIVER REVIEW DUE - ..." line in both
      modules' `_report`s but never changes the return code, kept
      deliberately distinct in wording and code path from the existing
      `resolved` GATE FAILURE (per the anti_patterns).
Prior notes (superseded by the decision above, kept for context):
Two open design questions to resolve before implementing:
  (a) Carrier shape for cross_surface.py's bare-`str` waivers (the majority
      of entries - see _READ_PRIMITIVES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES, and any others
      not yet converted to ClassifiedDivergence by the sibling TODO
      read-primitives-waivers-classified-divergence). Options: (i) add
      `review_by` as a THIRD optional field on `ClassifiedDivergence` and
      require every review_by-bearing waiver to at least be wrapped in
      `ClassifiedDivergence(reason=..., accepts=lambda _: True, review_by=...)`
      even if it has no real predicate yet (accepts-everything is
      explicit, not implicit, in this form) - this reuses one type instead
      of two; or (ii) introduce a small side-table
      `dict[str, date]` (e.g. `_REVIEW_BY: dict[str, date]`) keyed by the
      same divergence key, checked independently of the waiver's own
      shape - avoids touching the `known_divergences` Union type at all.
      Prefer (i) if the sibling TODO's ClassifiedDivergence conversion is
      expected to land first (fewer bare strings to carry the concern for
      long-term); prefer (ii) if this item lands independently and should
      not force every bare-string waiver into a dataclass. State and
      justify the choice here.
  (b) Same question for equivalence.py's plain `dict[str, str]` baselines
      (KNOWN_DIVERGENCES et al.) - these have no ClassifiedDivergence
      equivalent at all today, so a side-table (ii)-style
      `dict[str, date]` per baseline, or a small `@dataclass` wrapper
      (`KnownDivergence(reason: str, review_by: date | None = None)`)
      replacing the bare `str` value type, is the realistic choice. Note
      this is a wider blast radius (touches every existing baseline
      entry's type) - if it proves too invasive for zero-value-change
      entries, the side-table is likely the pragmatic default.
  (c) Warn vs fail: decide in this work unit, do not defer. Given the
      module already treats a stale-baseline `resolved` divergence as a
      hard gate FAILURE in cross_surface.py (line ~1191), a past-due
      `review_by` on a STILL-LIVE waiver is a weaker signal (the waiver
      may still be entirely correct) - default to WARN (print prominently,
      do not fail exit code) unless a strong case for FAIL emerges (e.g.
      "the gate is meant to be a hard forcing function and a warning is
      too easy to ignore"). Record the decision and rationale.

description:
The strategy doc says: "A dedicated `benchbox-results` repository remains
an optional future extraction if corpus size or contribution volume starts
to overwhelm the main repo. It is not a Phase 1 or early Phase 2
requirement."

Without an explicit checkpoint, this becomes a perpetually deferred
question that surfaces ad-hoc the first time someone gets annoyed about
repo size. The decision has real trade-offs (CI permissions, contributor
friction, SHA tracking across two repos, history rewrite risk) that
deserve a structured evaluation rather than a hot take.

This item creates the forcing function: a defined trigger condition, a
pre-written ADR template, and a lightweight evaluation procedure. When
the trigger fires, the evaluation produces a yes/no answer with rationale.
Until then, this TODO stays in planning as a marker that the decision is
intentional, not forgotten.

description:

sources of drift.

`benchbox/core/runner/dataframe_runner.py` is still load-bearing for CLI and

while adapter factory, capabilities, CLI/dry-run helpers, and the deprecated
runner use platform suffix/default-mode logic. A new DataFrame family or
registry default can therefore disagree with the lifecycle branch.

description:
Independent verification found two lifecycle/result consistency risks in
`benchbox/core/runner/runner.py`.

Driver metadata propagation exists in two places: the shared
`benchbox/core/results/driver_metadata.py:apply_driver_metadata()` helper
used by CLI/orchestrator paths, and runner-local
`_enrich_driver_runtime_metadata()` plus `_apply_driver_meta_to_dicts()`.
The original critic overstated precedence divergence: both paths prefer
adapter values over database config fallbacks. The real divergence is that
the runner also writes driver fields into `result.platform_info` with
`setdefault()`, while the shared helper only writes result attributes and
`execution_metadata`.

Post-load validation also conflates not-applicable validation with failed
validation. `_run_postload_validation()` returns `None` for `adapter is None`,
but returns a synthetic invalid `ValidationResult` when an adapter lacks
`create_connection`/`close_connection`. Consumers already treat `None` as
"no validation record" and aggregate `is_valid=False` as a failed stage.
preserves: Actual post-load validation exceptions still surface as failed validation, not as not-run.
Adapter-sourced driver metadata remains higher precedence than database_config fallbacks.
DataFrame post-load validation remains skipped unless a separate TODO changes DataFrame validation support.
Driver metadata still serializes through schema-v2 platform/execution blocks as before.
Existing platform_info keys are not overwritten by driver metadata propagation.

description:

too much, but also found that the original critic overstated the facts. The
dataclass currently has 78 fields, not roughly 205. It has several platform
metadata dictionaries, `_benchmark_id_override`, and a platform-specific
`native_comparison` field. The claimed `migration` top-level model field is
not a `BenchmarkResults` field; schema-v2 exports migration as a phase when
`ExecutionPhases.migration` is present, while a separate pg_mooncake script

`platform_extensions: dict[str, Any]`, is therefore directionally useful but
risky. Result JSON is a product boundary consumed by runtime loaders, CLI

narrow extension policy before any field move.

description:
Independent verification of the execution/results architecture review found
two adjacent duplication risks in the TPC metrics and power-test result path.

First, `benchbox/core/tpc_metrics.py` is an 877-line legacy module with no
production importers in the current tree. Production code imports
`benchbox.core.results.metrics.TPCMetricsCalculator`, which is re-exported
from `benchbox.core.results`. Only `tests/unit/core/test_tpc_metrics.py`
imports the legacy module. The module is therefore a deletion candidate, but
it contains richer validation/reporting classes that should be audited before
removal so useful behavior is not silently lost.

Second, `benchbox/platforms/base/execution.py` repeats TPC-H and TPC-DS
power-test result-dict conversion in four blocks, plus four
`power_test_error` sentinels. The duplication is smaller than the original
critic claimed, but it is still enough to make failure/result schema drift
likely when one TPC driver changes.
preserves: Do not weaken TPC compliance or row-count validation behavior as part of cleanup.
No result JSON schema change from metrics-module retirement or conversion-helper extraction.
Power-test failure sentinels still make all-query factory failures visible as FAILED runs.
TPC-H and TPC-DS Power@Size calculations continue using the canonical `results.metrics.TPCMetricsCalculator` formulas.

prior_art.concept: benchbox/core/results/builder.py: result-builder metric population - preserve as the production metric source.
benchbox/core/results/metrics.py: canonical lightweight TPC metric formulas - extend this rather than keeping a second calculator.
benchbox/platforms/base/execution.py: current TPC-H/TPC-DS power conversion blocks - consolidate locally first.
docs/reference/public-contracts.md: contract tier map - consult before deleting any import path that may be public.

title: Execution/results hardening: retire legacy TPC metrics and normalize power-result conversion

description:
The MCP server currently exposes only 11 tools while the CLI has ~34 commands.
This creates a significant gap in what AI agents can accomplish via MCP vs CLI.

Current MCP coverage:
- Discovery: 4 tools (list_platforms, list_benchmarks, get_benchmark_info, system_profile)
- Execution: 4 tools (run_benchmark, dry_run, validate_config, get_query_details)
- Results: 3 tools (list_recent_runs, get_results, compare_results)

Major gaps identified:
- Data preparation (datagen, convert)
- Query plan analysis (show-plan, plan-history)
- Dependency checking (check-deps)
- Performance analytics (report trends, regressions, rankings)
- Result aggregation and export

This TODO adds 7+ new MCP tools and 2 new MCP prompts to close the most important gaps.
title: Expand MCP tool surface area to match CLI capabilities

description:
Fingerprint fast-paths currently ignore core logical structure (join conditions,
grouping, projections, limits/offsets), so materially different plans hash the
same and are marked identical. Stored fingerprints are also trusted on ingest,
allowing stale/tampered hashes to bypass comparison. Tighten the structural
signature, recompute/verify fingerprints on load and before comparison, and
update regression/summary flows to refuse hashes that don’t match the current
tree. Ensure plan history and CLI outputs surface verification failures cleanly.
title: Expand query plan fingerprint coverage and verification

description:
The current CLI handling of `--tuning` argument uses implicit logic that can confuse users.
When users specify `--tuning tuned`, the system silently attempts to load a template from
`examples/tunings/{platform}/{benchmark}_tuned.yaml`. If not found, it falls back to basic
constraints without warning. Users have no visibility into which tuning file was loaded
or what settings are being applied.

Key issues identified:
1. Silent template loading - users don't know what template is used
2. Implicit fallback chain - silent fallback to basic config if template missing
3. No discovery mechanism - users must manually find tuning files
4. Path resolution ambiguity - custom paths resolved from cwd only
5. Error messaging - invalid path treated same as invalid keyword
6. "auto" mode unclear - documentation doesn't explain how it differs from "tuned"

This TODO addresses making tuning file resolution explicit and transparent so users
always know exactly what tuning configuration is being applied and where it came from.
title: Make tuning file resolution explicit and transparent in CLI

description:
Post-launch audit (2026-04-14) found that the explorer compare view
ships only 2 inline SVG components (grouped bar chart + simple ratio
table) while the CLI offers 15 chart types. The most strategically
important gap for the "dynamic comparison tool" claim is the absence
of charts that make per-query performance deltas legible at a glance:

  1. Normalized speedup chart (log scale, baseline-relative) - answers
     "how much faster/slower is platform B vs platform A per query?"
     The current grouped bar chart doesn't normalize, so a 1ms vs 2ms
     delta looks the same as a 100ms vs 200ms delta.

  2. Diverging bar chart (per-query improvement/regression) - answers
     "which queries got faster and which got slower?" A positive/negative
     bar per query makes regressions immediately obvious. The CLI's
     `diverging_bar` chart type is the primary tool for this.

These two charts close the most visible CLI parity gap and directly
support the compare view's core UX claim.

A phase breakdown (stacked load vs query time) and percentile ladder
are valuable but deferred - they require phase timing fields that are
not yet in the manifest.
preserves: Compare view URL format - chart selection is UI state, not URL state (no new query params needed)
Existing grouped bar chart - it is the default for 3+ result comparisons and remains accessible via the chart selector
Null-safety: if geomean_ms is missing, disable normalized speedup with a clear message
title: Add normalized speedup and diverging bar charts to explorer compare view

description:
Post-launch audit (2026-04-14) found that a visitor to a result detail
page cannot determine:
  - What the "Duration" number means (sum? mean? median?)
  - Whether tuning was applied (currently just a boolean)
  - Whether warmup queries are included in the timing
  - What execution mode was used (SQL vs DataFrame)
  - What hardware the result was produced on beyond OS/arch/CPU count

This matters because BenchBox's differentiator over ClickBench is
"rich per-query detail - execution plans, tuning configurations,
validation status". If a visitor can't interpret the numbers, that
claim is hollow. The absence of methodology disclosure also makes it
impossible to assess whether two results are meaningfully comparable.

This TODO adds a "How this was measured" disclosure section to the
ResultDetail page that surfaces the aggregation method, execution mode,
tuning state, test type, and key environment parameters.

description:
The strategy review (2026-04-15) identified that defaulting to geometric
mean as the single ranking metric across all benchmarks is wrong:

- TPC-H and TPC-DS define **power_score** (= 3600 / geomean × scale
  adjustment) as the standard metric. Users arriving from published
  TPC results expect to see that number.
- ClickBench and SSB have no published aggregate; geomean is a
  reasonable default there.
- Custom or ad-hoc benchmarks should expose both so users can pick.

This TODO introduces a per-benchmark-family ranking metric registry and
threads it through the pipeline and UI. The matrix leaderboard uses
`power_score` for TPC-H/TPC-DS and `geomean_ms` for everything else;
both are shown in each row, but the primary sort is the canonical one.

Scope excludes computing power_score (the CLI already does this) - this
TODO only ensures the explorer surfaces and ranks by the right metric.

approach:
Follow a research-first but opinionated cutover, not an additive
compatibility migration.

First, inventory every runtime metric fetch and every pipeline artifact that
currently feeds it. Then define the DuckDB schema and materializations that
replace those paths. After the research gate, wire the explorer pipeline
directly from committed JSON objects into DuckDB, move all metric surfaces
onto typed DuckDB queries, and remove metric-bearing JSON outputs and
loaders.

Temporary parity checks are allowed as verification scaffolding, but JSON is
not a second product contract. If a surface shows metrics to the user, those
metrics must exist in DuckDB first.

description:
Rework the results explorer so benchmark landing pages stay matrix-first
while DuckDB-WASM becomes the single runtime store for every user-visible
metric. Today the implementation is split-brain: `Query.tsx` already runs
against DuckDB, but `Home.tsx`, `PlatformIndex.tsx`, `BenchmarkIndex.tsx`,
`Compare.tsx`, and `ResultDetail.tsx` still fetch metric-bearing JSON
through `results-explorer/src/manifest.ts`.

The target contract is stricter than "prefer DuckDB when convenient":
committed JSON result objects are immutable source inputs; the explorer
pipeline projects them directly into `results.duckdb`; and every
user-visible metric, aggregate, rank, compare cell, detail timing, and
cohort summary is read from DuckDB. Any JSON that survives after this work
is bootstrap-only navigation metadata and must not carry user-visible
metrics.

This item still needs a research gate before implementation, but that gate
is for schema and cutover precision, not to re-open whether JSON remains a
first-class metric surface. The end state is DuckDB-only for explorer
metrics.

Verified current-state anchors:
  - `results-explorer/src/db.ts` attaches `/results/data/results.duckdb`
    with `ATTACH ... AS bench (READ_ONLY)`.
  - `results-explorer/src/pages/Query.tsx` already queries `bench.results`
    but still bootstraps schema from `results_schema.json`.
  - `results-explorer/src/manifest.ts` fetches `manifest.json`,
    `benchmarks/*.json.gz`, `details/*.json`, `compare/*.json`,
    `meta_leaderboard.json`, and `short_ids.json`, making JSON the
    dominant runtime read path today.
  - `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/duckdb_builder.py` currently emits only
    a thin `results` table plus `results_schema.json`, so DuckDB cannot yet
    serve Home, platform, benchmark, compare, and detail surfaces alone.
preserves: Any temporary bridge artifact used during W2-W4 page-by-page migration is regenerated from the same pipeline pass that writes DuckDB, never hand-patched, and cannot define, override, or outlive user-visible metrics
Benchmark landing pages remain matrix-first default routes; `/results/query` stays a secondary analysis surface rather than the primary explorer entrypoint
Committed JSON result objects remain immutable source inputs; the browser does not fetch them directly for metric rendering
DuckDB is always attached read-only in the browser; no implementation step may weaken `ATTACH ... (READ_ONLY)` or permit persistent mutation from the SQL workbench

Every result trusted enough to publish appears in the DuckDB published-results dataset with its identity preserved (`result_id`, `tuning_mode`, `trust_label`); the pipeline never silently collapses, dedupes, or hides publishable variants - users must be able to compare across tuning levels AND trust levels from the same store
Every user-visible metric, rank, aggregate, and detail timing shown in the explorer originates from DuckDB rather than JSON sidecars or TypeScript-only recomputation

Final-value parity for derived metrics is defined against the canonical Python reference computation in `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` (with read-only imports from `benchbox/core/results/`), NOT against pre-calculated CLI JSON, current TS reduction libs, or bridge artifacts
Raw JSON bundles under `public/data/bundles/` are a download-only affordance; no `src/pages/` or `src/components/` file fetches from `/results/data/bundles/` at runtime
Shareable compare flows remain available after cutover, but route convenience is subordinate to the DuckDB-only metric contract
The explorer remains static-hosted and browser-executed; no server API, auth dependency, or hosted query runtime is introduced by this TODO

work.notes:
Deliverables:
  1. A concrete call-site inventory for Home, PlatformIndex,
     BenchmarkIndex, Compare, ResultDetail, and Query showing the
     current data source and the target DuckDB table/view for each
     user-visible metric.
  2. A schema decision record mapping every user-visible explorer metric
     to DuckDB tables/views, plus the minimal bootstrap JSON that may
     remain and proof that it carries no metrics.
  3. A direct ingest contract documenting `committed JSON -> explorer
     pipeline -> DuckDB` and explicitly rejecting metric-bearing JSON as
     a steady-state runtime contract.
  4. A cutover/deletion order showing which JSON readers and JSON
     artifacts are removed or demoted once DuckDB parity is proven.
  5. A committed `visible_metrics.yaml` fixture enumerating every
     user-visible metric column across the ten canonical tables and
     classifying each as `raw_copy` (source-fidelity contract against
     the committed bundle field) or `derived` (final-value parity
     contract against the canonical Python reference computation).
     This file is the registry G-2 consumes and is required before W2
     starts.
  6. A definition-of-terms block pinning the meaning of the parity
     vocabulary used across this TODO:
       - "canonical Python reference computation" = the pipeline's own
         Python implementation inside
         `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` (plus read-only imports
         from `benchbox/core/results/`). TypeScript is never a
         reference oracle.
       - "final-value parity" = the rendered user-visible value
         produced by the DuckDB-backed read path equals the canonical
         Python reference computation for the same inputs, within a
         documented tolerance per metric. Parity is NOT defined
         against whatever the CLI, a pre-calculated JSON artifact, or
         the current TS reduction libraries happen to emit today.
       - "source-fidelity parity" = raw fields copied into DuckDB
         equal the corresponding field in the committed JSON bundle
         verbatim.
  7. A compute-ownership note answering: for every derived metric in
     `visible_metrics.yaml`, does the canonical Python reference
     computation already exist under
     `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` or `benchbox/core/results/`,
     or must a new module be added under
     `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` (the only write-legal home for
     new reduction code under this TODO's scope_limit)? If a derived
     metric is TS-only today (e.g. currently lives in
     `queryReduction.ts`, `chartMath.ts`, `ranking.ts`, or
     `compliance.ts`), record it here and plan to port the logic into
     `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` during W2.

Quantified research gates (each must be green or explicitly risk-accepted
before w2 starts; record findings in the schema decision record above):

  - RG-1 Cold-start init budget: measure time from page load to first
    successful SQL result against `results.duckdb` (cold cache, mid-tier
    laptop, Safari/Chrome/Firefox). Pass: p50 <1500ms, p95 <3500ms at
    current corpus; p95 <5000ms at 10x corpus.
  - RG-2 HTTP range-reads: verify `DuckDBDataProtocol.HTTP` with
    READ_ONLY ATTACH issues range requests and that benchbox.dev /
    GH Pages returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes` with 206 responses for a
    single-row `WHERE result_id = ?` query. Pass: the sum of HTTP
    Content-Length bytes transferred for a cold single-row lookup is
    ≤10% of the total `results.duckdb` file size, measured on the
    current corpus.
  - RG-3 DB size budget: build DB at 1x, 5x, 20x, 100x synthetic corpus
    (duplicated bundles with mutated ids). Record the `results.duckdb`
    file size on disk at each scale and publish the 1x baseline in the
    schema decision record. Pass: on-disk `results.duckdb` size grows
    sub-linearly in bundle count AND stays ≤20 MB at 100x. If the
    measured 1x baseline makes 20 MB at 100x structurally impossible
    (e.g. baseline already >1 MB per bundle), record a revised numeric
    ceiling in the decision record and escalate to RG-5 evaluation.
  - RG-4 COEP/COOP hosting: confirm either the `mvp` single-threaded
    DuckDB-WASM bundle meets RG-1 budgets, OR COEP/COOP headers can be
    served by the deploy target. Pass: a chosen WASM bundle works with
    the current hosting configuration.
  - RG-5 Single DB vs partitioned: only if RG-3 fails. Prototype
    multi-DB `ATTACH` from WASM. Default is single DB per the "one and
    only" rule; partitioning is a fallback, not a preference.
  - RG-6 View materialization budget: benchmark each canonical surface
     query cold against 100x corpus. Pass: <250ms p95 as a plain VIEW,
     otherwise promote to materialized `CREATE TABLE AS`.
  - RG-7 Attach-failure UX: every page renders a diagnostic ErrorMessage
    when the DB fails to attach (0-byte, 404, CORS). Pass: unit-tested
    per page, no silent JSON fallback.
  - RG-8 toJSON fidelity: round-trip every column type through
    `queryRows` in a Vitest matrix. Pass: no precision loss on DOUBLE /
    BIGINT / DECIMAL; date handling is explicit.
  - RG-9 Read-only fuzz: adversarial SQL (CREATE TABLE, ATTACH, COPY TO,
    INSTALL, LOAD, HTTPFS) against the READ_ONLY attached DB in WASM.
    Pass: all fail harmlessly with no side effects.

Research gate exit criterion: all RGs green or documented accepted-risk
note reviewed with the user, and a frozen `schema.sql` fixture committed
alongside the decision record.

Final names can change in w1, but every surface above must have an

Pipeline implementation rules:
  - `duckdb_builder.py` rewrites the 19-column stub (currently lines
    25-131) into a full-schema builder. Uses `CREATE OR REPLACE` on each
    build; the corpus is the only source of truth, so there are no
    migrations.
  - `pipeline.py` `run()` becomes: enumerate `bundles/*.json`, validate
    via `SchemaV2Validator`, compute derived values in memory (display
    timings, short_id, is_ranking_eligible, compliance_class, matrix
    cells, rankings, meta-leaderboard rows, cohort metadata), bulk
    insert in one transaction, copy raw bundles to
    `public/data/bundles/` for the raw-bundle download affordance ONLY.
  - All derived-value reductions consumed by the pipeline live under
    `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` or are imported read-only from
    `benchbox/core/results/`. This is the canonical Python reference
    computation for G-2 parity. If a reduction is currently TS-only
    (e.g. in `queryReduction.ts`, `chartMath.ts`, `ranking.ts`,
    `compliance.ts`), port the algorithm into
    `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` in this work item; the TS copy
    becomes dead code to be deleted in W4 once no page imports it.
  - W2 is ADDITIVE on the pipeline side. The pipeline starts emitting
    the ten canonical tables and keeps all existing metric-bearing
    JSON emitters running as bridge artifacts until the consuming
    page migrates in W4. No metric-JSON emitter is deleted at W2
    exit. This is the only reading that is consistent with "do not
    remove the artifact still backing a live page until that page
    migrates" - W4 removes each emitter in the same slice as its
    last consumer, and W7 does the final sweep.
  - Bridge artifacts are scaffolding, never a second accepted metric
    contract. During W2-W4, if a bridge artifact and DuckDB disagree,
    DuckDB is canonical by rule and the bridge artifact must be
    regenerated from the same pipeline pass, not hand-patched.
  - If `manifest.json` survives past W7, it is strictly non-metric
    route/navigation bootstrap derived from DuckDB-owned identities
    only. A key-whitelist contract test (see G-8) enforces this.
  - No TypeScript-side recomputation of display reductions, geomean,
    rank, compliance class, speedup ratios, or any other user-visible
    metric is permitted downstream. TS is allowed to do presentation
    formatting (locale formatting, unit suffixes, truncation) on
    values already produced by the canonical Python reference
    computation and read from DuckDB.

work.notes:
Surfaced during W2 contract tests: the same platform can legitimately
appear in a cohort more than once (different `tuning_mode`, different
`trust_label`, different run). The originating schema pinned
`cohort_metadata` PRIMARY KEY to `(cohort_key, platform_id)` and the
W2 builder silently deduplicated by keeping only the best-ranked row,
dropping the other publishable variant from the DuckDB store.

That violates the project principle: ALL results we trust enough to
publish must be available in the DuckDB published-results dataset so
users can compare across tuning levels AND trust levels from the same
store. The table is the per-cohort published-result set; the UI
decides any display-time grouping.

Empirical evidence recorded with this TODO (`/tmp/reproduce_cohort_duplicates.py`-style
two-bundle reproducer, same platform `duckdb`, tuning_mode
`tuned` vs `notuning`, both in `tpch-sf0.1-power`):
  - `meta_leaderboard.json` `cohorts[0].platforms` kept BOTH variants
    (tuned rank 1, notuning rank 2) - JSON artifact is correct.
  - DuckDB `cohort_metadata` after W2 dedup kept only the tuned row -
    silently discards the notuning variant.
  - `platform_agg` at `pipeline.py:240` overwrites the better rank
    (rank 1) with the worse rank (rank 2) via last-write-wins, so the
    JSON artifact `platforms[]` entry AND the DuckDB `meta_leaderboard`
    row BOTH report `avg_rank = 2.0` when the correct answer is 1.0.
    This is a pre-existing correctness bug in the meta-leaderboard
    that already affects today's Home surface, independent of the PK
    decision.

Implementation (Option B + bug fix):

Schema (`docs/development/browser-duckdb-schema.sql`):
  - `cohort_metadata` PRIMARY KEY changes from
    `(cohort_key, platform_id)` to `(cohort_key, result_id)`.
  - Add columns: `tuning_mode VARCHAR`, `trust_label VARCHAR NOT NULL`,
    `short_id VARCHAR NOT NULL`. These give Home the data it needs to
    label, group, or collapse variants without a secondary join.
  - Keep `idx_cohort_metadata_key (cohort_key)`; add
    `idx_cohort_metadata_platform (cohort_key, platform_id)` so
    platform-grouped queries stay cheap.

Python (`benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/duckdb_builder.py`):
  - `_create_schema` mirrors the new DDL (PK + 3 columns + index).
  - `_populate_cohort_metadata` deletes the `best` dedup dict and
    `_RANK_IDX` logic; inserts every row from
    `meta["cohorts"][*]["platforms"]`. Widens the insert tuple to
    include `tuning_mode`, `trust_label`, `short_id`.

Python (`benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/pipeline.py`):
  - `_build_meta_leaderboard` emits `tuning_mode`, `trust_label`,
    `short_id` on each entry in `cohort_platforms` so the builder has
    what it needs without re-joining. Thread `full_to_short` into
    the function, or resolve in the builder by looking up
    `short_id_map`.
  - Fix `platform_agg` last-write-wins at `pipeline.py:240`: when the
    same `platform_id` ranks in the same `cohort_key` more than once,
    KEEP THE BEST RANK (lowest integer). Correct for the Home
    meta-leaderboard semantics (one row per platform across cohorts
    - best variant represents the platform). Equivalent minimal
    edit: replace the blind dict assignment with a guarded update,
    or rely on `setdefault` since `sorted_rows` is already best-first.

Registry (`_project/planning/visible_metrics.yaml`):
  - Update `cohort_metadata` `rank` / `metric_value` / `speedup_vs_best`
    notes to clarify they are PER RESULT_ID, not per platform_id.
  - Add new rows: `cohort_metadata.tuning_mode`,
    `cohort_metadata.trust_label`, `cohort_metadata.short_id` with
    `kind: raw_copy` and appropriate `canonical_ref` pointers.

Tests:
  - Extend `test_distinct_tuning_modes_produce_distinct_rows` in
    `tests/unit/core/explorer_pipeline/test_benchmark_summary.py` with
    a DuckDB assertion: after the pipeline run, the cohort contains
    BOTH `result_id`s in `cohort_metadata` with distinct ranks.
  - Add a regression test in
    `tests/unit/core/explorer_pipeline/test_duckdb_browser_contract.py`
    (or a peer file) against the two-bundle same-platform-same-cohort
    fixture: assert `meta_leaderboard.avg_rank` equals the BEST rank
    (1.0, not 2.0), and `n_cohorts` equals the number of distinct
    cohort_keys (not the number of cohort-variants).
  - Add a `visible_metrics` drift test asserting the
    `cohort_metadata` PRIMARY KEY columns declared in the schema
    YAML match the frozen `browser-duckdb-schema.sql`.

Exit:
  - `cohort_metadata` PK is `(cohort_key, result_id)` in schema,
    builder, and visible_metrics.
  - Running the pipeline on a two-variant corpus lands BOTH rows in
    `cohort_metadata`; no silent deduplication anywhere in the
    pipeline.
  - `_build_meta_leaderboard` keeps the BEST rank per
    `(platform_id, cohort_key)`; regression test pinning
    `avg_rank == 1.0` on the two-variant reproducer is green.
  - All 217 pre-existing explorer pipeline tests remain green; the
    two new tests are green.
  - W3 does not start until this item is done, because the
    `duckdbQueries.getCohort` helper it builds must match the final
    key shape.

approach:
Start by making chart intent explicit in registry metadata, then update
ChartPanel navigation. Treat log scale and speedup as distinct encodings:
log scale for magnitude across orders of magnitude, speedup when the user is
asking relative winner/loser questions. Test chart math separately from Preact
rendering so scale regressions are easy to catch.
description:
Fix visualization choices that currently reduce trust or legibility in the
Results Explorer. Database benchmark latency often spans orders of magnitude,
so linear bar charts can compress meaningful differences and cause labels to
overlap. Chart navigation also exposes too many tiny chart chips without an
analytical hierarchy. The goal is to make charts answer clear questions:
overview, per-query behavior, distribution, cost, trend, and rank.
preserves: Benchmark ranking order continues to come from pipeline-emitted primary_metric/primary_order, not frontend guesses.
Chart registry remains the single source for chart availability and chart metadata.
Charts remain readable when only one platform/result is present.
Heatmaps remain keyboard navigable and retain existing role/grid accessibility behavior.
title: Explorer: chart correctness, log-scale latency encoding, and chart navigation

description:
`benchbox explorer build` (and the hidden `benchbox explorer build-contract`)
publish a static read-model for the `results-explorer` React app. They are
not benchmark-runner operations, yet they sit on the user-facing `benchbox`
CLI surface and ship under `benchbox/cli/commands/explorer.py` alongside a
7-file core package at `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/`.

Provenance audit (this session):
  - Both commands were added in commit `f9d08d38b` ("Migration: populate
    develop branch from private working tree (Phase 4 w4)", 2026-04-27).
    That was a bulk migration squash, not a discrete reviewed PR.
  - The breadcrumb at `.github/workflows/docs.yml:105` attributes them to
    PR #46, but #46 is `docs(contributing): name the version JSON key +
    non-uv fallback` — a contributing-results.md docs PR, unrelated to the
    CLI surface. The in-tree provenance trail lies.
  - No `_project/specs/` document scopes the explorer CLI surface; Phase-4
    migration TODO only lists the file paths as "to migrate", not as a
    command surface to design.

This TODO is the decision step. It does not move any code. It produces an
ADR that locks the destination so downstream migration (TODO
`explorer-cli-surface-migration`) has a concrete target.

The four candidate destinations are:

  1. **hide-only**: `hidden=True` on `explorer_group`. Cheapest. Does not
     solve intermingling — code stays in `benchbox/`, import surface stays
     public, only `--help` discoverability changes. Likely rejected.
  2. **new sibling package** `benchbox_explorer/` with its own
     `console_script` (e.g. `benchbox-explorer-publish`). Separate pip
     artifact; clean conceptual boundary; external CI/scripts can still
     script against a stable binary.
  3. **`_project/scripts/explorer/`** invoked via `uv run -- python -m
     _project.scripts.explorer.publish`. In-tree maintainer tool; not
     installed; tightest "this is not a public surface" signal.
  4. **co-locate in `results-explorer/`** as a Python sub-package called
     from `results-explorer/scripts/`. Tightest coupling to the only
     consumer. Mixes Python and Node trees.

The ADR must also resolve three gating sub-questions:

  a. Does `benchbox/core/explorer_pipeline/` ALSO relocate, or only the
     CLI wrapper? Argument for "yes": same intermingling concern; the
     package serves only the explorer site. Argument for "no": existing
     tests under `tests/unit/core/explorer_pipeline/` and import sites
     like `benchbox/cli/help.py` would need follow-up. Decision here
     shapes the migration cost.

  b. Backwards-compat alias for one release: keep
     `benchbox explorer build` as a thin deprecation shim that prints a
     `DeprecationWarning` and forwards to the new entry point, then drop
     it in the next minor release? Or hard-cut and update all known
     callers in the same PR? BenchBox is v0.2.x pre-1.0, so a hard cut
     is defensible; the ADR should still record the call.

  c. End-user error path when a stale snapshot is detected: today,
     `results-explorer/src/db.ts:196` tells the user to run
     `benchbox explorer build`. After the move, the message must point
     at the maintainer-only entry. For non-maintainers (e.g., someone
     running `npm run dev` against a downloaded snapshot), the message
     should redirect to "refresh the snapshot from the published site"
     or similar, not to a CLI they shouldn't be running.

No code is moved or renamed in this TODO. ADR-only.

approach:

highest-impact gap for benchmark credibility.

Per-chart workflow (apply uniformly):
  1. Read the CLI implementation (find the textcharts call site,
     identify input shape and reduction).
  2. Decide where the math lives. Default: in
     `transformer.py`, emitted via the appropriate artifact
     (BenchmarkSummary for cross-platform; DetailResult for
     single-result). Avoid TS-side computation.
  3. Generate parity fixtures.
  4. Build the SVG component using `chartTheme.ts` constants and
     `useElementSize` for responsiveness.
  5. Wire into the appropriate page (Compare, ResultDetail,
     BenchmarkIndex, PlatformIndex).
  6. Vitest unit + parity test.
  7. Manual smoke at 3 viewport widths.

This item is sequenced AFTER the foundational items
(`explorer-establish-cli-explorer-parity-tests`,
`explorer-emit-comparison-artifact-from-pipeline`,
`explorer-unify-visualization-foundations`) because each new chart
needs the parity fixtures, theme constants, and pipeline-emitted

description:
The 2026-04-15 review found that the CLI registers **16 canonical
chart types** in `benchbox/core/visualization/chart_types.py:17-45`,
but the explorer implements only **6 visualization components**
(QueryHeatmap, QueryTimingChart, GroupedQueryChart,
NormalizedSpeedupChart, DivergingBarChart, MetaLeaderboard) -
and only 3-4 of those have CLI counterparts that compute the same
values. **10 CLI chart types have no explorer equivalent.**

Missing chart types and their importance for benchmark credibility:

  | Chart                | Why it matters                                                   |
  |----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
  | `percentile_ladder`  | Tail-latency P50/P90/P95/P99 - central to fair benchmark claims  |
  | `cdf_chart`          | Distribution shape - exposes "fast median, slow tail" patterns   |
  | `rank_table`         | Compact per-query ranking - denser than heatmap for many queries |
  | `distribution_box`   | Box-plot of per-query latencies - shows variance/outliers        |
  | `query_histogram`    | Per-query latency distribution                                   |
  | `time_series`        | Trend over runs - regression detection                           |
  | `cost_scatter`       | Cost vs performance - central to cloud-warehouse comparisons     |
  | `power_bar`          | Dedicated TPC Power@Size visual                                  |
  | `sparkline_table`    | Compact metrics summary with embedded micro-charts               |
  | `stacked_phase`      | Phase breakdown (load/warmup/power/throughput)                   |

This item ports each missing chart type to the explorer in priority
order. Every new chart consumes pipeline-emitted data
(per `explorer-emit-comparison-artifact-from-pipeline` - extending
the artifact emission as needed) and ships with a parity fixture
(per `explorer-establish-cli-explorer-parity-tests`) so the math
is verified against the canonical Python implementation from day one.

Out of scope: building entirely NEW chart types that don't exist in
the CLI either. Those should be evaluated and added to both sides
through the canonical chart_types.py registry first.
preserves: BenchmarkSummary and DetailResult artifact backward compatibility - extensions add new fields, do not rename or remove existing ones
CLI chart_types.py registry as the single canonical source - explorer mirrors it, never the other way around
Existing 6 explorer chart components must continue to work - new charts add tabs/sections, do not replace existing visualizations
ResultDetail / BenchmarkIndex / PlatformIndex existing layouts and navigation patterns - additions are introduced as tabs or new sections, not page rewrites

description:
From the 2026-07-31 adversarial review of the #1340/#1368 mitigations. Three defects and one cleanup:

E1 (mitigation asymmetry): results-explorer/src/db.ts:410 returns any non-empty result immediately - the retry covers only ZERO-row cold reads. The repo's own record of the pass-1 bug says it surfaced as PARTIAL rows (e2e/failures/platform-index-cold-load.spec.ts:1-5; docs/operations/browser-ci.md: '1 of 5 rows'), and db.ts:444-450 itself argues readiness is not monotonic per query. A 3-of-5 cold read renders as truth. Probabilistic race - not deterministically reproducible; decide and document the policy (extend the cold-window retry to a completeness signal, or document explicitly why zero-only is the accepted trade-off).

E2 (blocking-gate coverage): playwright.config.ts:38 sets retries:2 in CI; only performance.spec.ts is exempted (package.json:17). The cold-load spec inherits retries, and each Playwright retry is a fresh browser context - a fresh roll of the cold-load dice. A reintroduced ~30% first-load race passes the blocking Chromium gate ~97% of the time as 'flaky but green', silently voiding browser-ci.md's 'if it flakes, that is signal' contract. Fix: retries:0 carve-out for e2e/failures/ (like the performance invocation).

E3 (helper contract): e2e/support/fixtures.ts:89 - waitForDataElement 'break's out of all remaining attempts when navigationKey(page.url()) changes, while its own docstring (lines 64-67) promises the remaining attempts just re-wait (naming app query-string canonicalization as the case). Effect: the #1368 mitigation is disabled for URL-rewriting routes and the thrown error ('Re-navigating between attempts did not help') is false. 

F4 (cleanup): db.ts:424-429 post-loop code is unreachable and the comment misattributes where the legit-empty return happens.

Disproven during review (do not re-fix): snapshotReadyAt window-state across re-init/online is correct (single write site, dbInstance never nulled, online forces full re-init); bad-id retry cost is ~300ms worst case inside the 15s window.

Note: results-explorer/e2e is not typechecked - tracked separately as explorer-e2e-typecheck-gap-20260730 (that item is slightly understated: playwright.config.ts is also unchecked and the package has no ESLint; src IS typechecked in CI via docs.yml).
preserves: Legitimately-empty results outside the cold window return immediately with zero retry cost (db.ts:459 behavior).
Retry bounds stay finite and small; no unbounded loops or sleeps in queryRows.
The cold-load spec stays genuinely cold: no helper it uses may navigate, retry, or warm the context before its first assertion.
WebKit/Firefox @smoke graduation policy is not changed here (tracked separately in the post-soak cleanup question).
