description:
The shared SQL/file loader at data_loading.py silently records 0 rows when
manifest-listed shard paths don't exist as files on disk (line 1972-1976).
This causes cryptic downstream query failures instead of an immediate,
actionable load error. Similarly, _load_single_file doesn't fully guard
against directory inputs or missing explicit single-file inputs, allowing
IsADirectoryError or silent skip behavior to propagate.

Root cause: stale Iceberg table directories (customer/, lineitem/) coexist
with valid manifest-tracked files. The exists() filter passes for directories,
but handlers can't load them. When all shards filter out, 0 rows is recorded
silently.

This is the highest-value fix because it protects users regardless of the
contamination source - stale Iceberg dirs, bad paths, permissions, etc.
preserves: Handler factory and FileFormatRegistry dispatch logic unchanged
Legitimate sharded loading still works when all shard files exist
Non-explicit discovery flows should not become noisier unless the loader can prove the missing path came from manifest or benchmark table input
title: Raise DataLoadingError instead of silent zero-row loads in SQL/file loader

description:
`pip-audit` (run in the `dependency-audit` CI job) flags lxml 6.0.2 for
PYSEC-2026-87, fixed in lxml 6.1.0. lxml is not a direct BenchBox
dependency (see the already-completed
`drop-lxml-dev-dep-or-port-test-to-stdlib` TODO, which removed it as a
direct dev dependency in 2026-04) - it is pulled in transitively by
`redshift-connector`.

`redshift-connector==2.1.13`'s own package metadata pins
`lxml>=4.6.5,<=6.0.2+`, so `uv lock --upgrade-package lxml` cannot move
past 6.0.2 without violating that constraint (verified via
`uv lock --upgrade-package lxml -v`, which shows uv's resolver refusing
to exceed the cap declared by redshift-connector). This is not fixable
by a version bump alone from the BenchBox side.

Until redshift-connector releases a version that relaxes or removes its
lxml upper bound, this finding is accepted as a temporary false
positive and suppressed via `PIP_AUDIT_IGNORE_VULNS=PYSEC-2026-87` in
`.github/workflows/pr.yml`, `.github/workflows/test.yml`, and
`.github/workflows/nightly.yml`, each referencing this TODO in a
comment.
preserves: PIP_AUDIT_IGNORE_VULNS carries only this one documented, triaged exception
dependency-audit stays a required, blocking CI check for every other finding
title: Unblock lxml PYSEC-2026-87 fix once redshift-connector relaxes its lxml pin

approach:
This is a mechanical default-flip across four locations plus a small
logic addition to `_existing_obt()` for a stale-file log message. No new
code paths, no new dependencies. The transformer already emits parquet
when asked.

Work order: w1 first (the actual flip), then w2 (UX improvement for
stale-file detection), then w3 (tests catch any accidental regression),
then w4 (docs), then w5 (end-to-end smoke).

Reference existing parquet path: `etl/transformer.py:730` already emits
`COPY ... TO '...' (FORMAT PARQUET)`. No changes needed to the export
logic itself.
description:
TPC-DS OBT currently defaults to pipe-delimited `.dat` output. At SF1 this
produces an 11GB uncompressed file (5,041,336 rows × 518 columns). The
schema is intentionally wide (One Big Table) - that is not a bug - but
`.dat` is a pathological storage choice for a 518-column table where:

- Every row carries ~300-400 NULL columns (store rows have NULL for all
  web_site_*, web_page_*, call_center_*, catalog_page_* columns; web rows
  are NULL for all store_* and call_center_* columns; etc.)
- Many dimension attributes repeat textual values (customer names,
  addresses, product descriptions) that compress trivially column-wise
- DataFrame platforms (DataFusion, Polars, Pandas) cannot practically
  load 11GB of pipe-delimited text into memory at SF1

Parquet's columnar encoding with null suppression and per-column
compression is expected to reduce the file materially - an order-of-
magnitude shrink is plausible given the null density and text repetition,
but the actual ratio is validated in w5. The transformer already
supports parquet output - the export
branch at `etl/transformer.py:730` emits parquet when
`output_format="parquet"` is passed. What is missing is making parquet
the default so DataFrame platforms work out of the box and SQL platforms
get a much smaller artifact for free.

This change:
- Flips the default `output_format` from `"dat"` to `"parquet"` in four
  places (benchmark `__init__`, `generate_data()`, `BenchmarkOptionSpec`,
  transformer `transform()`).
- Updates `_existing_obt()` to detect parquet first and trigger
  regeneration when only a stale `.dat` exists (it will not auto-delete).
- Keeps `.dat` available via explicit `--benchmark-option output_format=dat`
  so anyone reproducing older results or benchmarking a platform that
  cannot read parquet still has a path.

Downstream impact: DuckDB, ClickHouse, DataFusion-SQL, and all DataFrame
platforms read parquet natively via their existing CSV/parquet auto-detect
loaders. No platform-side code changes are expected. SQL platforms that
generate DDL first and then `COPY` from file will benefit from the smaller
artifact and faster load times.
preserves: DuckDB SQL platform still runs tpcds_obt to completion
Manifest JSON schema unchanged (same keys: table, mode, channels, column_count, rows_total, rows_by_channel, rows_with_returns, output_file, output_format, file_size_bytes, scale_factor)
Row counts match manifest (channel totals: store ~2.88M, catalog ~1.44M, web ~0.72M at SF1)
TPC-DS OBT query semantics unchanged - queries still reference the same column names and types
`.dat` format remains available when user explicitly passes `--benchmark-option output_format=dat`
`choices=('dat', 'parquet')` on the BenchmarkOptionSpec remains - don't narrow the allowed set
title: Make Parquet the default output format for TPC-DS OBT

description:
The datagen manifest validation (_validate_manifest_if_present in runner.py)
only checks that its own recorded files exist with correct sizes. It has no
concept of "unexpected entries" in the datagen directory. When stale Iceberg
table directories (customer/, lineitem/) coexist with valid manifest-tracked
files (customer.tbl.1.zst), validation passes but loading breaks.

Fix: add narrow collision detection that invalidates reuse when an untracked
directory shares a table name. This triggers regeneration (or raises under
no_regenerate), preventing users from ever reaching the broken load state.

Also add an entry type guard: if a manifest entry resolves to a directory but
is not marked is_directory, treat as invalid (catches corrupted state).

DataFrame paths also need narrow protection: if file-based loading encounters
a directory path, prefer colocated manifest file entries when available;
otherwise raise a clear error instead of surfacing IsADirectoryError.

title: Elevate MCP Feature on Landing Page and Documentation

approach: Revalidate the current seven-prompt server inventory and landing catalog first. Reuse the existing public MCP client adapters and transport fixtures. Exercise prompts/list and prompts/get through a real stdio subprocess and the stateless HTTP ASGI route, compare names, ordering, roles, and rendered text against the registered prompt contract, and assert no MCP session affinity is required. Wire the coverage into the MCP integration gate and document any intentional catalog-only differences.
description: Promoted from open deferral #462 on prompts-landing-phase5-mcp-parity. description: Found 2026-07-31 during the credential-egress review. Both MCP export paths construct ResultExporter(anonymize=False) - benchbox/mcp/tools/benchmark.py:289 and analytics.py:346 - and benchmark.py returns the entire un-anonymized result payload to the MCP client (:428, :441), including platform.config (which schema.py:526 extracts with no secret filtering). Additionally, every MCP error response embeds details['exception_message'] = str(exception) verbatim (benchbox/mcp/errors.py:338, reached from e.g. benchmark.py:443-456), so a driver error carrying 'motherduck_token=...' or a DSN reaches the client and its logs; driven proof: json.dumps(make_execution_error('x', exception=Exception('motherduck_token=SENT-123'))) contains the sentinel. Decide deliberately per surface: local-analysis payloads may legitimately stay un-anonymized, but exception text must at minimum have secret-assignment patterns scrubbed.

description:
Follow-up captured from the statistics-as-a-phase work (PR #980,
track2-joinorder-stats-phase). That change added an opt-in statistics phase
(load -> statistics -> query) reachable from the CLI via
`--phases ...,statistics`, which threads through
`LifecyclePhases.statistics` -> `RunConfig.gather_statistics` and is gated
per benchmark by the `supports_statistics_phase` registry flag
(joinorder/tpch/tpcds opt in).

The MCP `run_benchmark` tool does NOT yet expose this opt-in. Its phase
handling collapses the requested phases to a single `test_execution_type`
via `_map_phases_to_test_execution_type`

description:
Observed live 2026-07-23: PR #1288's medium-test job was cancelled at exactly 30:03 (the job's timeout-minutes: 30 in .github/workflows/pr.yml), failing ci-required-result, while the same PR's every other job was green and sibling runs that day completed medium-test in ~29 minutes (#1282: 20:31->21:00). The tier has grown to the edge of its own timeout: normal runtime ~29min vs 30min cap leaves <1 minute of scheduling headroom, so runner-side noise converts a healthy lane into a cancelled required check - the same failure symptom class as FAST_LANE_VIOLATION (budget outgrown by organic growth), but for wall-clock.

Same remediation shape as the fast-lane work (fast-lane-decouple-ceiling-contention-2): (a) immediate mechanical fix - raise timeout-minutes to restore real headroom (e.g. 45); (b) durable fix - record medium-tier wall time in dev-loop-metrics (the WS9 script already records the fast-test job; add the medium job name) and add a warning threshold well before the timeout, so growth is visible before it cancels runs; (c) consider whether the medium tier needs splitting/parallelizing (pytest-xdist or job sharding) once the trend data exists.
preserves: No test reclassification in this item - budget/observability only
medium-test remains a required (blocking) member of ci-required-result

Successful wall times (min): 20.2 21.4 21.5 21.8 26.5 26.8 26.8 26.9 26.9 27.4 27.6 29.2 29.5 29.6 29.6 29.8 29.8 29.9 29.9 -- min=20.2, median=27.4, max=29.9, p95=29.9. Eight of nineteen runs land at >=29.2min, i.e. within 48s of the cap; the max successful run finished 6s under it. IMPORTANT caveat: this distribution is CENSORED -- any run that would have exceeded 30min was cancelled and is excluded from the successful set, so the true upper tail is unknown and >=30. p95*1.3 = 38.9min, so 40 is the smallest round value meeting the >=30% headroom rule without the 'huge value' anti-pattern.

No CI workflow invokes this Make target or an equivalent selector across
the full tier. The develop-PR gate's `code-test` job explicitly documents

skips medium-marked tests, and only pin-points two specific medium nodes
by name as explicit exceptions (pr.yml:419-424

does not select the medium marker as a tier - it has its own fast-lane
test job and separate `integration` job, neither of which is `-m medium`.
So the ~79 other medium-marked files run only when a developer runs
`make test-medium` locally; nothing in CI exercises them as a tier.

RESULT: 1070.38s wall clock (~17.85 min), 1158 passed, 73 skipped, 15
failed, 44 errors. Well past "fast-lane-comparable" and squarely in
the TODO's own "10+ minutes -> nightly or post-merge" bucket.

FAILURE BREAKDOWN (important caveat below): the ONE failure this TODO
pre-flagged as known/expected was present as predicted:
`tests/unit/test_cross_surface_applicability.py::test_committed_artifact_is_current`.
Per this TODO's own instruction, I did NOT fix or regenerate that
artifact and did NOT exclude the test — see w2 notes for how the new
lane's known-issue is documented instead.

However 14 OTHER failures and 44 errors also occurred, which this
TODO did not anticipate:
  - tests/unit/test_error_handling.py::test_permission_denied_output_directory,
    ::test_readonly_filesystem_handling; tests/unit/cli/test_exceptions.py::
    test_validate_output_directory_local_invalid — these are classic
    "running pytest as root" artifacts: chmod-based permission-denial
    tests cannot produce PermissionError when the test process is
    root, which ignores file-mode permission bits. Root cause is this
    sandbox's execution user, not this session's edits.
  - tests/integration/test_dataframe_adapter_smoke.py (8 PySpark
    tests) — failed rather than cleanly skipped, alongside dozens of
    other PySpark tests elsewhere in the same run that DID skip
    cleanly with "Java not found" — suggests a partial/inconsistent
    JVM install in this sandbox, not a code regression.
  - tests/integration/validation/test_read_primitives_variant_parity.py
    (44 ERRORs, all in one file, spanning duckdb/datafusion/redshift/
    clickhouse reference-output fixtures) — the uniform failure shape
    across many parametrized cases in a single file is consistent
    with a fixture/session-level setup exception, and this session
    was running OTHER pytest invocations concurrently against the
    same tree with BENCHBOX_SKIP_TEST_LOCK=1 (bypassing this repo's
    own single-run lock) while this measurement was in flight, plus a
    second agent was independently running pytest against this same
    shared worktree at the same time (per the task's own instructions
    — this tree is explicitly shared with another concurrent agent).
    Concurrent DB-file/port/tmp-dir contention is a plausible cause.
  - tests/unit/cli/test_output_control_static.py::test_no_new_raw_print_in_benchbox_runtime
    — a static source-grep test; not obviously environment-related,
    and not touched by this session's edits (no benchbox/ source
    changed). Cause undetermined.

I could NOT re-run in isolation to separate "real develop regression"
from "sandbox/concurrency artifact" within this session's time budget
(a clean rerun takes ~18 min and this session had already produced
the required measurement). RECOMMENDATION: before relying on the new
develop-post-merge auto-revert wiring in production (see w2/w3), a
human or follow-up session should run `make test-medium` once, alone,
in a clean environment (ideally the actual GitHub Actions runner) to
get a trustworthy failure baseline. If the 14+44 are confirmed
environment noise, no code changes are needed; if any are real
regressions, they need their own fix TODOs before the auto-revert
wiring can be trusted not to fire spuriously. Original notes:
Run `time make test-medium` and record wall-clock time and pass/fail
count. This number drives w2's placement choice - a lane under a few
minutes is a candidate for a path-filtered PR job; a lane of 10+
minutes is a better fit for nightly or post-merge.

description:
Create a new Metadata Primitives benchmark to test cross-platform catalog/schema
introspection performance. This benchmark tests INFORMATION_SCHEMA views, SHOW commands,
and DESCRIBE operations that are essential for data discovery and tooling integration.

Unlike Read/Write/Transaction primitives that test data operations, this benchmark
focuses on metadata operations that are critical for:
- Data catalog integration
- Schema discovery tools
- IDE autocomplete performance
- BI tool connectivity
- Data governance workflows
title: Metadata Primitives Benchmark - INFORMATION_SCHEMA, SHOW, DESCRIBE

description:
Enhance the Metadata Primitives benchmark to stress-test metadata operations with
complex catalog scenarios that reflect real-world data warehouse characteristics.

The current implementation tests basic INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries against simple
schemas (TPC-H with 8 tables, ~60 columns total). Real production data warehouses
have significantly more complex metadata:

- Wide tables (100-1000+ columns) common in analytics/ML feature stores
- Nested view hierarchies (3-4+ levels) from BI tools like Looker, dbt, Tableau
- Complex data types (STRUCT, ARRAY, MAP, JSON) in modern data platforms
- Large catalogs (100s-1000s of tables) in multi-tenant environments
- Deep constraint/FK graphs in normalized operational databases

These complexity factors cause 5-100x slower metadata operations that are not
captured by the current benchmark. This enhancement adds a MetadataGenerator
component and new query categories to measure these performance characteristics.
title: Metadata Primitives Complexity Enhancements

description:
psycopg2-binary has been in maintenance-only mode since 2022. psycopg3 (PyPI package:
`psycopg`) is the designated successor from the same author (Daniele Varrazzo), built on
the same libpq foundation with active development, better wheel coverage (consistent
macOS ARM64 support), and native async support. psycopg2-binary bundles its own OpenSSL,
triggering security-scanner false positives; psycopg3[binary] has the same bundling model
but a cleaner, maintained build.

BenchBox uses psycopg2 across one shared mixin, five platform adapters, two dev scripts,
and four test files:

  Platform adapters:
    benchbox/platforms/base/psycopg2_mixin.py  - shared connection/cursor mechanics
    benchbox/platforms/postgresql.py            - most complex: copy_expert() bulk load
    benchbox/platforms/timescaledb.py           - psycopg2.sql for safe DDL composition
    benchbox/platforms/questdb.py               - inherits mixin; psycopg2.extras vestigial
    benchbox/platforms/pg_mooncake.py           - psycopg2.sql for GUC/DDL composition
    benchbox/platforms/pg_duckdb.py             - psycopg2.sql for GUC composition
    benchbox/platforms/redshift.py              - psycopg2 as fallback when redshift-connector absent

  pyproject.toml dependency declarations (4 sites):
    line 112: "psycopg2-binary>=2.9.0"  (extras:all)
    line 170: postgresql = ["psycopg2-binary>=2.9.0"]
    line 171: questdb = ["psycopg2-binary>=2.9.0", "requests>=2.28.0"]
    line 464: "psycopg2-binary>=2.9.0"  (dev group)

  Scripts: scripts/probe_mooncake_types.py, scripts/benchmark_mooncake_migration.py

  Tests:
    tests/unit/platforms/test_postgresql_adapter.py
    tests/unit/platforms/test_psycopg2_mixin.py
    tests/unit/core/test_platform_registry.py
    tests/integration/platforms/common.py

The only non-trivial code change is postgresql.py's two `cursor.copy_expert()` calls
(lines 500 and 505), which must be rewritten to use psycopg3's `cursor.copy()` context
manager. The psycopg.sql module (sql.SQL, sql.Identifier, sql.Literal) has an IDENTICAL
API to psycopg2.sql - no usage sites change beyond the import path.

This item was deferred from the `tighten-dependencies-phase-plan` audit as
"driver modernization - out of scope for an elimination audit. File separately when
product is ready."
preserves: All test fixtures remain functionally equivalent: mock.Mock() stubs must target the new import name (psycopg) and match the actual module structure post-migration.
PostgreSQL COPY bulk load correctness: same rows loaded, no data truncation or loss. The copy_expert() → cursor.copy() rewrite must produce identical database state.
Redshift fallback branch: psycopg3 replaces psycopg2 in the fallback only; the redshift-connector primary path is unchanged.
Streaming behavior for large TPC-H files: use 64KB chunk reads in cursor.copy() context manager, NOT whole-file f.read(), to preserve memory profile at high scale factors.

connection.autocommit = True pattern in postgresql.py and redshift.py: this property is still writeable in psycopg3 - do NOT replace with psycopg.connect(autocommit=True) unless doing a full connection-creation refactor.
psycopg2.sql-based safe identifier quoting in TimescaleDB, pg_mooncake, pg_duckdb: sql.Identifier() and sql.SQL() calls MUST remain - they are SQL injection guards.
title: Migrate PostgreSQL driver from psycopg2-binary to psycopg3 (psycopg)

approach:
Treat this as a contract unification, not a mechanical search-and-replace.
Start by codifying the CsvDialect behavior in tests, then migrate adapters in
groups whose load APIs are similar. Prefer small helper functions that accept
DataSource, table name, file path, and benchmark, and return the engine-native
option shape. This keeps platform SQL/API construction local while removing
dialect inference from each adapter.

The migrated Doris, PostgreSQL, QuestDB, and SingleStore implementations are
the reference pattern: resolve files with DataSourceResolver, call
resolve_csv_dialect() at the point where an engine-specific load statement or
API config needs delimiter/header/null semantics, and add tests that prove
manifest metadata beats filename suffixes.

description:
Commit 73f3a582e migrated only the Doris, PostgreSQL, QuestDB, and
SingleStore data-loading paths from ad-hoc filename heuristics to the shared
DataSourceResolver + resolve_csv_dialect pipeline. The remaining SQL,
embedded, cloud warehouse, Databricks, and Spark-family adapters still derive
CSV/TBL dialect from file extensions, benchmark csv_* attributes, or Spark's
CSV reader options directly.

This leaves BenchBox with two competing CSV dialect contracts. The resolver
path understands manifest-declared dialect metadata, treats null_marker=None
as a meaningful "no null marker" value, avoids mock pollution from raw
getattr(mock, "csv_*", None), and centralizes fallback logging. The remaining
adapters can still silently load manifest-described TBL/CSV data using stale
extension heuristics, especially for converted datasets, compressed files,
ClickBench-style empty strings, or benchmarks that expose dialect metadata
through manifests rather than benchmark attributes.

Current evidence from the live codebase:
- benchbox/platforms/duckdb.py:306,310,815 still uses get_delimiter_for_file()
  and is_tpc_format() in text loading paths.
- benchbox/platforms/clickhouse/workload.py:153 still uses is_tpc_format().
- benchbox/platforms/starrocks/workload.py:276,287 still uses is_tpc_format()
  and raw getattr(benchmark_instance, "csv_delimiter", None).
- benchbox/platforms/databend/adapter.py:461 still uses get_delimiter_for_file()
  after resolving files through DataSourceResolver.
- benchbox/platforms/firebolt.py:744,893 still uses get_delimiter_for_file()
  in copy/load SQL construction after DataSourceResolver resolution.
- benchbox/platforms/redshift.py:1351,1388 still uses get_delimiter_for_file()
  for COPY delimiter selection after DataSourceResolver resolution.
- benchbox/platforms/bigquery.py:1138 still uses get_delimiter_for_file()
  for LoadJobConfig field_delimiter.
- benchbox/platforms/databricks/adapter.py:1439,1458 still uses is_tpc_format()
  for CSV FORMAT_OPTIONS delimiter inference.
- benchbox/platforms/base/spark_execution_mixin.py:260 reads
  getattr(benchmark, "csv_delimiter", None) directly. spark.py, velox.py,
  and lakesail.py delegate to this mixin, so they share a parallel resolver
  bypass even though the mixin already creates a DataSourceResolver.

The goal is not just to replace function calls. The goal is to make every
adapter that builds a CSV/TBL load option consume the same resolved
CsvDialect object, including manifest table_metadata, benchmark attributes,
explicit None null markers, and safe fallback behavior.
preserves: ClickBench and other CSV-style benchmarks continue preserving empty strings according to their benchmark/manifest dialect.
DataSourceResolver remains the single source of table/file resolution and format preference selection; do not reimplement manifest walking inside adapters.
Existing platform upload/staging/compression behavior for Firebolt, Redshift, BigQuery, Databricks, Spark, Velox, and LakeSail remains unchanged.
SparkDataLoadMixin keeps LakeSail CSV-extension symlink compatibility and Spark compression option handling.
TPC-H/TPC-DS TBL inputs still load as pipe-delimited, headerless data on every migrated platform.
null_marker=None remains semantically distinct from a missing null marker; adapters must not replace explicit None with a default string.
resolve_csv_dialect() precedence remains manifest table_metadata first, then real benchmark csv_* attributes, then file-extension fallback with logging.

scope.path_glob: benchbox/core/manifest/ - manifest schema and parsing are not part of this migration unless a failing test proves metadata is not exposed.
benchbox/core/runner/ - runner orchestration should not need changes for CSV dialect routing.
benchbox/utils/file_format.py - keep low-level format helpers for callers outside migrated adapter load paths.
benchmark generation code - this item consumes existing manifest/dialect metadata; it does not change data generation.

description:
Follow-up to migrate-remaining-adapters-to-csv-resolver-pipeline (completed
2026-04-25). That work converted DuckDB, ClickHouse, StarRocks, Databend,
Firebolt, Redshift, BigQuery, Databricks, Spark, Velox, and LakeSail to
resolve_csv_dialect(). The adversarial review of that work flagged that the
TODO scope explicitly excluded several adapters that still drive CSV/TBL
load options through is_tpc_format() / get_delimiter_for_file(). Those
adapters need the same migration so the codebase converges on one CSV
dialect contract.

Current evidence from the live codebase (verified 2026-04-26):

- benchbox/platforms/snowflake.py:855 — _get_file_format_for_table() picks
  BENCHBOX_TBL_FORMAT vs BENCHBOX_CSV_FORMAT via is_tpc_format(first_file).
  Manifest-annotated .csv carrying TPC dialect metadata silently falls into
  the CSV format branch.
- benchbox/platforms/fabric_warehouse.py:945,950,1024 — branches on
  is_tpc_format(data_file) to pick field_terminator and reads
  get_delimiter_for_file(data_file) for COPY INTO statements.
- benchbox/platforms/datafusion.py:845 — _detect_csv_format() falls back
  to get_delimiter_for_file(file_paths[0]).
- benchbox/platforms/azure_synapse.py:541,610 — uses
  get_delimiter_for_file(first_file) for COPY INTO field_terminator and
  direct INSERT delimiter.
- benchbox/platforms/dataframe/{modin,cudf,pandas,pyspark,dask,lakesail}_df.py
  — use is_tpc_format(path) to gate has_trailing_delimiter() probing in
  DataFrame loaders. Same trailing-delimiter behaviour change addressed in
  DuckDB needs to be propagated through these read paths. (Note: the
  predecessor TODO migrated the SQL lakesail.py platform; lakesail_df.py
  and dask_df.py were not included and still use is_tpc_format.)
- benchbox/platforms/base/utils.py:45 — detect_file_format() uses
  is_tpc_format() to pick a default delimiter when no metadata is supplied.
  This is a shared utility — verify whether it should be migrated or
  documented as the legitimate "no-context" fallback.
preserves: DataSourceResolver remains the single source of table/file resolution; do not reimplement manifest walking inside adapters.
Dataframe adapter trailing-delimiter probing preserves the `null_marker is not None` gate so non-TPC CSVs do not pay the extra disk read.
Snowflake named file format objects (BENCHBOX_TBL_FORMAT, BENCHBOX_CSV_FORMAT) still load TPC and CSV data with their existing column/null/date semantics.
null_marker=None remains semantically distinct from a missing null marker; adapters must not replace explicit None with a default string.
resolve_csv_dialect() precedence remains manifest table_metadata first, then real benchmark csv_* attributes, then file-extension fallback with logging.

description:
Goal: let `make test-docker-*` run on Apple `container` via Mocker (a
Docker-compatible CLI over Apple's Containerization framework) instead of
Docker Desktop, removing Docker Desktop's always-on VM -- the dominant
source of the "Docker Desktop overhead" this effort started from. Apple
`container` itself has NO Docker Compose support; Mocker is the wrapper
that adds it.

BenchBox's integration layer is Compose-native. The generic targets call
(Makefile:436 / Makefile:480 / Makefile:489-540):
  docker compose -p <project> -f docker/<platform>/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
  docker compose -p <project> -f docker/<platform>/docker-compose.yml down -v
across DOCKER_PLATFORMS (Makefile:433): clickhouse trino presto postgresql
starrocks doris databend influxdb cedardb firebolt questdb singlestore.
Any backend must honor `-p`, `-f`, `up -d --wait` (healthcheck gating),
host->container port publishing, and `down -v` (named-volume removal).

Spike evidence (2026-06-30, host macOS 26.5 / arm64; container CLI 1.0.0;
Mocker 0.5.4 from us/tap) against UNMODIFIED docker/questdb (1 svc) and
docker/postgresql (2 svc, named volume):
  PASS  `-p` project naming                     (container bbspike-questdb-questdb-1)
  PASS  `up -d --wait` health gating            (-w/--wait + --wait-timeout real flags; up returned only once serving)
  PASS  host->container reachability            (localhost:19000/exec -> result; psycopg localhost:5432 -> PG 18.4, RW=42)
  PASS  `down` teardown                         (stopped+removed, ports closed)
  PASS  `restart: unless-stopped` parse
  FAIL  `down -v` named-volume removal          (-v documented but bbspike-pg-postgresql18-data SURVIVED; needed manual `mocker volume rm`)

The single blocker is the `down -v` volume leak: `make test-docker-down-*`
relies on `-v` for fresh state, so a leaked named volume means STALE DATA
carries across runs (e.g. a reused Postgres data dir) -- a correctness
risk for benchmarks, not a cosmetic one. Networking -- the feature every
Compose wrapper is reported to struggle with -- worked. Until `down -v`
is fixed or teardown is wrapped, Mocker is NOT safe as the default
test-docker-* backend.

FINDINGS (2026-07-03, mocker 0.5.4 / container 1.0.0 / macOS 26.5 arm64):
- w0: `down -v` still LEAKS the named volume (bbpg-postgresql18-data survived);
  no upstream fix -> w4 = option (b) teardown-wrap.
- w1: _project/scripts/mocker_compose_parity.sh drives the real make targets and
  asserts health-gated up, published-port reachability, no container/volume after
  teardown; exposed via `make test-docker-parity`.
- Parity MEASURED: PASS on BOTH docker and mocker for questdb + postgresql,
  including "no named volume after teardown" for postgres on mocker (the
  compose_down_fresh wrap prunes the leaked volume).
- w3: `CONTAINER_ENGINE=mocker make test-docker-questdb` -> 3 live_questdb tests
  (parquet load + query via connector) PASS; clean teardown.
- w2: databend multi-service -> mocker honors depends_on ordering (up --wait 4/4)
  BUT the stack does not stay healthy (minio exits, databend :8000 empty reply);
  the SAME stack on docker stays healthy and serves 200. So 3+ service stacks are
  NOT reliable on mocker -> keep docker default; mocker opt-in for single-service.
- w5: CONTAINER_ENGINE var (default docker) + COMPOSE seam; docker/*/*.yml
  unchanged; default NOT flipped. w6: AGENTS.md documents the CI boundary.
preserves: CI (.github/workflows/) continues to use docker on ubuntu; Mocker never enters CI.
Default `make test-docker-*` behavior on Docker is unchanged until the decision gate (w4) explicitly flips the default.
Fresh-state guarantee: after teardown, no named volume from the stack survives (the property the down -v bug breaks).
docker/*/docker-compose.yml remain standard Compose files usable by Docker and CI.

description:
DuckDB is currently a core (required) dependency in pyproject.toml at line 40:
  "duckdb>=1.4.0"

Because it's required, uv.lock pins it to an exact version (currently 1.4.3). When a
user runs `uv run benchbox run`, uv syncs the environment against uv.lock BEFORE Python
starts, silently reverting any manually installed version (e.g., duckdb==1.5.0.dev307)
back to 1.4.3. The user has no visibility into this until they check the result JSON.

Moving duckdb to an optional extras group removes it from the lock-enforced core set.
uv would no longer revert it - whatever the user has installed survives. Users who want
DuckDB can install it via `pip install benchbox[duckdb]` or the existing `all` extra.

Design decisions to resolve during implementation:
  1. Minimum version for the optional duckdb extra - keep >=1.4.0 or relax to >=1.0.0?
     Relaxing to >=1.0.0 gives users maximum flexibility (they can test any version),
     though some BenchBox features may require newer APIs.
  2. Backward compatibility - `pip install benchbox` currently installs duckdb; removing
     it from core will break existing installs. Options:
       a. Add duckdb to a "local" or "embedded" extras group and update install docs.
       b. Add duckdb to the existing `all` meta-extra and mark it as the recommended install.
       c. Keep a minimal >=1.0.0 pin in core (so something is installed) but remove the
          tight lock on a specific version by using a pre-release-tolerant spec.
  3. The `dev` extras group at line 66 also includes "duckdb>=1.4.0" - must be updated
     to match whatever approach is chosen.
  4. CI must still work - the CI install likely uses `pip install -e .[dev]` or similar.

The primary goal is: after `pip install benchbox` (or `uv add benchbox`), a user who
then runs `uv pip install "duckdb==X.Y.Z"` should have that version respected by
`uv run benchbox run` without being silently reverted.

pip install benchbox still results in a working DuckDB benchmark after install (either via an auto-included extra or clear documentation)

deferrals.reason: Root cause of this nightly failure, out of scope here (fix is in benchbox/, item is scoped to tests/unit/cli/**). benchbox/cli/__init__.py __getattr__ resolves 'main' by doing 'from benchbox.cli.main import main' then 'globals()[name] = main', caching the FUNCTION under the same name as the submodule. Whichever happens first in a given process wins: import the submodule first and the module binding survives; touch the attribute first and the function clobbers it. Python >= 3.11 hides this because unittest.mock._get_target uses pkgutil.resolve_name (imports the dotted path, module wins); 3.10 walks with getattr and lands on the function. Verified against the real package: with package-only import then attribute access, 3.10's resolver returns <function main> with has get_config_manager=False. Latent elsewhere - tests/unit/conftest.py:51, tests/unit/cli/test_run_driver_version_announcement.py:83, test_cli_main.py:152/206/276/379 (+ ConfigManager/SystemProfiler at 116/603/604/618), test_compression_cli.py:44/122/221 all still use the string target and are one test-distribution away from the same failure. Removing the shadow fixes all of them at once; patching each test file is a band-aid.

work.evidence: The recipe prints whatever its own shell considers the path to be; on Windows that shell is Git Bash/MSYS, which renders C:\\Users\\... as /c/Users/.... The assertion compared that against Path.resolve()'s native spelling, so it failed on spelling alone. Replaced the substring check with an exact comparison on a canonical form: normalize_path() lowercases and translates a leading /X/ drive segment, but ONLY when os.name == 'nt' - on POSIX a leading single-letter segment like /a/b is an ordinary directory and must not be rewritten. emitted_worktree_path() additionally asserts exactly one WORKTREE_PATH= line, so this is strictly stronger than the substring test it replaces. work.evidence: Platform-gated rather than 'fixed', because the test is POSIX-only by construction and the behaviour it exercises does not exist on Windows. It shims git with an extensionless '#!/bin/sh' script placed first on PATH, but Windows resolves git.exe/git.cmd and never executes an extensionless file, so the shim is bypassed entirely; it then drives the recipe's INT trap with 'kill -INT $PPID', which has no Windows equivalent. The nightly evidence matches exactly: returncode 0 with stderr "Switched to a new branch 'feature/signal-test'" - the real git ran, the claim succeeded, and there was no interrupt to trap, so 'assert result.returncode != 0' failed as 'assert 0 != 0'. Added pytest.mark.skipif(os.name == 'nt') to the module pytestmark with that reasoning as the skip reason. POSIX behaviour is untouched: the test still runs and passes on macOS/Linux (4 passed locally), and no script under _project/scripts was modified.
work.summary: Fix or platform-gate the INT-trap exit-code test

description:
Inconsistency surfaced during review of commit 495efcaa8 (psycopg3 migration
completion) and follow-up commit 1786150ec. The pg-family `_build_*_config`
builders disagree three ways on the fallback value used for `driver_package`
when `info` is None:

  - postgresql.py, timescaledb.py, pg_duckdb.py, pg_mooncake.py
    fall back to `"psycopg"` (bare distribution/import name).
  - cedardb.py:194 falls back to `"psycopg2-binary"` (psycopg2 pip extras
    variant - leftover from pre-psycopg3 migration; the registry metadata
    at platform_registry.py:616 already advertises `"psycopg"`, so this
    fallback string is stale).
  - questdb.py:1415 falls back to `"psycopg[binary]"` (psycopg3 with pip
    extras marker - the bracketed form is a pip-install requirement, not
    an import name).

In practice the fallback is rarely hit because PlatformRegistry.get_platform_info()
returns a populated `info` for every registered platform (all pg-family
entries in platform_registry.py advertise `driver_package: "psycopg"`), so
`info.driver_package` wins. But the divergence is a latent footgun: if
anything ever consumes driver_package as a pip-style requirement string vs.
an import-name string, the three forms behave differently. The bare name
`"psycopg"` is correct for `importlib.import_module()`; the bracketed form
is only valid for pip/uv install commands; and `"psycopg2-binary"` points
at an entirely different (legacy) distribution.

Action: pick one form (recommend bare `"psycopg"` since `driver_package` is
used elsewhere as an import target) and normalize cedardb.py and questdb.py
to match. Audit any consumer of `DatabaseConfig.driver_package` to confirm
import-name vs requirement-string usage before changing.
title: Normalize driver_package fallback string across pg-family config builders

driver resolution; _sync_driver_options also reads it. The DatabaseConfig
field is Optional[str] with no docstring distinguishing the two.

description:
Integrate Onehouse Quanton as a supported BenchBox platform for high-performance
managed Spark benchmarking with multi-table-format support.

Onehouse Quanton is a serverless managed Spark compute runtime that delivers:
- **2-3x better price-performance** vs AWS EMR and Databricks
- **No per-cluster fees** unlike Databricks Photon
- **Multi-table-format support**: Apache Hudi, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake
- **Apache XTable integration**: Cross-format metadata translation
- **OneSync catalog sync**: Tables accessible from Snowflake, Databricks, Trino, Ray
- **Serverless architecture**: Auto-scaling with intelligent cluster management
- **100% open-source compatible**: Standard Spark/SQL interfaces, no vendor lock-in

Key technical characteristics:
- Spark 3.x runtime with Quanton execution engine optimizations
- Serverless clusters in Onehouse Compute Runtime
- AWS-first with S3 integration (potentially multi-cloud)
- Smart ETL processing with incremental operations
- Proven TPC-DS, TPCx-BB, TPC-DI benchmark performance (3x faster on Iceberg)

This is a strategic platform addition because:
1. Growing enterprise interest in open lakehouse alternatives
2. Direct EMR/Databricks comparison validates performance claims
3. Multi-table-format support enables format comparison benchmarking
4. Founded by Apache Hudi creators - deep lakehouse expertise
5. Unique XTable integration for cross-format interoperability testing

Technical approach:
- Leverage existing managed Spark patterns (EMR Serverless, Dataproc Serverless)
- Compose CloudSparkConfigMixin and SparkTuningMixin
- Use Onehouse API/SDK for cluster and job management
- Support multiple table formats via configuration
- SQLGlot 'spark' dialect for query translation

Reference implementations:
- benchbox/platforms/aws/emr_serverless_adapter.py (serverless Spark pattern)
- benchbox/platforms/gcp/dataproc_serverless_adapter.py (serverless pattern)
- benchbox/platforms/base/cloud_spark/ (shared Spark infrastructure)
title: Add Onehouse Quanton platform support for managed Spark benchmarking

description:
BenchBox supports 34+ platform adapters and 5 open table formats (parquet, delta,
iceberg, vortex, ducklake) plus Hudi via Spark-based platforms. Several platforms are
known to support table formats that BenchBox does not yet register in format_capabilities.py.
This TODO tracks closing every verified gap.

## Current State (as of 2026-03-05)

### format_capabilities.py Registry
| Format   | Registered Platforms                                                    |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| parquet  | duckdb, datafusion, clickhouse, databricks, snowflake, bigquery,        |
|          | redshift, postgresql, sqlite                                            |
| delta    | databricks (NATIVE), duckdb (EXTENSION), datafusion (EXTENSION)         |
| iceberg  | duckdb (EXPERIMENTAL), datafusion (EXTENSION)                           |
| vortex   | duckdb (EXTENSION), datafusion (EXPERIMENTAL)                           |
| ducklake | duckdb (NATIVE)                                                         |

Note: ORC and Hive are NOT open table formats that BenchBox manages. ORC is a storage
format (like Parquet) used internally by Spark/Hive - BenchBox doesn't generate ORC data.
Hive is a metastore/catalog layer, not a table format - Presto/Trino use "hive" as a
catalog connector type, not as a `--table-format` value.

### Verified Gaps

**Gap 1: Hudi format missing from CAPABILITIES_REGISTRY**
- PySpark SQL / cloud_spark base: Hudi via hudi-spark-bundle (SparkTableFormat.HUDI)
- Quanton/OneHouse: Hudi is primary format (explicit --table-format hudi support)
- LakeSail: Hudi support
- hudi_maintenance.py exists with full ACID ops via PySpark
- NOTE: Databricks adapter does NOT have Hudi loading code (only PySpark path)

**Gap 2: Spark-based platforms missing from CAPABILITIES_REGISTRY**
- spark: not in PLATFORM_FORMAT_PREFERENCES (supports delta, iceberg, parquet via code)
- pyspark-sql: not in PLATFORM_FORMAT_PREFERENCES
- AWS EMR Serverless: supports delta, iceberg via Spark (cloud_spark base)
- GCP Dataproc/Serverless: supports delta, iceberg via Spark (cloud_spark base)
- Azure Synapse Spark: supports delta via Spark (cloud_spark base)

**Gap 3: Presto/Trino missing from CAPABILITIES_REGISTRY**
- Presto: supports iceberg, delta catalogs (explicit --table-format choices)
- Trino: supports iceberg, delta, hive catalogs (explicit --table-format choices)
- Neither appears in CAPABILITIES_REGISTRY or PLATFORM_FORMAT_PREFERENCES

**Gap 4: Cloud lakehouse platforms missing**
- Fabric Lakehouse: delta native (not registered)
- Fabric Spark: delta + parquet (not registered)
- Quanton: iceberg, hudi, delta (not registered, but adapter has full support)
- LakeSail: iceberg, hudi, delta (not registered)

**Gap 5: Snowflake Iceberg and Delta not registered**
- Snowflake supports Iceberg Tables (managed + unmanaged) since 2024
- Snowflake supports Delta Lake via external tables (TABLE_FORMAT=DELTA) and Delta Direct
- No code in snowflake.py adapter for Iceberg or Delta yet (adapter gap too)

**Gap 6: ClickHouse Delta/Iceberg not registered**
- ClickHouse can read Delta Lake and Iceberg via table functions
- No code in clickhouse.py adapter for these formats yet (adapter gap too)

**Gap 7: Redshift Delta/Iceberg not registered**
- Redshift Spectrum supports read-only queries on Delta Lake tables (since 2020, via manifest)
- Redshift has limited Iceberg preview support
- No code in redshift adapter for Delta or Iceberg loading yet (adapter gap too)

**Gap 8: BigQuery Delta not registered**
- BigQuery has native Delta Lake support via BigLake (since mid-2024)
- BigQuery also supports Iceberg via BigLake external tables
- No code in bigquery.py adapter for Delta or Iceberg loading yet (adapter gap too)

### Confirmed Non-Gaps (investigated and rejected)
- Databricks Hudi: Databricks platform supports Hudi via Spark runtime, but the BenchBox
  Databricks SQL adapter has zero Hudi code. Only PySpark-based adapters have Hudi support.
  (Tracked as deferred item d6.)
- ORC: Storage format, not an open table format BenchBox manages.
- Hive: Catalog/metastore layer, not a table format.
title: Close open table format support gaps across all BenchBox platforms

description:
The cross-surface gates are honestly documented per-benchmark, but the campaign
headline ("N benchmarks gated") hides that the gates are not equally strong
oracles. For DSL-generated benchmarks (SSB, ~40/43 ClickBench), both DataFrame
backends are generated from ONE spec, so the only independent signal is
SQL-vs-spec - a weaker check than SQL-vs-independent-handwritten-DataFrame (e.g.
CoffeeShop's hand-written impls). A reader who sees "guarded" may infer an
independent cross-check that, for several gates, does not exist.

Relatedly, the oracle coverage map already reports "guarded" on REGISTRATION, with
an Enforced column distinguishing enforced (CI-blocking) vs staged; surface the
independence dimension in the same table so "guarded" cannot be misread as
"independently verified".

description:
Follow-on from the PR #913 review (chatgpt-codex-connector, P2, thread
https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/pull/913#discussion_r3488713690). The
reference-independence axis shipped in oracle-coverage-map-reference-independence-disclosure,
but its cross-surface branch renders the per-gate SURFACE-PROVENANCE gradient
(shared-spec / mixed-provenance / separate-handwritten) directly in the
"Independence" column instead of the self-referential label that item's own w1
and its open-question DEFAULT specified ("cross-surface / variant-equivalence ->
self-referential"). The result conflates two orthogonal axes in one column.

Reproduced facts (verified by reading
_project/scripts/generate_oracle_coverage_map.py on develop):

- oracle_reference_independence()/oracle_independence_and_rationale() return
  gate.surface_independence for ORACLE_CROSS_SURFACE, so the Independence cell
  for amplab/coffeeshop/h2odb reads `separate-handwritten`, ssb/joinorder_synthetic
  read `shared-spec`, and clickbench/read_primitives read `mixed-provenance`.
- But for EVERY cross-surface gate the reference is the benchmark's own SQL
  surface, authored by the same person from the same spec understanding
  (benchbox/core/equivalence/cross_surface.py:15-19 states this explicitly:
  "the independence is always SQL-text vs DataFrame-code, authored by the same
  person from the same understanding"). On the reference-independence axis every
  cross-surface gate is therefore SELF-REFERENTIAL, regardless of whether the two
  surfaces were generated from one spec or hand-written separately.
- Net effect (the reviewer's concern): a reader skimming the Independence column
  sees `separate-handwritten` and may read it as "checked against an independent,
  separately-built implementation" and over-trust those value-level cells — the
  same coverage-theater the column was added to remove. The two facts a reader
  needs are distinct: (a) is the reference external to benchbox? (always "no" for
  cross-surface) and (b) how independent are the two compared surfaces from each
  other? (the shared-spec -> separate-handwritten gradient). One column cannot
  carry both without misleading on axis (a).

This item splits the single overloaded column into two orthogonal, derived
columns: Independence (reference-independence: self-referential vs
semi-independent vs independent) and Surface provenance (shared-spec /
mixed-provenance / separate-handwritten / — for non-cross-surface), updates the
disclosure prose and the classifier-truth tests accordingly, and regenerates the
committed map. It keeps everything GENERATED from live sources and ADDITIVE — it
does not change any oracle's actual strength, does not re-do Strength/Scale/Enforced,
and does not touch UNGUARDED breadth.

Note on parent status: oracle-coverage-map-reference-independence-disclosure is
still marked Not Started even though the axis shipped (PR #913); this follow-on
realigns the shipped behavior with that item's stated w1 design (cross-surface =
self-referential, provenance as a SEPARATE axis) per the reviewer, rather than
re-opening it.
preserves: The drift check (`make oracle-coverage-map-check`) stays green on a clean tree and on the required PR path; the new column/field regenerates deterministically and the provenance stamp stays out of the drift-compared body.
The map stays GENERATED from live sources — no hand-maintained per-benchmark classification — so neither axis can drift from reality.
The split is ADDITIVE: Strength/Scale/Enforced columns, the drift check, and every non-cross-surface Independence label stay exactly as they shipped.

description:
An adversarial falsification review of the oracle coverage-map disclosure work
(PR #867, reviewed on develop @ e4a04484 — an ancestor of origin/develop) found
that the Strength + Scale columns shipped in oracle-coverage-map-strength-disclosure
(#867, DONE) are honest as far as they go (the drift check, the derived-not-
hardcoded strength, and the staged-vs-enforced Enforced column all survived
attack), but the taxonomy omits the single axis that most determines how much a
green cell can be trusted: whether the oracle compares against an INDEPENDENT
reference or against itself.

Reproduced facts (verified by reading
_project/scripts/generate_oracle_coverage_map.py and the committed
_project/analysis/oracle-coverage-map.md on develop):

- The Strength taxonomy is exactly {value-level, cardinality-only,
  value+cardinality}. oracle_strength_and_scale returns STRENGTH_VALUE
  ("value-level") as an UNCONDITIONAL CONSTANT for every cross-surface / variant
  gate. It encodes WHAT is compared (full values vs row counts), never WHETHER
  the reference is independent of the system under test.
- The cells labelled "value-level" — ssb / amplab / coffeeshop / clickbench
  (cross-surface) — are SQL-vs-DataFrame self-comparisons: both surfaces derive
  from the same shared spec, so the SQL surface is effectively the reference for
  its own DataFrame surface. A parallel review found these catch transcription,
  not conceptual, bugs.
- tpch's "value+cardinality" is ALSO self-referential on the value axis: the
  reference digests were produced by running benchbox-on-DuckDB and frozen (see
  correctness-gate-value-digest-fidelity-followups). So even the strongest cell
  in the map is a regression snapshot, not an independent value oracle.
- Net effect: a reader who sees "value-level" reasonably infers "values are
  proven correct" and may skip manual inspection — the exact coverage-theater the
  map was built to remove, re-introduced one abstraction up. The map's honesty
  about the registered-vs-enforced axis makes this gap MORE likely to be missed,
  because the reader has already been taught the map is candid.

Two smaller disclosure defects from the same review:

- SF>1 VALUE-BLINDNESS NEEDS TWO COLUMNS TO SEE (NIT). tpch reads
  "value+cardinality | SF=1". The prose does say "tpch/tpcds values are unguarded
  above SF=1", but the table ROW alone (Strength without reading the Scale cell)
  lets a skimmer conclude tpch values are guarded generally. The most-run scale
  (SF>1) is value-blind and the row cell does not say so on its own.

- PROVENANCE SHA IS ORPHANED BY SQUASH-MERGE (NIT). The committed map stamps
  `revision: ddd96c47...` in its drift-ignored provenance header. Reproduced:
  that SHA is `git cat-file` "bad object" / unreachable from any ref — it was the
  pre-squash PR-branch HEAD, discarded when #867 landed as a squash. The stamp
  meant to let a reader locate the generation point points to a commit that does
  not exist in history. (The same squash-orphaning explains why this review's
  own brief cited merge SHAs f411d522/a0c62631 that are absent here; the squash
  landed as e4a04484.)

This item adds a reference-independence axis to the map, makes the SF>1 value gap
unmissable from a single row, and makes the provenance stamp survive squash-merge.
SCOPE BOUNDARY: it does NOT re-do the Strength/Scale/Enforced columns (#867, DONE),
does NOT close UNGUARDED breadth (benchmark-correctness-oracle-coverage-map), and
does NOT touch the registered-vs-verified-green axis (cross-surface-oracle-remediation).
preserves: The drift check (`make oracle-coverage-map-check`) stays green on a clean tree and on the required PR path; the new column and the new provenance stamp must regenerate deterministically and stay out of the drift-compared body.
The existing Strength/Scale/Enforced columns and the drift check stay exactly as #867 shipped them; the independence axis is an ADDITIVE column.
The map stays GENERATED from live sources — no hand-maintained classification — so it cannot drift from reality.

compare against a reference INDEPENDENT of the system under test, or against
itself? Derive from live sources, not a hand label:

comparison", not "values proven against an authority".

description:
An adversarial review of the oracle coverage map (#834, reviewed on develop)
found the map collapses very different guarantees into a single word, "guarded".
The drift machinery is sound and on the required PR path - it was verified to go
RED on a mutated artifact and a removed GATES entry - but it protects the map's
CONSISTENCY with the generator, not the TRUTH of what "guarded" implies.

Reproduced facts (verified against develop @ 8596ab51):

- `build_coverage_map` / `classify_oracles`
  (_project/scripts/generate_oracle_coverage_map.py) emit one primary oracle per
  benchmark and a boolean `guarded`. They do NOT record how STRONG that oracle is
  or at what SCALE it holds. The rendered map shows e.g.
  `tpch | expected-results | guarded` with no qualifier.
- The guaranteed strengths differ enormously and are not distinguished:
    * expected-results (tpch, tpcds): ROW-COUNT only today, and ONLY at SF=1
      (loader raises for other scales). Cardinality, one scale.
    * cross-surface (ssb, amplab, coffeeshop): VALUE-level (validate_results_exact
      sorts full result sets and compares cell-by-cell with tol 1e-10,
      benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py), but self-referential (SQL is the
      reference for its own DataFrame surface) at the bounded SF=0.1.
    * variant-equivalence (tpchavoc): value-level vs canonical TPC-H.
- A reviewer reading a green "guarded" cell reasonably infers "correctness is
  proven" and may skip manual value inspection. That is the coverage-theater risk
  the map was meant to remove, re-introduced one abstraction up: the map is honest
  about its DENOMINATOR (6/23 guarded, 17 named UNGUARDED) but not about the
  QUALITY of each guarded cell.

This item adds two disclosure axes to the generated map - oracle STRENGTH-TYPE
(value-level / cardinality-only / structural) and SCALE coverage - plus a
classifier-correctness test so the new axes cannot silently regress, and an
artifact-provenance note that addresses the review-staleness failure mode.

SCOPE BOUNDARY (do not duplicate): a separate, higher-priority axis -
"gate-registered vs verified-green" - is already owned by
cross-surface-oracle-remediation w9. This item owns the orthogonal STRENGTH-TYPE
+ SCALE + provenance axes and must layer onto whatever naming w9 lands.
preserves: The drift check (`make oracle-coverage-map-check`) stays green on a clean tree and on the required PR path; new columns must regenerate deterministically.
The existing summary semantics (N guarded / M UNGUARDED, the UNGUARDED dispatch lists) are preserved; strength/scale are additive columns.
The map stays GENERATED from live sources - no hand-maintained classification - so it cannot drift from reality.

description: generate_oracle_coverage_map.py has two holes in how it reads live cross-surface gate metadata. description:
Test-strategy review of packaging/config found three independent, low-risk
hygiene items in the top-level packaging and pytest config files:

1. **Stale `setup.py`.** `pyproject.toml` fully declares the project via
   PEP 621 `[project]` (`name = "benchbox"`, `version = "0.2.1"`, real
   `dependencies`) with `build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"`
   (pyproject.toml:1-7). `setup.py` separately declares
   `version="0.1.0"` and a tiny, wrong `install_requires=["pytest>=6.0.0",
   "pytest-cov>=2.10.0", "pytest-mock>=3.3.0"]` (test-only deps, not the
   real runtime dependency set). Since setuptools' PEP 517 build backend
   reads project metadata from `pyproject.toml`'s `[project]` table when
   present, `setup.py`'s `setup()` call is very likely vestigial for
   `uv build` / wheel builds today - but this must be verified, not
   assumed, before deleting it (see w1).

2. **Dead `setup.cfg` sections.** `setup.cfg` has `[flake8]` and
   `[isort]` sections, but the project's actual lint/format tooling is
   `ruff` (per `pyproject.toml`'s `[dependency-groups] dev` pinning
   `ruff==0.11.13`, and `make lint`/`make format` targets) - flake8 and
   isort are not installed or invoked anywhere. `setup.cfg` also has a
   `[tool:pytest]` section (`testpaths = tests`, a `markers` list) that
   is a SECOND pytest config in addition to `pytest.ini` and
   `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` - a third copy of the
   same settings, silently ignored (see #3).

3. **Three pytest config homes, only one active.** Pytest's config
   discovery picks the first of `pytest.ini` / `pyproject.toml` /
   `setup.cfg` / `tox.ini` it finds in the rootdir, in that priority
   order - `pytest.ini` exists at the repo root, so it always wins
   for a bare `uv run -- python -m pytest` invocation, making
   `pyproject.toml`'s `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` (lines 424-481) and
   `setup.cfg`'s `[tool:pytest]` section silently dead. This is visibly
   true from `pyproject.toml:426`: `minversion = "0.2.1"` - a copy-paste
   of the PROJECT version into a field pytest interprets as "minimum
   pytest version required," which is meaningless (pytest's real version
   is always >= "0.2.1" as a version-comparison string, so the check
   never fires) and clearly never validated against pytest's actual
   `minversion` semantics because nobody runs this config block.
   There is ALSO a fourth file, `pytest-ci.ini`, which IS actively used -
   explicitly passed via `-c pytest-ci.ini` in `Makefile:316` (`test-ci`)
   and `Makefile:547,550,553,556-558` (`coverage-fast`, `coverage-all`,
   `coverage-html`, `coverage-report`) - so any consolidation plan must
   account for THREE real config surfaces (`pytest.ini` for local/default
   runs, `pytest-ci.ini` for CI/coverage runs via explicit `-c`, and the
   dead `pyproject.toml`/`setup.cfg` copies), not two.

Separately (same TODO, same theme): `benchbox/__init__.py`,
`pyproject.toml`'s `[project].version`, `pyproject.toml`'s
`[tool.pytest.ini_options].minversion` (the meaningless copy above),
`README.md`, `docs/README.md`, and `benchbox/utils/VERSION_MANAGEMENT.md`
all separately hardcode `"0.2.1"` - 5 of these 6 are intentionally
tracked and cross-checked by `benchbox/utils/version.py`'s
`check_version_consistency()` (canonical source
`benchbox/__init__.py:17`, doc paths validated via
`_ADDITIONAL_VERSION_PATHS`/`DOCUMENTATION_VERSION_PATHS`,
`version.py:32-37`) - so the runtime-consistency risk is already
mitigated for those 5. The 6th (pytest's stray `minversion`) is NOT
tracked by that checker and is simply meaningless config, addressed by
item 3 above (whichever config file survives should not carry a
project-version-shaped `minversion`). `dynamic = ["version"]` (reading
version from `benchbox/__init__.py` at build time) would collapse the
`[project].version` copy specifically, but is scoped to a decision +
implementation work unit here, not a larger version-management rewrite.
preserves: Makefile targets test-ci, coverage, coverage-fast, coverage-all, coverage-html, coverage-report continue to work with pytest-ci.ini exactly as before - do not delete or restructure pytest-ci.ini without updating every Makefile reference in the same change.

The xdist safety shim behavior (_benchbox_pytest_xdist_safety.py, loaded via `-p _benchbox_pytest_xdist_safety` in pytest.ini's addopts) - if w3 picks option (A), this line must survive in pytest.ini unchanged; if option (B), it must be carried into pyproject.toml's addopts equivalent exactly.
benchbox/utils/version.py::check_version_consistency() continues to pass for whichever version-string copies remain after w4's decision.
make test-fast selection semantics (whatever marker expression / config file it currently resolves through) - verify with `make test-fast` before and after w3, comparing collected test counts.

benchbox-0.2.1-py3-none-any.whl with Version: 0.2.1 and 184
Requires-Dist entries from pyproject.toml's real dependency list
(not setup.py's 3 test-only deps). After deleting setup.py, the
identical build command produced the same wheel filename with an
identical file manifest and Requires-Dist list.

setup.py's coexistence was silently overriding
`requires-python`. Before deletion: `Requires-Python: >=3.10` plus
`Dynamic: requires-python` (setup.py's `python_requires=">=3.10"`
was winning over pyproject.toml's `requires-python =
">=3.10,<3.15"`, silently dropping the `<3.15` upper bound cap).
After deletion: `Requires-Python: <3.15,>=3.10` (correct, matches
pyproject.toml) and `Dynamic: requires-python` is gone. So
setup.py was not purely vestigial - it was shipping a wrong,
wider Python-version constraint in every built wheel. Deleting it
fixes a real (if minor) packaging bug, not just tidies dead code.

Scope is a DECISION plus (if adopted) a small implementation - not a
broader version-management rewrite. If adopted: set
`dynamic = ["version"]` in `pyproject.toml`'s `[project]` table,
remove the static `version = "0.2.1"` line, and add the
corresponding `[tool.setuptools.dynamic]` section pointing at
`benchbox.__version__` (setuptools supports `attr:
benchbox.__version__` for this). Verify `uv build` and `benchbox
--version` / `benchbox --version-json` still report the correct
version afterward, and that
`benchbox/utils/version.py::check_version_consistency()` still
passes (it may need a small update if it currently reads
`pyproject.toml`'s `[project].version` key directly via
`_PYPROJECT_CACHE` - check `version.py` for exactly how it sources
the "pyproject.toml version" side of its comparison before assuming
no change is needed). If NOT adopted, record the reasoning
(5 tracked copies + 1 runtime checker is judged sufficient
mitigation) as a one-line comment near
`_ADDITIONAL_VERSION_PATHS` in version.py so a future reader doesn't
re-raise the same question without context.

DECISION: NOT adopted. Confirmed by reading version.py:
`get_pyproject_version()` (line ~210) reads `[project].version`
directly out of the tomllib-parsed dict via `_PYPROJECT_CACHE` -
if `[project].version` becomes `dynamic = ["version"]`, that key
is simply absent from the static TOML parse (tomllib doesn't
resolve `[tool.setuptools.dynamic]` attr: pointers - that's a
setuptools build-time behavior, not a TOML-level fact), so
`get_pyproject_version()` would silently start returning None.
That flips "pyproject.toml" from a real tracked source to a
missing one in `check_version_consistency()`'s dev-mode
accounting, which is a regression the fix would have to
compensate for (e.g. teaching version.py to resolve
`attr:` dynamic version pointers itself) - real, non-trivial
version.py surgery for a decision framed as "small". The 5
tracked copies (`benchbox.__init__`, `installed-dist`,
`pyproject.toml`, `README.md`, `docs/README.md`,
`VERSION_MANAGEMENT.md`) plus `check_version_consistency()` are
already a solid drift-detection net for a single low-traffic
version string; collapsing one more copy isn't worth the added
complexity now. The actual motivating problem (pytest's
meaningless `minversion = "0.2.1"` copy-paste) is fully resolved
by w3 deleting the dead `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` block, so
there's no remaining live bug pushing toward adopting dynamic
version. Reasoning recorded as a comment block in
benchbox/utils/version.py directly above
`_ADDITIONAL_VERSION_PATHS` for future readers.

anti_patterns.why: they add dependencies; fcntl is stdlib and sufficient for macOS/Linux

anti_patterns.dont: use pytest_sessionstart hook

approach:
1. In tests/conftest.py, add after existing imports:
   - _TEST_LOCK_PATH = Path.home() / ".benchbox" / "test.lock"
   - _test_lock_fd: int | None = None  (module-level, keeps fd alive)
   - _should_acquire_test_lock(config) helper function
   - pytest_configure hook: acquires fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB), writes
     PID+timestamp+cmd to lock file, stores fd in _test_lock_fd
   - pytest_unconfigure hook: releases lock via flock(LOCK_UN) and closes fd

2. Error message format when blocked:
   "[benchbox] BLOCKED: A parallel test run is already active.
     Lock file : ~/.benchbox/test.lock
     Holder    : pid:XXXX started:YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS cmd:...
     Options:
       • Wait for the other run to finish and retry.
       • Run single-threaded (no lock):  pytest -n 0 ...
       • Bypass lock (dangerous):         BENCHBOX_SKIP_TEST_LOCK=1 pytest ..."

3. In Makefile, add test-unlock convenience target after test-fast:
   test-unlock:
       @echo "Removing stale BenchBox test lock..."
       @rm -f ~/.benchbox/test.lock
       @echo "Lock cleared."
description:
pytest.ini defaults to `-n auto`, which spawns one worker per logical CPU (10 on
this machine). When two agent sessions each trigger `make test-fast`, the result is
20+ concurrent pytest workers competing for CPU, bringing the machine to a halt.

Add an exclusive `fcntl.flock` lock in `tests/conftest.py` so that only one
parallel test run can be active at a time. A second concurrent attempt fails
immediately with a clear, actionable error message identifying the lock holder.

Chosen approach: `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)` on `~/.benchbox/test.lock`.
The OS auto-releases the lock when the holder process dies (no stale lock cleanup
needed). No new dependencies - `fcntl` is stdlib on macOS/Linux.
preserves: All 13,000+ fast-marked tests continue to pass after the hooks are added - confirm with `make test-fast` reporting 13052 passed
CI pipelines: lock is user-local (~/.benchbox/test.lock); CI containers with fresh filesystems must never see a pre-existing lock
Crash recovery: after kill -9 on a running test session, the next invocation must succeed without any manual cleanup (OS auto-releases flock on exit)
Single-threaded runs: numprocesses == 0 or None must bypass the lock entirely
xdist workers: hasattr(config, 'workerinput') check must prevent workers from competing for the lock - only the controller process acquires it
title: Prevent concurrent parallel test runs via fcntl.flock mutex

verifications.expected: tests pass (OS auto-released flock on kill)

description:
The TPC-DS dsdgen tool has broken stdout support due to two bugs that were
introduced when official TPC imports (v2.10.0, v4.0.0) reverted community fixes.

Bug 1 - Parameter name mismatch (params.h):
  - Help shows `_FILTER` but code calls `is_set("FILTER")` without underscore
  - fnd_param() uses prefix matching so "FILTER" never matches "_FILTER"

Bug 2 - fpOutfile overwrite (print.c):
  - Line 449 sets `fpOutfile = stdout` when FILTER is set
  - Line 485 unconditionally overwrites with `fpOutfile = pTdef->outfile` (NULL)
  - Result: "Failed to open output file!" error

These bugs affect both _sources/tpc-ds and the prebuilt binaries in _binaries/tpc-ds/.

Original fix by Greg Rahn (gregrahn) in commit 7992dbb of tpcds-kit repo.
title: Patch TPC-DS source to fix stdout data generation

description:
Apply patches to TPC-H dbgen source code to enable reliable stdout data generation
using the -z flag, matching the tpch-kit reference implementation.

The BenchBox TPC-H source (June 2021) lacks stdout output capability that was added
to tpch-kit (March 2025). This prevents streaming data generation workflows that
are critical for compression pipelines and efficient data loading.

Key differences identified between BenchBox and tpch-kit:
- Missing `zstdout` global variable declaration in dss.h
- Missing stdout conditional in print_prep() function in print.c
- Missing -z command-line flag handling in driver.c
- Money formatting bug in print.c (int vs long format specifier)
title: Patch TPC-H source to fix stdout data generation

description:
Add a pg_duckdb platform adapter that enables benchmarking PostgreSQL with
the pg_duckdb extension installed. pg_duckdb embeds DuckDB's vectorized
analytical engine inside PostgreSQL, accelerating OLAP queries by up to
1500x on certain workloads without requiring SQL changes.

This adapter should inherit from PostgreSQLAdapter (following the TimescaleDB
pattern) and add pg_duckdb-specific configuration: enabling the extension,
setting GUC parameters like duckdb.force_execution, configuring thread counts
for parallel scans, and optionally connecting to MotherDuck for hybrid queries.

Key benchmarking scenarios:
- pg_duckdb on regular PostgreSQL heap tables (row-oriented, DuckDB execution)
- pg_duckdb vs vanilla PostgreSQL (same data, same queries, different engine)
- pg_duckdb vs native DuckDB (comparing embedded vs standalone)
- pg_duckdb with MotherDuck cloud offload (deployment mode: motherduck)

The adapter should support TPC-H, TPC-DS, and ClickBench benchmarks, which
are the most relevant OLAP workloads for pg_duckdb's acceleration capabilities.

description:
Add a pg_mooncake platform adapter that enables benchmarking PostgreSQL with
the pg_mooncake extension installed. pg_mooncake adds native columnstore
tables (Iceberg/Delta Lake backed, Parquet storage) with DuckDB-powered
vectorized execution to PostgreSQL, achieving top-10 ClickBench performance.

Unlike pg_duckdb which accelerates queries on regular heap tables,
pg_mooncake uses a custom "columnstore" table access method (CREATE TABLE ...
USING columnstore) that stores data in Parquet format with Iceberg metadata.
This gives true columnar compression (5:1 to 20:1) and DuckDB-native
execution on columnar data.

This adapter should inherit from PostgreSQLAdapter and override schema
creation to use columnstore tables, handle the different data loading path
(COPY into columnstore creates Parquet files), and configure pg_mooncake-
specific GUC parameters.

Key benchmarking scenarios:
- pg_mooncake columnstore vs PostgreSQL heap tables (same queries)
- pg_mooncake vs native DuckDB (columnar vs columnar)
- pg_mooncake vs ClickHouse (ClickBench comparison - pg_mooncake is top 10)
- pg_mooncake with object storage backend (S3/GCS) vs local disk

description:
Implement comprehensive physical tuning DDL generation that bridges the gap between
the existing tuning configuration system and actual CREATE TABLE statement generation.

## Current State Analysis

BenchBox has a well-architected tuning configuration system with:
- `UnifiedTuningConfiguration` for holistic tuning management
- `TableTuning` with partitioning, clustering, distribution, sorting columns
- `PlatformOptimizationConfiguration` for Z-ordering, auto-optimize, bloom filters
- YAML config files in `examples/tunings/` with complete schema
- Platform compatibility matrix in `TuningType.is_compatible_with_platform()`

However, there's a significant gap: tuning configurations are **defined but not
consistently applied** during table creation. Many platforms log tuning info but
don't inject it into DDL statements.

## Gap Analysis by Platform

| Platform     | Config Support | DDL Generation | Post-Load Apply | Gap Level |
|--------------|----------------|----------------|-----------------|-----------|
| ClickHouse   | ✓ Full         | ✓ PARTITION BY, ORDER BY | ✓ OPTIMIZE | Low |
| Firebolt     | ✓ Full         | ✓ PRIMARY INDEX, PARTITION BY | - | Low |
| BigQuery     | ✓ Full         | ✓ PARTITION BY, CLUSTER BY | - | Low |
| Snowflake    | ✓ Full         | ✓ CLUSTER BY | ✓ ALTER CLUSTER | Low |
| Databricks   | ✓ Full         | ⚠ CLUSTER BY only | ✓ Z-ORDER | Medium |
| Spark        | ✓ Full         | ⚠ PARTITIONED BY only | ✓ Z-ORDER | Medium |
| DuckDB       | ✓ Full         | ✗ Logging only | - | High |
| Redshift     | ✓ Full         | ✗ Not implemented | - | High |
| PostgreSQL   | ✓ Full         | ✗ Not implemented | - | High |
| TimescaleDB  | ✓ Full         | ✗ Not implemented | - | High |
| Trino/Presto | ✓ Full         | ✗ Not implemented | - | High |
| Athena       | ✓ Full         | ✗ Not implemented | - | High |

## Missing Physical Tuning Features

### Distribution Strategies (Not Fully Implemented)
- **Redshift**: DISTSTYLE ALL/KEY/EVEN, DISTKEY(column)
- **Databricks**: Liquid clustering, hash distribution
- **BigQuery**: No explicit distribution (automatic)
- **Snowflake**: No explicit distribution (automatic micro-partitioning)

### Sort Key Variations (Partial)
- **Redshift**: SORTKEY(col), COMPOUND SORTKEY, INTERLEAVED SORTKEY
- **DuckDB**: ORDER BY in table definition (v0.10+)
- **ClickHouse**: ORDER BY (tuple) for MergeTree

### Partitioning Granularity (Not Configurable)
- Date partitioning: DAILY, MONTHLY, YEARLY
- Range partitioning: explicit boundaries
- Hash partitioning: bucket count
- List partitioning: explicit values

### Table Format-Specific Options (Not Covered)
- **Iceberg**: partition transforms (bucket, truncate, year, month, day, hour)
- **Delta Lake**: liquid clustering, deletion vectors
- **Hudi**: partition by, pre-combine field

## Proposed Architecture

A unified `DDLGenerator` interface that each platform implements:

```python
class DDLGenerator(Protocol):
    def generate_create_table_ddl(
        self,
        table_name: str,
        columns: list[ColumnDefinition],
        tuning_config: Optional[TableTuning] = None,
        platform_opts: Optional[PlatformOptimizationConfiguration] = None,
    ) -> str:
        """Generate CREATE TABLE with tuning clauses applied."""
        ...

    def generate_tuning_clauses(
        self,
        table_tuning: TableTuning,
    ) -> TuningClauses:
        """Generate platform-specific tuning SQL fragments."""
        ...
```
title: Implement Physical Tuning DDL Generation Across All Platforms

description:
Four independent robustness gaps in the plan-capture subsystem, each a separate
failure mode from the missing CI gate (tracked in plan-capture-blocking-ci-gate):

1. Implicit phase-eligibility. adapter.py:120 defaults
   plan_capture_phase_eligible=True and ~12 SaaS adapters inherit it implicitly.
   It is a correctness-critical flag (it decides whether plan capture is isolated
   from measured timing); a future non-EXPLAIN subclass would silently inherit
   True.
2. Timeout thread leak. On a capture timeout, result_capture.py:828 leaves a live
   EXPLAIN thread on the measurement connection (an accepted tradeoff). It cannot
   perturb MEASURED timing (post-measurement phase), but it can corrupt SUBSEQUENT
   captures in the same phase - untested.
3. Plan identity / misattribution. Plans are captured and attached by query_id,
   but for stream/seed-specific SQL (TPC power-test streams, unseeded variants)
   the SQL bound to a query_id can differ from the measured statement, so the
   attached plan may describe a different query text than the one timed.
4. Comparable-subset honesty. The cross-engine comparable subset is an
   operator-type multiset over a single query shape (test_cross_engine_
   conformance.py) with no tables/predicates - a meaningful harmonization check but
   near-trivial as "plan equivalence". Either strengthen it or relabel it so
   consumers do not over-trust it.
preserves: The centralized is_dml_query double-execution guard is unchanged.
The post-measurement capture phase stays isolated; measured timing is unaffected by any change here.

description:
Adversarial code reviews identified three issues that directly corrupt benchmark
measurement accuracy - the core purpose of BenchBox:

1. **Databend result cache never disabled** (PR #29): disable_result_cache=True is
   stored but never applied. Queries may return cached results, inflating performance
   numbers. Must execute SET enable_query_result_cache = 0.

2. **Databend USE database included in query timing** (PR #29): execute_query() starts
   the timer, then issues USE database before the actual query. Network latency of the
   USE statement contaminates every query measurement.

3. **Doris SET global modifies cluster-wide settings** (PR #30): configure_for_benchmark()
   uses SET global (e.g., SET global enable_sql_cache = false, SET global
   parallel_fragment_exec_instance_num = 8). This modifies settings for ALL sessions on
   the cluster, not just the benchmark session. If another workload is running, it gets
   disrupted. Should use session-level SET without the global keyword.

These are Critical priority because they silently produce wrong benchmark results -
the most dangerous class of bug in a benchmarking tool.

description:
Adversarial code reviews of PRs #27-33 identified cursor and connection resource
leaks in 5 of 6 new platform adapters: QuestDB, Databend, pg_duckdb, pg_mooncake,
and StarRocks. Common patterns:

1. **Cursor not closed on exception**: When cursor.execute() raises in execute_query(),
   the except block returns without calling cursor.close(). Under sustained query
   failures (common in benchmarking), this leaks server-side cursors.
2. **Orphaned cursors from mogrify()**: pg_duckdb and pg_mooncake create new cursors
   via conn.cursor().mogrify() for credential escaping, but never close them.
3. **Connection leaks in test/check methods**: Databend's test_connection() and
   check_server_database_exists() create BlockingDatabendClient instances without
   closing them.

These leaks accumulate during long benchmark runs and can exhaust server-side
connection/cursor limits.
