anti_patterns.dont: classify a platform as INFORMATIONAL in w2 based on 'common knowledge' or 'looks like Snowflake'
anti_patterns.instead: every classification must cite a vendor-doc URL or a reproducer
anti_patterns.why: vendor enforcement semantics shift between releases and connector layers (e.g. Trino-on-Iceberg differs from Trino-on-Hive)

anti_patterns.dont: combine the DEGRADED→INFORMATIONAL rename (w3) and the SKIPPED split (w4) into one work unit
anti_patterns.instead: ship them as two sequenced, individually-revertable commits
anti_patterns.why: both are closed-set transformations on the same enum file and combining doubles the diff and the revert blast radius

anti_patterns.dont: couple the coverage stream (w2/w5) to the SKIPPED-split stream (w4/w6)
anti_patterns.instead: the coverage stream depends only on w3 (the rename), not on w4
anti_patterns.why: that delays closing the silent-corruption window behind metadata refactoring

anti_patterns.dont: delete SupportLevel.DEGRADED or SupportLevel.SKIPPED without migrating every caller in the same change set
anti_patterns.instead: audit `grep -rn 'SupportLevel.DEGRADED' benchbox/ tests/ scripts/` (and the same for SKIPPED) before editing decision.py and fix every site in the same commit
anti_patterns.why: Python enums are closed sets and a half-migrated state will not import

anti_patterns.dont: delete the legacy_bypass tuple in benchmark.py before every w2-surfaced platform has a registered rule
anti_patterns.instead: delete the tuple as the LAST step of w5 after the parity test passes
anti_patterns.why: a half-migration leaves uncovered platforms with neither the legacy fallback nor a registry rule, fail-closed instead of fail-open

anti_patterns.dont: extend SupportLevel with a third skip value (e.g. SKIPPED_AUXILIARY) without ADR addendum sign-off
anti_patterns.instead: if a rule does not fit, raise it in w1 before code lands
anti_patterns.why: the taxonomy was deliberately frozen at four outcomes (BLOCKED / SKIPPED_QUERY / SKIPPED_DDL_FRAGMENT / INFORMATIONAL)

anti_patterns.dont: promote the reason-string lint from warn to error in the same slice that introduces the convention
anti_patterns.instead: ship warn-only here, promote in a follow-up
anti_patterns.why: the lint and the rule audit must land atomically if it is error-mode and that doubles the diff

anti_patterns.dont: regenerate docs/compat/*.md in a work unit that also changes the rule registry
anti_patterns.instead: always end the workstream with a clean docs-only regeneration commit (w9)
anti_patterns.why: a single commit then mixes 'registry change' with 'doc shape change' and reviewers cannot tell which drove which

anti_patterns.dont: register PK rules in w5 without first completing the w2 audit
anti_patterns.instead: every w5 rule must cite the audit row that justifies its bucket
anti_patterns.why: guessing at vendor enforcement semantics is exactly how silent-corruption originates

anti_patterns.dont: register a NATIVE PK rule for any adapter that inherits from NoConstraintEnforcementMixin
anti_patterns.instead: mixin members must classify as INFORMATIONAL or SKIPPED_DDL_FRAGMENT and the w5 parity test enforces this
anti_patterns.why: the mixin no-ops apply_constraint_configuration so the constraint never actually gets applied at runtime, registering NATIVE would create a registry/adapter parity bug

anti_patterns.dont: touch _pk_lock_bypass_required logic beyond removing the legacy_bypass tuple
anti_patterns.instead: if a rule cannot be expressed under the existing CompatAction values, raise it in w1, not w5
anti_patterns.why: the function is a stable consumer of the registry and changing its dispatch shape is out of scope

approach:
Two parallel streams gated on the ADR addendum (w1) and the
closed-set enum changes (w3, w4):

- Coverage stream (w2 → w5): audit PK enforcement on every supported
  platform with NoConstraintEnforcementMixin as a cross-check, then
  register the missing INFORMATIONAL rules and delete the legacy_bypass
  fallback tuple. Closes the silent-corruption window. Cannot start
  until w3 lands (uses the new INFORMATIONAL name from day one).

- Enum stream (w3 → w4): rename DEGRADED → INFORMATIONAL atomically,
  then split SKIPPED → SKIPPED_QUERY + SKIPPED_DDL_FRAGMENT atomically.
  Sequenced rather than combined so each is a single, individually-
  revertable closed-set transformation.

Then sequenced tail (w6 → w7 → w8 → w9):
- w6: migrate existing SKIPPED rules to refined values.
- w7: reason-string convention + warn-only lint, after w5 and w6 so
  reason updates touch each rule file once.
- w8: generator restructure into two doc sections.
- w9: final docs regeneration + verification.

Mirror the original pipeline's discipline: ADR before code, structural
change before content migration, convention before enforcement,
generator change before doc commit. Keep each enum change atomic - the
enum is a closed set so dual-run / shadow-mode is not feasible. The
reason-string lint stays warn-only in this TODO; promotion to error
mode is a separate follow-up after every rule complies.
description:
After build-sql-compat-phase-aware-pipeline shipped (w17/w18, 2026-04-26),
reviewing the eight skip/block/degrade rows in docs/compat/skip-reference.md
surfaced five problems with the as-shipped support_level surface. Three are
readability gaps; one is a real silent-corruption window the pipeline was
supposed to close; one is a naming choice that biases readers toward the
wrong interpretation.

1. SupportLevel.DEGRADED carries performance-regression connotations and
   reads as a judgement on the platform. The actual semantic - "the
   workload runs end-to-end, but a documented platform-level guarantee
   (typically PRIMARY KEY uniqueness) is not provided" - is closer to how
   vendors document this themselves. Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery, and
   Databricks docs use INFORMATIONAL or NOT ENFORCED. Renaming
   DEGRADED → INFORMATIONAL aligns with vendor terminology and removes
   the false suggestion that the platform is performing badly.

2. SupportLevel.SKIPPED is overloaded. The same enum value covers
   full-query exclusion (StarRocks vector_search Q2 is dropped from the
   result set entirely on platform_version < 3.2) and DDL-fragment
   suppression (DataFusion write_primitives / transaction_primitives
   lock-table DDL is skipped, but the workload itself runs end-to-end).
   The user-visible consequences are categorically different - one
   removes a query from the benchmark; the other only drops an internal
   coordination DDL - but the doc says "SKIPPED" for both.

3. Rule reason strings explain the platform deficiency ("DataFusion does
   not support PRIMARY KEY syntax", "QuestDB has no VECTOR column type")
   but not the user-visible consequence (benchmark refused at preflight /
   query omitted from results / workload runs with documented caveat).
   Readers consistently misread DDL-fragment skips as full-benchmark skips.

4. The generated skip-reference.md collapses BLOCKED, SKIPPED, and
   DEGRADED into a single per-platform table. Splitting "Will not run"
   (preflight refused or query omitted) from "Runs with caveats" (DDL
   fragment dropped, semantic enforcement gap) would make the page
   self-explaining.

5. PRIMARY KEY enforcement coverage is incomplete. Only four platforms
   have PK-capability rules registered (datafusion, clickhouse,
   starrocks, doris). Every other platform that accepts PRIMARY KEY DDL
   but does not enforce uniqueness silently breaks the
   write_primitives / transaction_primitives setup-lock semantics: the
   CREATE TABLE for write_primitives_setup_lock succeeds, both lock
   INSERTs succeed because uniqueness is not enforced, and concurrent
   setup workers think they own the lock at the same time. The
   legacy_bypass tuple in core/write_primitives/benchmark.py:62 is the
   fallback when no rule resolves; it lists exactly the four covered
   platforms, leaving Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery, Databricks, Synapse,
   Fabric Warehouse, Firebolt, Spark/PySpark, Trino/Presto/Athena/
   Starburst, Databend, and any other "accepts PK DDL, does not enforce"
   platform without protection.

Critical cross-reference for the audit: benchbox/platforms/base/no_constraint_mixin.py
defines NoConstraintEnforcementMixin, used by DataFusion, Polars, and cuDF.
Adapters using this mixin no-op apply_constraint_configuration at runtime,
meaning even if the registry resolved a NATIVE PK rule, the constraint
would never actually be applied. The mixin is direct, in-tree evidence of
"this platform does not enforce PK constraints". The w2 audit must use
it as a cross-check: every NoConstraintEnforcementMixin user must
classify as INFORMATIONAL (uniqueness not enforced but DDL accepted) or
SKIPPED_DDL_FRAGMENT (parser refuses DDL outright, like DataFusion).
Registering a NATIVE PK rule for a mixin user would be a parity bug.

This TODO addresses all five. The naming change (1) lands as a
closed-set enum rename. The structural change (2) lands as an enum
split with an ADR addendum and rule migration. The convention change
(3) lands as a reason-string format plus a lint check. The doc change
(4) is a generator restructure plus regenerated docs. The PK coverage
gap (5) lands as a per-platform audit followed by INFORMATIONAL rule
registrations and removal of the legacy_bypass tuple.

Coverage and taxonomy work proceed mostly in parallel after the ADR
addendum (w1) and the DEGRADED→INFORMATIONAL rename (w3); coverage
closes the bug-shaped gap; taxonomy is layered on after.
preserves: Every adapter inheriting from benchbox/platforms/base/no_constraint_mixin.NoConstraintEnforcementMixin resolves to a non-NATIVE PK rule after w5 - this is the structural parity guarantee the new test in w5 enforces
Existing tests under tests/unit/sql_compat/ continue to pass; if a test pins SupportLevel.DEGRADED or SupportLevel.SKIPPED it must be migrated to the appropriate new value, not deleted
Newly-registered INFORMATIONAL PK rules in w5 do not change behavior on the four already-covered platforms (datafusion, clickhouse, starrocks, doris) - their existing rules remain authoritative
NoConstraintEnforcementMixin behavior in benchbox/platforms/base/no_constraint_mixin.py is unchanged; the runtime no-op is a separate concern from the registry rule and remains as-is

REGISTRY.resolve() / resolve_all() / resolve_platform_rules() return decisions with the same action and payload for the same contexts after the rename and split - only the support_level enum value changes; reason strings change only in w7

The two existing DEGRADED rules (starrocks, doris) at write_primitives + transaction_primitives keep their action (REWRITE_DDL), payload (PKCapabilityPayload contents), and reason text after the w3 rename - only support_level renames

_pk_lock_bypass_required in core/{write,transaction}_primitives/benchmark.py continues to short-circuit lock acquire/release for every platform that resolves to a non-NATIVE PK rule (single-process behavior unchanged on covered platforms)
make compat-docs-check exits 0 after w9 and continues to be wired into .github/workflows/lint.yml
scripts/compat_lint.py continues to error on unregistered dialect branches in benchbox/core/ (the existing W16 acceptance gate)

description:
Adapters perform DDL rewrites via inline regex without registering them
under ``benchbox/sql_compat/``, bypassing the phase-aware compatibility
registry that the framework uses for governance and ``compat_lint`` audit.

Audit findings:

- SingleStore (benchbox/platforms/singlestore.py) does **four** DDL
  rewrites with **zero** registered rules: FK strip
  (``_strip_foreign_keys``, L103-120), SHARD KEY injection
  (``_transform_create_statement``, L847-853), SORT KEY injection
  (L856-859), REFERENCE TABLE rewrite (L830-837), plus lowercase
  identifier normalization (L810-823, MySQL-family operational detail
  that stays inline).
- **FK stripping is duplicated across six adapters** with slightly
  different regexes that have already drifted: SingleStore (L103-120),
  PostgreSQL (L117), Doris (L1435), StarRocks (workload.py L135),
  Databend (adapter.py L871), QuestDB (L482). Six implementations of the same intent.
- Other adapters (StarRocks, ClickHouse, Snowflake, Spark, Trino,
  Redshift, Presto) DO have registered rule stubs in
  ``benchbox/sql_compat/rules/ddl_optimize/`` — so the pattern exists,
  SingleStore and a few others are simply skipping it.
- ``benchbox/sql_compat/inventory.py`` (``compat_lint``) detects
  unregistered branching but doesn't fail CI today — so this drift is
  invisible.

Pattern (verified by reading
``benchbox/sql_compat/rules/ddl_optimize/starrocks_ddl_rewrites.py:25-45``):
a rule registers ``RewriteDDLPayload`` with a ``transformer_id`` for
governance/audit. The adapter still implements the transformation locally
via ``_optimize_table_definition()``. The registry advertises intent;
``compat_lint`` enforces that no adapter does an unregistered DDL rewrite.

This TODO:
1. Registers SingleStore's four DDL transforms under ``ddl_optimize``.
2. Extracts a single shared ``strip_foreign_keys()`` helper and
   migrates all six duplicating adapters to call it.
3. Audits every other adapter for unregistered DDL regex and registers
   them (or removes them) before flipping ``compat_lint`` to fail-CI.
4. Promotes the implicit ``_optimize_table_definition()`` pattern to a
   documented ``DdlOptimizer`` Protocol in ``benchbox/platforms/base/``.
5. Tightens ``compat_lint`` to **fail CI immediately** on unregistered
   DDL regex — strongest enforcement, per user direction.

**Decisions baked in (confirmed with user before authoring):**

- Sequential after ``harmonize-bypass-adapters-with-manifest`` (same
  adapter files, different code paths; lower merge-conflict risk).
- Extract shared FK-strip helper and migrate all six adapters
  (SingleStore + PostgreSQL + Doris + StarRocks + Databend + QuestDB).
- ``compat_lint`` flips to fail-CI in this TODO — no warn-only phase.
  Means w7 cannot land until w1-w5 have eliminated all drift across
  every adapter, not just the six in scope.

Out of scope: query_source rules (h2odb Q9 PERCENTILE_CONT and
vector_search variants are already correctly registered for ``mysql``
dialect at ``rules/query_source/h2odb_variants.py:95-114`` and
``rules/query_source/vector_search_variants.py``); VECTOR type mapping
(already in ``benchbox/core/vector_search/schema.py:_EMBEDDING_TYPE_MAP``);
identifier lowercasing in SingleStore (genuine MySQL-family detail);
SHARD KEY / SORT KEY / REFERENCE TABLE transformer relocation (registry
says register, not relocate — they stay in singlestore.py).
preserves: 13-benchmark SingleStore stress matrix that the band-aid commits validated — DDL transforms must produce byte-identical output before vs after w4/w6 refactor.

Existing query_source rules for mysql/SingleStore: rules/query_source/h2odb_variants.py:95-114 (Q9 PERCENTILE_CONT verbatim) and rules/query_source/vector_search_variants.py — these are correctly registered and must not be touched.

Existing registered rules in rules/ddl_optimize/ (clickhouse, starrocks, snowflake, spark, trino, redshift, presto) — w5 must not change their semantics, only ADD new rules for unregistered transforms.
Phase ordering and registry specificity tiers in benchbox/sql_compat/registry.py — additive changes only.
VECTOR(128, F32) mapping in benchbox/core/vector_search/schema.py:_EMBEDDING_TYPE_MAP — stays in benchmark schema, not sql_compat rules.

1. ``ddl_optimize.singlestore.all.strip_foreign_keys`` — references

   — ``transformer_id="singlestore_reference_table"``. Reason:
   "Small dimension tables (nation, region) benefit from REFERENCE
   TABLE replication to avoid broadcast joins."

description:
Independent verification at checked SHA e60986923 confirmed the registry is a
real single source of truth for benchmark listing/discovery, but found three
remaining drift/cost pockets around metadata:

1. `benchbox/cli/benchmarks.py` has local `_estimate_memory_usage()` and
   `_estimate_execution_time()` dictionaries. The execution-time dictionary
   duplicates registry `estimated_time_range`, and verification found one
   actual drift: `coffeeshop` is `(2, 8)` locally but `(3, 12)` in the
   registry. The original critic's missing-list details were partially stale:
   current local memory/time dicts have 18 entries and miss
   `ai_primitives`, `flightdata`, `tpchavoc`, `transaction_primitives`, and
   `vector_search`; `datavault` and `tpcds_obt` are present in both local
   dicts.

2. `benchbox/core/benchmark_registry.py` populates `data_source` metadata at
   import time by constructing exactly five probe benchmarks:
   `read_primitives`, `write_primitives`, `transaction_primitives`,
   `ai_primitives`, and `tpcds_obt`. Fresh-process verification measured
   registry import at 0.841s on this machine with those five constructor
   calls. The exact timing is environment-dependent, but the import-time
   instantiation count is structural and actionable.

3. `benchbox/mcp/tools/discovery.py` derives behavior from registry helpers
   but its `get_benchmark_info()` docstring repeats a prose benchmark list
   beginning `tpch, tpcds, ssb, clickbench...`, which can drift from the
   registry-owned list.

description:
Release bookkeeping in this repo has drifted from the actual published
state, in two independent ways confirmed against the repo and PyPI on
2026-07-03:

1. `CHANGELOG.md` line 10 has a `## [0.3.1] - 2026-05-30` section written
   in the same released-version format as every other dated entry (e.g.
   `## [0.3.0] - 2026-05-16` at line 53), but no `v0.3.1` git tag exists
   (`git ls-remote --tags origin 'refs/tags/v0.3.*'` returns only
   `refs/tags/v0.3.0`) and PyPI has never served `0.3.1`
   (`pip index versions benchbox` lists `0.3.0` as latest). The section
   reads as shipped when it is not.

2. `README.md:31` says `Current release: v0.2.1`, but that has been stale
   since `v0.3.0` published; PyPI-latest is `0.3.0`, not `0.2.1`
   (`pyproject.toml` and `benchbox/__init__.py` also still read `0.2.1`
   on `develop`, which is expected per the release-cut flow in
   `Makefile:977-1057` — version bumps happen only on the ephemeral
   release branch, not on `develop` — but README's human-facing claim
   needs to reflect the actual latest published release, not develop's
   working version file).

Compounding both: `v0.3.0` is PyPI-latest but fails a clean import
(`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'`, reverified live via
`uv run --isolated --no-project --with 'benchbox==0.3.0' -- python -c
'import benchbox'` run from outside the repo tree). So the CHANGELOG
currently implies a working, released `0.3.1` fix exists when the
PyPI-latest install is actually broken.

wording/dating, README's current-release line) and a durable guard so a
`CHANGELOG.md` released-version section can never again claim a version
with no corresponding git tag. It does NOT own cutting the real `v0.3.1`
release — that belongs to `release-recovery-v0-3-1`, which is already
Critical priority and already in flight.

description:
INDEPENDENT-VERIFICATION FINDING (2026-07-04 review of PR #952): the entire
scheduled release-canary lattice is inert. `.github/workflows/release-canary.yml`
declares `on.schedule: cron "0 8 * * *"` (line 5-7) and now carries three
jobs the repo's safety story leans on:

  1. `pypi-latest-installability` — the daily PyPI-latest install/import
     canary added by pypi-installability-canary-and-rollback (PR #952),
     whose DONE notes claim it "would have caught broken 0.3.0 in a day";
  2. `ruleset-drift` — the daily check that pins the develop ruleset's
     required-check wiring and the v* tag-creation ruleset via
     _project/scripts/ruleset_review_enforcement.py (it formerly also
     warned on the require_code_owner_review gap, but that target was
     retired 2026-07-18 and the warning removed — see
     docs/operations/repo-admin-settings.md);
  3. `credential-free-non-fast` — the scheduled non-fast test sweep.

None of them has ever executed. GitHub runs `on.schedule` workflows ONLY
from the DEFAULT branch's copy of the workflow file. The default branch is
`main` (`git remote show origin` → "HEAD branch: main"), and
`git ls-tree origin/main .github/workflows/` does NOT contain
release-canary.yml — it exists only on `develop`. Corroborating live
evidence gathered 2026-07-04:
  - the Actions "list workflows" API returns 19 workflows and
    release-canary is not among them (a workflow absent from the default
    branch with zero historical runs is never registered);
  - `GET /actions/workflows/release-canary.yml/runs` returns 404.

Consequence: the PyPI-latest canary cannot alert on the currently-broken
0.3.0 release (reconfirmed broken 2026-07-04: clean isolated install fails
with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'`), and the daily
ruleset-drift check that several governance TODOs treat as the live
detection layer (e.g. auto-merge-review-gate-admin-enforcement w2) is not
actually running. In this repo's flow, files reach `main` only at
release-cut, so without deliberate action the canary stays dead until the
next release — the exact window it is supposed to guard.

IMPORTANT EXPECTED STATE once activated: `pypi-latest-installability` will
correctly go RED every day until release-recovery-v0-3-1 ships a fixed
release. That is the desired signal, not a defect — do not "fix" the red
by weakening the canary.

side effects (PR opened, branch on origin, tag on main, PyPI
publish). Procedure:

   exist on develop before invoking them).
2. Get explicit user go-ahead (PyPI is irreversible).

   verifiable during the dry-run; w10/w11 verify on the next regular
   feature-PR cycle.

feature branch off develop, merge back, then bump to rc.2 and repeat.

description:
`.github/workflows/release.yml:3-5` triggers the whole workflow on any
`v*` tag push:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    tags: ['v*']
```

There is no job that asserts the tagged commit is actually an ancestor of
`main` before the `build` (line ~52) and `publish` (line ~98) jobs run.
The in-repo comment at the top of the file even documents the assumed
invariant ("the tag fired here has already been CI-validated" via the
`main-release-only` ruleset + squash-merge to `main`), but that invariant
is enforced entirely by out-of-band process (an admin/maintainer only
ever pushing tags after `release-finalize` merges to `main`), not by the
workflow itself. Anyone (or any compromised token) with tag-push
permission on any ref can trigger a real PyPI publish today.

Separately, `workflow_dispatch` (lines 6-13) lets a human manually run the
workflow from *any* ref with `test_pypi` defaulting to `false`. The
`publish` job's real-PyPI step (line 120-125:
`if: github.event.inputs.test_pypi != 'true'`) is gated only on that
boolean input, not on the ref being a tag at all — a manual dispatch from
a branch (e.g. a feature branch) with the default input publishes to real
PyPI. Only the downstream `github-release` job (line ~140:
`if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')`) checks the ref shape, and
that's after publish has already happened.

This TODO hardens the workflow itself so the *tooling* enforces the
on-main, validated-tag invariant, not just documented process + trust.
preserves: Test PyPI publishing via workflow_dispatch with test_pypi=true continues to work for pre-release validation (this is a legitimate, lower-risk path and should not be blocked by the ancestor-of-main check unless it's also dispatched from a non-main ref, which should already be unusual for that use case).

mismatches that create false confidence before any stronger release gate can
be made trustworthy.

Baseline evidence from 2026-05-25:

description:
Architecture review (Work Area E, structural remediation) found a layering
inversion: nine `benchbox/core/*/benchmark.py` modules import
`benchbox.cli.benchmark_hooks` at module level - e.g.
`benchbox/core/nyctaxi/benchmark.py:643`,
`benchbox/core/tpcdi/benchmark.py:2743`,
`benchbox/core/datavault/benchmark.py:477` (confirmed 10 importing modules
total: flightdata, tsbs_devops, tpcdi, nyctaxi, datavault, tpcds_obt,
vector_search, joinorder_synthetic, joinorder, tpch_skew) - and
`benchbox/platforms/__init__.py:593` imports `benchbox.cli.platform_hooks`,
which itself imports `benchbox.core.platform_registry` and
`benchbox.core.schemas` (`cli/platform_hooks.py:13-14`).

Both `benchbox/cli/benchmark_hooks.py` and `benchbox/cli/platform_hooks.py`
are dependency-free (or near-dependency-free) pure registries - lightweight
extension mechanisms letting benchmarks/platforms expose CLI option hooks
(`--benchmark-option K=V`) without changing core CLI code. Despite the
name/location, neither module actually depends on CLI parsing, click/argparse,
or terminal I/O; they are data-holding registries that `core/` and
`platforms/` should be able to depend on without reaching "up" into `cli/`.
Having `core -> cli` and `platforms -> cli` edges inverts the intended
`utils < core < platforms < cli` layering that `import-layering-enforcement`
(a separate TODO) will formalize.

This is a standalone structural fix, not a shrink-campaign item -
`_project/goal-shrink-core-code.md` scopes god-class/architecture
decompositions out of the autonomous shrink loop.
preserves: All 10 core benchmark modules and platforms/__init__.py continue to register their hooks at the same point in the import/registration sequence.
CLI --benchmark-option and platform-option parsing behavior (PlatformHookRegistry, PlatformOptionSpec, parse_bool, BenchmarkOptionError) is byte-identical after the move.
Existing imports of benchbox.cli.benchmark_hooks / benchbox.cli.platform_hooks from any external caller keep working via the shim for at least one release.

description:
Source: _project/audits/results-explorer-publication-adversarial-review.md
(develop_sha fddedf26), findings §2.9 (Critical), §2.10 (Required), §2.11
(Advisory).

§2.9 — The `ci-paths` job in `.github/workflows/pr.yml` declares only 7
outputs (pr.yml:20-26: safe-content-only, needs-code-ci,
content-guard-needed, changed-paths, code-paths, unknown-paths,
estimated-runner-minutes-saved). But `package-smoke` (pr.yml:770) and
`dependency-audit` (pr.yml:812) gate on
`needs.ci-paths.outputs.packaging-needed == 'true'`, and `parity-check`
(pr.yml:858) gates on `needs.ci-paths.outputs.viz-needed == 'true'`. The
classifier emits these only as STEP outputs
(scripts/path_filter_decision.py:196-200), never re-exported at the JOB
level, so `needs.ci-paths.outputs.packaging-needed`/`viz-needed` resolve to
the empty string and the `== 'true'` conditions are permanently false. All
three jobs are always skipped, and `ci-required-result` counts skipped as
pass (pr.yml:963-973). This directly defeats the work completed in
_project/DONE/main/pr-gate-package-and-audit-promotion.yaml, whose w1 notes
claim it emits "a `<group>-needed` GH Actions output" — it added the step
output and job gating but not the job-level `outputs:` declaration.

§2.10 — `_project/scripts/results_explorer_snapshot_invariants.py` enforces
12 read-model invariants and its docstring says it exists "so release gates
can run it," but nothing invokes it (grep across Makefile/.github/tests
returns only its own definition). docs.yml:110-118 builds the snapshot then
runs `npm run build` with no validation between, so a malformed snapshot
deploys ungated.

§2.11 — `make validate-imports` runs `scripts/validate_imports.py`, which
does not exist (the real gate is `make lint-imports` → `lint-imports`, used
by CI). A maintainer running the advertised target gets file-not-found.
preserves: Existing 7 ci-paths outputs and their consumers remain unchanged.
ci-required-result's skipped-counts-as-pass semantics for genuinely path-filtered-out jobs (a docs-only PR must still not pay packaging/viz cost).
docs.yml explorer steps remain gated on hashFiles('results-explorer/package.json') so main builds stay a deliberate no-op.

description:
An audit of the test suite (14,765 tests, 68% coverage) found systematic
coverage theater - tests that inflate metrics without catching bugs.  The root
cause is per-file coverage enforcement (via `test_check_per_file_coverage.py`
and `test_check_module_coverage.py`) which incentivised an agent to produce 92
coverage-specific test files (`*coverage*.py`, `*wave_remaining*.py`) whose
tests mock everything and assert only that mocks behave as configured.

Key findings:
- 79 files named `*coverage*.py` + 13 `*wave_remaining*.py` (92 total)
- ~933 tests from these files, mostly mock-verify-mock tautologies
- 1,366 `isinstance()` assertions across 295 files (many trivial)
- Pattern: mock class -> call method -> assert mock returned what you told it to
- Pattern: instantiate dataclass -> assert attributes equal constructor args
- Pattern: 300-line fake framework (test_unified_frame_coverage.py) that
  diverges from real API silently
- Estimated meaningful coverage: 30-40% (vs reported 68%)

This TODO remediates in phases: first remove perverse incentives, then triage
the 92 files, then write replacement tests for critical paths.
preserves: All e2e tests (tests/e2e/) must continue to pass unchanged
All existing integration tests (tests/integration/) must continue to pass unchanged
Coverage number may drop - this is expected and correct
tests/unit/core/test_dataframe_queries_coverage_wave_remaining.py must be kept (has real Polars execution)
title: Remediate test suite coverage theater: delete hollow tests, replace with behavior-verifying alternatives

work.summary: Remove per-file coverage enforcement and replace with suite-wide threshold
Triage the 92 coverage/wave_remaining test files into delete/keep/rewrite buckets
Delete files triaged as DELETE and verify suite still passes
Write behavior-verifying tests for platform adapters (DuckDB, SQLite, DataFusion)
Write file-based credential tests to replace mock CredentialManager tests
Add mutation testing for critical modules to measure test effectiveness

hardens defense-in-depth.

hardening improvement.

§2.20 — The publisher's canonical set is
benchbox/core/publishing/bundle_publisher.py:30
VALID_LABELS = (maintainer-run, community-submission, ci, local,
unofficial-research). But the explorer's TrustBadge config keys are
ci-verified, ci-validated, local-run
(results-explorer/src/components/TrustBadge.tsx:19-43) and ranking
eligibility is {maintainer-run, ci-verified} (models.py:82-89). So a bundle
labeled `ci` or `local` by the publisher renders under the "unrecognised —
contact maintainers" fallback and (for `ci`) is not ranking-eligible despite
the publisher treating it as first-class; `unofficial-research` has no
explorer badge at all. The two halves of the platform disagree on the label
vocabulary.

§2.21 — TrustBadge.tsx:64 `if (!trustLabel) return null;` hides the badge
entirely on an empty label instead of showing an explicit "unknown" (moot
today because the snapshot schema makes trust_label NOT NULL, but the
component contract is hide-on-missing).
preserves: Existing curated badge tones for maintainer-run and ci-verified.
is_ranking_eligible semantics: community-submission and local stay excluded from official rankings.

results-explorer/src/components/TrustBadge.tsx:TRUST_CONFIG — extend to cover every canonical label.
results-explorer/src/lib/displayLabels.ts:formatTrustLabel — reuse the existing 'unknown' rendering for the empty-state fix.

2026-07-06 FOLLOW-UP FIX (review-followup-sweep): the ci↔ci-verified
reconciliation only landed on the explorer badge side (TrustBadge.tsx
got a distinct `ci` entry alongside `ci-verified`) -- the ranking side
was missed. `bundle_publisher.VALID_LABELS` has never accepted
"ci-verified" as a label (it's parametrized as a bad/invalid case in
test_bundle_publisher_label.py); the publisher's real spelling is "ci".
But `RANKING_ELIGIBLE_TRUST_LABELS` in
`_project/scripts/explorer_pipeline/models.py` only listed
"ci-verified", so every bundle the publisher could actually produce
with the ci label was structurally excluded from official rankings --
the exact §2.20 defect this TODO was opened to close, still live.
Fixed by adding "ci" to RANKING_ELIGIBLE_TRUST_LABELS (kept
"ci-verified" too, since TrustBadge.tsx still renders it distinctly for
any historical data using that spelling). Added
test_ci_public_verified_is_eligible and extended
test_ranking_eligible_trust_labels_constant.

description:
Source: _project/audits/results-explorer-publication-adversarial-review.md
(develop_sha fddedf26), findings §2.1, §2.2, §2.3, §2.4 (all Required).

The community-vs-maintainer trust label is derived solely from the presence
of a `.manifest.json` sidecar and defaults to the most-trusted tier when the
sidecar is absent, and nothing in CI requires the sidecar:
  - _project/scripts/explorer_pipeline/pipeline.py:458-460 — trust stays the
    build default unless a manifest sidecar exists.
  - _project/scripts/explorer_publish.py:45-46 defaults --trust-label to
    "maintainer-run"; docs.yml:112 runs the build with no --trust-label.
  - scripts/generate_corpus_inventory.py:41-52 — same sidecar-or-default rule.
  - benchbox/validation/bundle.py:718-726 validates the manifest hash only
    `if manifest_path is not None`; a bundle with no sidecar yields no error.
  - models.py:82-89 — RANKING_ELIGIBLE_TRUST_LABELS = {maintainer-run,
    ci-verified}, so a mislabel flips a result from "displayed" to "ranked".
§2.1: a community bundle submitted without a sidecar is badged maintainer-run
and made ranking-eligible. §2.2: the explorer build discards the publish-time
label entirely (an `unofficial-research` bundle — required by
publish.py:97-110 for non-compliant TPC results — is re-badged maintainer-run;
the pipeline never reads a per-bundle label). §2.3: bundle_publisher.py:88
silently coerces an unknown label to maintainer-run for programmatic callers.
§2.4: a present-but-empty manifest emits only `vr.warn` and returns
(bundle.py:594-602); ValidationResult.ok ignores warnings (bundle.py:170-172),
so the sidecar grants the community label without the hash ever being verified.
preserves: Already-merged community bundles keep their community-submission label (legacy singleton submission-manifest.json still honored).
Existing manifest-hash traversal and symlink defenses in bundle.py.
The maintainer-run local publish flow (benchbox publish with a valid label) is unaffected.

`benchbox submit --dry-run` still succeeds against a source bundle whose `<bundle>.manifest.json` sidecar does not exist yet -- the new missing-sidecar hard error is scoped to the submission-corpus CI path, not validate_bundles() unconditionally.

description:
Remove SQL mode support from the Polars platform adapter since Polars SQL is
fundamentally incompatible with most BenchBox benchmarks. DataFrame execution
will be the only supported mode.

Analysis revealed that Polars SQL has critical limitations that prevent
TPC-H, TPC-DS, and SSB benchmarks from running:

1. **Implicit Joins Not Supported** - Polars requires explicit JOIN syntax;
   comma-separated tables in FROM clause fail (affects 17/22 TPC-H queries)
2. **EXISTS/NOT EXISTS Not Supported** - Correlated subqueries fail (Q4, Q21)
3. **Scalar Subquery Comparisons** - Only `=` supported, not `>`, `<` (Q22)
4. **Non-Equi Joins Not Supported** - LIKE in join conditions fails (Q13)
5. **Date/String Comparison Issues** - Type coercion problems

Only ClickBench (single-table, no joins) could potentially work in SQL mode,
but maintaining a separate SQL code path for one benchmark is not justified.

Polars is designed as a DataFrame library with SQL as a convenience layer.
BenchBox should embrace this by using Polars's native DataFrame API, which
has no such limitations and provides better performance.
title: Remove Polars SQL mode support - DataFrame only

approach:
Reuse existing DataFrameMaintenanceOperations protocol (maintenance_interface.py:300-427)
and get_maintenance_operations_for_platform() (maintenance_interface.py:783-866) as the
DataFrame backend's write layer. Follow the WritePrimitivesBenchmark pattern
(write_primitives/benchmark.py:1196-1287) for capability-driven DataFrame execution.

Extract SQL logic from benchmark.py into SQLETLBackend - this is a move, not a rewrite.
The _load_warehouse_data(), validate_etl_results(), and SCD processor SQL methods become
methods on SQLETLBackend. The existing run_etl_pipeline() becomes the shared orchestrator
that accepts a backend parameter instead of a connection.

Phase order matters: backend protocol first, then Transform refactor, then wiring, then
cleanup. Run tests after each phase.
description:
TPC-DI's execute_dataframe_workload() currently resolves a SQL connection via
SQLConnectionProvider.get_sql_connection() and passes it to run_etl_pipeline(),
which executes raw SQL INSERT INTO, executemany(), executescript(), and validation
via SELECT COUNT(*). The DataFrame variant should NEVER use SQL.

The fix: introduce a TPCDIETLBackend protocol with SQL and DataFrame implementations.
Extract a shared mode-agnostic ETL orchestrator for Extract + Transform, then create
separate Load/Validate/SCD backends. The DataFrame backend delegates to the existing
DataFrameMaintenanceOperations protocol (insert_rows, update_rows, merge_rows).
Additionally, eliminate the double CSV serialization in the Transform phase by having
transforms return DataFrames directly.

SQLConnectionProvider and get_sql_connection() are removed entirely from the
DataFrame subsystem since the concept is architecturally wrong - DataFrame adapters
should never be asked for SQL connections.

run_full_benchmark() and all SQL-mode TPC-DI entry points remain unbroken
title: Remove SQL coupling from TPC-DI DataFrame mode and unify ETL orchestration via backend protocol

description:
Two CLI parameter names on `benchbox run` don't clearly express user intent:

1. `--convert` is a verb describing the implementation action (converting files),
   not the user's intent (choosing a table format). Users think "I want to
   benchmark with Delta Lake", not "I want to convert my data."

2. `--data-format` coexists ambiguously with the new `--table-format`. It controls
   pre-sorted data generation (parquet-sorted, delta-sorted, iceberg-sorted) and
   pairs with `--sorted-ingestion-mode`/`--sorted-ingestion-method`.

Renaming to `--table-format` aligns with industry terminology ("open table formats"),
the BenchBox blog series title, and pairs naturally with `--table-mode`.

Renaming to `--presort` removes the "format" confusion and aligns with the
sorted-ingestion parameter family.

Alpha status: no backward compatibility needed.

Design decisions:
- `benchbox convert` subcommand: KEEP as-is (verb appropriate for subcommand)
- `FormatConversionOrchestrator`: KEEP as-is (internal; it IS a conversion orchestrator)
- Post-run summary label: "Convert" → "Table Format"
- `prompt_data_format()` → `prompt_table_format()` (feeds into --table-format, not --data-format)
- JSON output keys: clean break (convert_format → table_format, etc.)

Full plan: .claude/plans/lazy-hugging-unicorn.md

description:
DECISION MADE (do not re-litigate promote-vs-remove): keep
benchbox/experimental/concurrency/, but RENAME it -- the name "concurrency"
is a misnomer. It is not the TPC spec concurrency (that lives in
core/throughput/). It is a load-testing + workload-analysis framework:
- patterns.py: WorkloadPattern shapes (Steady/Burst/RampUp/Spike/Step/Wave)
  -- time-varying demand profiles.
- executor.py: ConcurrentLoadExecutor -- drives a pattern, per-stream
  connections, dynamic concurrency targeting, background resource monitor.
- pool_tester.py: ConnectionPoolTester -- pool exhaustion / churn / under-load.
- analyzer.py: ConcurrencyAnalyzer -- queue-dwell, contention, scaling curves.

The package name collides conceptually with core/throughput and hides what the
code does. Rename to `benchbox/experimental/load_testing/` (recommended). The
class names already use the operative term ("ConcurrentLoad*", "Workload*"),
so only the package name and one analyzer class are actually misleading.

SCOPE: this item is a rename + honest re-documentation ONLY. It stays under
benchbox.experimental (unsupported, no stability guarantees, not wired into
the CLI/registry). Hardening and any decision to wire it into the CLI/UAT are
DEFERRED to a separate future item -- do not do that work here.
preserves: All existing tests still pass after the path/class updates.
Public class names ConcurrentLoadExecutor/Config/Result, the WorkloadPattern family, and the pool-tester types keep working (only the package path and ConcurrencyAnalyzer change).
The package stays under benchbox.experimental and remains unsupported/undocumented as a product feature (no CLI/registry wiring in this item).

benchbox/experimental/nl2sql/, gpu/, multiregion/, aiml_functions/ — sibling experimental subsystems; keep the same 'experimental package, unsupported' shape and README/FAQ treatment.

description:
Adversarial review of the 14-TODO holistic-review remediation found a systemic
gap: several PRs landed real regression reproducers but parked them in
non-required CI lanes (manual env var, `slow`, `integration`/`medium`), so the
develop required gate `ci-required-result` does NOT execute them. The PR that
introduced each reproducer self-merged without ever running its own deepest
guard; the reproducers only fire one ring out, at the main-release boundary
(test.yml). Three concrete instances:

  1. #900 (plan-capture-blocking-ci-gate): the "gate catches a planted defect"
     proof is gated only by env var BENCHBOX_PLANT_PLAN_CAPTURE_GATE_DEFECT
     (tests/integration/test_plan_capture_gate.py:88), which NOTHING in CI sets.
     w3's no-silent-green claim is satisfied only as a one-time manual demo;
     there is no standing automated negative test.
  2. #901 (cross-surface-mutation-harness-scale-fidelity): the substantive
     mutation-catch assertions (test_mutation_sensitivity,
     test_unmutated_target_is_green) are module `slow`-marked and excluded from
     the required code-test lane; only the set-equality drift guard
     (test_targets_cover_every_enforced_gate, -m slow -n 0) runs in required CI.
  3. #909 (plan-capture-robustness-hardening): the w2 connection-fencing and w3
     plan-identity reproducers live in tests/integration/test_plan_capture_phase.py
     ([integration, medium]) and run only in test.yml; no required develop-PR
     job collects them.

Design principle this item establishes: a regression reproducer that proves a
fix MUST run in the required develop-PR gate, via an explicit-node step if its
marker excludes it from the fast lane. Cost is bounded by selecting only the
load-bearing cells, not whole slow matrices.
preserves: Every added step lives in a job already in ci-required-result.needs and is not continue-on-error.
No new always-on slow matrix in required CI — select only the load-bearing cells; keep wall-clock bounded.
The existing positive-path gate behavior and the fast-lane test selection are unchanged.

approach: This is a decision first, code second. Options: (a) extend restore-legacy in the todo-db repo to accept and load findings tables - correct if todo-db is meant to own the findings domain too, and the natural counterpart to the snapshot work; (b) migrate findings by a separate mechanism after the tracker cutover, accepting a window where they are absent; (c) accept the loss explicitly and record it, which is only defensible if the findings domain is being retired. Whichever is chosen, the importer should be made to REJECT unknown tables rather than ignore them, so a lossy snapshot can never again look like a successful migration. Coordinate with whoever owns the findings phases before choosing.
description: todo-db's restore_legacy() (src/todo_db/database.py:463 in ~/Developer/todo-db) checks only that its 12 required tables are present and IGNORES every other key in the snapshot, then rebuilds the destination from base=self.export() with items/events/tracker_tables overwritten. Findings tables are not in the required set, so findings never transfer. Worse, because unknown keys are ignored rather than rejected, a snapshot that DID carry findings would be accepted while silently discarding them - a migration that reports success and loses a domain. The findings domain is active work, not vestigial: phases 3/4/5 landed across #1341 (lossless mapping), #1347 (schema v4) and #1351 (corpus importer), and the hosted tracker holds at least one open finding (2026-07-18-190500-evidence-tree-sha-provenance-mismatch) plus an unsynced draft. Blocks a clean migrate-hosted-tracker-db-to-todo-db-0-3-schema cutover: 'legacy-tracker-snapshot-export-for-restore-legacy' makes the tracker tables transferable, but the findings domain still has no path across.
preserves: existing 'export --snapshot' output stays valid input for restore-legacy
the committed-export boundary: findings prose still never reaches Git (EXPORT_TABLE_ALLOWLIST stays findings-free)
title: restore-legacy silently discards findings; decide before any cutover

approach:
Start from measurement, not intuition. Use the existing marker census and
`scripts/analyze_test_timings.py` to capture the current fast-lane contents,
slowest selected tests, and startup-heavy files. Then tighten the default
policy in `tests/conftest.py` so unclassified tests land in `medium` unless
there is a specific reason they belong in `fast`.

After the default policy changes, audit every explicit `@pytest.mark.fast`
usage across `tests/unit` and `tests/integration`. Reclassify tests based on
actual behavior: subprocess/CLI startup, benchmark data generation, heavy
imports, table-format dependencies, cloud-adjacent fixtures, and expensive
file or database setup should move out of `fast`. Keep `fast` for true smoke
and lightweight developer-loop coverage.

Finish by updating command expectations and adding an automated guardrail that
checks both composition and runtime budget so future test additions cannot
silently re-inflate the fast lane.

description:
The current pytest fast lane no longer behaves like a lightweight developer
suite. On 2026-03-07, `uv run -- python -m pytest -m "fast" --tb=short`
selects 13,256 of 15,051 collected tests and produces a visible 10-30 second
system lock-up during startup under the default parallel settings.

The root cause is classification drift, not a single broken test. The marker
policy in tests/conftest.py currently defaults most unclassified unit tests to
`fast`, so recent testing improvements silently expanded the fast lane far
beyond its intended scope. This interacts badly with pytest-xdist startup and
heavy import/setup work, but parallel execution itself is not the problem and
must be preserved for the curated fast lane.

This TODO restores the original intent of the fast suite by performing a
comprehensive reclassification of tests, tightening default marker policy,
preserving parallel fast execution, and adding guardrails so the lane cannot
quietly bloat again. The outcome target is a truly lightweight parallel fast
suite aligned with the prior expectation that fast runs stay under roughly
80 seconds.
preserves: Broad unit coverage remains available through existing non-fast commands such as `test-unit`; reclassification must not hide tests from routine quality workflows.
Existing explicit slow, stress, and resource_heavy coverage remains runnable after reclassification.
The resource-heavy/stress split in `test-all` continues to protect machines from known heavyweight suites.
`uv run -- python -m pytest -m "fast" --tb=short` remains a parallel run; do not force `-n 0` as the primary fix.
title: Restore lightweight fast test lane with comprehensive test reclassification

approach:
Compose with existing SchemaV2Validator (schema.py) as the first structural check.
If SchemaV2Validator raises, record FAIL and short-circuit structural checks.
Otherwise run all three tiers in sequence.

Benchmark specs are hardcoded from reference runs (not dynamically derived from
benchmark modules) - dynamic derivation creates transitive import issues and makes
the validator less self-contained.

Two-tier severity model:
  FAIL = mathematical impossibility or known-bad value (corrupted result)
  WARN = suspicious-but-plausible (degraded result, may still be valid)

The CLI script uses validate_file / validate_directory from the core module
directly - no duplication of logic.
description:
The live integration test suite produces JSON result files after each benchmark
run but there is no systematic way to evaluate whether those files are
structurally sound, complete, and believable. A silent failure - missing queries,
zero-time measurements, wrong row counts - can pass undetected.

This task implements a three-tier validator (structural → completeness →
believability) using the 20 DuckDB SF1 reference runs as ground-truth baselines.
The validator serves three consumers:
  1. CI/post-run scripts: batch-validate a results directory, non-zero exit on failure
  2. Live integration tests: importable function called after running a benchmark
  3. Interactive analysis: MCP tool for Claude-assisted review

Three-tier check system:
  STRUCTURAL  - schema version, required keys, cross-field math, non-negative
                timings, percentile ordering, valid phase enums
  COMPLETENESS - expected query IDs for known benchmarks, measurement iterations
                 present, power phase completed, tables object when required
  BELIEVABILITY - avg between min/max, geomean plausible, success rate above
                  benchmark floor, SF1 row counts within 1%, no duplicate
                  (id, iter, stream) combos

Reference DuckDB SF1 files live in benchmark_runs/results/ and match
the glob *_sf1_duckdb_*_2026*.json (55 files total). There are 20 current
benchmark IDs plus 8 legacy aliases (e.g., star_schema→ssb,
amplab_big_data→amplab, h2o_database→h2odb, tpc_di→tpcdi,
joinorderbenchmark→joinorder, nyc_taxi_olap→nyctaxi,
flight_data_olap→flightdata, data_vault→datavault).
The validator must handle both current and legacy benchmark IDs.
preserves: All 20 DuckDB SF1 reference files produce overall_status != FAIL
SchemaV2Validator in schema.py - compose with it, do not modify or duplicate
load_result_file() and find_latest_result() in loader.py - no changes to these
register_analytics_tools() signature in analytics.py - only ADD a new @mcp.tool() inside it
title: Build result integrity validator for benchmark JSON output

description:
Complete redesign of the benchmark result JSON output schema from v1.1 to v2.0.

The current v1.1 schema has significant issues:
- Extensive duplication (platform in 4 locations, timing in 2+ locations)

- Single source of truth for all data
- Compact query format (1 line vs 7 lines per query)
- Companion files for query plans and tuning details

description:
Benchmark results currently capture the client host environment and a
platform-specific `platform_info` block, but they do not fully describe where
the measured database engine actually ran. This is misleading for common local
development and integration-test workflows where BenchBox runs on macOS while
the data platform runs in a Linux Docker container because the platform is not
natively compatible with macOS.

The same gap exists for cloud runs. Some adapters capture useful fields such
as region, warehouse size, workgroup, storage bucket, reservation, or cluster
metadata, but those fields are adapter-specific and exported as raw config
rather than a stable result contract. Downstream consumers cannot reliably
compare or filter benchmark results by runtime type, container image, cloud
provider, region, compute shape, storage configuration, or whether a field was
requested by the user vs observed from the platform.

Build a normalized execution-environment contract for result artifacts that
separates:
  - the BenchBox client process host;
  - the measured platform runtime;
  - requested platform options;
  - observed platform deployment details;
  - cloud provider, region, compute, and storage facets;
  - raw adapter metadata retained for compatibility; and
  - anonymized/redacted public export behavior.
preserves: Anonymized exports never include raw passwords, tokens, private keys, access keys, credential file paths, or full connection strings.
Benchmarks do not fail when Docker, cloud metadata APIs, or permissioned system introspection are unavailable; results must record unavailable metadata explicitly.
Existing `platform_info`, `platform.config`, `system_profile`, `driver_metadata`, and `engine_version` consumers keep receiving equivalent data during the migration.
Existing cloud adapters remain lazy about optional SDK imports and do not require cloud credentials during unit tests.
Existing result JSON artifacts without normalized environment fields continue to load and export through the compatibility path.
No benchmark timing path includes Docker or cloud metadata collection in the measured query execution duration.
title: Results pipeline: complete benchmark execution environment capture

anti_patterns.dont: canonicalize already-checked-in bundles without also updating their per-bundle manifest hashes
anti_patterns.why: the manifest SHA-256 contract is byte-exact.

anti_patterns.dont: canonicalize the primary bundle while leaving `.plans.json` or `.tuning.json` companions vulnerable
anti_patterns.why: `companion_hashes` are validated by the same manifest path.

anti_patterns.dont: change the manifest's hash function or schema
anti_patterns.instead: only change the writer side, then keep the same SHA-256 contract.

anti_patterns.instead: the durable fix is byte-stable emission.
anti_patterns.why: every future tool that touches bundle bytes will re-trip the hash mismatch

approach:
Treat bundle and companion files as a binary contract. The `bundle_hash` and
`companion_hashes` fields commit the writer to byte-stable output; honour
that by emitting primary and companion JSON through a single canonical
serializer and hashing the post-serialization bytes. Land in two PRs if
needed: the writer/hash canonicalization first (W1-W3), then the pre-commit
exclusion removal (W4) once the writer is in place and any in-flight bundles
have been re-emitted or grandfathered.
description:
The bundle emitter (`benchbox/core/results/exporter.py`) writes the primary
result JSON and companion `.plans.json` / `.tuning.json` files without a
canonical trailing-newline / whitespace policy. The submit manifest writer
(`benchbox/cli/commands/submit.py`) then records SHA-256 hashes for the
emitted bundle and companions. Tools that round-trip the file —
pre-commit's `end-of-file-fixer` and `trailing-whitespace` hooks, GitHub's
rich JSON viewer, editors that auto-save with a final newline — change
bytes the manifest's `bundle_hash` SHA-256 was computed against.

The W3 corpus-integration PR
(`results-explorer-uat-corpus-integrate-validated-bundles`) hit this when
staging 188 community-submission bundles into `results-data/bundles/`: the
EOF-fixer added trailing newlines and broke every hash. The PR landed by
excluding `results-data/bundles/*.json` from those hooks
(`.pre-commit-config.yaml:106-118`). That fix is correct but it is a
band-aid: any future submitter running a different tool, GitHub PR review
flow, or editor that touches the bytes will hit the same wall, and the
exclusion does not protect them.

The durable fix is to emit the primary bundle and companion JSON files in a
canonical byte-stable form (single serializer with a fixed trailing-newline
policy and stable key ordering) AND compute `bundle_hash` and
`companion_hashes` against that canonical form, so EOF-fixing /
pretty-printing within the canonical form is a no-op.

Originating blind-spot finding:
`_project/blind-spots/2026-05-03-090105-mixed-tooling-data-pr-review-gap.md`.

The hosted-results contract treats phase mismatch as a warning, but the Explorer cohort key and Compare UI treat phase as identity. Resolve those semantic contradictions before making a broad Database Leaderboards claim.

trapped-page navigation defect is largely remediated. The follow-up

supported-benchmark catalog instead of the current public result corpus. The

actionable public result pages from no-data placeholders.

should either list only benchmarks with public results for the current
explorer corpus, or it should visibly mark/disable no-result options with an
explicit empty-state affordance. Do not remove the empty benchmark route

approach: Re-run the lockfile audit, trace each advisory to direct/transitive and runtime/build/test reachability, inspect upstream fixes, and prefer lockfile-compatible updates. Add CI enforcement at an agreed severity with a machine-readable exception file containing advisory, rationale, owner, expiry, and removal condition. Fail closed on new or expired high/critical advisories while avoiding blind npm audit fix upgrades.
description: The release review found npm audit reporting four advisories, three high and one low, in the Vite/PostCSS and transitive test/build dependency graph. No vulnerable code path in the shipped browser bundle or exploit was reproduced. Establish a proportionate policy that distinguishes runtime, build-time, and test-only exposure, fixes safe updates, and records narrowly scoped expiring exceptions instead of leaving audit output unmanaged.
preserves: A new critical or high advisory cannot hide behind an unrelated existing exception.
Application runtime behavior and production bundle size remain unchanged unless a reviewed dependency fix requires otherwise.
Every exception names an owner, exact advisory/package range, expiry date, exposure analysis, and removal trigger.
Major upgrades are evaluated explicitly and never accepted through npm audit fix --force.
The npm lockfile remains deterministic under npm ci.

UI copy.

at least one test name still describe the retired "dark BenchBox shell +
light analytical data panels" contract even though the current product
contract is user-selectable light/dark theming. These stale artifacts are a
root cause for repeated retheme regressions: implementers can follow an old
"final decision" and reintroduce mixed-theme assumptions.

not redesign Home, the theme system, or the corpus model. It should make the
current intended contract explicit, update assertions to match it, add
count-aware corpus summary labels, and add a compact stale-contract scan so
future PRs cannot silently revive the old contract.

approach: Define one recursive public-egress policy that classifies values as credentials, identifying local paths, allowed non-identifying paths, URLs, or ordinary strings. Reuse the existing anonymization specifications and submission validator, then assert the same policy against exporter output, submitted bundles and companions, corpus inventory inputs, and the exact Explorer publication output. description: Release-readiness review evidence at 17c0c098a found 650 machine-local absolute-path values across 183 of 207 curated bundles, including working directories and driver-runtime executables. No email, credential-key, or URL-query secret was reproduced, but the path values conflict with the public anonymization contract and are copied into the Explorer download surface. This item prevents recurrence at the producer, submission validator, and Explorer publication boundary. It does not rewrite the existing corpus; that is owned by the dependent backfill item.
preserves: Existing hash, symlink, traversal, trust-label, and vendor-governance validation remains at least as strict.
Local-only anonymize=False consumers retain their documented non-secret diagnostic metadata; the fail-closed rule applies at public egress boundaries.
Secret-looking values remain redacted rather than reversibly hashed.
The public contract is recursive across bundle, manifest, and companion objects and cannot be bypassed by renaming a field.
URLs, SQL text, benchmark identifiers, and legitimate relative source references are not corrupted by a blanket slash regex.

prior_art.concept: The publication pipeline is the last chance to reject legacy curated data before it becomes directly downloadable.
Existing recursive public anonymization and path-key classifier are the single policy seam; extend rather than parallelize them.
Existing hostile-input and manifest validation is the public admission boundary; add the path-privacy decision there.

description:
The post-remediation review found that Results Explorer now has better
duplicate-name disambiguation, but it still leaks conflicting run identities
and removes receipt/detail reachability from high-use benchmark views.

Benchmark Matrix and Ranks views can show the runs a user wants to inspect,
but those rows no longer expose a result-detail or receipt affordance. Compare
selection trays also display compact compare IDs such as `d28345e6` while row
labels and result-detail routes show different public result IDs such as
`a62d0d72`. This makes the same run appear to have two identities.

This TODO defines a single public run-identity contract, separates URL
transport IDs from visible IDs, and restores compact detail/receipt reachability
in Matrix and Ranks without reintroducing tall frozen rows.
preserves: Existing shareable compare URLs must continue to resolve for supported ID aliases.
Matrix and Ranks density improvements must not be undone by stacking receipt text, trust badges, version, and source in one cell.
Run identity disambiguation must remain concise in tables and complete in titles/aria labels.
Selection controls must remain keyboard reachable and screen-reader labelled.

four real product bugs, plus one open question about a possibly-removed UI
control. This item tracks the investigation and remediation of each.

work.notes:
DECISION: B2 is real and intermittent. The casing/projection bug
and the equality-mismatch bug are both ruled out. The mechanism
that produces the intermittency is NOT YET PINNED — w3 must
instrument before implementing a fix.

Evidence (what we know):
  - Direct DuckDB inspection: `platform_index_rows` for the
    production corpus contains clean ASCII slugs ('duckdb',
    'polars', 'datafusion', 'sqlite') with no whitespace, casing,
    or NULL oddities. → rules out the projection/casing class.
  - PlatformIndex.tsx:48 filter is `r.platform_id === platform`
    (strict-equality ASCII strings). The same code path renders
    the same data shape for every platform; if it failed for
    "polars" it would also fail for "sqlite". → rules out the
    equality-mismatch class.
  - Three serial invocations of the original manual repro produced
    P/F, F/F, P/P with the warm run finishing in 1-3s — strong
    intermittency signal correlated with WASM warmth.

Mechanism (NOT confirmed — three plausible candidates):
  1. DuckDB-WASM cold-load partial data: a SELECT resolves
     before the runtime has fetched all of the table's pages.
     Underlying range-read issue tracked as
     `enable-duckdb-wasm-http-range-reads-for-registered-urls`
     (see results-explorer/src/db.ts:67-77).
  2. Preact useEffect cleanup race: PlatformIndex.tsx:24-40
     uses `let cancelled = false; if (!cancelled) setRows(r)`.
     A fast navigation between platform pages could drop the
     setRows call.
  3. Shared `initPromise` race in db.ts:48-96: `getDb()` reuses
     `initPromise` across mounts; component-ordering quirks
     could leave the cached `dbInstance` in an inconsistent
     state.

None of the three has direct evidence yet. Picking a fix without
instrumentation risks fixing the wrong layer.

The manual overlay repro was replaced in w3 by the route-backed
regression guard at
`results-explorer/e2e/failures/platform-index-cold-load.spec.ts`.
work.summary: Investigate B2 — root-cause empty PlatformIndex for duckdb/polars

work.notes:
DECISION: No toggle should exist. The original Q1 framing was
based on an incomplete read of the code; the actual contract is
stronger than "URL-only" — it is "benchmark-derived, not
user-configurable."

Evidence:
  - `git log -G"primaryMetric"` returns ONE commit ever
    touching the symbol in pages/ — f9d08d38b, the migration
    that originally populated develop. There is no removed
    button in history.
  - ResultDetail.tsx:64-66 calls
    `getPrimaryMetricForBenchmark(data.benchmark)` and feeds
    the result into `setPrimaryMetric`. Compare.tsx:82-84 does
    the same with `details[0]!.benchmark`. The setter is NEVER
    fired from a user-driven event in either file.
  - The metric is therefore determined by the benchmark family's
    ranking config (e.g. ClickBench → power_score, TPC-H →
    display_geomean_ms). Letting users override it via a toggle
    would produce incorrect cross-benchmark comparisons.
  - Cross-benchmark comparisons are foreclosed by Compare.tsx:64-71,
    which rejects mixed-benchmark sets with "Cannot compare results
    from different benchmarks: ...". Since every Compare and
    ResultDetail view is single-benchmark, the per-benchmark metric
    is unambiguous — a toggle would only enable wrong metric choices,
    not legitimate ones.

Implication for w7:
  - Drop §4.2 ("Primary metric toggle (power_score ↔
    display_geomean_ms) updates the chart") from the test plan.
  - Drop §5.3 (same expectation in Compare).
  - Optionally add a positive assertion that confirms the
    benchmark-derived contract — but capture the actual axis-label
    text emitted by chartRegistry.ts:233-240 for each benchmark's
    primary_metric (run the relevant pages once and copy the
    rendered label). Do NOT guess the text; the labels are
    generated, not hard-coded.

No follow-up TODO needed; the feature should not be added.

work.notes:
Implemented approach (a): inside BenchmarkIndex.tsx, after
results finish loading and before the title is rendered, check
whether `benchmarkResults.length === 0` (no row in the loaded
set whose `benchmark` matches the URL slug). Approach (b) —
maintaining a known-benchmarks set from cohort_metadata — was
rejected because `results` already carries the answer; threading
a second source of truth would invite drift.

Post-review (W5 review): the original guard conflated "unknown
slug" with "known slug, no data yet." The published corpus has
data for 2 of the 8 entries in BENCHMARK_LABELS (src/utils.ts);
the other 6 (tpcds, clickbench, nyctaxi, h2odb, datavault, plus
ssb-as-alias) all 404'd, suggesting they were unsupported. Now
a 3-state guard:
  - Unknown slug (not in BENCHMARK_LABELS) →
    <NotFound message="Benchmark X is not part of the published corpus." />
  - Known benchmark with no rows → an inline empty-corpus state
    ("No published results yet for ClickBench. The benchmark is
    supported by BenchBox but no runs have been ingested into
    the public corpus.").
  - Known benchmark with rows → the existing BenchmarkIndex flow.

Supporting changes:
  - utils.ts: BENCHMARK_LABELS exported; new helper
    isKnownBenchmark(slug) returns slug in BENCHMARK_LABELS.
  - NotFound: gained an optional `message` prop so callers can
    give the user a more specific 404 reason than the default
    "Page not found.".

Comment near the guard documents an incidental safety property:
the summary-fetch useEffect is safe for both empty cases because
its `phases.length === 0` early-return catches them. A future
decoupling of `phases` from `benchmarkResults` would need to add
its own early-return.

approach:
Investigate before patching. w1 and w2 are research/decision units
that produce explicit outputs (root cause; delete-vs-implement
decision). Run them first. Once they settle:

  Phase A (parallel-safe mechanical fixes):  w3, w4, w5, w7, w8, w9, w10, w11
  Phase B (depends on Phase A):              w12 (needs w2), w6 (needs w1)
  Phase C (depends on Phases A+B):           w13 docs, w14 e2e
  Phase D (acceptance gate):                 w15 re-run QA

Reuse existing patterns:
  - Sort handlers: copy ResultDetail's `<th><button onClick=
    toggleSort()>` pattern verbatim (w3).
  - Stable Preact keys: every result row already has a `result_id` —
    use it directly (w4).
  - URL-state validation: `useUrlState` + `replaceState` on hydrate
    is the right shape for w7 + w8; consider extracting a small
    helper if both ship.
  - Document title: a tiny `useEffect`-based `useDocumentTitle`
    hook under `src/lib/` is sufficient — no need for a head-manager
    dependency (w10).
  - Loading-state gating: `Home.tsx`'s existing
    `if (!results) return <LoadingSpinner ... />` is the obvious
    surface for w6; just AND it with `metaLeaderboard !== null` if
    H1/H3 wins.

Do NOT batch fixes into one mega-commit. Each work unit is its own
commit per the skill's commit framework. Run lint + relevant tests
per slice. Vertical slices: implement → test → verify → commit.

For the failing cold-load (N1), do NOT skip the diagnosis step —
jumping to a "just add a spinner" fix risks masking a deeper
data-layer race that will resurface as soon as the corpus grows.

work.notes:
DECISION: N1 is a loading-state/data-readiness race where
`listResults()` can briefly resolve to an empty array on a cold
DuckDB-WASM attach, and Home treats that empty array as loaded
final state while the meta-leaderboard data is allowed to arrive
independently.

Evidence:
  - QA pass-2 captured the exact mixed state: `0 Results / 0
    Benchmarks / 0 Platforms` plus "No leaderboard cells match";
    a later module probe against the same snapshot returned 12
    rows, and warm reloads rendered correctly
    (`_project/audits/results-explorer-qa-pass2-findings.md:46-65`).
  - `Home.tsx:34-43` launches `listResults()` and
    `getMetaLeaderboardData()` independently. `Home.tsx:135`
    gates only on `!results`, so `[]` is considered loaded.
  - Once `results === []`, `resultById` is empty
    (`Home.tsx:53-55`). If `metaLeaderboard` then resolves,
    `filteredMetaLeaderboard` drops every cohort because each
    cohort requires at least one platform row whose `result_id`
    exists in `resultById` (`Home.tsx:74-83`), producing an
    empty `cohorts` array (`Home.tsx:117-121`).
  - The visible zero cards are rendered directly from the
    empty `results` array (`Home.tsx:200-203`), and the empty
    leaderboard copy renders when `filteredMetaLeaderboard` is
    truthy with `cohorts.length === 0` (`Home.tsx:283-286`).
  - `db.ts:106-110` already has the pass-1 PlatformIndex
    projection-readiness fence, so the next fix should not
    broaden `db.ts` first. The Home-specific bug is that its UI
    can combine an empty result snapshot with non-empty cohort
    metadata and make that transient look authoritative.

Winning hypothesis: H2 is the likely cold-load trigger
(`listResults()` can resolve `[]` before the snapshot is fully
useful), and H3 is the UI paint condition that turns the trigger
into a visible bug. H1 alone is too narrow because the recorded
state includes zero result stat cards, not just a leaderboard
placeholder.

Code surfaces for w6:
  1. `results-explorer/src/pages/Home.tsx` -- introduce an
     explicit Home data loading state that waits for both
     `listResults()` and `getMetaLeaderboardData()` to settle
     before rendering stat cards and MetaLeaderboard. Preserve
     the legitimate no-leaderboard case by distinguishing
     "leaderboard still loading" from "leaderboard loaded as
     null because the corpus has no eligible 2+ platform
     cohorts."
  2. `results-explorer/src/pages/__tests__/Home.test.tsx` --
     add a regression test with staged promises: resolve
     `listResults()` to `[]` first, keep meta-leaderboard
     pending/then resolve it, and assert the page keeps showing
     the loading spinner rather than 0/0/0 or "No leaderboard
     cells match."
  3. `results-explorer/e2e/routes/home.spec.ts` -- add or
     strengthen a cold-load assertion that the empty-corpus copy
     never appears before `Recent Results`/leaderboard data is
     visible.

Reproduce on a hard refresh of `/results/` (DevTools "Disable cache"
checked, "Preserve log" on). Capture the timing of:
  - Initial render (which strings appear first — "Loading..." or "0 Results"?)
  - DuckDB-WASM .duckdb fetch start/end
  - getMetaLeaderboardData() resolve
  - listResults() resolve

Hypothesis ladder, narrowest first:
  H1  Race in `Home.tsx`: the loading guard is `if (!results)`,
      but `setResults([])` may run before the meta-leaderboard
      `getMetaLeaderboardData()` resolves, briefly painting an
      empty corpus before the leaderboard fills in.
  H2  `listResults()` returns `[]` (not throw) when the DuckDB
      view isn't attached yet; the `null`-vs-`[]` distinction is
      being lost before the spinner can render.
  H3  StatCard counts (`results.length`, `benchmarks.length`,
      `platformIds.length`) are computed unconditionally from
      `results ?? []`, so an in-flight empty array paints the
      zero state for one frame.

Output of this unit: a one-paragraph diagnosis on this work
unit's notes naming the winning hypothesis with file:line evidence,
and a short list of code surfaces that need to change in w6.
work.summary: Investigate N1 — root-cause cold-load empty corpus on Home

`primaryMetric` state/setter from ResultDetail and Compare, then

Currently `BenchmarkIndex.tsx:42-44` reads `sf` as a string with
no validator, then keys data fetches off `effectiveSf =
scaleFilter ?? scaleFactors[0] ?? "0.01"`. If the URL is

pattern — extract a small helper if w7 ships first).

description:
PR #276 (`fix(explorer): tighten Query workbench desktop intro to keep
results panel above the fold`) closed the failing `responsive.spec.ts`
desktop assertion by trimming 12px of vertical space above the grid at
lg+ widths only. That fix passes the numeric `expectTopWithin(...,
maxY=900)` check (panel.top is now 897), but it leaves two related soft
issues that the PR #276 review surfaced and explicitly deferred:

1) **Layout/test-name semantic mismatch.** The test is titled
   "query workbench renders summary, active filters, and rows
   **before deep controls** at desktop", but the `query-visible-columns`
   element (locate by `data-testid="query-visible-columns"` in
   `results-explorer/src/pages/Query.tsx`) keeps the `lg:order-1`
   class, so at desktop the column-toggle UI still renders **above**
   the summary and rows. The numeric assertion passes but the test
   name promises ordering the layout does not deliver. This is the
   durable concern and survives any future visible-columns
   restructure.

2) **Brittle 3px desktop budget (state-dependent).** Immediately
   after PR #276 landed, panel.top = 897 against `maxY = 900` at
   desktop — any future change adding a border, a font-metrics tick,
   or a half-line wrap on the intro paragraph would retrip the
   assertion. The block comment above `VIEWPORTS` in
   `results-explorer/e2e/responsive.spec.ts` (added by PR #278
   alongside this TODO) documents the brittleness. **Important
   state-dependence:** PR #277 (concurrent, may land before this
   TODO is actioned) restructures `query-visible-columns` from a
   div into a default-collapsed `<details>`/`<summary>` affordance,
   which collapses the visible-columns block from ≈494px to ≈54px
   by default at lg:order-1. Once PR #277 is in develop, the live
   panel.top drops to ≈457 and the brittleness rationale evaporates;
   only the semantic mismatch (1) remains. Re-measure with the live
   DOM probe before deciding which resolution to pick. (Numbers in
   this block corrected post-PR-291 against the captured w0.log to
   match the observed measurement at the time; the original draft
   estimated 30px / 445 from a smaller probe.)

Resolving (1) structurally also resolves (2) regardless of PR #277's
merge state: if `query-visible-columns` drops `lg:order-1` (or moves
to `lg:order-5` so the right-column flex order at desktop becomes
summary → panel → details → visible-columns), panel.top falls into
the low hundreds and the desktop budget stops being a recurring
concern.

Two reasonable resolutions:
  a) **Restructure the layout to match the test name.** Drop
     `lg:order-1` from `query-visible-columns` so the section's flex
     order at desktop is summary → panel → details → visible-columns,
     matching the test's "rows before deep controls" promise. UX
     change: the column-toggle UI moves from the top of the right
     column to the bottom at desktop. Mobile/tablet ordering is
     already this way (visible-columns at the bottom via `order-5`).
  b) **Rename the test and document the lg-order intent.** Keep the
     `lg:order-1` placement (PR #120's design intent of putting
     column configuration above the table at desktop) and rename the
     test to something like "renders summary, results panel, and
     deep controls within the desktop viewport budget" so the title
     matches what the assertions actually check.

Resolution (a) is preferable because it removes a documented
inconsistency and gives the desktop budget durable headroom; (b) is
acceptable if PR #120's design intent is still load-bearing.
preserves: All `data-testid`s on `query-visible-columns`, `query-results-panel`, `query-result-summary`, and `query-mobile-filter-drawer` — downstream tests rely on them.
Mobile/tablet ordering: results panel above visible-columns (the existing `order-3` < `order-5` invariant).
`maxY=1200` budgets at mobile/tablet.

scope.path_glob: results-explorer/e2e/responsive.spec.ts (test title + comment if resolving (b); update the `VIEWPORTS` budget comment under (a) to reflect the new headroom)
results-explorer/src/pages/Query.tsx (one to two lines around the `query-visible-columns` and intro container if resolving (a); else untouched)

Query workbench restructuring (mobile drawer + filter bar reorganization),
not with the post-merge follow-up PR #272. PR #272 was only able to
validate its own affordance + document-overflow changes by running them in
isolation because `responsive.spec.ts` runs serially and this test fails
before the affordance loop runs.

Two reasonable resolutions:
  1) Trim 9px of vertical space above the results panel on the Query
     workbench at lg+ widths (e.g. tighten `mt-*` / `gap-*` between the
     result summary and the panel).
  2) Relax `viewport.maxY` for desktop from 900 to ~960. The original 900
     choice equals the viewport height itself, leaving zero margin for
     layout drift. Tablet uses 1200/900=1.33, mobile uses 1200/900=1.33;
     desktop's 900/900=1.0 is the only "no margin" pick in the matrix.

Resolution (1) is preferable because it forces every future PR to keep the
result panel above the fold; (2) is acceptable if the post-PR-270 layout
is intentional and we only want a guardrail against gross regressions.
preserves: PR #270's contract that mobile drawer + Query controls remain reachable above the fold at every viewport
PR #272's affordance + overflow tests continue to pass at 390/768
Serial mode for `responsive.spec.ts` if its current invariants depend on it
