description:
Follow-up review of `testing-approach-correctness-gates` found that #737
added valuable CI plumbing but left important correctness gaps in the
bounded real-result gate. The rebuttal agrees with the architectural shape:
a single bounded DuckDB/TPC-H cell is acceptable for routine develop PRs,
and `medium` does not automatically need to become a full CI lane. The
valid defects are narrower and more actionable:

  - the current gate validates only row counts, and the configured query
    subset `6,14,15,17,19` has SF=1 expected cardinality of exactly one row
    for every query, making it weak against wrong joins, filters, or
    aggregate values that still emit one row;
  - strict expected-result enforcement can still be silently disarmed by
    scale/benchmark drift because the hard assertion is guarded by
    `benchmark_name == "tpch" and scale_factor >= 1.0`;
  - the Makefile target can pass if the selected pytest node is skipped;
  - `tests/README.md` still references nonexistent `tests/specialized/`
    files, while the prior TODO claims that reference was removed;
  - the `medium` marker policy is documented, but the large medium-only
    population needs an explicit product-risk triage rather than an
    assumption that every medium test is either CI-worthy or irrelevant.

Correct the testing approach by keeping the bounded-gate design, making the
oracle materially discriminating, proving strict mode fails when disarmed,
adding a skip-as-failure guard for the selected node, repairing stale docs,
and converting the medium-marker debate into a concrete triage decision.
preserves: Databricks coverage-theater fixes from #737 remain intact; do not reintroduce constructor-bypass tests or `_build_query_result_with_validation` stubs.
Default non-strict stress matrix behavior continues to skip unsupported expected-results validation rather than failing unrelated opt-in matrix cases.
Develop PR feedback remains bounded; do not run the full stress matrix on every routine PR.
Main/release and develop workflow aggregators continue to require the correctness gate for code-impacting paths where they do today.
Strict gate mode fails when configured expected-results checks do not actually evaluate.
`make test-correctness-gate` still executes a real DuckDB/TPC-H benchmark through generate, load, and power phases.

anti_patterns.dont: hard-kill or forcibly interrupt threads

description:
throughput-timeout-leak-and-success-gates (#1106) fixed the real timeout bug
(the per-stream timeout was dead code because `as_completed()` only yields
already-done futures) and added opt-in cooperative cancellation. But a residual
remains, explicitly accepted by that item as out of scope:
`StreamRunner.execute()` runs its streams inside a `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...)`
block (benchbox/core/throughput/runner.py), and the context manager's `__exit__`
calls `shutdown(wait=True)`. So even though a timed-out stream is now correctly
surfaced (logged + recorded in `result.errors`), `execute()` still cannot
RETURN until every worker thread finishes. With cooperative cancellation OFF
(the default), a genuinely hung stream blocks `execute()` -- and therefore the
whole throughput phase, and any subsequent phase (e.g. maintenance) -- for as
long as the stream keeps running against the DB.

Goal: allow the executor to return promptly once its timeout/accounting window
closes, without waiting on a zombie stream, while still never hard-killing a
thread (Python cannot do so safely). The likely mechanism is to manage the
pool manually (`ThreadPoolExecutor(...)` without the `with` block, or
`shutdown(wait=False)`) so the leaked thread is abandoned to run out in the
background -- with its connection ownership and resource accounting clearly
documented -- rather than blocking the main thread. This must compose with the
already-shipped leak surfacing and cooperative-cancel opt-in.

Note the subtlety: abandoning a thread that still holds a DB connection has its
own hazards (connection not closed until the thread ends; a later phase running
while the zombie hammers the DB). The design must decide and document what
happens to the leaked stream's connection and how TTT/accounting treat the
overlap -- this is why #1106 deferred it rather than squeezing it in.
preserves: Opt-in cooperative cancellation (config.cancel_on_timeout default False) keeps working and still bounds a stream to ~one more query.
The already-shipped leak surfacing: a timed-out/leaked stream is still logged (logger.warning) and recorded in result.errors.
The robust cancel-event guard (honor only a real set threading.Event) added in #1106 stays intact.
as_completed accounting semantics (streams_executed / successful / errors) for the normal, non-hung path.

benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py / benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py — the cooperative-cancel poll (config.cancel_on_timeout, per-stream threading.Event) this must compose with.
docs/development/throughput-result-alignment.md — documents the timed-out-stream leak behavior; update alongside any change to shutdown semantics.

anti_patterns.dont: open N real connections for embedded DuckDB
anti_patterns.why: cursor sharing is the correct model there

description:
The production throughput path gives every concurrent stream a separate
*cursor* on ONE shared underlying platform connection, not an independent
session. In benchbox/platforms/base/execution.py the connection_factory
closures (TPC-H lines 375-383, TPC-DS lines 244-252) call
`_make_stream_cursor(connection)` -> `connection.cursor()`
(benchbox/platforms/base/connection_wrappers.py:121-129) against the single
connection passed into the driver.

This is safe and intentional for DuckDB (its Python client is documented as
thread-safe at cursor level and cursors share the embedded DB), and the
DuckDB caveat is documented in docs/benchmarks/tpc-h.md. But TPC throughput
semantics model N INDEPENDENT concurrent users/sessions, and for
client/server engines a single connection is a single session:
- Many DB-API drivers (e.g. psycopg, Snowflake, Databricks SQL, Trino) do not
  support truly concurrent statement execution across cursors of one
  connection — calls serialize on the connection lock or raise.
- Even where they don't error, all streams share one session's server-side
  resources, so it is not a real multi-user concurrency measurement.

Fix: make the per-stream connection acquisition a platform capability. Engines
that model concurrency at the connection level (server engines) must hand each
stream its OWN connection/session from a factory or pool; embedded engines
(DuckDB) keep the cursor-sharing fast path. The throughput driver already
calls `connection_factory()` per stream (throughput_test.py) -- the gap is
that the adapter closure returns cursors of one connection instead of
independent sessions.
preserves: Connections are still closed per stream in _execute_stream's finally block.
DuckDB throughput continues to use cursor sharing (documented, correct) with no perf regression.

description:
The TPC-H and TPC-DS throughput tests generate each query INSIDE the timed,
concurrent per-stream loop, and query generation shells out to a subprocess.

- TPC-H: `TPCHThroughputTest._execute_stream` (benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py:207-228)
  captures `query_start = mono_time()` (line 208) and THEN calls
  `self.benchmark.get_query(...)` (line 223). `get_query` -> `QGen.generate`
  (benchbox/core/tpch/queries.py:28-78) spawns a `qgen` subprocess, creates a
  `TemporaryDirectory`, and `shutil.copy2` copies `dists.dss` on EVERY call.
- TPC-DS: `TPCDSThroughputTest._execute_single_query`
  (benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py:333-346) captures `query_start`
  then calls `_get_stream_query_text` -> `get_query` -> `dsqgen`
  (benchbox/core/tpcds/c_tools.py:933) subprocess.

Two distinct second-order problems, both of which distort the throughput
measurement the test exists to produce:

1. MEASUREMENT CONTAMINATION: subprocess spawn + temp-dir + file-copy time is
   counted inside `execution_time_seconds`, so per-query timings and the
   derived `query_throughput` include query-generation cost, not just DB
   execution. TTT itself (first-stream-start -> last-stream-end) is also
   inflated by generation done during the concurrent window.
2. ARTIFICIAL BOTTLENECK UNDER CONCURRENCY: with N streams, N threads each
   fork a `qgen`/`dsqgen` process, create a temp dir, and copy a dists file
   concurrently. Process creation, the GIL around subprocess management, and
   filesystem contention serialize what is supposed to be parallel DB work.
   The more streams you add (the whole point of a throughput test), the worse
   the generation contention becomes -- so the harness can mask real platform
   scaling behind its own driver overhead.

Fix: generate the full per-stream query text (the ordered list of SQL strings
for each stream) BEFORE `StreamRunner.execute` starts the concurrent window,
and have `_execute_stream` iterate over pre-materialized SQL. The timed region
must contain only connection use and DB execution. This mirrors how a real
TPC driver submits a prepared query set per session.

USE THE NATIVE BATCH STREAM MODE, don't reassemble by hand. Both binaries can
emit a whole stream in ONE subprocess call:
- TPC-H: qgen's `-p <stream>` flag generates all 22 queries in the official
  permuted order for a stream in a single invocation. BenchBox ALREADY wraps
  this in TPCHStreamManager._generate_stream_queries_qgen
  (benchbox/core/tpch/streams.py) -- but the throughput test bypasses it and
  calls the per-query QGen.generate (queries.py:28) inside the timed loop
  instead. Route throughput generation through the existing native `-p` path
  (or an equivalent single-call batch) so one qgen call replaces 22, per
  stream, before the timed window.
- TPC-DS: the analogous fix is `dsqgen -STREAMS N`, owned by
  tpcds-throughput-permutation-compliance (which also restores official
  ordering + per-stream parameters). This item and that one share the same
  "batch-generate all streams up front" mechanism; coordinate so TPC-H and
  TPC-DS converge on the same pre-generated-workload shape.

So the per-query subprocess churn is not just moved out of the timed loop --
it is collapsed from O(streams x queries) subprocess spawns to O(streams) (or
even one), using each binary's native stream capability that BenchBox already
has a wrapper for (TPC-H) or should adopt (TPC-DS).
preserves: Per-stream, per-position seeds remain `seed + stream_id*1000 + position` so generated SQL is byte-identical to today (only WHEN it is generated changes).
TPC-H PERMUTATION_MATRIX stream ordering and TPC-DS StreamQuery ordering are unchanged.
dry-run captured_items still records the labeled SQL for every stream/position.

title: Pre-generate throughput query streams outside the timed concurrent loop

Generation cost is excluded from measured execution time

work.notes:
In TPCHThroughputTest.run, before StreamRunner.execute, build a
{stream_id: [sql, ...]} map. Route generation through the EXISTING native
`qgen -p <stream>` path (TPCHStreamManager._generate_stream_queries_qgen)
so one subprocess emits a stream's 22 queries in official permuted order,
instead of 22 QGen.generate calls with per-call temp-dir + dists.dss copy.
_execute_stream then consumes pre-built SQL; the qgen call leaves the timed
loop entirely. Preserve the per-position seed (`seed + stream_id*1000 +
position`) so generated SQL is byte-identical to today.

IMPLEMENTED WITH A DEVIATION from "route through the native qgen -p
path": did not use _generate_stream_queries_qgen. Verified by reading
_sources/tpc-h/dbgen/qgen.c main() and rnd.c that the -p path seeds a
SINGLE subprocess invocation with `rng_seed + stream_id` and derives
all 22 per-query seeds internally from that one Park-Miller LCG chain
(Seed[0]=rndm; for i=1..22: Seed[0]=NextRand(Seed[0]); Seed[i]=Seed[0];
qsub indexes Seed[qnum] by query NUMBER, not position). This throughput
test's seed formula (`seed + stream_id*1000 + position`) instead starts
a FRESH LCG chain per query, keyed by position -- a different scheme
that produces different SQL for the same nominal seed. Confirmed no
accidental convergence anywhere in the codebase (TPCHStreams is never
instantiated by TPCHThroughputTest). Routing through the batch path
would have silently changed every query's substitution parameters,
violating must_preserve. Instead: added TPCHThroughputTest.
_pregenerate_stream_queries() (benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py),
which calls the EXISTING self.benchmark.get_query() path (same seed
formula, same call signature) for all streams via a ThreadPoolExecutor,
entirely before StreamRunner.execute; _execute_stream reads the result
from an instance-attribute cache (self._pregenerated_queries) so its
signature/call-site stayed untouched (required -- out-of-scope tests
tests/unit/core/test_tpc_reporting_execution.py and
tests/unit/tpch/test_tpch_compliance.py call/monkeypatch _execute_stream
with the historical 3-arg signature). Complementary fix in
benchbox/core/tpch/queries.py: QGenBinary now lazily creates and reuses
ONE working directory across all generate() calls (thread-safe via a
lock) instead of a fresh tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() + dists.dss copy
per call -- qgen only reads dists.dss and writes to stdout in this
mode, so sharing one dir concurrently is safe. This addresses the
TODO's stated overhead complaint (per-call temp-dir + copy churn) even
though subprocess count remains O(streams x queries) rather than
collapsing to O(streams). Byte-identity verified empirically: script
generated the same 2 streams x 22 queries via the pre-change inline
formula and the new _pregenerate_stream_queries() path at SF 0.01,
zero mismatches (not committed -- ad hoc verification script).
work.summary: Pre-generate ordered SQL per stream for TPC-H via the native qgen -p batch path, before the concurrent window

test_tpc_reporting_execution.py, tests/unit/core/tpcds/
test_throughput_test_coverage.py) and had to keep its exact behavior

order with `stream_seed = config.base_seed + stream_id*1000 +
position`, missing the `+ stream_id` seed offset real execution
applies via `seed = config.base_seed + stream_id`, and never resolves
variants/permutation -- so it was already only an approximate
pre-check, not a faithful capture of what a stream actually runs).
Added TPCDSThroughputTest._pregenerate_stream_queries()
(benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py), which for each stream calls
the existing _build_stream_queries() (untouched -- TPC-DS stream/
permutation logic in streams.py is out of scope and unmodified) to

each entry's SQL via the existing _get_stream_query_text() using the

Raises immediately on any failure (fail-fast, matching the historical

incidentally removes a latent race: create_standard_streams's
permutation generator calls Python's global random.seed() per stream,
which the OLD code invoked concurrently (once per thread) inside

every stream's ordering sequentially, single-threaded, before any
concurrency starts. Byte-identity verified empirically the same way as

zero mismatches).

description:
Result handling inside the concurrent streams both distorts measurement and
is inconsistent between the two benchmarks.

1. FULL MATERIALIZATION UNDER THE GIL: every stream calls
   `cursor.fetchall()` for every query:
   - TPC-H: benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py:238 `rows = cursor.fetchall()`
     then `result_count = len(rows)`.
   - TPC-DS: benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py:314-315 fetchall() then
     the result is DISCARDED.
   fetchall materializes the entire result set into Python objects while
   holding the GIL. For embedded engines (DuckDB) that release the GIL during
   query execution but not during Python-object materialization, this
   serializes result handling across streams -- an artificial bottleneck that
   grows with result size and stream count, again masking real platform
   scaling. It is also timed inside execution_time_seconds.

2. INCONSISTENT ROW-COUNT SEMANTICS: TPC-H reports len(rows); TPC-DS hardcodes
   result_count = 0 (throughput_test.py:365). Downstream the adapter maps this

description:
Strong evidence that the number of concurrent streams a user requests never
reaches the throughput test, which silently runs at the hard-coded default
(2). Two independent breaks in the chain:

1. `run-official --streams N` VALIDATES that --streams is provided
   (benchbox/cli/commands/run_official.py:36-38), prints it (line 46, 52-53
   "Note: Stream configuration ({streams} streams) applies when supported"),
   then invokes `run` WITHOUT passing `streams`
   (run_official.py:56-67). The value is discarded.

2. Through the main pipeline, the run config carries `concurrent_streams`
   (from BenchmarkConfig.concurrency): benchbox/cli/execution_pipeline.py:106,
   benchbox/cli/orchestrator.py:494, benchbox/core/runner/runner.py:726,
   benchbox/core/schemas.py:98 (`RunConfig.concurrent_streams`). But the
   throughput drivers read a DIFFERENT key:
   - benchbox/platforms/base/execution.py:368
     `num_streams = run_config.get("num_streams", run_config.get("streams", 2))`
   - benchbox/platforms/base/execution.py:233 (TPC-DS) `run_config.get("num_streams", 2)`.
   Neither `num_streams` nor `streams` is ever populated from
   `concurrent_streams`, so both default to 2 regardless of user input.

Net effect: `benchbox run ... --phases throughput` and `run-official
--streams 8` both execute 2 streams. The headline throughput metric is
computed for the wrong concurrency level, and QphH/QphDS composed from it is
wrong. This is a functional defect, not just a UX gap.

NOTE (w0): confirm the break end-to-end with a live run before fixing, since
a legacy alias could exist somewhere not yet found. If a path is found that
DOES honor the count, narrow the fix accordingly.

description:
Two smaller robustness/consistency issues in the throughput executor.

1. TIMED-OUT STREAM LEAK: StreamRunner.execute enforces per-stream timeout via
   `future.result(timeout=...)` but cannot cancel a running thread
   (benchbox/core/throughput/runner.py:87-113). A timed-out stream keeps
   executing in the background, still holding its connection and consuming
   CPU/server resources, while the executor records it as failed and moves on.
   During a long throughput run this means the reported TTT window can overlap
   zombie streams that are still hammering the DB -- skewing both the failed
   run's accounting and any subsequent phase (e.g. maintenance) that starts
   while zombies run. At minimum this should be surfaced; ideally streams
   should be cooperatively cancellable or isolated so a timeout actually stops
   work.

2. DIVERGENT SUCCESS GATES: TPC-H throughput uses a configurable
   min_success_rate (default 0.99) (benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py:38,
   135-137) while TPC-DS hardcodes 0.70
   (benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py:186, and again per-stream at :393).
   The divergence is documented as intentional
   (benchbox/core/throughput/runner.py:11-15 and
   docs/development/throughput-result-alignment.md) but 0.70 vs 0.99 is a large
   gap that changes whether a run is declared successful. Reconcile against the
   TPC-DS spec: make the TPC-DS gate configurable like TPC-H (keeping the
   spec-derived default) and document the spec citation for each threshold.
preserves: Default TPC-H gate stays 0.99; default TPC-DS gate stays its current spec value unless the spec says otherwise.
as_completed accounting (streams_executed/successful/errors) semantics.

work.notes:
Discovered the per-stream timeout was dead code: StreamRunner.execute()
called future.result(timeout=timeout) on a future already yielded by
as_completed() (which only yields done() futures), so TimeoutError could
never actually raise in real usage -- verified with a standalone repro
before changing anything. Fixed by passing timeout to
as_completed(pending, timeout=...) itself, with a fallback loop that
classifies any still-pending future as timed-out/leaked when that call
raises. streams_executed/streams_successful/errors accounting is
unchanged (shared via a small _record_completed_future helper used by
both the main loop and the fallback). A leaked stream now always logs
via logger.warning(...) (previously gated on config.verbose, so it could
be entirely silent) and result.errors gets an explicit message noting
Python cannot forcibly cancel the running thread.
work.summary: Surface timed-out (leaked) streams: annotate the result and log that background execution may continue

work.notes:
Added config.cancel_on_timeout (default False) on both
TPCHThroughputTestConfig and TPCDSThroughputTestConfig. When enabled,
StreamRunner.execute() creates one threading.Event per stream, exposed
via a runtime-only config._stream_cancel_events attribute (not a
declared config field, so unaffected configs/test doubles are
unaffected), and sets the timed-out stream's own event only (never
every stream's event -- one slow stream must not cancel healthy ones).
Each spec's _execute_stream query loop polls its own event once per
query and breaks early if set, marking the stream unsuccessful with an
explicit cancellation error message. Never hard-kills a thread. Even
with this enabled, exiting execute()'s ThreadPoolExecutor context still
blocks until every submitted thread returns (implicit
shutdown(wait=True)); cooperative cancellation shortens that wait to
roughly one more query's execution time instead of leaving it
unbounded.
work.summary: Add a cooperative-cancellation or isolation option so a stream timeout can actually stop work (opt-in)

work.notes:
Added TPCDSThroughputTestConfig.min_success_rate (default 0.70,
mirroring TPCHThroughputTestConfig.min_success_rate). Replaced all
THREE independently hard-coded 0.7 literals (run()'s overall gate,
_finalize_stream_success()'s per-stream gate, and
validate_results()'s gate -- the TODO's own description only names the
first two, but a third existed) with reads of this single field.
Checked both bundled spec PDFs (_sources/tpc-h/specification.pdf,
_sources/tpc-ds/specification/specification_4.0.0.pdf) directly for a
partial-success/acceptable-failure-rate clause: none exists in either
spec. TPC-H 5.1.1.6 defines a failed run as one that "did not complete
successfully due to unforeseen system failures" -- no tolerance
percentage. The prior TPC-H comment ("TPC-H spec allows up to 1% query
failures") was an invented citation (the spec's only 1%/0.99
occurrences are unrelated numeric result-value tolerances, Clause
2.2.4.2) and has been corrected. Both 0.99 and 0.70 are now documented
as BenchBox-internal usability tolerances, not official TPC compliance
gates, on each config dataclass and in
docs/development/throughput-result-alignment.md.

description:
TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension for time-series data that deserves
first-class platform status in BenchBox. Currently it's only supported as
a flag on PostgreSQL (--postgres-enable-timescale).

A dedicated TimescaleDB adapter would:
- Appear as a separate platform in the interactive wizard
- Leverage hypertables for time-series optimized storage
- Use TimescaleDB-specific compression and retention policies
- Support TSBS (Time Series Benchmark Suite) in addition to TPC benchmarks
- Provide TimescaleDB-specific tuning profiles

This builds on the existing PostgreSQL adapter infrastructure.

**Code Review Findings (2024-12-24):**
The following TimescaleDB-related code already exists:
- `--postgres-enable-timescale` CLI flag (platforms/postgresql.py:116-119)
- `enable_timescale` config stored but NOT USED (platforms/postgresql.py:209)
- `get_platform_info()` detects TimescaleDB version (platforms/postgresql.py:676-686)
- `tsbs_devops/schema.py` has `timescale` dialect with hypertable creation
- `nyctaxi/schema.py` has `timescale` dialect handling

Key decision: Created separate TimescaleDBAdapter class extending PostgreSQLAdapter.
title: Create first-class TimescaleDB platform adapter

description:
The TimescaleDB adapter (benchbox/platforms/timescaledb.py) uses f-string interpolation
to construct SQL queries with user-controlled values, creating SQL injection vulnerabilities.

Identified in code review on 2025-12-24 (commit e58ed40e).

Affected locations:
- Lines 300-310: create_hypertable() with chunk_interval parameter
- Lines 362-380: add_compression_policy() with compression_after parameter
- Line 410: ANALYZE with qualified_table

Example vulnerable code:
```python
cursor.execute(f"""
    SELECT create_hypertable(
        '{qualified_table}',  # table_name from config
        'time',
        chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '{self.chunk_interval}',  # user-controlled!
        ...
    )
""")
```

If chunk_interval contains `'; DROP TABLE users; --`, it could execute arbitrary SQL.
title: Fix SQL injection vulnerabilities in TimescaleDB adapter

approach: Distinguish 'the collect subprocess failed' from 'the policy was violated'. When returncode is non-zero, emit a distinct diagnostic naming the interpreter and the missing dependency (and exit non-zero as a tooling error), rather than appending to the policy-violation list. Optionally resolve pytest via the project venv explicitly instead of sys.executable, so the script behaves the same however it is launched.

deferrals.reason: (1) todo verify grades solely on exit code (todo_db.py:1809 'passed = proc.returncode == 0'), ignoring the prose expectation. Rung 1 runs the script under --strict in the broken env; the CORRECT behaviour there is a non-zero exit, because a policy check that never ran must not report success -- otherwise CI goes green on a broken environment. So the rung can only ever report fail. Verified the rung's intent manually instead: 0 FAST_LANE_VIOLATION lines, no 'Fast lane policy violations' summary, exactly 1 FAST_LANE_ENVIRONMENT_ERROR naming the interpreter, exit 1. Verifications are create-time-only so the rung cannot be amended. (2) tests/unit/scripts/test_timing_policy_modes.py is outside only_modify, but its test_emit_fast_count_unparseable_output_fails_closed asserted the exact string 'could not parse' -- the wording this fix deliberately replaces -- so it had to be updated or CI would go red.
deferrals.summary: Verification rung 1 is unsatisfiable as authored, and the fix needs a test file outside only_modify

description: _run_pytest_collect() shells out to [sys.executable, '-m', 'pytest', ...]. Invoked the documented agent way -- 'uv run --project _project/scripts -- python _project/scripts/timing_policy_check.py --strict' -- sys.executable is the _project/scripts venv, which has neither pytest nor benchbox installed. Every collect subprocess exits 1 with no parseable count, and the script converts that into policy violations: 'Fast lane policy violations: 4' with four 'could not parse collect count' lines. Nothing is actually wrong with the fast lane. Run from the project env instead ('uv run -- python _project/scripts/timing_policy_check.py --strict') the same tree reports 'Fast lane policy violations: 0'. Found during the 2026-07-24 benchmark-runs batch (PRs #1299-#1302); verified pre-existing by stashing all batch changes and reproducing on a clean tree. Real-world cost: an agent following the pre-approved command list sees 4 FAST_LANE_VIOLATIONs, cannot tell them from a genuine cap breach, and may 'fix' a cap that was never exceeded. CI is unaffected because its lint job invokes the script with the project environment.
preserves: A real fast-lane cap breach still fails with a clear FAST_LANE_VIOLATION
CI's lint invocation keeps its current pass/fail semantics for a genuine max_fast_tests breach

description:
During the 2026-06-08 TODO prioritization pass, 6 priority fields were edited
and committed without running validate_todo.py first. The PR gate already
handles this: pr-content-guard runs validate_todo.py on each changed TODO path
when the diff routes to the content-only CI path. So PR merges are protected.

pushing or opening a PR) and only discover the error in CI. Adding a pre-commit
hook closes this gap by failing the commit immediately.

edit outside a PR (e.g. a direct push to a feature branch) could introduce
invalid YAML in unreviewed files. Belt-and-suspenders: add a validate --all
step to pr-preflight for the content-only code path as well.

description:

approach: For (a), lint cannot execute rungs against a hypothetical fixed tree, so it cannot prove falsifiability in general. Two tractable options: require rung commands to be self-asserting in form (assert/grep -q/test, not a bare suite invocation), or record the pre-fix exit status at create time and reject a rung that already exits 0. The second is stronger and cheap - the author is standing in the unfixed tree when they create the item. For (b), a heuristic that would have caught the real case: if only_modify names a source file whose conventional test file exists, that test file should also be in scope. Keep it a warning - some work genuinely edits source without touching tests.
description: lint returns 0 findings for items whose verification rungs cannot gate and whose scope omits files the work will touch. Both shipped on real items on 2026-07-30/31. (a) NON-GATING RUNG: anonymization-secret-list-diverged-from-platform-options carried the rung 'pytest tests/unit/core/results/test_platform_options_capture.py -q', which passed on the unfixed tree (44 passed, exit 0). It asserted 'the suite still passes', never 'the defect is fixed'. A rung that cannot fail for the reason it exists is not a gate, and it is more dangerous than a broken one because it reports green. (b) INCOMPLETE SCOPE: the same item listed anonymization.py in only_modify but not tests/unit/core/results/test_anonymization.py, which exists and is where that module's tests live - so the work could not land in scope. This is a DIFFERENT check from the sibling item todo-lint-unresolvable-scope-and-ladder-paths, which only catches paths that do not exist. IMPORTANT ORDERING CONSTRAINT, verified 2026-07-31: a prose-placeholder rung exits 2 and a genuinely unmet criterion exits 1, so a naive 'rung must fail before the fix' check is VACUOUSLY SATISFIED by a broken rung. Falsifiability therefore depends on todo-lint-unrunnable-verification-commands landing first; it does not subsume it.

description:
Two related blind-spots flagged that TODOs whose safety predicate rests
on external/transient evidence (upstream behavior, harness output,
dependency-resolved version) have no schema-level mechanism to record
or verify the evidence durability:

- `2026-05-04-074634` -- the /todo review rubric scores write-time
  quality, not implement-time freshness. A TODO that sits in planning/
  for weeks may have evidence that has silently rotted.
- `2026-05-04-083819` -- W0 verification-only commits cite evidence in
  free-text commit messages; a reviewer landing the PR days later
  cannot replay it.

This TODO ships three thin conventions:

1. Optional `freshness_check` block in the TODO schema, OR a strong-
   convention "w0: re-validate evidence" first work unit for upstream-
   dependent items (w1 picks).
2. A new freshness axis on the /todo review rubric -- unconditionally,
   regardless of which mechanism w1 picks. The rubric must score
   freshness whether the schema field exists or the convention is
   review-time-only.
3. A `_project/verification-logs/<todo-id>/<work-id>.log` committed-
   artifact convention for verification-only commits.

The companion `extend-five-axis-review-rubric` TODO ships the
/code review side (verification-only / evidence-durability branch);
this TODO owns the /todo review side and the artifact convention.
preserves: /todo review rubric existing axes (clarity / completeness / actionability / freshness / guardrails / work-breakdown) are unchanged in name and weight.

approach: Decide what is safely mutable before an item reaches done: description and verification command/expected are strong candidates, scope globs likely too. Add an 'amend' verb restricted to those fields, log every change via the existing event log so auditability is preserved, and refuse amendment once state=done. Separately, let promote() carry --only-modify/--do-not-modify/--preserve/--verify/--work so promoted items are not born guardrail-less.

deferrals.reason: Implemented update in _project/scripts/todo_db.py, then tests/unit/scripts/test_todo_wrapper.py::TestSkillThinness failed with 'standalone_only_commands overlaps wrapper handlers: [update]'. The todo-db skill states it outright: 'Standalone-only actions -- declared machine-readably in the skill sidecar as standalone_only_commands, currently update -- exist only in todo-db >= 0.3.' Two tests enforce the boundary and one of them hardcodes update as THE example of a wrapper-unsupported verb, with the comment that the sets 'must stay disjoint'. So amendment is already solved upstream in todo-db >= 0.3; this repo's embedded wrapper deliberately omits it, and reimplementing it here is the wrong fix. I reverted that half. Remaining real work, unaddressed anywhere: adopt todo-db >= 0.3 as the project's CLI (or route the wrapper's unsupported verbs to it) so amendment becomes available to this repo -- that is a dependency/adoption decision, not a code patch, and it is out of this item's only_modify allowlist of todo_db.py + tests. The promote-guardrails half WAS in scope and shipped: promote now accepts --only-modify/--do-not-modify/--preserve/--verify/--work/--category/--approach, so promoted items are no longer born without scope or a ladder.

description: The tracker has no update/edit verb (create, claim, release, deps, unblock, start, done, defer, promote, dismiss, complete, drop, block, list, ready, stats, check-scope, verify, lint, sweep-stale, migrate, config, export, finding). Combined with scope/verifications being create-time-only, an item authored with a mistake stays wrong forever. Three distinct instances hit in the 2026-07-25 follow-up batch alone: (1) promote() accepts only title/priority/worktree/description, so all four promoted items shipped with NO scope globs, NO verification ladder and NO work units -- check-scope passes trivially rather than meaningfully, and scope had to be self-policed in the PR body each time; (2) timing-policy-check-misreports-pytest-failure-as-violation rung 1 is unsatisfiable as authored and cannot be amended, so it reads fail forever despite a correct fix; (3) todo-verify-grades-only-on-exit-code's description proposes an approach that research disproved (evaluating expected against stdout would fail 2787 of 2939 verifications), and the description could not be corrected -- the rebuttal had to live in PR #1311's body instead. Dropping and recreating is not a workaround: drop is terminal and reserves the id forever, and dependents would need new ids. See verification-rungs-authored-with-unsatisfiable-commands for the rung-specific sweep; this item is about the ergonomics gap that produced them.
preserves: Existing item history stays auditable - amendments are logged, not silent overwrites
drop keeps its terminal, id-reserving semantics
title: Scope, verifications and descriptions are create-time-only, so a mis-authored item can never be repaired

description: todo_db.py:1809 sets 'passed = proc.returncode == 0'. The per-verification 'expected' text authored at create time is displayed but never evaluated, so any rung whose intent is about OUTPUT rather than exit status cannot be expressed. Concrete case from timing-policy-check-misreports-pytest-failure-as-violation (PR for it): rung 1 runs the checker under --strict in a deliberately broken environment and expects it to 'report a tooling/environment error, not Fast lane policy violations: 4'. The correct behaviour there is a NON-ZERO exit -- a policy check that never ran must not report success -- so the rung reports fail forever even though the implementation is right. Because verifications are create-time-only, the item's author cannot repair the rung afterwards either. Options: evaluate the expected string against stdout/stderr when it is not an exit-code phrase; or add an explicit expected_exit_code / expect_failure field; or at minimum document that rungs must be phrased as exit-code assertions so authors stop writing output expectations. Related create-time-only constraint: promote() cannot set scope/verifications at all, so promoted items get no ladder.
title: todo verify grades rungs solely on exit code, so 'expected output' verifications are unsatisfiable

description:
The TPC-DI scalability test's memory assertion checks absolute process RSS:

  max_memory_mb = 1000 * scale_factor + 2000
  assert metrics["peak_memory_mb"] <= max_memory_mb

This was raised from 600 MB to 2000 MB base in commit 8c0ddcb46 because observed
absolute RSS at SF 0.01 was 1943 MB - xdist workers, loaded modules, and pandas
internals dominate the measurement, not the benchmark itself.

The problem: absolute RSS is immune to memory leaks. A 300 MB regression at SF 0.01
would push actual usage to ~2243 MB, which still passes the 2010 MB ceiling (since
ceiling is 1000*0.01 + 2000 = 2010 MB). The test no longer catches regressions.

The fix is already 90% done: `memory_growth_mb = peak_memory - start_memory` is
already computed and stored in performance_results[scale_factor] at line 144 of
test_multi_scale_factor_performance_analysis. The validation method at line 301
just ignores it, checking peak_memory_mb instead.

Switching to delta restores regression sensitivity: the baseline process RSS
(1800-2000 MB of OS/Python/xdist overhead) is subtracted out, leaving only the
memory actually allocated by the benchmark. A tight ceiling on growth catches leaks
without being affected by CI environment variability.
preserves: All four scale factors (0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0) continue to be tested
No changes to data collection logic in test_multi_scale_factor_performance_analysis - only _validate_performance_thresholds changes
memory_growth_mb key continues to exist in performance_results dict (used by _save_performance_baseline)
peak_memory_mb key remains in performance_results (other methods may reference it)
title: Refactor TPC-DI memory validation to check growth (delta) instead of absolute RSS

description:
Running TPC-DS on PySpark fails with ~60 queries due to missing UnifiedExpr methods
and Polars-specific code in the DataFrame queries.

The TPC-DS dataframe queries currently use Polars-specific functions (pl.concat, pl.when)
and call methods on expressions that don't exist in the UnifiedExpr wrapper class.
This prevents TPC-DS from running on PySpark.

Root causes:
- 7 missing UnifiedExpr methods: is_between, fill_null, is_null, is_not_null, rank, over, cum_sum
- 2 missing context functions: concat() and when() - queries use pl.concat/pl.when directly
- Type unwrapping issues where UnifiedExpr isn't converted to native PySpark Column
title: TPC-DS PySpark Compatibility - Add missing UnifiedExpr methods and context functions

anti_patterns.instead: adopt dsqgen's ordering and back it with a checked-in output diff.

description:
BenchBox bypasses dsqgen's official multi-stream mode and hand-rolls TPC-DS
throughput stream ordering and per-stream parameters. This is the core
compliance gap; two symptoms and the root cause:

ROOT CAUSE -- dsqgen -STREAMS is never used. dsqgen (the official binary) has
a -STREAMS N mode (with -INPUT templates.lst) that emits the official
per-stream query ORDERING and the official per-stream substitution PARAMETERS
in a single invocation. BenchBox never calls it (grep: no -STREAMS anywhere).
Instead, DSQGenBinary.generate (benchbox/core/tpcds/c_tools.py:161-259) calls
dsqgen ONE query template at a time (`-TEMPLATE queryN.tpl -RNGSEED <seed>
-FILTER Y`), and the higher layers reconstruct streams by hand:

1. HOME-GROWN ORDERING: stream query order comes from a deterministic swap
   with hardcoded PERMUTATION_SEED = 19620718 in
   benchbox/core/tpcds/streams.py (TPCDS_STANDARD mode, ~lines 77-104), NOT the
   official dsqgen permutation. (TPC-H by contrast uses the real 41x22
   PERMUTATION_MATRIX from permute.h, benchbox/core/tpch/streams.py:39-81.)
2. HOME-GROWN PER-STREAM PARAMETERS: stream_id passed to generate() never
   reaches dsqgen; it only seeds a Python RNG jitter in
   _generate_parameter_variations (c_tools.py:437+,
   `effective_seed = base_seed*7919 + stream_id*3037`). So per-stream parameter
   diversity is invented in Python, not produced by dsqgen's stream seeding.

SECONDARY -- suspicious per-stream regeneration:
TPCDSThroughputTest._build_stream_queries
(benchbox/core/tpcds/throughput_test.py:264-293) calls
`create_standard_streams(num_streams=stream_id + 1, base_seed=seed +
stream_id)` then picks `streams.get(stream_id, [])`. Each stream regenerates
the full set with a DIFFERENT num_streams and a shifted seed, so a stream's
ordering depends on its index rather than the run's stream count -- looks
unintended vs TPC-H's single PERMUTATION_MATRIX[stream_id % 41] index.

FIX DIRECTION: adopt `dsqgen -STREAMS N` to generate all throughput streams in
one call. This simultaneously (a) restores official ordering + official
per-stream substitution parameters (compliance), and (b) collapses the
per-query subprocess spawns into ONE generation pass -- directly serving
throughput-pregenerate-query-streams (which needs streams materialized before
the timed window anyway). Retire the home-grown permutation and RNG jitter for
the throughput path.

This is soundness-critical (query ordering + substitution parameters feed the
QphDS compliance story) -- back every change with a dsqgen-output diff.
preserves: Deterministic, reproducible streams for a fixed (num_streams, seed) — now anchored to dsqgen output rather than the Python permutation.
Single-query get_query (non-throughput uses like power/dry-run) keeps working via the existing per-template path.

approach: Rebuild dbgen and qgen from _sources/tpc-h/dbgen/ with an explicit lower MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET (e.g. 15.0) or on an older runner, verify with `vtool -show` that minos <= 15.0, confirm generation still matches the reference query/data set, then re-bless benchbox/_binaries/tpc-h/darwin-arm64/checksums.md5.
description:
chatgpt-codex-connector review finding on merged PR #1256 (P2), deferred from the first PR-review sweep (PR #1259) and tracked in GitHub issue #1260.

The packaged darwin-arm64 binaries committed in #1256 were built on macOS 26 and carry LC_BUILD_VERSION minos 26.0 (verified with `vtool -show` on both qgen and dbgen; the previous packaged qgen had minos 15.0). On macOS 15.x and earlier dyld rejects a binary whose minos exceeds the host OS. Because benchbox/_binaries/tpc-h/darwin-arm64/checksums.md5 MATCHES these binaries, ensure_tpc_binaries() selects the precompiled path instead of rebuilding, so TPC-H data/query generation fails on Apple Silicon installs running macOS <= 15.
Thread: https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/pull/1256#discussion_r3626428542
Issue: https://github.com/joeharris76/BenchBox/issues/1260

Why this was deferred from the code sweep: re-blessing a committed binary's checksum is provenance-governed (make audit-sha-check, SHA-provenance evidence tree), the rebuilt bytes depend on the local toolchain, and TPC spec-correctness of the rebuilt generator needs verification beyond a code-fix sweep.

Related open item: resync-tpch-darwin-x86-64-binaries covers the x86_64 drift; consider doing both rebuilds in one controlled session.
preserves: TPC-H generated data and queries stay spec-correct and byte-comparable to the reference set
The EOL_HANDLING trailing-pipe framing guard still passes for the rebuilt dbgen
checksums.md5 stays in the GNU 'hash filename' format the verifier parses
title: Rebuild darwin-arm64 TPC-H qgen/dbgen with a lower MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET (minos 26.0 breaks macOS <= 15)

description:
Canonical TPC-H Q11 renders its value threshold as 0.0001 / SF (qgen does
this, and PR #770 made the SQL run path scale-faithful for both TPC-H and
TPC-Havoc). The DataFrame surface only gets the scale-correct fraction when a
qgen seed is provided: dataframe_runner._setup_parameter_overrides extracts
parameters from rendered qgen SQL and injects them via
set_parameter_overrides. Without a seed, every Q11 DataFrame implementation
(canonical TPC-H and all TPC-Havoc variants) reads
TPCH_DEFAULT_PARAMS[11]["fraction"] = 0.0001 - the SF=1 value - regardless of
the benchmark's actual scale factor. At SF=0.1 the executed Q11 threshold is
10x too small (wrong row count and timing); at SF=10 it is 10x too large.

The TPC-Havoc DataFrame equivalence gate
(benchbox/core/tpchavoc/dataframe_equivalence.py, see
tpchavoc-dataframe-variant-equivalence-gate) works around this inside the
gate by injecting {11: {"fraction": 0.0001 / SF}} through the same public
set_parameter_overrides seam that seeded runs use. That keeps the gate
honest but does not fix the unseeded product run path.

Fix at the seam where scale is known: the DataFrame runner (or the
parameter-override setup it calls) should derive the unseeded Q11 fraction
from the run's scale factor, exactly as the SQL side derives {q11_fraction}
during query rendering. Then drop the gate-local injection in
dataframe_equivalence.find_dataframe_divergences (the gate should pass with
no override once defaults are scale-aware).
preserves: Seeded runs keep using qgen-extracted parameters unchanged.
The TPC-Havoc DataFrame equivalence gate stays green throughout.

benchbox/core/tpch/dataframe_queries.py:TPCH_DEFAULT_PARAMS / get_tpch_parameters / set_parameter_overrides - the parameter seam; defaults are static and scale-blind

benchbox/core/tpchavoc/dataframe_equivalence.py:find_dataframe_divergences - the gate-local workaround to remove once defaults are scale-aware

description:
Promoted from the deferred item in
[[tpch-throughput-seed-validation-fix]] (surfaced by the UAT-effort
assessment, 2026-07-16). The seed-validation fix currently EXCLUDES Q11,

cardinality for the seed in use, so Q11/16/18/20 are validated like the rest.

path; this strengthening only makes sense once that path exists and is green.

description:
TPC-H throughput fails row-count validation for queries 11, 16, 18, and 20 on
EVERY stream, at SF=1 on DuckDB, for ANY seed choice (reproduced with seed=42,
seed=7, and no seed). This is NOT a concurrency bug: the identical 4 queries
fail identically in single-stream POWER mode with a non-reference seed, while
POWER mode with no seed (qgen defaults, exact validation against the official
answer files) passes cleanly.

ROOT CAUSE (hypothesis, to confirm in w0): the throughput driver derives each
stream's per-query seed as `seed + stream_id*1000 + position`
(benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py), so no throughput query (beyond
possibly the first query of stream 0) can ever land on the reference-seed
exact-match validation path. Every throughput query therefore falls back to
the LOOSE (+-50%) tolerance in benchbox/core/expected_results/tpch_results.py,
which is not wide enough for these 4 TPC-H-spec-sanctioned non-deterministic
queries (their row counts legitimately vary with substitution parameters).
tpch_results.py's own docstring flags a RANGE mode as "reserved for future
use" and NOT yet wired up for TPC-H (tpch_results.py:23-26) -- almost certainly
the intended fix: validate these queries against a spec-derived acceptable
RANGE rather than an exact reference or a blanket +-50% band.

Discovered during throughput-uat-and-ci-coverage (#1094) verification against a
live SF=1 DuckDB run. Previously invisible because the throughput driver was
only ever exercised against Mock connections before
throughput-real-db-integration-tests (#1074), and that item's new tests run at
SF=0.01, which does not reproduce this SF=1-scale manifestation.

BLAST RADIUS TODAY: the nightly throughput UAT cell's `uat-sweep` step is
marked `continue-on-error: true` (.github/workflows/nightly.yml:591-596)
specifically to tolerate this known defect; the concurrency invariant that
item protects (requested stream count reaches the driver) is hard-gated by a
separate step, but the cell's overall clean-pass status stays red until this
is fixed. Closing this lets that continue-on-error be removed so a NEW
correctness regression in the throughput cell fails the nightly outright.
preserves: Do not widen validation for queries that are actually deterministic -- only the spec-sanctioned non-deterministic queries move to RANGE.
EXACT validation (reference-seed path) still fires and stays strict for deterministic queries and power/no-seed runs.
The concurrency invariant already hard-gated in nightly (requested stream count reaches the driver) keeps its own independent gate.

description:
DECISION (user, 2026-07-11): fix this as part of the UAT hardening effort.
It is the single defect that neutralizes the nightly throughput UAT gate.

The defect (documented in .github/workflows/nightly.yml:580-595 and
tests/uat/throughput.py:116-129, verified on develop @ fc31f3604):
TPC-H throughput mode derives per-stream/per-position query parameters as
`seed + stream_id * 1000 + position`
(benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py), so queries 11/16/18/20 -- TPC-H's
parameter-sensitive, answer-set-boundary queries -- never land on the
reference-seed exact-match validation path after the first query of
stream 0. They then fail BenchBox's LOOSE (+-50%) row-count check on
every stream. Reproduced upstream with a custom seed, a different custom
seed, and no seed at all; confirmed independent of concurrency (same 4
queries fail in single-stream POWER mode with a non-reference seed).

Consequence: every throughput cell is permanently red, which forced
`continue-on-error: true` on the nightly sweep (nightly.yml:596) and
reduced the CI signal to a single stream-count assertion. Restoring the
gate (nightly-throughput-gate-restoration) depends on this fix.

Prior-art policy to mirror: the bounded correctness gate ALREADY excludes
Q11/Q16/Q18/Q20 "for answer-set boundary sensitivity"
(docs/operations/release-guide.md:33-35); the fix brings the loose
validation path in line with that established policy instead of inventing
a new one. Expected shape: when a query's substitution parameters differ
from the reference seed AND the query is in the documented
parameter-sensitive set, row-count validation records
"not validated (parameter-sensitive, non-reference params)" instead of a
failure; validation status for the run treats these as neither pass nor
fail (mirroring how the correctness gate's exclusion works). Value: a
clean throughput run becomes achievable and Throughput@Size is computed,
un-neutralizing validate_throughput_metric.
preserves: Per-stream seed derivation formula unchanged (it is TPC-compliant stream permutation behavior).
Reference-seed runs keep EXACT-match validation for all queries including Q11/16/18/20 -- the exclusion applies only to non-reference parameters.
TPC-H/TPC-DS throughput success-gate defaults (0.99/0.70) from PR #1106 unchanged.
The correctness gate (make test-correctness-gate) behavior and its exclusion list are untouched.

benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py -- per-stream seed derivation (the mechanism stays; only validation policy changes).
docs/operations/release-guide.md:33-35 + make test-correctness-gate -- the existing Q11/16/18/20 exclusion policy and its rationale. Reuse the policy and the query set constant.

work.notes:
Seam, precisely:
1. benchbox/core/validation/query_validation.py QueryValidator.
   validate_query_result() is the single dispatch point for row-count
   validation (EXACT/RANGE/LOOSE/SKIP) -- called from ~20 platform
   adapter execute_query() implementations (benchbox/platforms/*, out
   of scope_limit) plus benchbox/core/benchmark_mixins.py (also out of
   scope_limit, core/ but not core/validation|tpch|expected_results|
   results/). None of those call sites are touched by this fix.
2. benchbox/core/expected_results/registry.py
   ExpectedResultsRegistry.get_expected_result() decides EXACT vs SKIP
   purely from stream_id (>0 => SKIP, "no answer files for streams>0")
   -- it has NO visibility into which seed produced the current query's
   parameters.
3. benchbox/core/expected_results/tpch_results.py
   get_tpch_expected_results() registers EVERY TPC-H query with
   ValidationMode.EXACT unconditionally (never LOOSE) -- so the LOOSE
   mode described in that file's own module docstring ("BenchBox
   automatically switches to LOOSE validation" for custom seeds) is
   DEAD in practice.
4. benchbox/core/tpch/power_test.py TPCHPowerTest.__init__ computes an
   `actual_validation_mode` string ("exact"/"loose"/"disabled") from
   comparing the seed to get_reference_seed(scale_factor) (lines
   ~140-195), stores it on TPCHPowerTestConfig.validation_mode -- but
   grep confirms `.validation_mode` is read ONLY when building
   to_dict() metadata; it is NEVER consulted to change how
   validate_query_result() is called. The "auto-switch to loose"
   plumbing is entirely vestigial. Root cause is NOT "wrong tolerance
   chosen" -- it's "no seed-awareness reaches the validator at all".
5. Confirms exact match to TODO's "queries 11/16/18/20 ... never land
   on the reference-seed exact-match path" framing: registry.py only
   ever exact-validates stream_id in (None, 0); power_test.py's own
   warmup/measurement iteration renumbering
   (benchbox/core/tpch/platform_power.py current_stream_id = i for
   warmup, warm_up_iterations+i for measurement) means only the
   WARMUP run is ever tagged stream_id=0 and reaches EXACT validation
   at all -- and platform_power.py's warmup loop (lines ~104-129)
   never checks power_test_result.success, so those failures are
   silently absorbed and never surface in the CLI's printed
   success/PASSED verdict (only the measurement runs, tagged stream 1-3
   and therefore already SKIPped, are checked). This means today,
   POWER mode's Q11/16/18/20 failures are invisible unless you inspect
   the exported JSON's queries[] array directly -- worth flagging as a
   separate follow-up (spawned as a background task, not fixed here;
   out of this TODO's scope which is validation-policy-only).
6. SEPARATE BUG FOUND (not fixed here, see below): throughput_test.py
   _execute_stream()'s `connection.set_query_context(query_id)` call
   (line ~475) omits `stream_id=stream_id` -- so EVERY throughput
   stream is treated as stream_id=None -> "stream 0" by the registry,
   meaning ALL streams (not just stream 0) attempt EXACT validation.
   This is WHY w0's throughput repro found stream 1 also failing
   Q11/16/18/20, not just stream 0. Chose NOT to fix this omission in
   this TODO: the parameter-sensitive exclusion (w2) resolves it
   completely regardless, because the exclusion check does not depend
   on stream_id or the registry's skip logic -- it is computed
   independently from the actual per-query seed
   (base_seed + stream_id*1000 + position) vs the reference seed.
   Leaving the stream_id omission in place does not reintroduce any
   failure for THIS defect (confirmed: the other 18 "answer-stable"
   queries already tolerate stream>0's different derived parameters
   without EXACT mismatches in the w0 throughput repro -- 8/44 failed,
   all and only {11,16,18,20} x 2 streams). Flagged as a spawn_task
   follow-up per review-protocol instead of silently leaving it
   undocumented.
7. No existing PARAMETER_SENSITIVE/BOUNDARY_SENSITIVE Python constant
   in benchbox/core/expected_results/ (confirmed via grep) -- the only
   prior art is Makefile's CORRECTNESS_GATE_QUERY_IDS (the INCLUDED 18,
   inverse of the excluded 4), consumed only by
   tests/integration/test_local_platform_benchmark_matrix.py via the
   BENCHBOX_CORRECTNESS_GATE_QUERY_IDS env var -- test-only plumbing,
   not importable production code. Defining a new constant, not
   duplicating.

PINNED FILE LIST for w2 (narrowed from the full scope_limit):
  - benchbox/core/expected_results/tpch_results.py (new constant)
  - benchbox/core/validation/query_validation.py (context channel +
    exclusion check)
  - benchbox/core/tpch/power_test.py (compute + set/clear context)
  - benchbox/core/tpch/throughput_test.py (compute + set/clear context)
Design constraint driving the context-channel approach (rather than a
new function parameter threaded through validate_query_result's
callers): threading an explicit "is_reference_seed" argument would
require editing every platform adapter's execute_query() signature
(~20 files under benchbox/platforms/, all outside scope_limit) plus
benchbox/core/benchmark_mixins.py (also outside scope_limit). Instead,
benchbox/core/tpch/{power_test,throughput_test}.py set a thread-local
"is this query using the reference seed's parameters" flag immediately
before calling connection.execute() (the same call site that already
calls set_query_context() via hasattr-duck-typing, so no platform code
needs to know this channel exists), and
benchbox/core/validation/query_validation.py reads it. Defaults to
None (unset) for every caller that never sets it (TPC-DS, DataFrame
validation, any other QueryValidator user) -- preserves their exact
pre-existing behavior untouched, satisfying must_preserve.

approach:
These are shared variant queries, so a change affects all platforms. Fix

description:
While fixing the DuckDB SF1 hang in tpchavoc 10_v8 (uat-duckdb-reference-triage),
the root cause was a correlated subquery whose unqualified columns
(`l2.l_orderkey = l_orderkey`) silently bound to the INNER alias (l2)
instead of the outer table, degenerating the intended correlated
semi-join into an uncorrelated full scan. 10_v8 was fixed by qualifying
the correlation to the outer table.

Two more variants carry the identical pattern but do NOT currently break
any platform (they execute in <0.1s at SF1 on DuckDB because the
degenerate subquery folds to a cheap one-time scalar), so they were left
out of the duckdb-reference-triage scope:

- q11 variant 1 ("Scalar subqueries"): subquery
  `from partsupp ps2, ... where ps2.ps_partkey = ps_partkey` — unqualified
  `ps_partkey` binds to ps2, so the threshold becomes an uncorrelated
  avg over all German partsupp rows instead of per-part.
- q17 variant 8 ("EXISTS pattern"): EXISTS subquery
  `from (...) avg_calc where avg_calc.l_partkey = l_partkey` — unqualified
  `l_partkey` binds to avg_calc, dropping the per-part correlation.

These likely produce semantically-incorrect variant results on EVERY
platform (tpchavoc validates execution, not result equivalence, so the
defect is silent). This item is about correctness of the shared variant
SQL, not a DuckDB-specific failure.
preserves: All tpchavoc variants must still parse, bind, and execute on every supported platform.
DuckDB tpchavoc must remain 100% green at 0.01/0.1/1.0 after the changes.

description:
The TPC-Havoc SQL equivalence gate landed in PR #770 proves every variant is
result-equivalent to canonical TPC-H on ONE engine: DuckDB at SF=0.1. But the
variants are written once and run, after dialect translation, on ~20 platforms
(Postgres-family, ClickHouse, DataFusion, Spark, Snowflake, BigQuery, Trino,
etc.). "Equivalent on DuckDB" does not imply "equivalent everywhere":

  - Dialect translation can change semantics (NULL ordering, integer vs float
    division, DISTINCT/window edge cases, implicit casts, date arithmetic).
  - Engines differ in window-function, QUALIFY, and aggregate-filter support;
    the variant families lean on exactly these (the gate's burndown touched
    QUALIFY, window rank columns, and FILTER variants).
  - The existing PostgreSQL execution-filter skip-list
    (benchbox/sql_compat/rules/execution_filter/postgres_tpchavoc.py) already
    encodes ~17 variants Postgres can't even execute - evidence that
    cross-engine behavior diverges structurally, not just numerically.

So a variant can be execution-green AND wrong on engine X while the DuckDB gate
stays green - the precise silent-divergence failure mode the SQL gate exists to
kill, just one engine over. This TODO does NOT try to gate all 20 engines in
routine CI (too slow, too flaky). It adds a SECOND, bounded engine sample to
catch the largest class of translation-induced divergence, and decides from the
evidence whether a broader matrix is warranted.

PostgreSQL is the natural first second-engine: a Postgres service container
already exists in the PR CI (the postgres-integration job added on develop),
and its skip-list gives a ready-made expected-exception set.

approach:
Mirror benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py one-to-one for the DataFrame
surface: same data builder, same canonical reference, same validator, same
bounded SF=0.1 DuckDB cell, same empty-baseline fail-on-divergence policy, same

its result to ordered row tuples. Land report-mode first (w1), burn down (w2),
then flip the gate (w3). Do not duplicate the comparator or the data builder.
description:
PR #770 landed a hard result-equivalence gate for the TPC-Havoc *SQL*
variants: it executes canonical TPC-H plus every SQL variant on a bounded
SF=0.1 DuckDB cell, compares with float tolerance, and fails CI on any
divergence (KNOWN_DIVERGENCES is empty). That gate found and drove out 24
silent correctness defects (value clamping, join fan-out, schema leakage,
scale-threshold, QUALIFY-vs-WHERE filtering).

The DataFrame variants (benchbox/core/tpchavoc/dataframe_queries/) get NO such
guard. TPC-Havoc claims the 10 DataFrame variants of each query are
semantically equivalent to canonical TPC-H exactly as the SQL variants do, and
`TPCHavocBenchmark.supports_dataframe_mode()` returns True, so the DataFrame
surface is a shipped, runnable benchmark whose core invariant is unchecked.

Crucially, the SQL gate proves NOTHING about this surface. Review evidence
from PR #770: the DataFrame variants are INDEPENDENT designs, not mirrors of
the SQL variants. The same variant id encodes a DIFFERENT transformation per
surface (e.g. SQL q9_v10 had nation-bucketing + negative-profit clamping
defects; DataFrame q9_v10 is a benign algebraic reformulation of the profit
term). None of the 24 SQL-side divergences had a DataFrame analog when spot-
checked, but "spot-checked, no analog found" is not "gated, proven equivalent"
- the same defect CLASSES (clamping a value via a conditional, dropping/adding
an output column, filtering the inner frame instead of the outer row) are all
expressible in DataFrame code and would be equally silent.

This TODO builds the DataFrame analog of the SQL gate: execute every DataFrame
variant against the same small-SF data, compare each to canonical TPC-H with
the SAME validator/tolerance, drive any divergence to zero (fix or declared
exception), and wire it into the same bounded CI job. It is the natural
completion of tpchavoc-variant-equivalence-gate across both execution
surfaces.
preserves: ResultValidator tolerance and checksum semantics are unchanged; reuse, do not fork, the comparator.
The SQL equivalence gate and its empty KNOWN_DIVERGENCES stay green and unchanged.
benchbox run --benchmark tpchavoc DataFrame mode default (execution-only) behavior stays available; the gate is additive.

description:
SOUNDNESS-CRITICAL COMPARATOR SURFACE: this TODO's work is in
benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py, the blocking TPC-Havoc SQL equivalence
gate. It is adjacent to, and shares helpers with, benchbox/core/tpchavoc/validation.py
(covered by .github/CODEOWNERS as `benchbox/core/**/validation.py @joeharris76`)
and mirrors the discipline of benchbox/core/equivalence/cross_surface.py
(covered as `benchbox/core/equivalence/** @joeharris76`). Even though
`benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py` itself is not literally matched by
either existing CODEOWNERS glob (verified: only `core/**/validation.py` and
`core/equivalence/**` are listed in .github/CODEOWNERS as of this writing),
it IS the hard, blocking correctness gate for TPC-Havoc and must be treated as
soundness-critical - request code-owner review on the PR explicitly rather
than relying on the glob to force it, and flag in the PR description that
CODEOWNERS coverage for this file may itself be worth extending.

Verified by reading benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py on this branch:

- `build_postgres_with_tpch` (lines 370-431) verifies every TPC-H table loaded
  >0 rows before sampling (lines 412-419: `table_stats.get(table, 0) <= 0`
  raises `RuntimeError`), with the comment "A silent empty/partial load would
  make every variant compare empty-vs-empty and report a FALSE green."
- `build_datafusion_with_tpch` (lines 588-618) has the identical guard (lines
  611-614).
- `build_clickhouse_with_tpch` (lines 770-808) has the identical guard (lines
  800-803).
- `build_duckdb_with_tpch` (lines 296-316), the BLOCKING gate builder that
  every other engine's builder was modeled after, has NO such guard: it calls
  `DuckDBAdapter(database=":memory:").load_data(tpchavoc, connection, data_dir)`
  and returns immediately, never checking the load actually populated rows.
  A silent partial/empty DuckDB load would make `find_divergences` compare
  empty-vs-empty for every affected query and the hard gate would report a
  FALSE green - the exact failure mode the three sibling engines were
  explicitly hardened against.
- `find_divergences` (lines 198-274) has no per-query vacuity check: it never
  inspects whether `original` (the canonical query's row count) is empty
  before comparing to each variant. Compare this to
  `benchbox/core/equivalence/cross_surface.py`'s `legitimately_empty` /
  vacuous-cell handling (`CrossSurfaceGate.legitimately_empty`,
  cross_surface.py:372-382, and the FAILURE line at cross_surface.py:1183-1187
  `GATE FAILURE - vacuous empty-vs-empty queries ... not classified`), which
  fails the gate on any unclassified 0-row reference rather than silently
  passing an empty-vs-empty comparison.
- `_report` (lines 434-470), shared by every TPC-Havoc engine, returns
  `1 if new else 0` (line 470) - it does NOT fail when `resolved` (a
  previously-known divergence that no longer reproduces) is non-empty; it
  only PRINTS a message to update the baseline (line 466-467). Compare this
  to the cross-surface gate's own `_report`
  (benchbox/core/equivalence/cross_surface.py:1188-1196), which explicitly
  fails on `resolved`: "GATE FAILURE - previously-known divergences now
  equivalent ... remove the stale baseline entry in a reviewed change" and
  `return 1 if (new or resolved or missing_backends or unclassified_empty) else 0`.
  So today a stale TPC-Havoc `KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`/`POSTGRES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES`/
  etc. entry (whose divergence has since been fixed) can sit indefinitely
  without forcing anyone to prune it, unlike the cross-surface gate's
  behavior.
preserves: The DuckDB SQL equivalence gate stays the hard, blocking gate; `make tpchavoc-equivalence-report` reports `checked 220 variants - 0 divergent, 220 equivalent` (or the then-current true count) with exit 0 on a healthy tree, unchanged by this hardening.

The Postgres/DataFusion/ClickHouse samples (`make tpchavoc-equivalence-report-postgres/-datafusion/-clickhouse`) stay green; the shared `_report` change in w3 must not newly fail them on entries that are still live.
find_divergences, validate_variant_equivalence, and _report remain shared/engine-agnostic - no per-engine fork introduced by this hardening.

approach:
Mirror the second/third-engine pattern for ClickHouse - a build helper, a
find_clickhouse_divergences, a run_clickhouse_sample, an engine-keyed
CLICKHOUSE_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES, and (only if needed) a CLICKHOUSE_TPCHAVOC_SKIPS
execution-filter (w0). Run the oracle in report mode and classify divergences,
expecting the first real result-semantic differences because ClickHouse uses a
NATIVE non-Postgres dialect (w1). Fix translation bugs at the seam and declare
irreducible engine-semantic result differences as justified exceptions (w2),
pick a bounded routine-CI posture from evidence (w3), and update the cross-engine
conclusion to a dialect-FAMILY claim (w4). DuckDB stays the hard gate.
description:
The TPC-Havoc cross-dialect equivalence oracle now samples THREE engines: the
DuckDB SQL gate (PR #770, the hard blocker, KNOWN_DIVERGENCES empty), the
PostgreSQL sample (PR #803, 203/203 executable, POSTGRES_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES
empty), and the DataFusion sample (PR #806, 206/206 executable,
DATAFUSION_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES empty). The three-engine conclusion (PR #806 w4)
was that translation divergence is SYSTEMATIC-ZERO: every variant an engine can
execute is result-equivalent to canonical TPC-H run through the SAME translation
on the SAME instance; cross-engine differences live only in WHICH variants
execute (bounded by per-engine skip-lists), never in the RESULTS of the ones
that do.

But there is a confound: all three engines translate through a PostgreSQL-shaped
seam. SQLGlot normalizes "datafusion" -> "postgres"
(benchbox/utils/dialect_utils.py:normalize_dialect_for_sqlglot), and "netezza"
(the TPC-H source dialect) -> "postgres" too, so DuckDB, Postgres, and DataFusion
all receive SQL that is essentially Postgres-family. The systematic-zero result
may therefore reflect that the seam emits one dialect family faithfully - NOT
that it is faithful to an engine with genuinely different result semantics.

This TODO closes that gap with a FOURTH engine that translates through a NATIVE,
non-Postgres SQLGlot dialect and has known result-semantic differences:
ClickHouse. Unlike DataFusion, "clickhouse" is a first-class SQLGlot write
dialect (normalize_dialect_for_sqlglot("clickhouse") == "clickhouse"), so the
variants and canonical are rendered through a DIFFERENT code path in the seam.
ClickHouse also differs on exactly the result-semantic axes the earlier TODOs
flagged as the highest-information contrast: integer vs float division, NULL
ordering/placement, implicit casts, and Decimal-vs-Float aggregation. If the
systematic-zero result holds here, it is strong evidence the seam is faithful
across dialect FAMILIES; if it breaks, the divergences localize precisely the
result-semantic gaps a Postgres-shaped sample structurally cannot see.

This is the `deferred` follow-on recorded in BOTH
tpchavoc-cross-dialect-equivalence-sampling.yaml and
tpchavoc-third-engine-equivalence-sampling.yaml. It remains a SAMPLE: the DuckDB
gate stays the hard blocker; this does NOT gate all ~20 platforms.
preserves: Only an unreachable/unusable engine is a SKIP (mirror run_postgres_sample's connect-only skip); schema/load/translation/sweep failures must propagate.
Reuse find_divergences, validate_variant_equivalence, and _report; no per-engine fork of the comparator/oracle.
The DuckDB SQL equivalence gate stays the hard, blocking gate with empty KNOWN_DIVERGENCES (220/220, exit 0).
The PostgreSQL and DataFusion samples stay green; POSTGRES_/DATAFUSION_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES and their TPCHAVOC_SKIPS semantics are unchanged.

work.notes:
RESOLVED. Added to benchbox/core/tpchavoc/equivalence.py: CLICKHOUSE_TARGET_DIALECT
= "clickhouse", build_clickhouse_with_tpch, find_clickhouse_divergences,
run_clickhouse_sample, and `--engine clickhouse` in main(). RUN MODE: in-process
ClickHouse via chDB (ClickHouseLocalAdapter / clickhouse-local) - the cheapest
faithful engine, no service container (chDB 4.1.6 is already a dev dependency).
The chDB client exposes execute(sql).fetchall() natively and raises per query, so
find_divergences' per-query error isolation works with no autocommit transaction.
Canonical via tpch.get_query(q, dialect="clickhouse") and variants via
translate_query_text(sql, "netezza", "clickhouse") - both through the SAME native
clickhouse seam (NOT normalized to postgres) so shared translation cancels out. The
comparator and _report are reused verbatim - no per-engine fork. Each table's row
count is verified (>0) so a partial load cannot produce a false green. MergeTree
ORDER BY (PK-derived by the adapter) is physical layout only and never changes
results. CLICKHOUSE_SESSION_SETTINGS={"join_use_nulls":1} configures SQL-standard
LEFT JOIN NULL semantics (the semantics canonical TPC-H and the variants assume,
and that the other three engines use natively); this is documented, NOT used to
mute a divergence - the residual divergences are still reported and the JOIN-NULL
default is itself recorded as an engine-semantic difference in w4. A
comparator-robustness fix in validation.py (_numeric_values_equal coerces both
operands to float) lets the reused comparator compare ClickHouse's Decimal averages
against canonical Float64 instead of crashing on `float - Decimal`; it is
engine-agnostic and keeps DuckDB/Postgres/DataFusion green.
work.summary: Wire the ClickHouse build helper + sample path, reusing find_divergences and _report

work.notes:
RESOLVED. Ran `python -m benchbox.core.tpchavoc.equivalence --engine clickhouse` at
SF=0.1. The raw sweep (no skip-list, ClickHouse default settings) surfaced 28
divergences - the richest surface of any sampled engine, as expected for the first
native non-Postgres dialect. Classification:

(a) translation-layer bugs: NONE. The native-clickhouse translation is faithful;
    every divergence is an execution gap or an engine-semantic result difference,
    so there was no seam bug to fix (w2).

(b) irreducible engine-semantic RESULT differences -> CLICKHOUSE_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES
    (7 entries, three classes):
      - decimal-division-truncation (1_v4): ClickHouse SUM(decimal)/COUNT keeps the
        operand Decimal scale (avg_qty = Decimal('25.53')) where canonical AVG
        returns full Float64 (25.5376...). The "Decimal-vs-Float" axis this engine
        was chosen to surface.
      - sum-empty-group-zero (3_v7, 7_v7, 10_v7, 10_v8): ClickHouse SUM/sumIf over
        an all-filtered group returns 0, not NULL, so variants emulating a WHERE
        filter with SUM(...) FILTER(...) + HAVING <agg> IS NOT NULL never drop the
        empty groups canonical's WHERE removes (extra rows: e.g. 3_v7 15224 vs 1216).
      - correlated-subquery-decorrelation (2_v8, 13_v1): ClickHouse's partial,
        experimental correlated-subquery decorrelation computes a different result
        for these shapes (13_v1 correlated scalar COUNT -> NULL for an empty
        correlation; 2_v8 doubly-correlated NOT EXISTS -> different row set).
    The LEFT JOIN NULL-fill cases (14_v5, 16_v3, 16_v5) were the documented
    join_use_nulls=0 default; configuring SQL-standard join_use_nulls=1 (w0)
    resolves them, so they are NOT listed (the default itself is recorded as an
    engine-semantic note rather than a per-variant exception).

(c) real variant defects the DuckDB gate missed: NONE. Every variant still passes
    the DuckDB gate (220/220); the ClickHouse divergences are engine-semantic or

engine, and that is the informative outcome - it localizes exactly the
result-semantic gaps a Postgres-shaped sample structurally cannot see. Across four

netezza/datafusion -> postgres, so they all received one dialect family. ClickHouse
- the first engine on a NATIVE non-Postgres dialect - confirms the seam is still
FAITHFUL (zero translation-layer bugs: every divergence is an engine-semantic result
difference or an executability gap, none a mistranslation), but it is faithful

ClickHouse surfaces are precisely the axes the earlier TODOs predicted: Decimal-vs-

(resolved by standard join_use_nulls=1), and partial correlated-subquery
decorrelation. So the four-engine claim is: the dialect-translation seam is faithful
across dialect FAMILIES; what differs between engines is (1) WHICH variants execute
(per-engine skip-lists) and (2) on a native-dialect engine, a small, enumerable set

work.notes:
RESOLVED (review follow-up to the two #817 threads).

(1) Transform-wrapper parity. The sample now routes both canonical and variant SQL
through the SAME production query-time rewrites the real ClickHouse adapter applies
(ClickHouseQueryTransformer.transform - Decimal/Float casts + safe division - then
add_query_settings), via a new engine-agnostic `execute_transform` hook on
find_divergences and `_clickhouse_execute_transform`. Applied identically to both
sides, so shared transforms still cancel out. Re-verified at SF=0.1: the classified
surface is UNCHANGED (7 CLICKHOUSE_KNOWN_DIVERGENCES still diverge, no new
unclassified ones).

Surfaced and fixed a real production bug: safe_division wrapped a WINDOWED divisor
`SUM(x) OVER (...)` as the invalid `NULLIF(SUM(x), 0) OVER (...)` (ClickHouse:
'NULLIF ... OVER' is not a window function), which would also fail variant 8_v9 and
any windowed-division TPC-DS query on real ClickHouse runs. The operand scanner now
treats `agg(...) OVER (...)` as one operand, so it wraps as
`NULLIF(SUM(x) OVER (...), 0)`.

(2) NULL-ordering scope. The order-insensitive comparator (it sorts both sides)
structurally cannot observe a difference that shows up only as NULL placement within
an ORDER BY, so that axis is NOT sampled by this row-set oracle - now documented
explicitly in the equivalence module docstring. Covering it would need a separate
order-sensitive check on the NULL-bearing-sort-key subset; left out of scope here.

(systematic-zero) and a non-Postgres-family engine (faithful + a fully classified
result-semantic residue) agreeing that the seam introduces no translation
divergence. A fifth engine would re-confirm executability/result-semantics that are
already engine-documented, at the cost of another CI surface, without testing a new
seam path. The DuckDB gate stays the hard blocker; the three samples stay
non-blocking.

description:
While verifying PR #756 (correlated-subquery self-binding fixes), a SECOND,
different class of equivalence defect surfaced in the TPC-Havoc variant set.
`q2_v10` (the "CASE expressions" variant) returns the correct 460-row key set
at SF=1 but reformulates its output projection as
`case when s_acctbal > 0 then s_acctbal else 0 end as s_acctbal`. The 38
suppliers in the result whose `s_acctbal` is negative are therefore reported
as `0.00` instead of their real (negative) balance, so q2_v10 diverges from
canonical TPC-H Q2 and from its nine sibling variants on those rows.

This is NOT the self-binding pattern PR #756 addressed; it is
projection-faithfulness drift - an output reformulation (CASE / COALESCE /
NULL-handling wrappers) that changes projected VALUES while leaving the
filtered row set correct. Like self-binding, it is silent today because
TPC-Havoc validates execution, not result equivalence (see the companion
`tpchavoc-variant-equivalence-gate` TODO).

Fix q2_v10 to project the true `s_acctbal`, then sweep every variant set for
the same class: projection expressions that can alter a value relative to the
canonical query (CASE wrappers that substitute defaults, COALESCE-to-0 on
nullable measures, casts that round/truncate). Fix any found WITHOUT changing
a variant's structural identity.
preserves: DuckDB tpchavoc remains 100% execution-green at SF 0.01 / 0.1 / 1.0.
Each touched variant keeps its declared structural identity (q2_v10 stays the 'CASE expressions' variant).
Row/key sets already correct are not changed - only value-faithfulness of projected columns.
